individual_results.question: What is the process for the Board to review the structure of bargaining units if it is deemed that they are no longer appropriate for collective bargaining, and what actions can the Board take if the parties do not reach an agreement?
individual_results.answer:
## Board Review of Bargaining Unit Structure

### Initiation of Review

The Board can review the structure of bargaining units upon application by the employer or a bargaining agent. This review is initiated when the Board is satisfied that the bargaining units are "no longer appropriate for collective bargaining." This determination is made after considering the circumstances and potentially conducting a representation vote or other inquiry.
"On application by the employer or a bargaining agent, the Board may review the structure of the bargaining units if it is satisfied that the bargaining units are no longer appropriate for collective bargaining."

### Process When Parties Reach Agreement

If the parties reach an agreement on the determination of bargaining units and any related questions within a reasonable period, the Board is obligated to facilitate the implementation of that agreement.
"If the Board reviews, pursuant to subsection (1) or section 35 or 45, the structure of the bargaining units, the Board (a) must allow the parties to come to an agreement, within a period that the Board considers reasonable, with respect to the determination of bargaining units and any questions arising from the review; and (b) may make any orders it considers appropriate to implement any agreement."

### Board Determination When Parties Do Not Reach Agreement

If the parties fail to reach an agreement within a reasonable period, the Board is empowered to determine any questions that arise and issue orders to implement its determination.
"If the Board is of the opinion that the agreement reached by the parties would not lead to the creation of units appropriate for collective bargaining or if the parties do not agree on certain issues within the period that the Board considers reasonable, the Board determines any question that arises and makes any orders it considers appropriate in the circumstances."

### Actions the Board Can Take

When the Board determines the structure of bargaining units, it has a wide range of actions it can take to implement its decision. These actions include:

*   Determining which trade union shall be the bargaining agent for the employees in each bargaining unit that results from the review.
*   Amending any certification order or description of a bargaining unit contained in any collective agreement.
*   Deciding which collective agreement is in force if more than one collective agreement applies to employees in a bargaining unit.
*   Amending, to the extent that the Board considers necessary, the provisions of collective agreements respecting expiry dates or seniority rights, or amending other such provisions.
*   Deciding which terms and conditions of employment apply to employees until the time that a collective agreement becomes applicable to the unit or the conditions of those paragraphs are met with respect to the unit.
*   Authorizing a party to a collective agreement to give notice to bargain collectively.
"For the purposes of subsection (3), the Board may (a) determine which trade union shall be the bargaining agent for the employees in each bargaining unit that results from the review; (b) amend any certification order or description of a bargaining unit contained in any collective agreement; (c) if more than one collective agreement applies to employees in a bargaining unit, decide which collective agreement is in force; (d) amend, to the extent that the Board considers necessary, the provisions of collective agreements respecting expiry dates or seniority rights, or amend other such provisions; (e) if the conditions of paragraphs 89(1)(a) to (d) have been met with respect to some of the employees in a bargaining unit, decide which terms and conditions of employment apply to those employees until the time that a collective agreement becomes applicable to the unit or the conditions of those paragraphs are met with respect to the unit; and (f) authorize a party to a collective agreement to give notice to bargain collectively."

## Flexibility of the Board in Making Decisions and Issuing Orders

### Section 251.12: Flexibility in Ordering Actions to Give Effect to Decisions

The Board possesses significant flexibility when formulating orders to ensure their decisions are implemented. Section 251.12(1) explicitly states,
"The Board may, in an appeal under this Part, make any order that is necessary to give effect to its decision, including an order to (a) confirm, rescind or vary, in whole or in part, the decision being appealed; (b) direct payment to any specified person of any wages or other amounts held in trust by the Receiver General that relate to the appeal; (c) award costs in the proceedings; and (d) order a party, whose conduct in the proceedings has, in the Board’s opinion, unduly delayed the determination of the appeal, to pay to the Receiver General an amount that is equal to all or part of the expenses incurred in the proceedings by the Board."

This provision demonstrates the Board's broad discretion. It can "confirm, rescind or vary" its prior decision, indicating adaptability based on the appeal. Furthermore, it can issue orders related to financial matters, such as directing payment of wages or awarding costs. Notably, the Board can also impose financial penalties on parties who have unduly delayed the appeal process, showcasing its power to influence procedural conduct. The phrase
"...any order that is necessary to give effect to its decision..." underscores the Board's freedom to tailor its orders to achieve the desired outcome.

### Section 244(1): Flexibility in Filing Orders in Federal Court

The Board also exhibits flexibility in the timing and manner of filing orders in the Federal Court. Section 244(1) allows
"Any person affected by an order of the Board under subsection 242(4), or the Head on the request of such a person, may, after 14 days from the day on which the order is made, or from the day provided in the order for compliance, whichever is later, file in the Federal Court a copy of the order, exclusive of reasons."

This flexibility is evident in the two possible deadlines for filing the order. The filer can wait 14 days from the order's date or until the compliance date specified in the order, whichever is later. This allows for adjustments based on the practicalities of implementing the Board's decision. Additionally, the option for the Head to file the order upon request further enhances the Board's adaptability to the needs of affected parties.

### Section 243(1): Finality of Board Orders

While the Board has flexibility in *making* decisions and issuing orders, Section 243(1) establishes the *finality* of those orders. It states,
"Every order of the Board is final and shall not be questioned or reviewed in any court."

This provision, echoed in Section 156(1), signifies a limitation on judicial review. Once an order is issued, it is binding and cannot be challenged in court. This finality is crucial for ensuring the efficient and effective administration of the Canada Labour Code. The Board's flexibility in crafting orders is balanced by the principle that those orders are not subject to further judicial scrutiny.

### Section 251.11(2): Flexibility in Providing Copies of Decisions

The Board also demonstrates flexibility in how it disseminates its decisions. Section 251.11(2) mandates,
"The Board shall send a copy of the decision, with reasons, to each party to the appeal and to the Head."

This provision ensures transparency and allows all relevant parties to understand the Board's reasoning behind its decision. The flexibility lies in the Board's ability to tailor the distribution of copies to the specific needs of the appeal process, ensuring that all stakeholders are informed.

## Board Decision on Some Issues with Reserved Jurisdiction

### Section 20(1)
"Where, in order to dispose finally of an application or complaint, it is necessary for the Board to determine two or more issues arising therefrom, the Board may, if it is satisfied that it can do so without prejudice to the rights of any party to the proceeding, issue a decision resolving only one or some of those issues and reserve its jurisdiction to dispose of the remaining issues."

This section directly addresses the question. It explicitly states that the Board has the power to issue a decision on a subset of issues within a proceeding while retaining the authority to address the remaining issues later. The condition for doing so is that the Board must be satisfied that it can resolve the initial issues without negatively impacting the rights of any party involved. This demonstrates a flexible approach to decision-making, allowing the Board to manage complex cases by addressing manageable parts first and reserving judgment on the more intricate aspects.

### Section 156(1)
"Every order or decision made or direction issued by the Board under this Part is final and shall not be questioned or reviewed in any court."

While this section focuses on the finality of Board decisions, it indirectly supports the Board's ability to issue partial decisions. The finality of a decision on some issues does not preclude the Board from later issuing a decision on the remaining issues. The Board's jurisdiction is not limited to issuing complete decisions at once; it can proceed incrementally, issuing final decisions on parts of the case while reserving authority over the rest.

### Section 16.1
"The Board may decide any matter before it without holding an oral hearing."

This section indicates the Board's flexibility in its decision-making process. It can issue a decision on some issues without requiring an oral hearing on all issues. This further supports the Board's ability to issue partial decisions, as it is not bound by a requirement to address all issues simultaneously through a full hearing.

individual_results.question: What are the general responsibilities of The Board in relation to the Canada Labour Code?
individual_results.answer:
## General Responsibilities of The Board Under the Canada Labour Code

### Powers to Assist Parties in Resolving Disputes

The Board possesses significant powers to facilitate the resolution of disputes arising under the Canada Labour Code. Section 15.1(1) explicitly states:
"The Board, any member of the Board or any external adjudicator — or an employee of the Administrative Tribunals Support Service of Canada who is authorized by the Board — may, if the parties agree, assist the parties in resolving any issues in dispute at any stage of a proceeding and by any means that the Board considers appropriate, without prejudice to the Board’s power to determine issues that have not been settled." This indicates a proactive role for the Board in encouraging settlement through various methods, provided the parties consent.

### Powers to Determine Complaints

When settlement is not achieved, the Board retains the authority to make a determination of the complaint. Section 98(1) outlines this power:
"Subject to subsection (3), on receipt of a complaint made under section 97, the Board may assist the parties to the complaint to settle the complaint and shall, where it decides not to so assist the parties or the complaint is not settled within a period considered by the Board to be reasonable in the circumstances, determine the complaint." This highlights the Board's ultimate responsibility to adjudicate disputes when other avenues for resolution have failed.

### Powers to Conduct Investigations and Gather Evidence

The Board has extensive powers to conduct thorough investigations into matters brought before it. Section 16(a) details these powers:
"(a) to summon and enforce the attendance of witnesses and compel them to give oral or written evidence on oath and to produce such documents and things as the Board deems requisite to the full investigation and consideration of any matter within its jurisdiction that is before the Board in the proceeding..." This demonstrates the Board's ability to gather information through witness testimony and document production.

### Powers to Administer Oaths and Solemn Affirmations

To ensure the reliability of evidence, the Board is empowered to administer oaths and solemn affirmations. Section 16(b) states: "(b) to administer oaths and solemn affirmations." This is a standard procedure for verifying the truthfulness of sworn statements.

### Powers to Examine Evidence and Documents

The Board has the authority to examine evidence and documents submitted to it. Section 16(c) specifies:
"(c) to receive and accept such evidence and information on oath, affidavit or otherwise as the Board in its discretion sees fit, whether admissible in a court of law or not..." This indicates a flexible approach to accepting evidence, prioritizing its relevance to the proceeding.

### Powers to Conduct Representation Votes

A key responsibility of the Board is to conduct representation votes to determine appropriate bargaining units. Section 16(i) outlines this power:
"(i) to order, at any time before the proceeding has been finally disposed of by the Board, that (i) a representation vote or an additional representation vote be taken among employees affected by the proceeding in any case where the Board considers that the taking of such a vote would assist the Board to decide any question that has arisen or is likely to arise in the proceeding, whether or not such a representation vote is provided for elsewhere in this Part, and (ii) the ballots cast in any representation vote ordered by the Board pursuant to subparagraph (i) or any other provision of this Part be sealed in ballot boxes and not counted except as directed by the Board..." This highlights the Board's role in ensuring fair representation in collective bargaining.

### Powers to Issue Declaratory Opinions

The Board can also provide declaratory opinions upon request. Section 15.1(2) states:
"(2) The Board, on application by an employer or a trade union, may give declaratory opinions." This allows parties to seek the Board's interpretation of legal questions related to the Canada Labour Code.

### Powers to Make Regulations

The Board has the authority to make regulations of general application to support its functions. Section 15(a) details these powers:
"(a) the establishment of rules of procedure for its pre-hearing proceedings and hearings; (a.1) the use of means of telecommunication that permit the parties and the Board or its members to communicate simultaneously for pre-hearing conferences, hearings and Board meetings; (b) the determination of units appropriate for collective bargaining; (c) the certification of trade unions as bargaining agents for bargaining units; (d) the conduct of representation votes; (e) the specification of the period of time after which the Board may receive an application from a trade union for certification as the bargaining agent for a unit where the Board has refused an application from the trade union for certification in respect of the same or substantially the same unit; (f) the specification of the period of time after which the Board may receive an application from an employee for revocation of a trade union’s certification as the bargaining agent for a unit where the Board has refused an application for revocation in respect of the same unit; (g) the hearing or determination of any application, complaint, question, dispute, difference or appeal that may be made or referred to the Board; (g.1) an expeditious procedure and matters that may be determined under that procedure; (h) the forms to be used in respect of any proceeding that may come before the Board; (i) the time within which and the circumstances under which the Board may exercise its powers under section 18; (j) any inquiry that the Board may make under subsection 34(2); (k) the form in which and the period during which evidence and information may be presented to the Board in connection with any proceeding that may come before it; (l) the specification of the time within which and the parties or persons to whom notices and other documents shall be sent and the circumstances in which such notices or other documents shall be deemed to have been given or received by the Board or any party or person; (m) the determination of the form in which and the period during which evidence as to (i) the membership of any employees in a trade union, (ii) any objection by employees to the certification of a trade union, or (iii) any signification by employees that they no longer wish to be represented by a trade union shall be presented to the Board on an application made to it pursuant to this Part; (n) the criteria for determining whether an employee is a member of a trade union; (o) the circumstances in which evidence referred to in paragraph (m) may be received by the Board as evidence that any employees wish or do not wish to have a particular trade union represent them as their bargaining agent, including the circumstances in which the evidence so received by the Board may not be made public by the Board; (o.1) the conditions for valid strike or lockout votes; (p) the authority of any person to act on behalf of the Board and the matters and things to be done and the action to be taken by that person, including the authority of an employee of the Administrative Tribunals Support Service of Canada to make decisions on uncontested applications or questions; (p.1) the manner and criteria for selecting external adjudicators; and (q) any other matters and things that may be incidental or conducive to the proper performance of the duties of the Board under this Act." This extensive list demonstrates the Board's broad range of responsibilities in administering the Canada Labour Code.

individual_results.question: Under what conditions can an order or decision made by the Board be reviewed or questioned in a court?
individual_results.answer:
## Conditions for Review or Questioning of Board Orders or Decisions in Court

### General Finality of Board Orders and Decisions

Several sections of the Canada Labour Code establish the finality of Board orders and decisions. Section 246.5 states,
"Every decision of the Board made under this Division is final and shall not be questioned or reviewed in any court." This indicates a broad principle of non-reviewability. Similarly, Section 243(1) and Section 156(1) reiterate this finality, asserting that
"Every order of the Board is final and shall not be questioned or reviewed in any court." These statements collectively emphasize the limited grounds upon which a Board order or decision can be challenged in a court of law.

### Exceptions to Finality

However, the finality of Board orders and decisions is not absolute. Section 22(1) outlines the specific exceptions to this rule. It states,
"Subject to this Part and to any regulations made under paragraph 111.01(1)(g), every order or decision made by the Board under this Part is final and is not to be questioned or reviewed in any court, except in accordance with the Federal Courts Act on the grounds referred to in paragraph 18.1(4)(a), (b) or (e) of that Act." This exception is narrowly defined and pertains only to grounds for review available under the Federal Courts Act. These grounds include, but are not limited to, jurisdiction of the Board, exceeding its jurisdiction, or a failure of the Board to exercise its jurisdiction.

### No Review by Certiorari, etc.

Multiple sections explicitly prohibit review by certain types of court proceedings. Section 246.5(2) declares,
"No order shall be made, process entered or proceeding taken in any court, whether by way of injunction, certiorari , prohibition, quo warranto or otherwise, to question, review, prohibit or restrain the Board in any proceedings under this Division." This statement is echoed in Section 243(2), Section 156(2), and Section 251.12(3), reinforcing the general prohibition against challenging Board proceedings through these specific court mechanisms.

### Review under the Federal Courts Act

The Federal Courts Act provides the limited avenue for review of Board orders and decisions. Section 22(1) specifies that review can only occur
"...in accordance with the Federal Courts Act on the grounds referred to in paragraph 18.1(4)(a), (b) or (e) of that Act." This means that any attempt to question a Board order in court must be based on one of the specific grounds for review outlined in the Federal Courts Act. These grounds relate to the Board's jurisdiction, exceeding its jurisdiction, or a failure of the Board to exercise its jurisdiction.

### Review of Board Decisions in Appeal Proceedings

Section 251.12(1) addresses the review of Board decisions in appeal proceedings. It states,
"The Board may, in an appeal under this Part, make any order that is necessary to give effect to its decision, including an order to (a) confirm, rescind or vary, in whole or in part, the decision being appealed..." This indicates that in an appeal, the Board has the power to review its own prior decisions and make new orders to implement its revised position. However, this review is specifically within the context of an appeal under that Part of the Code.

individual_results.question: What is the purpose of filing a copy of an order or decision of the Board in a court, and what are the implications of such registration?
individual_results.answer:
## Purpose of Filing a Board Order or Decision in Court

### Facilitating Review and Enforcement

The primary purpose of filing a copy of a Board order or decision in a court is to facilitate review and enforcement. Section 23(1) of the Canada Labour Code states:
"The Board shall, on the request in writing of any person or organization affected by any order or decision of the Board made under this Part, file a copy of the order or decision, exclusive of reasons, in the Federal Court, unless, in the opinion of the Board, (a) there is no indication of failure or likelihood of failure to comply with the order or decision; or (b) there is other good reason why the filing of the order or decision in the Federal Court would serve no useful purpose." This provision establishes a mechanism for parties affected by a Board decision to seek judicial review if they believe the order is flawed or likely to be non-compliant.

Furthermore, Section 246.6(2) elaborates on the implications of such registration:
"On filing in the Federal Court under subsection (1), an order of the Board shall be registered in the Court and, when registered, has the same force and effect, and all proceedings may be taken in respect of it, as if the order were a judgment obtained in that Court." This indicates that once an order is filed and registered in the Federal Court, it gains the status of a judgment. This has significant implications for enforcement, as it allows for the use of all available court processes to ensure compliance with the Board's order.

### Providing a Basis for Judicial Proceedings

Section 23(2) further clarifies the effect of registration:
"Where the Board files a copy of any order or decision in the Federal Court pursuant to subsection (1), it shall specify in writing to the Court that the copy of the order or decision is filed pursuant to that subsection and, where the Board so specifies, the copy of the order or decision shall be accepted for filing by, and registered in, the Court without further application or other proceeding." This streamlines the process of judicial proceedings related to the Board's order. The registration in the Federal Court provides a clear basis for any subsequent actions taken in that court, such as applications for injunctions or other remedies.

## Implications of Registration

### Judgment Status and Enforcement

The registration of a Board order or decision in the Federal Court transforms it into a judgment. As stated in Section 246.6(2),
"...when registered, has the same force and effect, and all proceedings may be taken in respect of it, as if the order were a judgment obtained in that Court." This judgment status is crucial for enforcement purposes. It allows for the use of all available court mechanisms to compel compliance with the Board's order, including the issuance of injunctions or the imposition of penalties.

### Standing of the Board

Section 22(1.1) addresses the Board's standing in proceedings referred to in subsection (1):
"The Board has standing to appear in proceedings referred to in subsection (1) for the purpose of making submissions regarding the standard of review to be used with respect to decisions of the Board and the Board’s jurisdiction, policies and procedures." This provision grants the Board the authority to participate in judicial review proceedings to advocate for its own decisions and to clarify its jurisdictional boundaries and procedures.

### No Further Review in Court

Section 22(1) explicitly states the finality of Board orders and decisions:
"Subject to this Part and to any regulations made under paragraph 111.01(1)(g), every order or decision made by the Board under this Part is final and is not to be questioned or reviewed in any court, except in accordance with the Federal Courts Act on the grounds referred to in paragraph 18.1(4)(a), (b) or (e) of that Act." This provision reinforces the principle of finality of Board orders and decisions, limiting the scope of judicial review to very specific grounds outlined in the Federal Courts Act.

individual_results.question: What are the rules and restrictions surrounding the timing of a trade union's application for certification as a bargaining agent for a unit of employees?
individual_results.answer:
## Timing Rules and Restrictions for Trade Union Certification Applications

### General Applicability of Application Timing Rules

Section 24(1) of the Canada Labour Code outlines the general rules and restrictions regarding the timing of a trade union's application for certification as a bargaining agent for a unit of employees. It states:
"A trade union seeking to be certified as the bargaining agent for a unit that the trade union considers constitutes a unit appropriate for collective bargaining may, subject to this section and any regulations made by the Board under paragraph 15(e), apply to the Board for certification as the bargaining agent for the unit." This establishes that a trade union can apply for certification at any time, subject to certain conditions and limitations detailed in subsequent subsections.

### Application Timing Based on Collective Agreement Status

Section 24(2) provides a detailed breakdown of when a trade union can make an application for certification based on the status of a collective agreement applicable to the unit. It outlines several scenarios:

#### No Collective Agreement in Force and No Certified Union
"Subject to subsection (3), an application by a trade union for certification as the bargaining agent for a unit may be made (a) where no collective agreement applicable to the unit is in force and no trade union has been certified under this Part as the bargaining agent for the unit, at any time..."

This indicates that a trade union can apply for certification at any point in time when there is no existing collective agreement and no other union has been certified.

#### No Collective Agreement in Force but a Certified Union Exists
"(b) where no collective agreement applicable to the unit is in force but a trade union has been certified under this Part as the bargaining agent for the unit, after the expiration of twelve months from the date of that certification or, with the consent of the Board, at any earlier time..."

Here, a trade union can apply for certification after twelve months from its previous certification, or earlier with the Board's consent, provided there is no current collective agreement.

#### Collective Agreement in Force for Not More Than Three Years
"(c) where a collective agreement applicable to the unit is in force and is for a term of not more than three years, only after the commencement of the last three months of its operation..."

In this case, a trade union can apply for certification only after the final three months of the existing collective agreement's term.

#### Collective Agreement in Force for More Than Three Years
"(d) where a collective agreement applicable to the unit is in force and is for a term of more than three years, only after the commencement of the thirty-fourth month of its operation and before the commencement of the thirty-seventh month of its operation and, thereafter, only (i) during the three month period immediately preceding the end of each year that the collective agreement continues to operate after the third year of its operation, and (ii) after the commencement of the last three months of its operation."

This scenario has the most complex timing rules. A trade union can apply for certification only after the thirty-fourth month of the existing collective agreement's term and before the thirty-seventh month. Subsequently, applications can be made only during the three-month period immediately preceding the end of each year after the third year of the agreement's operation, and again after the last three months of its operation.

### Application Timing During Strikes or Lockouts

Section 24(3) imposes a restriction on applying for certification during certain industrial actions. It states:
"An application for certification under subsection (2) in respect of a unit must not, except with the consent of the Board, be made during a strike or lockout that is not prohibited by this Part and that involves employees in the unit." This means that a trade union cannot apply for certification while a strike or lockout is ongoing, unless the Board grants its consent.

### Restrictions on Changing Terms of Employment After Application

Section 24(4) outlines restrictions on employers altering terms of employment after a trade union has made an application for certification. It states:
"Where an application by a trade union for certification as the bargaining agent for a unit is made in accordance with this section, no employer of employees in the unit shall, after notification that the application has been made, alter the rates of pay, any other term or condition of employment or any right or privilege of such employees until (a) the application has been withdrawn by the trade union or dismissed by the Board, or (b) thirty days have elapsed after the day on which the Board certifies the trade union as the bargaining agent for the unit, except pursuant to a collective agreement or with the consent of the Board." This provision prevents employers from unilaterally changing employment terms once a certification application has been made, until the application is withdrawn, dismissed, or the Board certifies the union.

individual_results.question: Under what conditions may the Board refuse to certify a trade union as the bargaining agent for a unit of employees?
individual_results.answer:
## Conditions for Refusal of Certification

### Section 26: Prohibited Certification for Overlapping Units

The Board is explicitly prohibited from certifying a trade union as the bargaining agent for both a bargaining unit comprised of private constables and a bargaining unit comprised of employees other than private constables if any or all of the employees in both such bargaining units are employed by the same employer.
"The Board shall not certify a trade union as, and a trade union shall not act as, the bargaining agent for both a bargaining unit comprised of private constables and a bargaining unit comprised of employees other than private constables if any or all of the employees in both such bargaining units are employed by the same employer."

This section directly addresses a specific condition under which the Board may refuse certification. It prevents a single union from representing two distinct but overlapping bargaining units where the same employer employs all members of both units. This restriction is likely intended to avoid conflicts of interest and ensure that each bargaining unit has a dedicated representative.

### Section 28: Requirement for Majority Support

The Board is obligated to certify a trade union as the bargaining agent for a bargaining unit only if it is satisfied that, as of the date of the filing of the application or of any other date that the Board considers appropriate, a majority of the employees in the unit wish to have the trade union represent them as their bargaining agent.
"The Board shall, subject to this Part, certify a trade union as the bargaining agent for a bargaining unit if the Board (a) has received from the trade union an application for certification as the bargaining agent for a unit; (b) has determined the unit that constitutes a unit appropriate for collective bargaining; and (c) is satisfied that, as of the date of the filing of the application or of any other date that the Board considers appropriate, a majority of the employees in the unit wish to have the trade union represent them as their bargaining agent."

This condition highlights the importance of demonstrating majority support for a union's certification. The Board's certification is contingent upon a clear indication that a majority of the employees in the unit desire the union to act as their bargaining agent. This ensures that the union has a legitimate mandate to represent the interests of the employees.

### Section 29: Minimum and Maximum Union Membership Percentage

The Board may order a representation vote if it is satisfied that not less than 35% and not more than 50% of the employees in the unit are members of the trade union.
"If a trade union applies for certification as the bargaining agent for a unit in respect of which no other trade union is the bargaining agent, and the Board is satisfied that not less than 35% and not more than 50% of the employees in the unit are members of the trade union, the Board shall order that a representation vote be taken among the employees in the unit."

This condition sets a threshold for the Board to order a representation vote. The Board will only order a vote if the union's membership falls within the specified percentage range. This requirement aims to ensure that the union has a substantial base of support within the unit before certification is considered.

### Section 28: Established Practice of Membership Without Eligibility Requirements

The Board may disregard membership eligibility requirements if it is satisfied that a trade union has an established practice of admitting persons to membership without regard to the eligibility requirements of its charter, constitution or by-laws.
"Where the Board is satisfied that a trade union has an established practice of admitting persons to membership without regard to the eligibility requirements of its charter, constitution or by-laws, the Board may disregard those requirements in determining whether a person is a member of a trade union."

This condition provides the Board with flexibility in determining union membership when a union has a history of lax membership requirements. The Board may disregard these requirements if it is convinced that the union has a genuine practice of admitting members without strict adherence to its own eligibility criteria. This ensures that the certification process is not unduly hindered by technicalities in membership rules.

individual_results.question: What factors influence the Labour Board's decision when determining a unit that is appropriate for collective bargaining?
individual_results.answer:
## Factors Influencing the Labour Board's Decision on Appropriate Bargaining Units

### General Considerations

The Labour Board's determination of an appropriate bargaining unit is guided by several factors. Primarily, the Board assesses whether the proposed unit is suitable for collective bargaining. This involves considering the employees' similarities in terms of their duties, responsibilities, and working conditions. The Board has the authority to modify the unit proposed by the trade union seeking certification.
"In determining whether a unit constitutes a unit that is appropriate for collective bargaining, the Board may include any employees in or exclude any employees from the unit proposed by the trade union." This quote directly addresses the Board's flexibility in defining bargaining units. It highlights that the Board is not bound by the trade union's initial proposal and can adjust the unit based on its own assessment of appropriateness.

### Specific Employee Categories

The Board's decision is also influenced by the specific categories of employees involved. When a trade union applies for certification representing professional employees, the Board must determine if the unit is comprised solely of professional employees, unless such a unit would not otherwise be appropriate for collective bargaining.
"Where a trade union applies under section 24 for certification as the bargaining agent for a unit comprised of or including professional employees, the Board, subject to subsections (2) and (4), shall determine that the unit appropriate for collective bargaining is a unit comprised of only professional employees, unless such a unit would not otherwise be appropriate for collective bargaining." This passage emphasizes the Board's scrutiny of units seeking to represent professional employees. It states that the Board will generally limit the unit to only professional employees, but it retains the discretion to broaden the unit if it would not otherwise be suitable for collective bargaining.

### Supervisory and Private Constable Employees

The Board also has specific rules regarding the inclusion of supervisory and private constable employees in bargaining units. Supervisory employees can be included in a bargaining unit if the Board determines that the unit proposed in the application is appropriate for collective bargaining. However, private constables must be excluded from a unit with other employees.
"Where a trade union applies for certification as the bargaining agent for a unit comprised of or including employees whose duties include the supervision of other employees, the Board may, subject to subsection (2), determine that the unit proposed in the application is appropriate for collective bargaining." This quote indicates the Board's discretion in including supervisory employees. It states that the Board can include them if it deems the unit otherwise appropriate for collective bargaining.
"The Board shall not include a private constable in a unit with other employees." This passage provides a clear exception to the general rule regarding supervisory employees. It explicitly prohibits the inclusion of private constables in a bargaining unit with other employees.

### Successor Rights and Activity Changes

When a sale or change of activity occurs, the Board may review the structure of the bargaining units to determine if the affected employees constitute one or more appropriate units for collective bargaining.
"In the case of a sale or change of activity referred to in section 44, the Board may, on application by the employer or any trade union affected, determine whether the employees affected constitute one or more units appropriate for collective bargaining." This quote explains the Board's role in reviewing bargaining units following a change in business ownership or operations. It allows the Board to reassess the appropriateness of the existing units based on the new circumstances.

individual_results.question: What are the requirements for a trade union to be certified as the bargaining agent for a unit of employees?
individual_results.answer:
## Requirements for Trade Union Certification as Bargaining Agent

### Section 28: Duty to Certify Trade Union

#### Subtitle: General Requirements for Certification
"The Board shall, subject to this Part, certify a trade union as the bargaining agent for a bargaining unit if the Board (a) has received from the trade union an application for certification as the bargaining agent for a unit; (b) has determined the unit that constitutes a unit appropriate for collective bargaining; and (c) is satisfied that, as of the date of the filing of the application or of any other date that the Board considers appropriate, a majority of the employees in the unit wish to have the trade union represent them as their bargaining agent."

This section outlines the fundamental prerequisites for a trade union to be certified as the bargaining agent for a bargaining unit. The Board is obligated to certify a union if it meets three core criteria. First, the Board must have received a formal application for certification from the trade union. Second, the Board must have identified the specific unit of employees for which the union seeks certification, deeming it appropriate for collective bargaining. Finally, and crucially, the Board must be satisfied that a majority of the employees within that unit have expressed a desire for the trade union to represent them as their bargaining agent. This majority requirement is a cornerstone of the certification process, ensuring that the union has the support of the majority of the employees it intends to represent.

### Section 29: Representation Vote

#### Subtitle: When a Representation Vote is Ordered
"The Board may, in any case, for the purpose of satisfying itself as to whether employees in a unit wish to have a particular trade union represent them as their bargaining agent, order that a representation vote be taken among the employees in the unit."

This section details a mechanism the Board can employ to ascertain whether a majority of employees in a unit genuinely desire the trade union to act as their bargaining agent. The Board has the authority to order a representation vote if it needs further assurance about the employees' preference. This vote provides a direct expression of the employees' wishes, supplementing the general majority requirement outlined in Section 28.

#### Subtitle: Mandatory Vote Based on Union Membership
"If a trade union applies for certification as the bargaining agent for a unit in respect of which no other trade union is the bargaining agent, and the Board is satisfied that not less than 35% and not more than 50% of the employees in the unit are members of the trade union, the Board shall order that a representation vote be taken among the employees in the unit."

This subsection specifies a scenario where a representation vote is mandatory. If a trade union applies for certification for a unit where no other union is currently the bargaining agent, and the Board determines that between 35% and 50% of the employees are members of that union, the Board is compelled to order a representation vote. This threshold indicates a significant level of support for the union within the unit, triggering a formal vote to confirm the employees' preference.

### Section 36: Effect of Certification

#### Subtitle: Exclusive Authority and Revocation of Prior Certifications
"(1) Where a trade union is certified as the bargaining agent for a bargaining unit, (a) the trade union so certified has exclusive authority to bargain collectively on behalf of the employees in the bargaining unit; (b) the certification of any trade union that was previously certified as the bargaining agent for any employees in the bargaining unit is deemed to be revoked to the extent that the certification relates to those employees..."

This section explains the consequences of a trade union being certified as the bargaining agent. Firstly, the certified union gains "exclusive authority" to bargain collectively on behalf of all employees within the bargaining unit. This means no other union can represent those employees in collective bargaining. Secondly, any prior certifications held by other unions for employees within the same bargaining unit are automatically revoked to the extent they relate to those employees. This ensures that only one union holds the exclusive right to bargain for the unit's employees.

#### Subtitle: Substitution as Party to Collective Agreement
"(c) the trade union so certified is substituted as a party to any collective agreement that affects any employees in the bargaining unit, to the extent that the collective agreement relates to those employees, in the place of the bargaining agent named in the collective agreement or any successor thereto; and (d) the trade union so certified is deemed to be the bargaining agent for the purposes of paragraph 50(b)."

This subsection further elaborates on the impact of certification. The certified union is legally substituted as a party to any existing or future collective agreements that cover the bargaining unit's employees. This means that all future collective bargaining will occur between the certified union and the employer. Additionally, the certified union is deemed to be the bargaining agent for the purposes of a specific paragraph (50(b)), further solidifying its exclusive representation rights.

individual_results.question: Under what circumstances may or must the Board order a representation vote among employees in a unit to determine their bargaining agent?
individual_results.answer:
## Circumstances for Ordering a Representation Vote

### General Authority for Ordering a Representation Vote

The Board possesses the authority to order a representation vote under various circumstances. Section 29(1) states,
"The Board may, in any case, for the purpose of satisfying itself as to whether employees in a unit wish to have a particular trade union represent them as their bargaining agent, order that a representation vote be taken among the employees in the unit." This establishes a broad power for the Board to initiate a vote whenever it deems necessary to ascertain the employees' preference for a specific union.

### Mandatory Vote Based on Union Membership

Section 29(2) outlines a specific condition under which the Board *must* order a representation vote. It states,
"If a trade union applies for certification as the bargaining agent for a unit in respect of which no other trade union is the bargaining agent, and the Board is satisfied that not less than 35% and not more than 50% of the employees in the unit are members of the trade union, the Board shall order that a representation vote be taken among the employees in the unit." This provision mandates a vote when a union has a significant, but not majority, membership within the unit. The Board's satisfaction with this membership range triggers the requirement for a vote to definitively determine the employees' support for that union.

### Mandatory Vote Based on Membership Eligibility

Section 29(3) provides another mandatory vote scenario. It specifies,
"Where the Board is satisfied that a trade union has an established practice of admitting persons to membership without regard to the eligibility requirements of its charter, constitution or by-laws, the Board may disregard those requirements in determining whether a person is a member of a trade union." This condition necessitates a vote when a union has lax membership standards. The Board's determination that the union disregards eligibility criteria allows it to mandate a vote to accurately gauge the employees' support for the union based on its actual membership.

### Mandatory Vote Based on Vote Results

Section 30(2) details a mandatory vote triggered by the results of a previous representation vote. It states,
"Where the Board orders that a representation vote be taken on an application by a trade union for certification as the bargaining agent for a unit in respect of which no other trade union is the bargaining agent, the Board shall include on the ballots a choice whereby an employee may indicate that they do not wish to be represented by any trade union named on the ballots." This provision mandates a vote when a previous vote did not yield a majority support for any single union. The Board's inclusion of a "no preference" option in the ballots ensures that the employees' lack of support for any particular union is also reflected in the outcome.

### Other Circumstances for Ordering a Representation Vote

Section 30(1) broadens the Board's authority by stating,
"Where the Board orders that a representation vote be taken among employees in a unit, the Board shall (a) determine the employees that are eligible to vote; and (b) make such arrangements and give such directions as the Board considers necessary for the proper conduct of the representation vote, including the preparation of ballots, the method of casting and counting ballots and the custody and sealing of ballot boxes." This provision indicates that the Board can order a vote at any time it deems necessary to determine the employees' bargaining agent, and it is responsible for ensuring the vote is conducted properly.

individual_results.question: What are the responsibilities of the Board when ordering a representation vote among employees in a unit, and what choices must be included on the ballots?
individual_results.answer:
## Responsibilities of the Board When Ordering a Representation Vote

### Determining Eligible Voters and Conducting the Vote

The Board bears several responsibilities when ordering a representation vote. First, it is tasked with "determine[ing] the employees that are eligible to vote." This involves establishing the boundaries of the unit and identifying who among the employees fall within that unit and are therefore entitled to participate in the vote.

Furthermore, the Board is responsible for
"...such arrangements and give such directions as the Board considers necessary for the proper conduct of the representation vote..." This encompasses a range of logistical tasks, including
"...the preparation of ballots, the method of casting and counting ballots and the custody and sealing of ballot boxes." The Board essentially oversees the entire process to ensure it is fair, accurate, and conducted according to established procedures.

### Choices to be Included on the Ballots

When ordering a representation vote on an application for certification as the bargaining agent for a unit where no other trade union is currently the bargaining agent, the Board must include a specific choice on the ballots. This choice allows an employee to indicate that they do not wish to be represented by any trade union named on the ballots.

The text explicitly states,
"Where the Board orders that a representation vote be taken on an application by a trade union for certification as the bargaining agent for a unit in respect of which no other trade union is the bargaining agent, the Board shall include on the ballots a choice whereby an employee may indicate that they do not wish to be represented by any trade union named on the ballots." This provision ensures that employees have the option to remain unrepresented by any particular union, even if multiple unions are seeking certification.

### Exceptions to the "No Representation" Choice

However, there are exceptions to the requirement of including the "no representation" choice. The Board is not required to include this choice in the ballots for a second or subsequent representation vote if the employees in a unit have cast ballots in favor of all trade unions involved totaling more than fifty per cent of all the ballots cast, but have not given majority support to one trade union in that vote. In such cases, a second vote is deemed unnecessary to determine the majority preference.

The text clarifies this exception by stating,
"Notwithstanding subsection (2), where the employees in a unit have cast ballots in favour of all trade unions involved in a representation vote totalling more than fifty per cent of all the ballots cast but have not given majority support to one trade union in that vote and, as a result, a second or subsequent representation vote is required, the Board shall not be required to include the choice referred to in subsection (2) in the ballots for the second or subsequent vote." This prevents the inclusion of the "no representation" choice in situations where a majority of employees have supported multiple unions, but none have achieved a clear majority.

individual_results.question: Under what conditions does the Board consider a representation vote valid and how does it determine the outcome?
individual_results.answer:
## Validity and Outcome Determination of Representation Votes

### Conditions for a Representation Vote to be Valid

The Board considers a representation vote valid under specific conditions.
"Where the Board orders that a representation vote be taken among employees in a unit, the Board shall (a) determine the employees that are eligible to vote; and (b) make such arrangements and give such directions as the Board considers necessary for the proper conduct of the representation vote, including the preparation of ballots, the method of casting and counting ballots and the custody and sealing of ballot boxes."

This section outlines the Board's responsibilities when ordering a representation vote. It emphasizes the Board's duty to first identify the eligible voters and then to establish the necessary procedures for conducting the vote fairly and effectively. This includes preparing ballots, determining the voting method, and ensuring the secure handling of ballots.

Furthermore, the Board can order a representation vote when a trade union applies for certification as the bargaining agent for a unit where no other trade union currently holds that status, and the Board determines that at least 35% and no more than 50% of the employees in the unit are members of the trade union.
"If a trade union applies for certification as the bargaining agent for a unit in respect of which no other trade union is the bargaining agent, and the Board is satisfied that not less than 35% and not more than 50% of the employees in the unit are members of the trade union, the Board shall order that a representation vote be taken among the employees in the unit."

This condition ensures that the vote is conducted only when the trade union has a significant existing membership within the bargaining unit.

### Determining the Outcome of a Representation Vote

The Board determines the outcome of a representation vote based on the ballots cast by the majority of employees voting.
"Subject to subsection (2), the Board shall determine the result of a representation vote on the basis of the ballots cast by the majority of employees voting."

This statement clearly indicates that the Board's determination of the vote's outcome rests solely on the ballots cast by the majority of eligible voters.

However, the Board can declare a representation vote void if less than thirty-five percent of the employees who are eligible to vote have actually voted.
"Where, on considering the result of a representation vote, the Board determines that less than thirty-five per cent of the employees who are eligible to vote have voted, the Board shall determine that the representation vote is void."

This provision safeguards the integrity of the vote by invalidating it if voter turnout is insufficient. The Board requires a minimum level of participation to ensure that the results accurately reflect the will of the majority of employees.

Finally, the Board recognizes that a vote by the majority of employees voting in a representation vote is strong evidence of the majority of employees in the unit holding the opinion expressed in the vote.
"A vote by the majority of the employees voting in a representation vote is evidence that a majority of employees in the unit in respect of which the vote was ordered are of the opinion expressed in the vote of the majority of employees voting."

This passage highlights the weight the Board gives to a clear majority vote as an indication of the employees' preference for a particular trade union as their bargaining agent.

individual_results.question: What are the implications for a council of trade unions and its member trade unions when the council is certified as the bargaining agent for a unit?
individual_results.answer:
## Implications of Certification of a Council of Trade Unions

### Collective Agreement Obligations
"Where a council of trade unions is certified by the Board as the bargaining agent for a bargaining unit, (a) the council of trade unions and each trade union forming the council of trade unions is bound by any collective agreement entered into by the council of trade unions and the employer concerned; and (b) this Part applies, except as otherwise provided, as if the council of trade unions were a trade union."

This section clearly outlines the implications of a council of trade unions being certified. It establishes that the certified council, along with each member trade union of the council, becomes bound by any collective agreement negotiated by the council with the employer. This means that the council acts as the single bargaining agent for the entire unit, and all its member unions are obligated to abide by the terms of the resulting collective agreement. The provision further clarifies that the entire council is treated as a single trade union for the purposes of the Canada Labour Code, streamlining the bargaining process and ensuring consistency in the agreement.

### Membership in the Council
"Membership in any trade union that forms part of a council of trade unions is deemed to be membership in the council of trade unions."

This point emphasizes the interconnectedness of the trade unions within a council. It states that if a trade union is a member of a council, it is also considered a member of the council itself. This simplifies the certification process and ensures that all member unions are automatically bound by any collective agreement negotiated by the council. It also clarifies that the council acts as a unified bargaining entity, with all its member unions participating in the process.

### Effect of Certification on Individual Trade Unions
"The Board may certify a council of trade unions as the bargaining agent for a bargaining unit where the Board is satisfied that the requirements for certification prescribed by or pursuant to this Part have been met."

This section explains the Board's authority to certify a council of trade unions. It states that the certification occurs when the Board is convinced that all the necessary requirements for certification have been fulfilled. This implies that the Board will assess whether the council meets the criteria for certification, such as demonstrating a majority of employees in the unit desiring the council to represent them.

### Designation of Employers’ Organization
"Where a council of trade unions is certified by the Board as the bargaining agent for a bargaining unit, (a) the council of trade unions and each trade union forming the council of trade unions is bound by any collective agreement entered into by the council of trade unions and the employer concerned; and (b) this Part applies, except as otherwise provided, as if the council of trade unions were a trade union."

This reiterates the comprehensive implications of certification. It reinforces that the certified council and its member unions are bound by any collective agreement it enters into with the employer. Furthermore, it clarifies that the entire council is treated as a single trade union for the purposes of the Canada Labour Code, simplifying the bargaining process and ensuring consistency in the agreement.

individual_results.question: What happens when an employers' organization is designated as the employer for a unit of employees of two or more employers in the context of collective bargaining under the Canada Labour Code?
individual_results.answer:
## Designation of Employers’ Organization as the Employer

### Section 33(1)
"Where a trade union applies for certification as the bargaining agent for a unit comprised of employees of two or more employers who have formed an employers’ organization, the Board may designate the employers’ organization to be the employer if it is satisfied that each of the employers forming the employers’ organization has granted appropriate authority to the employers’ organization to enable it to discharge the duties and responsibilities of an employer under this Part."

This section outlines the process by which an employers’ organization can be designated as the employer for a bargaining unit. The Board has the authority to make this designation if it is convinced that each of the constituent employers has given the employers’ organization the necessary power to act as an employer under the Canada Labour Code. This designation is a crucial step in facilitating collective bargaining when multiple employers are involved in a single bargaining unit.

### Section 33(1.1)
"The Board may, on application by the employers’ organization, include in the designation referred to in subsection (1) any employer that becomes a member of the employers’ organization if it is satisfied that that employer has granted appropriate authority to the employers’ organization to enable the employers’ organization to discharge the duties and responsibilities of an employer and that such an inclusion would ensure the fulfilment of the objectives of this Part."

This subsection provides a mechanism for adding new employers to a designated employers’ organization. If an employer joins an existing designated employers’ organization and grants the necessary authority, the Board can include that employer in the designation. This ensures that the designated employers’ organization remains representative of all employers within the bargaining unit.

### Section 33(2)
"Where the Board designates an employers’ organization as an employer pursuant to subsection (1), (a) the employers’ organization and each employer forming the employers’ organization is bound by any collective agreement entered into by the employers’ organization and the trade union concerned; and (b) this Part applies, except as otherwise provided, as if the employers’ organization were an employer."

This section details the legal consequences of the Board’s designation of an employers’ organization as the employer. Firstly, the designated employers’ organization and each employer forming it are bound by any collective agreement negotiated between the employers’ organization and the trade union. Secondly, the entire Part of the Canada Labour Code applies as if the employers’ organization were an employer. This means that all the rules and procedures outlined in the Code regarding collective bargaining, certification, and other related matters apply to the designated employers’ organization.

### Section 33(3)
"Where an employer ceases to be a member of an employers’ organization or withdraws the authority referred to in subsection (1) or (1.1) that the employer granted to the employers’ organization, the employer (a) continues to be bound by any collective agreement applicable to the employer’s employees that was entered into by the employers’ organization; and (b) may be required to commence collective bargaining in accordance with section 48."

This section addresses what happens when an employer leaves a designated employers’ organization. The employer remains bound by any collective agreement previously entered into by the employers’ organization and the trade union. However, the employer may be required to commence collective bargaining in accordance with section 48 of the Canada Labour Code. This ensures that the bargaining unit remains representative of all employers involved, even after an employer withdraws from the designated organization.

individual_results.question: What is the process for determining a bargaining unit for employees in the long-shoring industry or other designated industries, and what is the role of the employer representative in collective bargaining?
individual_results.answer:
## Determining a Bargaining Unit for Employees in the Long-shoring Industry or Other Designated Industries

### Board's Determination of Appropriate Unit

The process for determining a bargaining unit for employees in the long-shoring industry or other designated industries involves the Board's assessment of what constitutes an appropriate unit for collective bargaining. Section 34(1) states:
"Where employees are employed in (a) the long-shoring industry, or (b) such other industry in such geographic area as may be designated by regulation of the Governor in Council on the recommendation of the Board, the Board may determine that the employees of two or more employers actively engaged in the industry in the geographic area constitute a unit appropriate for collective bargaining and may, subject to this Part, certify a trade union as the bargaining agent for the unit." This indicates that the Board has the authority to make this determination based on the industry and geographic area.

### Recommendation of the Board

The Board's determination is often preceded by a recommendation. Section 34(2) outlines the conditions under which the Board will make such a recommendation:
"No recommendation under paragraph (1)(b) shall be made by the Board unless, on inquiry, it is satisfied that the employers actively engaged in an industry in a particular geographic area obtain their employees from a group of employees the members of which are employed from time to time by some or all of those employers." This ensures that the unit proposed by the Board is genuinely representative of the employees in the industry and geographic area.

### Certification of Bargaining Agent

Once the Board determines an appropriate bargaining unit, it may certify a trade union as the bargaining agent for that unit. Section 34(1) also mentions this:
"...and may, subject to this Part, certify a trade union as the bargaining agent for the unit." This certification grants the union the legal authority to bargain collectively on behalf of all employees within the unit.

## The Role of the Employer Representative in Collective Bargaining

### Board's Appointment of Employer Representative

The Board plays a crucial role in establishing an employer representative when employees are employed in the long-shoring industry or other designated industries. Section 34(3) details this process:
"Where the employers fail to comply with an order made under paragraph (3)(a), the Board shall, after affording to the employers a reasonable opportunity to make representations, by order, appoint an employer representative of its own choosing." This means that if the employers in the unit fail to agree on a representative, the Board will step in and appoint one.

### Employer Representative as Employer for the Purposes of This Part

Section 34(5) clarifies the status of the employer representative:
"An employer representative shall be deemed to be an employer for the purposes of this Part and, by virtue of having been appointed under this section, has the power to, and shall, discharge all the duties and responsibilities of an employer under this Part on behalf of all the employers of the employees in the bargaining unit, including the power to enter into a collective agreement on behalf of those employers." This highlights the significant authority vested in the employer representative, enabling them to act on behalf of all employers in the bargaining unit.

### Employer Representative's Responsibilities and Costs

The employer representative has several responsibilities, including requiring each employer in the unit to remit their share of the costs incurred in fulfilling their duties and responsibilities under this Part and the terms of the collective agreement. Section 34(5.1) states:
"The employer representative may require each employer of employees in the bargaining unit to remit its share of the costs that the employer representative has incurred or estimates will be incurred in fulfilling its duties and responsibilities under this Part and under the terms of the collective agreement." Additionally, the employer representative must act in a non-arbitrary, non-discriminatory, and good-faith manner in the representation of all employers in the unit. Section 34(6) emphasizes this:
"In the discharge of the duties and responsibilities of an employer under this Part, an employer representative, or a person acting for such a representative, shall not act in a manner that is arbitrary, discriminatory or in bad faith in the representation of any of the employers on whose behalf the representative acts."

### Board's Role in Resolving Disputes

The Board retains the authority to resolve any questions that arise under this section, including those relating to the choice or appointment of the employer representative. Section 34(7) clarifies this:
"The Board shall determine any question that arises under this section, including any question relating to the choice or appointment of the employer representative." This ensures that the process for determining the bargaining unit and appointing the employer representative is fair and impartial.

individual_results.question: Under what circumstances can the Board declare multiple employers and their federal works, undertakings, or businesses as a single entity for collective bargaining purposes?
individual_results.answer:
## Board Declaration of Single Employer

### Circumstances for Declaration

The Board has the authority to declare multiple employers and their associated federal works, undertakings, or businesses as a single entity for collective bargaining purposes under specific circumstances. This power is granted to facilitate more efficient and comprehensive bargaining within interconnected federal operations.

#### Operation by Common Control or Direction

The primary circumstance under which the Board can make such a declaration is when
"...associated or related federal works, undertakings and businesses are operated by two or more employers having common control or direction..." This indicates that the various federal entities are linked through a shared level of authority or influence.
"Where associated or related federal works, undertakings and businesses are operated by two or more employers having common control or direction, the Minister may, after affording to the employers a reasonable opportunity to make representations, by order, declare that for all purposes of this Part the employers and the federal works, undertakings and businesses operated by them that are specified in the order are, respectively, a single employer and a single federal work, undertaking or business."

This section explicitly states the condition for the Minister (acting on the Board's recommendation) to make the declaration. It emphasizes the requirement of "common control or direction" among the multiple employers.

#### Application Following Declaration

Once the Board makes such a declaration, significant implications arise for collective bargaining.
"...subsection (1), (a) the employers’ organization and each employer forming the employers’ organization is bound by any collective agreement entered into by the employers’ organization and the trade union concerned; and (b) this Part applies, except as otherwise provided, as if the employers’ organization were an employer."

This passage details the legal consequences of the declaration. It establishes that the employers' organization, encompassing the multiple employers, becomes bound by any collective agreement reached with the trade union. Furthermore, the entire entity is treated as a single employer for all purposes of the Part, with the exception of specific provisions outlined in the legislation.

#### Board's Consideration of Bargaining Units

The Board also has the power to determine whether the employees affected by the declaration constitute one or more units appropriate for collective bargaining.
"The Board may, in making a declaration under subsection (1), determine whether the employees affected constitute one or more units appropriate for collective bargaining."

This provision highlights the Board's role in analyzing the structure of the federal operations and identifying the most suitable bargaining units for effective negotiation.

In summary, the Board can declare multiple employers and their federal works, undertakings, or businesses as a single entity for collective bargaining purposes when they are operated by two or more employers having common control or direction. This declaration has far-reaching consequences, binding the employers' organization to any collective agreement and treating the entire entity as a single employer for all relevant provisions of the Part. The Board also has the authority to determine the appropriate bargaining units for the affected employees.

individual_results.question: What are the protections in place for employees in an affected bargaining unit from the date of certification until a first collective agreement is entered into, specifically regarding dismissal or discipline?
individual_results.answer:
## Protections for Employees During Certification Period

### Section 36.1(1) - Just Cause Requirement
"During the period that begins on the date of certification and ends on the date on which a first collective agreement is entered into, the employer must not dismiss or discipline an employee in the affected bargaining unit without just cause."

This section establishes a crucial protection for employees during the certification period. It mandates that employers cannot terminate or discipline employees in the bargaining unit without a legitimate, non-discriminatory reason. The employer must demonstrate "just cause" for any such action. This provision aims to prevent employers from retaliating against employees who supported a unionization effort.

### Section 36.1(2) - Arbitration for Disagreements
"Where a disagreement relating to the dismissal or discipline of an employee during the period referred to in subsection (1) arises between the employer and the bargaining agent, (a) the bargaining agent may submit the disagreement to an arbitrator for final settlement as if it were a difference; and (b) sections 57 to 66 apply, with the modifications that the circumstances require, to the disagreement."

This subsection provides a mechanism for resolving disagreements between the employer and the bargaining agent concerning employee dismissals or disciplines. It allows the bargaining agent to refer the dispute to an arbitrator for a binding decision. This arbitration process ensures a fair and impartial resolution, protecting employees from arbitrary or retaliatory actions by the employer.

### Section 36.1(3) - Limitation on Application for Certification
"Subsection (2) does not apply to a trade union certified as a result of an application made under section 24.1."

This limitation clarifies that the arbitration provision in subsection (2) does not apply to unions certified as a result of an application made under section 24.1. This exception likely addresses specific circumstances related to the certification process under that section.

This section of the Canada Labour Code explicitly outlines the standard of behavior expected of a trade union or its representative when representing employees. It mandates that such representatives must act
"...not act in a manner that is arbitrary, discriminatory or in bad faith..." This standard encompasses several key principles. "Arbitrary" behavior would involve decisions or actions taken without reason or justification. "Discriminatory" behavior would involve treating employees differently based on protected characteristics or other irrelevant factors. "Bad faith" behavior would involve acting with dishonest or deceitful intentions, undermining the collective agreement process.

The quote emphasizes the obligation of trade unions to represent their members fairly and ethically. It prohibits actions that are capricious, biased, or intended to obstruct the bargaining process. This standard is crucial for ensuring that employees' rights under the collective agreement are protected and that the bargaining process is conducted with integrity.

## Conditions for Employee Application to Revoke Certification

### General Conditions

An employee can apply to revoke the certification of a trade union as the bargaining agent for a bargaining unit under several conditions.
"If a trade union has been certified as the bargaining agent for a bargaining unit, any employee who claims to represent a majority of the employees in the bargaining unit may, subject to subsection (5), apply to the Board for an order revoking the certification of that trade union." This passage outlines the fundamental condition for an employee to initiate a revocation process. The employee must demonstrate that they represent a majority of the employees in the bargaining unit.

### Specific Grounds for Application

Employees can apply for revocation based on various grounds.
"Where a council of trade unions has been certified as the bargaining agent for a bargaining unit, in addition to any circumstances in which an application for revocation of the certification of the council of trade unions may be made pursuant to section 38 or subsection 40(1), any employee in the bargaining unit, the employer of the employees in the bargaining unit or a trade union that forms part of the council of trade unions may apply to the Board for revocation of the certification on the ground that the council of trade unions no longer meets the requirements for certification of a council of trade unions." This passage details a specific ground for application: alleging that the certification was obtained through fraud. "An application for an order pursuant to subsection (1) may be made in respect of a bargaining agent for a bargaining unit, (a) where a collective agreement applicable to the bargaining unit is in force, only during a period in which an application for certification of a trade union is authorized to be made pursuant to section 24 unless the Board consents to the making of the application for the order at some other time; and (b) where no collective agreement applicable to the bargaining unit is in force, at any time after a period of one year from the date of certification of the trade union." "An application under subsection (1) or (3) must not, except with the consent of the Board, be made in respect of the bargaining agent for employees in a bargaining unit during a strike or lockout of those employees that is not prohibited by this Part." "If a collective agreement applicable to a bargaining unit is in force but the bargaining agent that is a party to the collective agreement has not been certified by the Board, any employee who claims to represent a majority of the employees in the bargaining unit may, subject to subsection (5), apply to the Board for an order declaring that the bargaining agent is not entitled to represent the employees in the bargaining unit."
