## Revocation of Certification and Declaration of Non-Entitlement

### Conditions for Revocation of Certification

The Board has several grounds upon which it can revoke the certification of a trade union as the bargaining agent for a bargaining unit.

#### Application by an Employee
"Where a trade union is certified as the bargaining agent for a bargaining unit, (a) the trade union so certified has exclusive authority to bargain collectively on behalf of the employees in the bargaining unit; (b) the certification of any trade union that was previously certified as the bargaining agent for any employees in the bargaining unit is deemed to be revoked to the extent that the certification relates to those employees; (c) the trade union so certified is substituted as a party to any collective agreement that affects any employees in the bargaining unit, to the extent that the collective agreement relates to those employees, in the place of the bargaining agent named in the collective agreement or any successor thereto; and (d) the trade union so certified is deemed to be the bargaining agent for the purposes of paragraph 50(b)." This section outlines the effect of certification, including the revocation of prior certifications. It also details the substitution of the newly certified union as a party to any existing collective agreement.

#### Application for Revocation Based on Fraud
"Where a trade union has been certified as the bargaining agent for a bargaining unit, (a) any employee in the bargaining unit, (b) the employer of the employees in the bargaining unit, or (c) any trade union that appeared before the Board in the certification proceeding, that alleges that the certification was obtained by the fraud of the trade union so certified, may apply to the Board, at any time, for revocation of the certification." This subsection specifies who can apply for revocation based on allegations of fraud. It states that any employee, employer, or other trade union that participated in the certification proceeding and alleges fraud can file an application.

#### Application for Revocation Where Majority No Longer Wishes Representation
"If, on receipt of an application for an order made under subsection 38(1) or (3) in respect of a bargaining agent for a bargaining unit, and after any inquiry by way of a representation vote or otherwise that the Board considers appropriate in the circumstances, the Board is satisfied that a majority of the employees in the bargaining unit no longer wish to have the bargaining agent represent them, the Board shall, subject to subsection (2), by order, (a) in the case of an application made under subsection 38(1), revoke the certification of the trade union as the bargaining agent for the bargaining unit; or (b) in the case of an application made under subsection 38(3), declare that the bargaining agent is not entitled to represent the employees in the bargaining unit." This section details the Board's action when a majority of employees no longer desire the current bargaining agent to represent them. It states that the Board will issue an order either revoking the certification or declaring the bargaining agent not entitled to represent the employees.

#### Application for Revocation Based on Failure to Bargain in Good Faith
"If no collective agreement applicable to a bargaining unit is in force, an order shall not be made under paragraph (1)(a) in relation to the bargaining agent for the bargaining unit unless the Board is satisfied that the bargaining agent has failed to make a reasonable effort to enter into a collective agreement in relation to the bargaining unit." This subsection clarifies a condition under which the Board will not issue an order revoking certification. It requires the bargaining agent to have made a reasonable effort to negotiate a collective agreement before the Board will consider revocation.

### Conditions for Declaration of Non-Entitlement

The Board can also declare that a bargaining agent is not entitled to represent the employees in the bargaining unit under specific circumstances.

#### Application for Declaration of Non-Entitlement
"If a collective agreement applicable to a bargaining unit is in force but the bargaining agent that is a party to the collective agreement has not been certified by the Board, any employee who claims to represent a majority of the employees in the bargaining unit may, subject to subsection (5), apply to the Board for an order declaring that the bargaining agent is not entitled to represent the employees in the bargaining unit." This section outlines the process for applying to the Board for a declaration of non-entitlement when the bargaining agent is not certified but a collective agreement is in force. It allows any employee claiming a majority to file such an application.

#### Application for Declaration of Non-Entitlement Based on Fraud
"On receipt of an application under subsection (1) in respect of a trade union certification as the bargaining agent for a bargaining unit, the Board shall, by order, revoke the certification of the trade union as the bargaining agent for the bargaining unit if the Board is satisfied that the evidence in support of the application (a) was not and could not, by the exercise of reasonable diligence, have been presented to it in the certification proceeding; and (b) is such that the Board would have refused to certify the trade union as the bargaining agent for the bargaining unit if the evidence had been presented to it in the certification proceeding." This subsection details the Board's action upon receiving an application for a declaration of non-entitlement based on fraud. It states that the Board will issue an order revoking the certification if the evidence of fraud could not have been presented during the certification proceeding and would have led to a refusal of certification.

#### Application for Declaration of Non-Entitlement Where Majority No Longer Wishes Representation
"If, on receipt of an application for an order made under subsection 38(1) or (3) in respect of a bargaining agent for a bargaining unit, and after any inquiry by way of a representation vote or otherwise that the Board considers appropriate in the circumstances, the Board is satisfied that a majority of the employees in the bargaining unit no longer wish to have the bargaining agent represent them, the Board shall, subject to subsection (2), by order, (a) in the case of an application made under subsection 38(1), revoke the certification of the trade union as the bargaining agent for the bargaining unit; or (b) in the case of an application made under subsection 38(3), declare that the bargaining agent is not entitled to represent the employees in the bargaining unit." This section reiterates the Board's action when a majority of employees no longer wish the current bargaining agent to represent them, stating that it will issue an order either revoking certification or declaring non-entitlement.

individual_results.question: Under what circumstances can a trade union's certification as a bargaining agent be revoked?
individual_results.answer:
## Revocation of Certification of a Bargaining Agent

### Grounds for Revocation

A trade union's certification as a bargaining agent can be revoked under several circumstances, as outlined in the Canada Labour Code.

#### Application for Revocation Based on Fraud

One primary circumstance for revocation arises when fraud is alleged in the certification proceeding. Section 40(1) states:
"Where a trade union has been certified as the bargaining agent for a bargaining unit, (a) any employee in the bargaining unit, (b) the employer of the employees in the bargaining unit, or (c) any trade union that appeared before the Board in the certification proceeding, that alleges that the certification was obtained by the fraud of the trade union so certified, may apply to the Board, at any time, for revocation of the certification." This indicates that any party with evidence of fraud can petition the Board for revocation.

Section 40(2) elaborates on the Board's process in such cases:
"On receipt of an application under subsection (1) in respect of a trade union certification as the bargaining agent for a bargaining unit, the Board shall, by order, revoke the certification of the trade union as the bargaining agent for the bargaining unit if the Board is satisfied that the evidence in support of the application (a) was not and could not, by the exercise of reasonable diligence, have been presented to it in the certification proceeding; and (b) is such that the Board would have refused to certify the trade union as the bargaining agent for the bargaining unit if the evidence had been presented to it in the certification proceeding." This highlights that the Board will only revoke certification if the evidence of fraud was not presented during the original certification process and would have led to a denial of certification.

#### Application for Revocation Based on Lack of Majority Support

Another circumstance for revocation occurs when a majority of the employees in the bargaining unit no longer wish to have the bargaining agent represent them. Section 39(1) specifies this:
"If, on receipt of an application for an order made under subsection 38(1) or (3) in respect of a bargaining agent for a bargaining unit, and after any inquiry by way of a representation vote or otherwise that the Board considers appropriate in the circumstances, the Board is satisfied that a majority of the employees in the bargaining unit no longer wish to have the bargaining agent represent them, the Board shall, subject to subsection (2), by order, (a) in the case of an application made under subsection 38(1), revoke the certification of the trade union as the bargaining agent for the bargaining unit; or (b) in the case of an application made under subsection 38(3), declare that the bargaining agent is not entitled to represent the employees in the bargaining unit." This demonstrates that the Board can revoke certification if a majority of the employees express a lack of desire for the current bargaining agent to continue representing them.

#### Application for Revocation Based on Failure to Bargain in Good Faith

Section 39(2) provides a limitation on the revocation process when no collective agreement is in force:
"If no collective agreement applicable to a bargaining unit is in force, an order shall not be made under paragraph (1)(a) in relation to the bargaining agent for the bargaining unit unless the Board is satisfied that the bargaining agent has failed to make a reasonable effort to enter into a collective agreement in relation to the bargaining unit." This indicates that the Board will not revoke certification solely based on a lack of collective agreement if the bargaining agent has not made a good faith effort to negotiate one.

#### Application for Revocation Based on Certification Obtained by Fraud

Section 40(1) also covers the revocation of certification based on fraud that was not disclosed during the original certification proceeding:
"Where a trade union has been certified as the bargaining agent for a bargaining unit, (a) any employee in the bargaining unit, (b) the employer of the employees in the bargaining unit, or (c) any trade union that appeared before the Board in the certification proceeding, that alleges that the certification was obtained by the fraud of the trade union so certified, may apply to the Board, at any time, for revocation of the certification." This reiterates the ability to seek revocation based on undisclosed fraud.

### Time Limits for Application

The Canada Labour Code specifies time limits for applying to the Board for revocation of certification. Section 38(2) outlines these:
"An application for an order pursuant to subsection (1) may be made in respect of a bargaining agent for a bargaining unit, (a) where a collective agreement applicable to the bargaining unit is in force, only during a period in which an application for certification of a trade union is authorized to be made pursuant to section 24 unless the Board consents to the making of the application for the order at some other time; and (b) where no collective agreement applicable to the bargaining unit is in force, at any time after a period of one year from the date of certification of the trade union." This indicates that an application for revocation can be made at any time after one year from the date of certification if no collective agreement is in force, or only during a specific period if a collective agreement is in force.

## Revocation of Certification of a Council of Trade Unions

### General Circumstances for Revocation

Section 41(1) outlines the general circumstances under which an application can be made to revoke the certification of a council of trade unions as a bargaining agent. It states:
"Where a council of trade unions has been certified as the bargaining agent for a bargaining unit, in addition to any circumstances in which an application for revocation of the certification of the council of trade unions may be made pursuant to section 38 or subsection 40(1), any employee in the bargaining unit, the employer of the employees in the bargaining unit or a trade union that forms part of the council of trade unions may apply to the Board for revocation of the certification on the ground that the council of trade unions no longer meets the requirements for certification of a council of trade unions."

This section broadens the grounds for revocation beyond those applicable to individual trade unions. It specifies that any stakeholder within the bargaining unit – employee, employer, or a constituent trade union of the council – can apply for revocation if the council
"...no longer meets the requirements for certification of a council of trade unions." This indicates that the certification of a council of trade unions can be challenged based on a failure to continue satisfying the criteria for such certification.

### Specific Grounds for Revocation

Section 41(1) further elaborates on specific grounds for revocation by listing who can make the application and the reason for it. It mentions:
"...any employee in the bargaining unit, the employer of the employees in the bargaining unit or a trade union that forms part of the council of trade unions may apply to the Board for revocation of the certification on the ground that the council of trade unions no longer meets the requirements for certification of a council of trade unions."

This clarifies that the application can originate from various sources within the bargaining unit, including individual employees, the employer, or a member trade union of the council. The underlying reason for the application is that the council
"...no longer meets the requirements for certification of a council of trade unions." This suggests that the council's continued certification is contingent upon it maintaining compliance with the criteria established for certification of a council of trade unions.

### Application Period

Section 41(3) specifies the timeframe within which an application for revocation of certification of a council of trade unions can be made. It states:
"An application under subsection (1) may be made in respect of a council of trade unions that has been certified as the bargaining agent for a bargaining unit only during a period in which an application for an order revoking the certification of that council of trade unions is authorized to be made under section 38."

This indicates that an application for revocation of certification of a council of trade unions can only be made during a specific window, which coincides with the period when an application for an order revoking the certification of the council is authorized under section 38. This temporal restriction suggests a coordinated process for challenging the certification of a council of trade unions.

individual_results.question: What happens to a collective agreement between a trade union and an employer if the Board makes an order revoking the trade union's certification, and what restrictions are placed on the employer?
individual_results.answer:
## Revocation of Certification and Effect on Collective Agreements and Employer Bargaining

### Effect of Revocation on Collective Agreements

Section 42 of the Canada Labour Code directly addresses the consequences of the Board making an order revoking a trade union's certification. It states:
"Where the Board makes an order under section 39, subsection 40(2) or section 41 revoking the certification of a trade union or council of trade unions, or declaring that a trade union is not entitled to represent the employees in a bargaining unit, (a) any collective agreement between the trade union or council of trade unions and the employer of the employees in the bargaining unit that applies to the bargaining unit ceases to have effect from the time the order is made or from such later time as the Board considers appropriate; and (b) the employer shall not bargain collectively, or enter into a collective agreement with the trade union or council of trade unions, for a period of one year from the date of the order, unless the trade union or council of trade unions is certified by the Board under this Part during that period as the bargaining agent for a bargaining unit comprised of employees of the employer."

This passage clearly outlines the immediate impact of a certification revocation order on existing collective agreements. Subsection (a) declares that
"...any collective agreement between the trade union or council of trade unions and the employer of the employees in the bargaining unit that applies to the bargaining unit ceases to have effect from the time the order is made or from such later time as the Board considers appropriate..." This means that the previously in-force collective agreement is terminated as of the date the Board issues the order.

Subsection (b) then imposes a restriction on the employer's bargaining activities. It prohibits the employer from
"...collectively, or enter into a collective agreement with the trade union or council of trade unions, for a period of one year from the date of the order..." This one-year restriction is contingent upon the Board subsequently certifying a new bargaining agent for the bargaining unit within that period. The employer cannot engage in collective bargaining with the previously certified union until a new union is certified.

### Restrictions Placed on the Employer

Following the revocation of certification, the employer faces a significant one-year restriction on bargaining with the former bargaining agent. As stated in Section 42(b):
"...the employer shall not bargain collectively, or enter into a collective agreement with the trade union or council of trade unions, for a period of one year from the date of the order, unless the trade union or council of trade unions is certified by the Board under this Part during that period as the bargaining agent for a bargaining unit comprised of employees of the employer."

This restriction is designed to provide a period of stability and to allow for the potential certification of a new bargaining agent. The employer is barred from any collective bargaining activity with the now-decertified union for a full year unless the Board re-certifies the union as the bargaining agent for the same bargaining unit within that timeframe. This ensures that the employer cannot continue bargaining with a union that has lost its legal standing to represent the employees.

individual_results.question: What happens to the rights, privileges, and duties of a trade union when it is succeeded by another trade union due to a merger, amalgamation, or transfer of jurisdiction?
individual_results.answer:
## Successor Rights and Obligations: Mergers, etc., of Trade Unions

### Section 43(1)
"Where, by reason of a merger or amalgamation of trade unions or a transfer of jurisdiction among trade unions, a trade union succeeds another trade union that, at the time of the merger, amalgamation or transfer of jurisdiction, is a bargaining agent, the successor shall be deemed to have acquired the rights, privileges and duties of its predecessor, whether under a collective agreement or otherwise."

This section directly addresses the question. It states that when one trade union takes over the rights, privileges, and duties of another due to a merger, amalgamation, or transfer of jurisdiction, the successor union is legally considered to have acquired those rights, privileges, and duties. This means that the successor union steps into the shoes of the predecessor union, inheriting all associated obligations and entitlements, whether they are found within a collective agreement or elsewhere. The use of the term "deemed to have acquired" is crucial, as it highlights the legal effect of the succession – the successor union is treated as if it had always possessed those rights, privileges, and duties.



### Section 43(2)
"Where, on a merger or amalgamation of trade unions or a transfer of jurisdiction among trade unions, any question arises concerning the rights, privileges and duties of a trade union under this Part or under a collective agreement in respect of a bargaining unit or an employee therein, the Board, on application to it by a trade union affected by the merger, amalgamation or transfer of jurisdiction, shall determine what rights, privileges and duties have been acquired or are retained."

This section outlines the role of the Board in resolving any disputes that may arise concerning the rights, privileges, and duties of a trade union following a merger, amalgamation, or transfer of jurisdiction. It specifies that the Board will make a determination upon application from a trade union affected by the change. The Board's determination will clarify which rights, privileges, and duties have been acquired or are retained by the successor union. This provision ensures that any ambiguities or disagreements are resolved through a formal process overseen by the Board.



### Section 43(3)
"Before determining, pursuant to subsection (2), what rights, privileges and duties of a trade union have been acquired or are retained, the Board may make such inquiry or direct that such representation votes be taken as it considers necessary."

This section details the methods the Board may employ to gather information and make its determination regarding the successor union's rights, privileges, and duties. It states that the Board may conduct inquiries or direct representation votes as it deems necessary. This allows the Board to gather relevant information from the affected trade unions and their members to ensure a fair and accurate determination. The Board's flexibility in choosing the appropriate inquiry or voting method underscores its commitment to resolving disputes effectively.

individual_results.question: What happens to the labour relations of employees when a business is sold, particularly in terms of their bargaining agent and collective agreements?
individual_results.answer:
## Successor Rights and Obligations: Changes in Labour Relations Upon Business Sale

### Section 44(1) and (2) of the Canada Labour Code

Section 44(1) addresses the continuity of labour relations when a business is sold. It states,
"Where an employer sells a business, (a) a trade union that is the bargaining agent for the employees employed in the business continues to be their bargaining agent; (b) a trade union that made application for certification in respect of any employees employed in the business before the date on which the business is sold may, subject to this Part, be certified by the Board as their bargaining agent; (c) the person to whom the business is sold is bound by any collective agreement that is, on the date on which the business is sold, applicable to the employees employed in the business; and (d) the person to whom the business is sold becomes a party to any proceeding taken under this Part that is pending on the date on which the business was sold and that affects the employees employed in the business or their bargaining agent."

This section clearly outlines the continuity of the bargaining agent. It explicitly states that
"...a trade union that is the bargaining agent for the employees employed in the business continues to be their bargaining agent..." This ensures that the employees retain their existing bargaining representative. Furthermore, it provides a mechanism for a trade union that had previously applied for certification to be certified by the Board, subject to the provisions of this Part.

Section 44(2) elaborates on the binding nature of existing collective agreements. It specifies,
"(c) the person to whom the business is sold is bound by any collective agreement that is, on the date on which the business is sold, applicable to the employees employed in the business..." This means that the collective agreement in place at the time of the sale remains in effect for the employees of the newly acquired business.

### Section 47(1) and (2) of the Canada Labour Code

Section 47(1) further clarifies the successor rights and obligations. It states,
"Where the name of any portion of the federal public administration specified from time to time in Schedule I, IV or V to the Financial Administration Act is deleted and that portion of the federal public administration is established as or becomes a part of a corporation or business to which this Part applies, or where a portion of the federal public administration included in another portion of the federal public administration specified in those Schedules is severed from the portion in which it was included and established as or becomes a part of such a corporation or business, (a) a collective agreement or arbitral award that applies to any employees in that portion of the federal public administration and that is in force at the time the portion of the federal public administration is established as or becomes a part of such a corporation or business continues in force, subject to subsections (3) to (7), until its term expires; and (b) the Federal Public Sector Labour Relations Act applies in all respects to the interpretation and application of the collective agreement or arbitral award."

This section reinforces the continuity of collective agreements. It explicitly states that
"...a collective agreement or arbitral award that applies to any employees in that portion of the federal public administration and that is in force at the time the portion of the federal public administration is established as or becomes a part of such a corporation or business continues in force, subject to subsections (3) to (7), until its term expires..." This ensures that the existing collective agreement remains in effect until its expiration date.

Section 47(2) addresses the application of the Federal Public Sector Labour Relations Act. It specifies,
"(b) the Federal Public Sector Labour Relations Act applies in all respects to the interpretation and application of the collective agreement or arbitral award." This ensures that the collective agreement or arbitral award is interpreted and applied in accordance with the provisions of the Federal Public Sector Labour Relations Act.

### Section 47.1 of the Canada Labour Code

Section 47.1 provides additional details regarding successor rights and obligations when a business is sold. It states,
"Where, before the deletion or severance referred to in subsection 47(1), notice to bargain collectively has been given in respect of a collective agreement or arbitral award binding on employees of a corporation or business who, immediately before the deletion or severance, were part of the federal public administration, (a) the terms and conditions of employment contained in a collective agreement or arbitral award that, by virtue of section 107 of the Federal Public Sector Labour Relations Act , are continued in force immediately before the date of the deletion or severance or that were last continued in force before that date, in respect of those employees shall continue or resume in force on and after that date and shall be observed by the corporation or business, as employer, the bargaining agent for those employees and those employees until the requirements of paragraphs 89(1)(a) to (d) have been met, unless the employer and the bargaining agent agree otherwise; (b) the Federal Public Sector Labour Relations Act applies in all respects to the interpretation and application of any term or condition continued or resumed by paragraph (a); (c) on application by the corporation or business, as employer, or the bargaining agent for those employees, made during the period beginning on the one hundred and twentieth day and ending on the one hundred and fiftieth day after the date of the deletion or severance, the Board shall make an order determining (i) whether the employees of the corporation or business who are represented by the bargaining agent constitute one or more units appropriate for collective bargaining, and (ii) which trade union shall be the bargaining agent for the employees in each such unit; (d) where the Board makes the determinations under paragraph (c), the corporation or business, as employer, or the bargaining agent may, by notice, require the other to commence collective bargaining under this Act for the purpose of entering into a collective agreement; and (e) this Part, other than section 80, applies in respect of a notice given under paragraph (d)."

This section reiterates the continuity of collective agreements and the application of the Federal Public Sector Labour Relations Act. It also addresses the process for determining bargaining units and certifying a new bargaining agent if necessary. It further clarifies that the provisions of this Part apply to any notice to bargain collectively given prior to the deletion or severance.

individual_results.question: What is the role of the Board in the event of a sale or change of activity affecting employees' collective bargaining units?
individual_results.answer:
## The Board's Role in Sales or Changes of Activity Affecting Collective Bargaining Units

### Determining Appropriate Bargaining Units

Section 45 outlines the Board's role when a sale or change of activity affects employees' collective bargaining units. It states,
"In the case of a sale or change of activity referred to in section 44, the Board may, on application by the employer or any trade union affected, determine whether the employees affected constitute one or more units appropriate for collective bargaining." This indicates that the Board has the authority to review and redefine bargaining units following such events. The Board's determination is made upon application from either the employer or a trade union impacted by the sale or change of activity.

### Review of Bargaining Unit Structure

Section 18.1 further elaborates on the Board's power to review bargaining unit structures. It specifies,
"On application by the employer or a bargaining agent, the Board may review the structure of the bargaining units if it is satisfied that the bargaining units are no longer appropriate for collective bargaining." This power is exercised at the Board's discretion, contingent upon its assessment that the existing units are no longer suitable for effective collective bargaining.

### Determining Bargaining Unit Composition

Section 45 reiterates the Board's role in determining the appropriate bargaining units. It mentions,
"...the Board may, on application by the employer or any trade union affected, determine whether the employees affected constitute one or more units appropriate for collective bargaining." This underscores the Board's function as the ultimate arbiter of bargaining unit composition in the context of sales or changes of activity.

### Board's Authority to Make Orders

Section 18.1 details the Board's broad authority to make orders regarding bargaining units following a review. It states,
"...may make any orders it considers appropriate to implement any agreement." This gives the Board the power to implement any agreement reached between the parties regarding bargaining unit determination. Furthermore, it lists specific orders the Board may make, including
"...determine which trade union shall be the bargaining agent for the employees in each bargaining unit that results from the review..." and
"...amend any certification order or description of a bargaining unit contained in any collective agreement..." This demonstrates the Board's comprehensive control over bargaining unit structure in these situations.

### Board's Determination of Collective Agreements

Section 46 clarifies the Board's responsibility in addressing questions arising from a sale or change of activity. It states,
"The Board shall determine any question that arises under section 44, including a question as to whether or not a business has been sold or there has been a change of activity of a business, or as to the identity of the purchaser of a business." This indicates that the Board is tasked with resolving any ambiguities or disputes that may arise concerning the status of the business and the identity of the new owner.

### Application of Orders

Section 18.1 further explains the application of orders made by the Board. It states,

"Where the name of any portion of the federal public administration specified from time to time in Schedule I, IV or V to the Financial Administration Act is deleted and that portion of the federal public administration is established as or becomes a part of a corporation or business to which this Part applies, or where a portion of the federal public administration included in another portion of the federal public administration specified in those Schedules is severed from the portion in which it was included and established as or becomes a part of such a corporation or business, (a) a collective agreement or arbitral award that applies to any employees in that portion of the federal public administration and that is in force at the time the portion of the federal public administration is established as or becomes a part of such a corporation or business continues in force, subject to subsections (3) to (7), until its term expires..."

It states that any existing collective agreement or arbitral award applicable to the employees in that transferred portion
"...continues in force, subject to subsections (3) to (7), until its term expires..." This means that the existing agreements are not automatically terminated. Instead, they remain in effect until their scheduled expiration date. The subsequent subsections (3) through (7) outline the procedures and considerations for the future of these agreements within the new corporate structure.

### Application of the Federal Public Sector Labour Relations Act
"...and (b) the Federal Public Sector Labour Relations Act applies in all respects to the interpretation and application of the collective agreement or arbitral award."

This part of Section 47(1) clarifies which legislation governs the interpretation and application of the continued-in-force collective agreement or arbitral award. It explicitly states that the Federal Public Sector Labour Relations Act applies "in all respects." This ensures consistency and uniformity in how the agreements are understood and enforced within the new corporate entity. The Federal Public Sector Labour Relations Act provides the framework for resolving disputes and interpreting the terms of the collective agreement or arbitral award.

## Governor in Council Exclusion of Federal Public Administration from Sections 47 and 47.1

### Circumstances for Exclusion

The Governor in Council has the authority to exclude a portion of the federal public administration from the operation of sections 47 and 47.1 through an order. This exclusion can occur under specific circumstances.

#### Deletion or Severance of Federal Public Administration

The primary circumstance for exclusion is the deletion or severance of a portion of the federal public administration. Section 47.2 states,
"The Governor in Council may, by order, exclude from the operation of sections 47 and 47.1 any portion of the federal public administration that is deleted or severed as described in subsection 47(1) where the Governor in Council, on the recommendation of the Minister after consultation with the Treasury Board and the Minister responsible for that portion of the federal public administration, is of the opinion that it is in the public interest to do so." This indicates that when a portion of the federal public administration is deleted or severed, the Governor in Council can issue an order to exclude it from the application of sections 47 and 47.1.

#### Public Interest

The Governor in Council's decision to exclude a portion of the federal public administration from sections 47 and 47.1 must be based on the public interest. Section 47.2 elaborates on this, stating that the exclusion can occur
"...where the Governor in Council, on the recommendation of the Minister after consultation with the Treasury Board and the Minister responsible for that portion of the federal public administration, is of the opinion that it is in the public interest to do so." This highlights the importance of considering the broader public good when making such exclusion decisions.

### Process for Exclusion

The process for exclusion involves a recommendation from the Minister, consultation with the Treasury Board and the Minister responsible for the portion of the federal public administration in question, and a final decision by the Governor in Council. Section 47.2 outlines this process:
"The Governor in Council may, by order, exclude from the operation of sections 47 and 47.1 any portion of the federal public administration that is deleted or severed as described in subsection 47(1) where the Governor in Council, on the recommendation of the Minister after consultation with the Treasury Board and the Minister responsible for that portion of the federal public administration, is of the opinion that it is in the public interest to do so." ## Requirements for an Employer Taking Over Services from a Previous Contractor

### Section 47.3(1) - Definition of Successive Contracts for Services
"In this section, means an employer who, under the terms of a contract or other arrangement that is no longer in force, (a) provided services at an airport to another employer, or to a person acting on behalf of that other employer, in an industry referred to in paragraph (e) of the definition federal work, undertaking or business in section 2; (b) provided prescribed services to another employer, or to a person acting on behalf of that other employer, in a prescribed industry; or (c) provided prescribed services at a prescribed location to another employer, or to a person acting on behalf of that other employer, in a prescribed industry."

This section defines what constitutes a "successive contract for services" employer. It specifies that an employer taking over services must have previously provided similar services to another employer or a representative acting on their behalf, within a defined industry or location. This establishes the context for the subsequent requirements.

### Section 47.3(2) - Remuneration Requirements
"An employer who succeeds a previous contractor as the provider of services, in accordance with a contract or other arrangement, must pay to the employees providing the services under that contract or arrangement remuneration not less than that which the employees of the previous contractor who provided the same or substantially similar services were entitled to receive under the terms of a collective agreement to which this Part applied."

This section outlines the key requirement for an employer succeeding a previous contractor: they must pay their employees remuneration
"...not less than that which the employees of the previous contractor who provided the same or substantially similar services were entitled to receive under the terms of a collective agreement to which this Part applied." This ensures that employees are not disadvantaged when a contractor transition occurs. The reference to a collective agreement is important, as it provides a benchmark for determining appropriate remuneration.

### Section 47.3(3) - Regulations
"The Governor in Council may, on the Minister’s recommendation, make regulations prescribing anything that is to be prescribed under subsection (1)."

This section grants the Governor in Council the authority to create regulations to further specify the requirements outlined in subsection (1). This allows for flexibility and adaptation to changing circumstances.

### Section 24(2) - Application for Certification Timing

This indicates that a certified bargaining agent, or an employer initiating the certification process, can begin collective bargaining as soon as a union applies for certification when no existing collective agreement covers the unit.

### Section 36(2) - Duty of Fair Representation
"Where a disagreement relating to the dismissal or discipline of an employee during the period referred to in subsection (1) arises between the employer and the bargaining agent, (a) the bargaining agent may submit the disagreement to an arbitrator for final settlement as if it were a difference; and (b) sections 57 to 66 apply, with the modifications that the circumstances require, to the disagreement."

While this section addresses disagreements during the certification period, it indirectly supports the initiation of collective bargaining. It highlights the bargaining agent's right to seek arbitration to resolve disputes. This implies that even when no collective agreement is in force, the bargaining agent has a mechanism to address issues that arise during the bargaining process.

### Section 36(2) - Requirement to Commence Bargaining
"Where, pursuant to paragraph (1)(c), a trade union is substituted as a party to a collective agreement, the trade union may, within three months after the date on which it is certified as the bargaining agent for a bargaining unit affected by the collective agreement, require the employer who is a party to the collective agreement to commence collective bargaining for the purpose of renewing or revising the collective agreement or entering into a new collective agreement."

This section directly addresses the employer's obligation to commence collective bargaining after a trade union is certified. It states that the certified bargaining agent can
"...require the employer who is a party to the collective agreement to commence collective bargaining..." within three months of certification. This confirms that the certified bargaining agent has the power to initiate collective bargaining when no collective agreement is in force.

### Section 36(2) - Renewal or Revision of Collective Agreement
"Where, pursuant to paragraph (1)(c), a trade union is substituted as a party to a collective agreement, the trade union may, within three months after the date on which it is certified as the bargaining agent for a bargaining unit affected by the collective agreement, require the employer who is a party to the collective agreement to commence collective bargaining for the purpose of renewing or revising the collective agreement or entering into a new collective agreement."

This subsection further clarifies the certified bargaining agent's role in initiating collective bargaining. It specifies that the certified bargaining agent can
"...require the employer who is a party to the collective agreement to commence collective bargaining for the purpose of renewing or revising the collective agreement or entering into a new collective agreement." individual_results.question: What are the requirements for a party to a collective agreement to initiate collective bargaining for the purpose of renewing, revising, or entering into a new collective agreement?
individual_results.answer:
## Requirements for Initiating Collective Bargaining for Renewal, Revision, or New Agreement

### Section 48: Notice to Bargain to Enter into a Collective Agreement
"Where the Board has certified a bargaining agent for a bargaining unit and no collective agreement binding on the employees in the bargaining unit is in force, the bargaining agent may, by notice, require the employer of those employees, or the employer may, by notice, require the bargaining agent to commence collective bargaining for the purpose of entering into a collective agreement."

This section outlines the initial step for either party to initiate collective bargaining for a new agreement. It states that either the bargaining agent (after certification) or the employer can issue a notice to the other party to begin negotiations. This notice serves as the formal trigger for the collective bargaining process. The requirement is a written notification, allowing both sides to prepare for discussions.

### Section 49: Notice to Bargain to Renew or Revise a Collective Agreement or Enter a New Collective Agreement
"(1) Either party to a collective agreement may, within the period of four months immediately preceding the date of expiration of the term of the collective agreement, or within the longer period that may be provided for in the collective agreement, by notice, require the other party to the collective agreement to commence collective bargaining for the purpose of renewing or revising the collective agreement or entering into a new collective agreement."

This section details the timeframe and method for initiating collective bargaining for a renewal, revision, or new agreement. It specifies that either party can issue a notice within a defined period before the existing agreement expires, or within a longer period stipulated in the existing collective agreement. The notice is a formal request to begin negotiations for a new or modified agreement.
"(2) Where a collective agreement provides that any provision of the collective agreement may be revised during the term of the collective agreement, a party entitled to do so by the collective agreement may, by notice, require the other party to commence collective bargaining for the purpose of revising the provision."

This subsection addresses the possibility of revising specific provisions within an existing collective agreement. It clarifies that if the agreement allows for such revisions, either party can issue a notice to initiate bargaining specifically for that provision. The notice is a formal request to begin negotiations for a revision of the particular provision.

### Section 36: Certification of Bargaining Agents and Related Matters: Effect of certification
"(1) Where a trade union is certified as the bargaining agent for a bargaining unit, (a) the trade union so certified has exclusive authority to bargain collectively on behalf of the employees in the bargaining unit; (b) the certification of any trade union that was previously certified as the bargaining agent for any employees in the bargaining unit is deemed to be revoked to the extent that the certification relates to those employees; (c) the trade union so certified is substituted as a party to any collective agreement that affects any employees in the bargaining unit, to the extent that the collective agreement relates to those employees, in the place of the bargaining agent named in the collective agreement or any successor thereto; and (d) the trade union so certified is deemed to be the bargaining agent for the purposes of paragraph 50(b)."

While this section primarily focuses on the effect of certification, it indirectly supports the requirement for initiating collective bargaining. It establishes that once a bargaining agent is certified, they have the exclusive authority to bargain collectively. This means that any request to begin collective bargaining must be directed to the certified bargaining agent.

### Section 50: Obligation to Bargain Collectively: Duty to bargain and not to change terms and conditions
"Section 50 Where notice to bargain collectively has been given under this Part, (a) the bargaining agent and the employer, without delay, but in any case within twenty days after the notice was given unless the parties otherwise agree, shall (i) meet and commence, or cause authorized representatives on their behalf to meet and commence, to bargain collectively in good faith, and (ii) make every reasonable effort to enter into a collective agreement; and (b) the employer shall not alter the rates of pay or any other term or condition of employment or any right or privilege of the employees in the bargaining unit, or any right or privilege of the bargaining agent, until the requirements of paragraphs 89(1)(a) to (d) have been met, unless the bargaining agent consents to the alteration of such a term or condition, or such a right or privilege."

This section reinforces the legal obligation to bargain collectively upon receiving a notice to do so. It mandates that both the bargaining agent and the employer must meet and commence bargaining in good faith within a specified timeframe. This underscores the formal process for initiating collective bargaining.

"Where, before the deletion or severance referred to in subsection 47(1), notice to bargain collectively has been given in respect of a collective agreement or arbitral award binding on employees of a corporation or business who, immediately before the deletion or severance, were part of the federal public administration, (a) the terms and conditions of employment contained in a collective agreement or arbitral award that, by virtue of section 107 of the Federal Public Sector Labour Relations Act , are continued in force immediately before the date of the deletion or severance or that were last continued in force before that date, in respect of those employees shall continue or resume in force on and after that date and shall be observed by the corporation or business, as employer, the bargaining agent for those employees and those employees until the requirements of paragraphs 89(1)(a) to (d) have been met, unless the employer and the bargaining agent agree otherwise..."

"(b) the Federal Public Sector Labour Relations Act applies in all respects to the interpretation and application of any term or condition continued or resumed by paragraph (a)..."

This subsection clarifies that the Federal Public Sector Labour Relations Act governs the interpretation and application of any terms and conditions that are continued or resumed after the deletion or severance. This ensures consistency and clarity in the application of labour relations law.

#### Board Order Determining Bargaining Units and Bargaining Agents
"(c) on application by the corporation or business, as employer, or the bargaining agent for those employees, made during the period beginning on the one hundred and twentieth day and ending on the one hundred and fiftieth day after the date of the deletion or severance, the Board shall make an order determining (i) whether the employees of the corporation or business who are represented by the bargaining agent constitute one or more units appropriate for collective bargaining, and (ii) which trade union shall be the bargaining agent for the employees in each such unit..."

This subsection outlines the Board's role in determining bargaining units and bargaining agents after the deletion or severance. It states that upon application within a specific timeframe, the Board will issue an order determining whether the employees constitute one or more appropriate bargaining units and which trade union will be the bargaining agent for each unit. This ensures that bargaining is conducted within appropriate units and that a clear bargaining agent is identified.

#### Requirement for Collective Bargaining
"(d) where the Board makes the determinations under paragraph (c), the corporation or business, as employer, or the bargaining agent may, by notice, require the other to commence collective bargaining under this Act for the purpose of entering into a collective agreement..."

This subsection details the process for initiating collective bargaining after the Board's determinations. It states that either party can issue a notice requiring the other to commence collective bargaining for the purpose of entering into a collective agreement. This ensures that bargaining is promptly initiated once the bargaining units and bargaining agents have been determined.

#### Application of the Part
"(e) this Part, other than section 80, applies in respect of a notice given under paragraph (d)."

This subsection clarifies the scope of Part I of the Canada Labour Code in relation to the notice to bargain process. It states that this Part applies in respect of a notice given under paragraph (d), with the exception of section 80. This ensures that the provisions of Part I are applicable to the bargaining process initiated after the Board's determinations.

individual_results.question: Under what conditions do sections 52, 54, and 55 of the Canada Labour Code not apply to an employer and a bargaining agent who are bound by a collective agreement in the context of a technological change?
individual_results.answer:
## Conditions Where Sections 52, 54, and 55 Do Not Apply to Employers and Bargaining Agents Bound by Collective Agreements in the Context of Technological Change

### Section 51(2)
"Sections 52, 54 and 55 do not apply, in respect of a technological change, to an employer and a bargaining agent who are bound by a collective agreement where (a) the employer has given to the bargaining agent a notice in writing of the technological change that is substantially in accordance with subsection 52(2), (i) prior to the day on which the employer and the bargaining agent entered into the collective agreement, if the notice requiring the parties to commence collective bargaining for the purpose of entering into that collective agreement was given pursuant to section 48, or (ii) not later than the last day on which notice requiring the parties to commence collective bargaining for the purpose of entering into the collective agreement could have been given pursuant to subsection 49(1), if the notice was given under that subsection; (b) the collective agreement contains provisions that specify procedures by which any matters that relate to terms and conditions or security of employment likely to be affected by a technological change may be negotiated and finally settled during the term of the agreement; or (c) the collective agreement contains provisions that (i) are intended to assist employees affected by any technological change to adjust to the effects of the technological change, and (ii) specify that sections 52, 54 and 55 do not apply, during the term of the collective agreement, to the employer and the bargaining agent."

Section 51(2) outlines several conditions under which sections 52, 54, and 55 of the Canada Labour Code do not apply to employers and bargaining agents bound by a collective agreement in the context of a technological change.

One condition is that the employer has provided the bargaining agent with a notice in writing of the technological change that is substantially in accordance with subsection 52(2). This notice must be provided either before the collective agreement was entered into (if the notice requiring the parties to commence collective bargaining was given pursuant to section 48) or no later than the last day on which such notice could have been given (if the notice was given under subsection 49(1)).

Another condition is that the collective agreement contains provisions that specify procedures by which any matters that relate to terms and conditions or security of employment likely to be affected by a technological change may be negotiated and finally settled during the term of the agreement. This indicates that the existing collective agreement already addresses potential technological changes through established negotiation mechanisms.

A third condition is that the collective agreement contains provisions that are intended to assist employees affected by any technological change to adjust to the effects of the technological change, and that these provisions specifically state that sections 52, 54, and 55 do not apply during the term of the collective agreement. This demonstrates a proactive approach within the collective agreement to manage the impact of technological change without triggering the requirements of sections 52, 54, and 55.

### Section 55
"Where a bargaining agent applies to the Board for an order under subsection 54(1), the employer in respect of whom the application is made shall not effect the technological change in respect of which the application is made until (a) the Board has made an order refusing to grant leave to the bargaining agent to serve on the employer a notice to commence collective bargaining; or (b) the Board has made an order granting leave to the bargaining agent to serve on the employer a notice to commence collective bargaining and (i) an agreement has been reached as a result of collective bargaining, or (ii) the requirements of paragraphs 89(1)(a) to (d) have been met."

Section 55 specifies the conditions under which an employer is prohibited from implementing a technological change while a bargaining agent is seeking an order to commence collective bargaining.

The employer must not proceed with the technological change
"...until (a) the Board has made an order refusing to grant leave to the bargaining agent to serve on the employer a notice to commence collective bargaining; or (b) the Board has made an order granting leave to the bargaining agent to serve on the employer a notice to commence collective bargaining and (i) an agreement has been reached as a result of collective bargaining, or (ii) the requirements of paragraphs 89(1)(a) to (d) have been met." This means that the employer is temporarily barred from making the technological change if the Board denies the bargaining agent's request for an order to begin bargaining, or if the Board grants the request but no agreement is reached through collective bargaining, or if the requirements of paragraphs 89(1)(a) to (d) are not satisfied.

individual_results.question: What are the requirements for an employer bound by a collective agreement to implement a technological change that is likely to affect the terms and conditions or security of employment of a significant number of employees?
individual_results.answer:
## Requirements for Employers Implementing Technological Change Under a Collective Agreement

### Notice of Technological Change

#### Timing of Notice
"An employer who is bound by a collective agreement and who proposes to effect a technological change that is likely to affect the terms and conditions or security of employment of a significant number of the employer’s employees to whom the collective agreement applies shall give notice of the technological change to the bargaining agent bound by the collective agreement at least one hundred and twenty days prior to the date on which the technological change is to be effected." This section clearly establishes the mandatory timeframe for providing notice. The employer must inform the bargaining agent a minimum of 120 days before the technological change is implemented. This extended period is intended to allow for collective bargaining and adjustments to the existing collective agreement.

#### Contents of the Notice
"The notice referred to in subsection (1) shall be in writing and shall state (a) the nature of the technological change; (b) the date on which the employer proposes to effect the technological change; (c) the approximate number and type of employees likely to be affected by the technological change; (d) the effect that the technological change is likely to have on the terms and conditions or security of employment of the employees affected; and (e) such other information as is required by the regulations made pursuant to subsection (4)." This subsection meticulously details the information that must be included in the written notice. The notice must specify the type of technological change, the planned implementation date, the estimated number and type of affected employees, the anticipated impact on employment terms and conditions, and any additional information mandated by regulations. This comprehensive requirement ensures that the bargaining agent has a clear understanding of the proposed change and its potential consequences.

#### Additional Information Upon Request
"An employer who has given notice under subsection (1) to a bargaining agent shall, on request from the bargaining agent, provide the bargaining agent with a statement in writing setting out (a) a detailed description of the nature of the proposed technological change; (b) the names of the employees who will initially be likely to be affected by the proposed technological change; and (c) the rationale for the change." This provision mandates that the employer must provide further details to the bargaining agent upon request. This additional information, including a detailed description, initial affected employees, and the reasoning behind the change, further facilitates the bargaining process.

### Conditions Precedent to Technological Change

#### Board Order Granting Leave to Bargain
"Where a bargaining agent alleges that sections 52, 54 and 55 apply to an employer in respect of an alleged technological change and that the employer has failed to comply with section 52, the bargaining agent may, not later than thirty days after the bargaining agent became aware, or in the opinion of the Board ought to have become aware, of the failure of the employer to comply with section 52, apply to the Board for an order determining the matters so alleged." This section outlines the initial step in the process. If the bargaining agent believes that technological change triggers the requirements of sections 52, 54, and 55 and that the employer has failed to comply with section 52, the agent can apply to the Board for an order.
"On receipt of an application for an order determining the matters alleged under subsection (1) and after affording an opportunity for the parties to make representations, the Board may, by order, (a) determine that sections 52, 54 and 55 do not apply to the employer in respect of the alleged technological change; or (b) determine that sections 52, 54 and 55 apply to the employer in respect of the alleged technological change and that the employer has failed to comply with section 52 in respect of the technological change." This further clarifies the Board's potential actions. After allowing parties to present their views, the Board can either rule that the technological change does not trigger the requirements of sections 52, 54, and 55, or it can rule that they do apply and that the employer has failed to comply with section 52.

#### Board Order Directing Delay or Reinstatement
"The Board may, in any order made under paragraph (2)(b), or by order made after consultation with the parties pending the making of any order under subsection (2), (a) direct the employer not to proceed with the technological change or alleged technological change for such period, not in excess of one hundred and twenty days, as the Board considers appropriate; (b) require the reinstatement of any employee displaced by the employer as a result of the technological change; and (c) where an employee is reinstated pursuant to paragraph (b), require the employer to reimburse the employee for any loss of pay suffered by the employee as a result of their displacement." This subsection details the remedies the Board can order. The Board can direct the employer to delay the technological change for up to 120 days, order the reinstatement of any displaced employees, and require the employer to compensate reinstated employees for lost wages.

#### Board Order Granting Leave to Bargain
"An order of the Board made under paragraph (2)(b) in respect of an employer is deemed to be a notice of technological change given by the employer pursuant to section 52, and the Board shall concurrently, by order, grant leave to the bargaining agent to serve on the employer a notice to commence collective bargaining for the purpose referred to in subsection 54(1)." This provision states that a Board order delaying the technological change is considered a formal notice of the change from the employer. Simultaneously, the Board will grant the bargaining agent permission to serve a notice to commence collective bargaining.

#### Employer Prohibition on Proceeding with Change
"Where a bargaining agent applies to the Board for an order under subsection 54(1), the employer in respect of whom the application is made shall not effect the technological change in respect of which the application is made until (a) the Board has made an order refusing to grant leave to the bargaining agent to serve on the employer a notice to commence collective bargaining; or (b) the Board has made an order granting leave to the bargaining agent to serve on the employer a notice to commence collective bargaining and (i) an agreement has been reached as a result of collective bargaining, or (ii) the requirements of paragraphs 89(1)(a) to (d) have been met." This section outlines the conditions under which the employer can proceed with the technological change. The employer must wait until the Board either denies the bargaining agent leave to bargain or grants leave and either an agreement is reached or the requirements of specific paragraphs are met.

individual_results.question: What can a bargaining agent do if they allege that an employer has failed to comply with the requirements related to technological changes, and what are the potential outcomes of such an action?
individual_results.answer:
## Bargaining Agent Actions Upon Alleged Technological Change Compliance Failure

### Application for Order Determining Alleged Non-Compliance

Section 53 outlines the procedure a bargaining agent can take if they believe an employer has failed to comply with the requirements related to technological changes, specifically section 52.
"Where a bargaining agent alleges that sections 52, 54 and 55 apply to an employer in respect of an alleged technological change and that the employer has failed to comply with section 52, the bargaining agent may, not later than thirty days after the bargaining agent became aware, or in the opinion of the Board ought to have become aware, of the failure of the employer to comply with section 52, apply to the Board for an order determining the matters so alleged."

This indicates that the bargaining agent must formally apply to the Board within thirty days of becoming aware of the alleged non-compliance. The application seeks an order from the Board to determine whether sections 52, 54, and 55 actually apply to the employer in the context of the alleged technological change and whether the employer has indeed failed to comply with section 52.

### Potential Outcomes of the Application

Section 53 further details the potential outcomes of such an application.

#### Board Determination on Non-Application
"On receipt of an application for an order determining the matters alleged under subsection (1) and after affording an opportunity for the parties to make representations, the Board may, by order, (a) determine that sections 52, 54 and 55 do not apply to the employer in respect of the alleged technological change; or (b) determine that sections 52, 54 and 55 apply to the employer in respect of the alleged technological change and that the employer has failed to comply with section 52 in respect of the technological change."

The Board has two potential outcomes when considering the application. First, it can determine that sections 52, 54, and 55 do not apply to the employer in the situation described. Second, it can determine that these sections *do* apply and that the employer has failed to comply with section 52.

#### Board Directives Upon Finding Non-Compliance
"The Board may, in any order made under paragraph (2)(b), or by order made after consultation with the parties pending the making of any order under subsection (2), (a) direct the employer not to proceed with the technological change or alleged technological change for such period, not in excess of one hundred and twenty days, as the Board considers appropriate; (b) require the reinstatement of any employee displaced by the employer as a result of the technological change; and (c) where an employee is reinstated pursuant to paragraph (b), require the employer to reimburse the employee for any loss of pay suffered by the employee as a result of their displacement."

If the Board determines that the employer has failed to comply with section 52, it has several potential directives. It can order the employer to halt the technological change for a period not exceeding one hundred and twenty days. It can also require the reinstatement of any employee who was displaced as a result of the technological change. Furthermore, if an employee is reinstated, the Board can order the employer to reimburse the employee for any lost wages.

#### Board Order Deemed Notice
"An order of the Board made under paragraph (2)(b) in respect of an employer is deemed to be a notice of technological change given by the employer pursuant to section 52, and the Board shall concurrently, by order, grant leave to the bargaining agent to serve on the employer a notice to commence collective bargaining for the purpose referred to in subsection 54(1)."

Crucially, the Board's order finding non-compliance is treated as a formal notice of the technological change given by the employer. This allows the bargaining agent to immediately proceed with the process of initiating collective bargaining, as outlined in section 54. The Board will concurrently grant the bargaining agent leave to serve this notice on the employer.

individual_results.question: What recourse does a bargaining agent have when it receives notice of a technological change that may adversely affect the terms and conditions or security of employment of a significant number of employees bound by a collective agreement?
individual_results.answer:
## Recourse for a Bargaining Agent Upon Receiving Notice of Technological Change

### Application for Order to Serve Notice to Bargain

Section 54(1) outlines the recourse available to a bargaining agent upon receiving notice of a technological change. It states:
"Where a bargaining agent receives notice of a technological change pursuant to section 52, the bargaining agent may, in order to assist the employees affected by the change to adjust to the effects of the change, apply to the Board, within thirty days after the date on which it receives the notice, for an order granting leave to serve on the employer a notice to commence collective bargaining for the purpose of (a) revising the existing provisions of the collective agreement by which they are bound that relate to terms and conditions or security of employment; or (b) including new provisions in the collective agreement that relate to terms and conditions or security of employment."

This section clearly indicates that a bargaining agent, upon receiving the required notice under section 52, can petition the Board for an order to serve a notice to commence collective bargaining. The purpose of this notice is twofold: either to revise existing collective agreement provisions related to terms and conditions or security of employment, or to include new provisions addressing these matters. This provides the bargaining agent with a mechanism to proactively address the potential adverse effects of the technological change on the employees.

### Board's Discretion to Grant Leave

Section 54(2) further elaborates on the Board's authority to grant this leave. It specifies:
"Where the Board has received from a bargaining agent an application for an order under subsection (1), and it is satisfied that the technological change in respect of which the bargaining agent has received notice given pursuant to section 52 is likely, substantially and adversely, to affect the terms and conditions or security of employment of a significant number of employees to whom the collective agreement between the bargaining agent and the employer applies, the Board may, by order, grant leave to the bargaining agent to serve on the employer a notice to commence collective bargaining for the purpose referred to in subsection (1)."

This passage highlights the Board's role in assessing the potential impact of the technological change. The Board has the discretion to grant the bargaining agent leave to serve a notice to bargain if it determines that the change is "likely, substantially and adversely" to affect a "significant number of employees." This ensures that the Board intervenes when the technological change poses a serious threat to the employees' terms and conditions of employment.

### Conditions Precedent to Technological Change

Section 54(1) also touches upon conditions precedent to technological change. It states:
"Section 54 (1) Where a bargaining agent receives notice of a technological change pursuant to section 52, the bargaining agent may, in order to assist the employees affected by the change to adjust to the effects of the change, apply to the Board, within thirty days after the date on which it receives the notice, for an order granting leave to serve on the employer a notice to commence collective bargaining for the purpose of (a) revising the existing provisions of the collective agreement by which they are bound that relate to terms and conditions or security of employment; or (b) including new provisions in the collective agreement that relate to terms and conditions or security of employment."

This section implies that the bargaining agent's recourse is available *after* receiving the required notice under section 52. This notice serves as the trigger for the bargaining agent to seek an order to serve a notice to bargain.

In summary, a bargaining agent, upon receiving notice of a technological change that may adversely affect the terms and conditions or security of employment of a significant number of employees bound by a collective agreement, has recourse to apply to the Board for an order granting leave to serve a notice to commence collective bargaining. This notice serves to proactively address the potential negative impacts of the technological change by allowing the parties to negotiate revisions or additions to the existing collective agreement. The Board has the discretion to grant this leave if it determines that the technological change is likely to have a substantial and adverse effect on the employees' terms and conditions of employment.
