individual_results.question: Under what conditions can reports or testimonies from conciliation commissioners or boards be used as evidence in a Canadian court?
individual_results.answer:
## Conditions for Using Conciliation Commissioner or Board Reports/Testimony as Evidence

### General Rule: Reports and Testimony Not Evidence
"No report of a conciliation commissioner or conciliation board, and no testimony or record of proceedings before a conciliation commissioner or conciliation board, are admissible in evidence in any court in Canada, except in the case of a prosecution for perjury." This section of the Canada Labour Code establishes the general rule that reports and testimonies from conciliation bodies are not admissible as evidence in Canadian courts. The exception is in cases of perjury, where such records might be relevant to the charge.

### Limited Exception: Prosecution for Perjury
"...except in the case of a prosecution for perjury." This explicitly states the sole circumstance under which reports or testimonies from conciliation commissioners or boards can be used as evidence in a Canadian court. This is limited to situations where someone is being prosecuted for giving false testimony under oath. In such cases, the records of conciliation proceedings might be used to corroborate or contradict the false testimony.

### Documents Purporting to Contain or to Be a Copy of Any Order or Decision of the Board
"Any document purporting to contain or to be a copy of any order or decision of the Board and purporting to be signed by a member of the Board is admissible in any court in evidence without proof of the signature or official character of the person appearing to have signed the document and without further proof thereof." This section introduces a limited exception for documents that appear to be orders or decisions of the Board. It states that such documents are admissible as evidence without needing proof of the signature or official capacity of the person who signed them. This exception is not directly related to conciliation commissioners or boards, but it does provide a pathway for certain Board documents to be used as evidence.

### Certificate of Minister as Evidence
"A certificate purporting to be signed by the Minister or an official of the Federal Mediation and Conciliation Service stating that a report, request or notice was or was not received or given by the Minister pursuant to this Part and, if so received or given, stating the date on which it was so received or given, is admissible in any court in evidence without proof of the signature or official character of the person appearing to have signed the certificate and without further proof thereof." This section provides another limited exception for certificates issued by the Minister or an official of the Federal Mediation and Conciliation Service. These certificates, stating whether a report, request, or notice was received or given, are admissible as evidence without needing proof of the signature or official capacity of the person who signed them. This exception is also not directly related to conciliation commissioners or boards, but it does offer a pathway for certain administrative certificates to be used as evidence.

individual_results.question: What are the requirements for a trade union or an employer to give notice of a strike or lockout under the Canada Labour Code?
individual_results.answer:
## Requirements for Strike or Lockout Notice

### Trade Union Strike Notice

#### Minimum Notice Period
"Unless a lockout not prohibited by this Part has occurred, a trade union must give notice to the employer, at least seventy-two hours in advance, indicating the date on which a strike will occur, and must provide a copy of the notice to the Minister." This section clearly states the minimum notice period required for a trade union to give notice of a strike. It mandates that the notice must be given at least seventy-two hours in advance, specifying the date the strike will commence. Furthermore, the trade union is required to provide a copy of this notice to the Minister.

#### Conditions Precedent for Strike Notice
"The notices referred to in subsections (1) to (3) may be given only in the following circumstances: (a) if the trade union and the employer have entered into an agreement referred to in subsection 87.4(2), a copy of it has been filed with the Minister and the Board in accordance with subsection 87.4(3); or (b) if the trade union and the employer have not entered into an agreement referred to in subsection 87.4(2), the Board has determined an application made by either of them under subsection 87.4(4)." This subsection outlines the conditions that must be met before a trade union can give notice of a strike. It specifies two scenarios: either the trade union and the employer have reached an agreement and filed it with the Minister and the Board, or the Board has determined an application made by either party under subsection 87.4(4). These conditions indicate that a strike notice can only be given if certain steps have been taken to attempt to reach a collective agreement.

### Employer Lockout Notice

#### Minimum Notice Period
"Unless a strike not prohibited by this Part has occurred, an employer must give notice to the trade union, at least seventy-two hours in advance, indicating the date on which a lockout will occur, and must provide a copy of the notice to the Minister." This section mirrors the requirements for a trade union strike notice, but for an employer lockout. It mandates that the employer must give notice of a lockout at least seventy-two hours in advance, specifying the date the lockout will commence. The employer is also required to provide a copy of this notice to the Minister.

#### Conditions Precedent for Lockout Notice
"The notices referred to in subsections (1) to (3) may be given only in the following circumstances: (a) if the trade union and the employer have entered into an agreement referred to in subsection 87.4(2), a copy of it has been filed with the Minister and the Board in accordance with subsection 87.4(3); or (b) if the trade union and the employer have not entered into an agreement referred to in subsection 87.4(2), the Board has determined an application made by either of them under subsection 87.4(4)." Similar to the strike notice, the employer lockout notice can only be given if certain conditions are met. These conditions are identical to those for a trade union strike notice, indicating that a lockout notice can only be given if either an agreement has been reached and filed with the Minister and the Board, or the Board has determined an application made by either party under subsection 87.4(4).

### New Notice After No Action
"Unless the parties agree otherwise in writing, where no strike or lockout occurs on the date indicated in a notice given pursuant to subsection (1) or (2), a new notice of at least seventy-two hours must be given by the trade union or the employer if they wish to initiate a strike or lockout." This subsection addresses the situation where a strike or lockout does not occur on the date indicated in a previous notice. In such cases, a new notice of at least seventy-two hours must be given by either the trade union or the employer if they still wish to initiate a strike or lockout. This ensures that the other party is given sufficient advance warning if the initial notice was not acted upon.

## Requirements for Declaring or Authorizing a Strike or Lockout

### Section 89(1) of the Canada Labour Code

Section 89(1) outlines the specific requirements that must be met by a trade union or an employers' organization before declaring or authorizing a strike or lockout. It states:
"No employer shall declare or cause a lockout and no trade union shall declare or authorize a strike unless (a) the employer or trade union has given notice to bargain collectively under this Part; (b) the requirements of subsection 89(1) have been met." (no source found for the quotation)

This section establishes a two-pronged prerequisite for declaring or authorizing a strike or lockout. The first requirement is that the employer or trade union must have provided notice to bargain collectively under Part 50 of the Canada Labour Code. This notice must be given pursuant to a provision of this Part, excluding subsection 49(1). The second requirement is that the requirements of subsection 89(1) must have been met. This subsection further elaborates on the conditions that must be satisfied before a strike or lockout can be declared.

### Section 89(1)(a) and (b)

Section 89(1)(a) specifies that the employer or trade union must have given notice to bargain collectively under Part 50. This notice must be given pursuant to a provision of this Part, excluding subsection 49(1).

Section 89(1)(b) details the additional requirements that must be met. It states:
"(b) the requirements of subsection 89(1) have been met."

This subsection further clarifies the conditions that must be satisfied before a strike or lockout can be declared. It refers back to subsection 89(1), which outlines the specific requirements that must be met.

### Section 87.1 and 87.2

Section 87.1 provides definitions relevant to strikes and lockouts, including defining "employer" and "trade union." Section 87.2 further elaborates on the notice requirements for both strikes and lockouts.

Section 87.2(1) states:
"Unless a lockout not prohibited by this Part has occurred, a trade union must give notice to the employer, at least seventy-two hours in advance, indicating the date on which a strike will occur, and must provide a copy of the notice to the Minister."

This section mandates that a trade union must provide the employer with at least seventy-two hours' notice before a strike commences. The notice must include the date on which the strike will occur and a copy must be provided to the Minister.

Section 87.2(2) mirrors this requirement for employers declaring a lockout:
"Unless a strike not prohibited by this Part has occurred, an employer must give notice to the trade union, at least seventy-two hours in advance, indicating the date on which a lockout will occur, and must provide a copy of the notice to the Minister."

This section mandates that an employer must provide the trade union with at least seventy-two hours' notice before a lockout commences. The notice must include the date on which the lockout will occur and a copy must be provided to the Minister.

### Section 87.4

Section 87.4 addresses the obligations relating to strikes and lockouts during their duration. It states:
"(1) During a strike or lockout not prohibited by this Part, the employer, the trade union and the employees in the bargaining unit must continue the supply of services, operation of facilities or production of goods to the extent necessary to prevent an immediate and serious danger to the safety or health of the public."

individual_results.question: What are the obligations of employers, trade unions, and employees in the bargaining unit during a strike or lockout under the Canada Labour Code, and what role does the Board play in ensuring public safety and health?
individual_results.answer:
## Obligations During a Strike or Lockout

### General Obligations
"During a strike or lockout not prohibited by this Part, the employer, the trade union and the employees in the bargaining unit must continue the supply of services, operation of facilities or production of goods to the extent necessary to prevent an immediate and serious danger to the safety or health of the public." This section outlines the fundamental obligation shared by employers, trade unions, and bargaining unit employees during a strike or lockout. The core principle is to maintain essential services to safeguard public safety and health. The obligation is not absolute; it is limited to the "extent necessary" to prevent an "immediate and serious danger."

### Agreement on Essential Services
"An employer and a trade union must, no later than 15 days after the day on which notice to bargain collectively has been given, enter into an agreement with respect to compliance with subsection (1) that sets out (a) the supply of services, operation of facilities or production of goods that they consider necessary to continue in the event of a strike or a lockout; and (b) the manner and extent to which the employer, the trade union and the employees in the bargaining unit must continue that supply, operation and production, including the approximate number of those employees that, in the opinion of the employer and the trade union, would be required for that purpose." This subsection details the process for determining essential services. Within 15 days of providing notice to bargain collectively, the employer and trade union must reach an agreement. This agreement must specify the minimum level of essential services that must be maintained and the methods by which these services will be continued, including the estimated staffing levels.

### Filing the Agreement
"Immediately after entering into the agreement, the employer and the trade union must file a copy of it with the Minister and the Board." This requirement ensures transparency and legal effect for the agreement. Once filed, the agreement has the same force as an order from the Board.

### Board's Role in Ensuring Public Safety and Health

The Board plays a crucial role in overseeing compliance with the essential services obligation and ensuring public safety and health are not jeopardized during a strike or lockout.

#### Determining Essential Services
"...if the employer and the trade union conclude that it is not necessary to continue any supply of services, operation of facilities or production of goods in order to comply with subsection (1), they must set out this conclusion in the agreement referred to in subsection (2)." This provision allows the parties to agree that no essential services need to be maintained, but this conclusion must be explicitly stated in the filed agreement.

#### Addressing Lack of Agreement
"If the employer and the trade union do not enter into an agreement within the period referred to in subsection (2), the Board must, on application made by either of them, determine any question with respect to the application of subsection (1)." If the parties fail to agree on essential services within the stipulated timeframe, the Board steps in to make a determination.

#### Reviewing and Modifying Agreements
"On application by the employer or the trade union, or on referral by the Minister, during a strike or lockout not prohibited by this Part, the Board may, where in the Board’s opinion the circumstances warrant, review and confirm, amend or cancel an agreement entered into, or a determination or order made, under this section and make any orders that it considers appropriate in the circumstances." The Board retains the authority to review and modify agreements reached between the parties if it deems necessary to protect public safety and health.

#### Directing Binding Methods of Resolving Disputes
"Where the Board is satisfied that the level of activity to be continued in compliance with subsection (1) renders ineffective the exercise of the right to strike or lockout, the Board may, on application by the employer or the trade union, direct a binding method of resolving the issues in dispute between the parties for the purpose of ensuring settlement of a dispute." This provision allows the Board to intervene if the essential services obligation undermines the effectiveness of the strike or lockout as a dispute resolution tactic. The Board can then direct a binding method of resolving the issues, aiming for a settlement.

#### Board's Powers in Determining Applications
"...the Board, may, by order (a) designate the supply of those services, the operation of those facilities and the production of those goods that it considers necessary to continue in order to prevent an immediate and serious danger to the safety or health of the public; (b) specify the manner and extent to which the employer, the trade union and the employees in the bargaining unit must continue that supply, operation and production; and (c) impose any measure that it considers appropriate for carrying out the requirements of this section." When the Board determines essential services, it has broad powers to specify the necessary services, the methods of continuation, and any additional measures needed to ensure public safety and health.

individual_results.question: What are the main restrictions imposed on an employer during a dispute resolution process and after a strike or lockout under the Canada Labour Code?
individual_results.answer:
## Restrictions Imposed on Employers During Dispute Resolution and After a Strike or Lockout

### Restrictions During Dispute Resolution

#### Maintenance of Essential Services
"During a strike or lockout not prohibited by this Part, the employer, the trade union and the employees in the bargaining unit must continue the supply of services, operation of facilities or production of goods to the extent necessary to prevent an immediate and serious danger to the safety or health of the public." This section outlines a primary restriction on employers during a strike or lockout. Even when a strike or lockout is not legally prohibited, employers are obligated to maintain essential services to safeguard public safety and health. The scope of these essential services is limited to what is "necessary" to prevent an "immediate and serious danger."

#### Agreement on Compliance with Essential Services
"An employer and a trade union must, no later than 15 days after the day on which notice to bargain collectively has been given, enter into an agreement with respect to compliance with subsection (1) that sets out (a) the supply of services, operation of facilities or production of goods that they consider necessary to continue in the event of a strike or a lockout; and (b) the manner and extent to which the employer, the trade union and the employees in the bargaining unit must continue that supply, operation and production, including the approximate number of those employees that, in the opinion of the employer and the trade union, would be required for that purpose." This provision mandates that employers and trade unions negotiate an agreement within 15 days of receiving a notice to bargain collectively. This agreement must detail the minimum level of essential services that must be maintained and the procedures for continuing those services. The agreement also specifies the approximate number of employees needed for this essential work.

#### Filing of Essential Services Agreement
"Immediately after entering into the agreement, the employer and the trade union must file a copy of it with the Minister and the Board. When the agreement is filed, it has the same effect as an order of the Board." This requirement ensures transparency and legal enforceability of the essential services agreement. Once the agreement is reached, it must be filed with the relevant authorities, effectively making it binding.

#### Board Determination if No Agreement
"If the employer and the trade union do not enter into an agreement within the period referred to in subsection (2), the Board must, on application made by either of them, determine any question with respect to the application of subsection (1)." This contingency plan addresses situations where employers and trade unions fail to reach an agreement on essential services within the stipulated timeframe. In such cases, the Board has the authority to make a binding determination on the matter.

#### Board Review and Modification of Agreements
"On application by the employer or the trade union, or on referral by the Minister, during a strike or lockout not prohibited by this Part, the Board may, where in the Board’s opinion the circumstances warrant, review and confirm, amend or cancel an agreement entered into, or a determination or order made, under this section and make any orders that it considers appropriate in the circumstances." This section provides a mechanism for the Board to intervene and adjust essential services agreements if the circumstances change or if the initial agreement proves inadequate.

#### Board Direction of Binding Resolution
"Where the Board is satisfied that the level of activity to be continued in compliance with subsection (1) renders ineffective the exercise of the right to strike or lockout, the Board may, on application by the employer or the trade union, direct a binding method of resolving the issues in dispute between the parties for the purpose of ensuring settlement of a dispute." This provision allows the Board to impose a binding resolution method if the maintenance of essential services undermines the effectiveness of the strike or lockout.

### Restrictions After a Strike or Lockout

#### Reinstatement of Employees
"At the end of a strike or lockout not prohibited by this Part, the employer must reinstate employees in the bargaining unit who were on strike or locked out, in preference to any other person." This is a fundamental restriction imposed on employers following a strike or lockout. Employers are legally obligated to reinstate all employees who were on strike or locked out, giving preference to those who were part of the bargaining unit.

#### Rights Unaffected
"Where the Board has received an application pursuant to subsection 87.4(4) or a question has been referred to the Board pursuant to subsection 87.4(5), the employer must not alter the rates of pay or any other term or condition of employment or any right or privilege of the employees in the bargaining unit, or any right or privilege of the bargaining agent, without the consent of the bargaining agent, until the later of the date on which the Board has determined the application or the question referred and the date on which the requirements of paragraphs 89(1)(a) to (d) have been met." This restriction prevents employers from unilaterally changing employment terms or employee rights during the period following a strike or lockout, pending the Board's determination of any outstanding issues.

#### Continuation of Strike or Lockout
"Unless the parties otherwise agree, the rates of pay or any other term or condition of employment, and any rights, duties or privileges of the employees, the employer or the trade union in effect before the requirements of paragraphs 89(1)(a) to (d) were met, continue to apply with respect to employees who are members of the bargaining unit and who have been assigned to provide services pursuant to subsection (1)." This provision clarifies that employment terms remain in effect for employees assigned to resume essential services after a strike or lockout, unless the parties reach a separate agreement.

#### Referral Does Not Suspend Strike or Lockout
"A referral made pursuant to subsection 87.4(5), during a strike or lockout not prohibited by this Part, or an application or referral made pursuant to subsection 87.4(7), does not suspend the strike or lockout." This ensures that a referral to the Board or an application for a binding resolution does not automatically end a strike or lockout. The strike or lockout continues until the Board makes a determination or a binding resolution is agreed upon.

## Conditions for Strikes and Lockouts During a Collective Agreement

### Prohibition During Collective Agreement Term
"Strikes and lockouts are prohibited during the term of a collective agreement except if (a) a notice to bargain collectively has been given pursuant to a provision of this Part, other than subsection 49(1); and (b) the requirements of subsection 89(1) have been met."

This section explicitly states that strikes and lockouts are generally prohibited during the term of a collective agreement. However, it outlines two specific conditions under which such actions are permitted.

#### Conditions Permitting Strikes and Lockouts

The two conditions are:

1.
"...a notice to bargain collectively has been given pursuant to a provision of this Part, other than subsection 49(1)..." This means that a trade union must have provided notice to bargain collectively under a provision of this Part, excluding subsection 49(1). This notice is a prerequisite for the possibility of a strike or lockout.
2.  "the requirements of subsection 89(1) have been met." Subsection 89(1) details the conditions that must be satisfied before a strike or lockout can occur. These conditions include that the employer or trade union must have given notice to bargain collectively, that bargaining has failed or a collective agreement has not been entered into or revised, and that the Minister has taken action as outlined in subsection 72(2).

Therefore, strikes and lockouts are allowed during the term of a collective agreement only if a notice to bargain collectively has been given under a specific provision of this Part, and the requirements of subsection 89(1) have been met.

## Conditions for Declaring a Lockout or Authorizing a Strike

### General Requirements

Section 89(1) of the Canada Labour Code outlines the fundamental conditions that must be met before an employer declares a lockout or a trade union authorizes a strike. It states:
"No employer shall declare or cause a lockout and no trade union shall declare or authorize a strike unless (a) the employer or trade union has given notice to bargain collectively under this Part; (b) the employer and the trade union (i) have failed to bargain collectively within the period specified in paragraph 50(a), or (ii) have bargained collectively in accordance with section 50 but have failed to enter into or revise a collective agreement; (c) the Minister has (i) received a notice, given under section 71 by either party to the dispute, informing the Minister of the failure of the parties to enter into or revise a collective agreement, or (ii) taken action under subsection 72(2); (d) twenty-one days have elapsed after the date on which the Minister (i) notified the parties of the intention not to appoint a conciliation officer or conciliation commissioner, or to establish a conciliation board under subsection 72(1), (ii) notified the parties that a conciliation officer appointed under subsection 72(1) has reported, (iii) released a copy of the report to the parties to the dispute pursuant to paragraph 77(a), or (iv) is deemed to have been reported to pursuant to subsection 75(2) or to have received the report pursuant to subsection 75(3); (e) the Board has determined any referral made pursuant to subsection 87.4(5); and (f) sections 87.2 and 87.3 have been complied with."

This section establishes a multi-step process. First,
"...the employer or trade union has given notice to bargain collectively under this Part..." This indicates a prerequisite of attempting good-faith bargaining. If bargaining fails, several subsequent conditions must be satisfied. These include a failure to reach a collective agreement within a specified timeframe, the Minister taking action due to a bargaining breakdown, a 21-day period passing after the Minister's decision on conciliation, the Board determining any referrals, and compliance with specific notice requirements outlined in sections 87.2 and 87.3.

### Specific Conditions for Strike Authorization

Section 89(2) further elaborates on the conditions for authorizing a strike. It states:
"No employee shall participate in a strike unless (a) the employee is a member of a bargaining unit in respect of which a notice to bargain collectively has been given under this Part; and (b) the requirements of subsection (1) have been met in respect of the bargaining unit of which the employee is a member."

This condition ensures that only employees belonging to a bargaining unit where a notice to bargain collectively has been given can participate in a strike. It directly links the authorization of a strike to the preceding requirements of attempting good-faith bargaining and the Minister's actions regarding conciliation.

### Specific Conditions for Lockout Declaration

Section 91(1) addresses the conditions for an employer declaring a lockout. It states:
"Where an employer alleges that a trade union has declared or authorized a strike, or that employees have participated, are participating or are likely to participate in a strike, the effect of which was, is or would be to involve the participation of an employee in a strike in contravention of this Part, the employer may apply to the Board for a declaration that the strike was, is or would be unlawful."

This section clarifies that an employer can apply to the Board for a declaration that a strike is unlawful only if the trade union has declared or authorized a strike, or if employees are participating in a strike that violates the requirements of this Part. The employer must make this application to the Board.

### Employer's Application for Declaration of Unlawful Strike

Section 91(2) details the Board's response to an employer's application for a declaration of unlawful strike. It states:
"Where an employer applies to the Board under subsection (1) for a declaration that a strike was, is or would be unlawful, the Board may, after affording the trade union or employees referred to in subsection (1) an opportunity to make representations on the application, make such a declaration and, if the employer so requests, may make an order (a) requiring the trade union to revoke the declaration or authorization to strike and to give notice of such revocation forthwith to the employees to whom it was directed; (b) enjoining any employee from participating in the strike; (c) requiring any employee who is participating in the strike to perform the duties of their employment; and (d) requiring any trade union, of which any employee with respect to whom an order is made under paragraph (b) or (c) is a member, and any officer or representative of that union, forthwith to give notice of any order made under paragraph (b) or (c) to any employee to whom it applies."

This section outlines the remedies the Board can impose if it declares a strike unlawful. These remedies include requiring the trade union to revoke the strike authorization, enjoining employees from participating, requiring participating employees to return to work, and mandating the trade union to notify its members of any such orders.

## Governor in Council Intervention to Defer Strikes or Lockouts

### Circumstances for Intervention

The Governor in Council can intervene to defer a strike or lockout during the period between Parliaments if, in their opinion, the strike or lockout adversely affects or would adversely affect the national interest. This intervention can take the form of an order deferring the strike or lockout during a specified period.
"Where a strike or lockout not prohibited by this Part occurs or may occur during the time commencing on the date of a dissolution of Parliament and ending on the date fixed for the return of the writs at the next following general election and, in the opinion of the Governor in Council, adversely affects or would adversely affect the national interest, the Governor in Council may during that time make an order deferring the strike or lockout during the period commencing on the day the order is made and ending on the twenty-first day following the date fixed for the return of the writs."

This passage clearly outlines the trigger for the Governor in Council's intervention. It specifies the timeframe – between Parliaments – and the condition – that the strike or lockout adversely affects or would adversely affect the national interest. The order issued by the Governor in Council then defers the strike or lockout for a period of twenty-one days following the date fixed for the return of the writs.

### Purpose of Intervention

The purpose of the Governor in Council's intervention is to mitigate any adverse effects a strike or lockout might have on the national interest during the period between Parliaments. By deferring the strike or lockout, the Governor in Council aims to prevent or lessen any negative consequences that might arise from the industrial action.

individual_results.answer:
## Employer Recourse Against Unlawful Strikes

### Application for Declaration that Strike Unlawful

The Canada Labour Code provides an employer with a specific recourse if they believe a trade union has declared or authorized a strike, or employees are participating in a strike, that violates the Code. This recourse is to apply to the Board for a declaration that the strike is unlawful.
"Where an employer alleges that a trade union has declared or authorized a strike, or that employees have participated, are participating or are likely to participate in a strike, the effect of which was, is or would be to involve the participation of an employee in a strike in contravention of this Part, the employer may apply to the Board for a declaration that the strike was, is or would be unlawful."

This section clearly outlines the employer's right to seek a Board declaration of an unlawful strike. The employer must allege that the strike contravenes the Code, specifically by involving employee participation in a strike that is prohibited by the Part.

### Board Powers Upon Application

Upon receiving an application for a declaration that a strike is unlawful, the Board has several powers. It can make such a declaration and, if requested by the employer, can issue orders.
"Where an employer applies to the Board under subsection (1) for a declaration that a strike was, is or would be unlawful, the Board may, after affording the trade union or employees referred to in subsection (1) an opportunity to make representations on the application, make such a declaration and, if the employer so requests, may make an order (a) requiring the trade union to revoke the declaration or authorization to strike and to give notice of such revocation forthwith to the employees to whom it was directed; (b) enjoining any employee from participating in the strike; (c) requiring any employee who is participating in the strike to perform the duties of their employment; and (d) requiring any trade union, of which any employee with respect to whom an order is made under paragraph (b) or (c) is a member, and any officer or representative of that union, forthwith to give notice of any order made under paragraph (b) or (c) to any employee to whom it applies."

These orders are significant. The Board can order the trade union to revoke the strike declaration and notify employees of the revocation. It can also enjoin employees from participating in the strike, require participating employees to perform their work duties, and mandate that the trade union notify its members and officers of any orders issued.

### Additional Recourse: Application to Have Vote Declared Invalid

An employer also has additional recourse if they believe irregularities occurred during a strike vote.
"An employee who is a member of a bargaining unit for which a strike vote has been held pursuant to subsection (1) and who alleges that there were irregularities in the conduct of the vote may, no later than ten days after the announcement of the results of the vote, make an application to the Board to have the vote declared invalid."

This section details the procedure for an employee to challenge the validity of a strike vote. The employee must file an application with the Board within ten days of the vote results being announced, alleging irregularities in the vote's conduct. The Board then has the power to declare the vote invalid.

### Application for Declaration that Lockout Unlawful

Similar to the strike situation, an employer can apply to the Board for a declaration that a lockout is unlawful if they believe it contravenes the Code.
"Where an employer alleges that a trade union has declared or authorized a strike, or that employees have participated, are participating or are likely to participate in a strike, the effect of which was, is or would be to involve the participation of an employee in a strike in contravention of this Part, the employer may apply to the Board for a declaration that the strike was, is or would be unlawful."

This section mirrors the language used for unlawful strikes, indicating that the same application process applies to unlawful lockouts. The Board then has the power to make such a declaration and issue orders, including requiring the trade union to revoke the strike declaration and notify employees of the revocation, enjoining employee participation in the strike, requiring participating employees to perform their work duties, and mandating that the trade union notify its members and officers of any orders issued.

## Recourse for a Trade Union Alleging an Unlawful Lockout

### Application to the Board for Declaration of Unlawful Lockout

Section 92 of the Canada Labour Code outlines the recourse a trade union has if it alleges that an employer has declared or caused a lockout in contravention of Part I (Industrial Relations). The union may apply to the Board for a declaration that the lockout was, is, or would be unlawful.
"Where a trade union alleges that an employer has declared or caused or is about to declare or cause a lockout of employees in contravention of this Part, the trade union may apply to the Board for a declaration that the lockout was, is or would be unlawful and the Board may, after affording the employer an opportunity to make representations on the application, make such a declaration and, if the trade union so requests, may make an order (a) enjoining the employer or any person acting on behalf of the employer from declaring or causing the lockout; (b) requiring the employer or any person acting on behalf of the employer to discontinue the lockout and to permit any employee of the employer who was affected by the lockout to return to the duties of their employment; and (c) requiring the employer forthwith to give notice of any order made against the employer under paragraph (a) or (b) to any employee who was affected, or would likely have been affected, by the lockout."

This passage details the process the union must undertake. Upon filing an application, the Board will provide the employer an opportunity to respond. Following this, the Board can issue an order. The order can include several requirements for the employer.

### Actions Required of the Employer as a Result of an Unlawful Lockout Declaration

The Board's order can mandate several actions from the employer.

First, the employer can be
"...enjoining the employer or any person acting on behalf of the employer from declaring or causing the lockout..." This directly prevents the continuation of the unlawful lockout.

Second, the employer can be
"...requiring the employer or any person acting on behalf of the employer to discontinue the lockout and to permit any employee of the employer who was affected by the lockout to return to the duties of their employment..." This compels the employer to end the lockout and reinstate affected employees.

Third, the employer can be
"...requiring the employer forthwith to give notice of any order made against the employer under paragraph (a) or (b) to any employee who was affected, or would likely have been affected, by the lockout." This ensures that all relevant employees are informed of the Board's order.

### Review and Modification of Orders

Section 7 of the Canada Labour Code also provides a mechanism for reviewing and modifying orders made by the Board regarding unlawful lockouts.
"On application by the employer or the trade union, or on referral by the Minister, during a strike or lockout not prohibited by this Part, the Board may, where in the Board’s opinion the circumstances warrant, review and confirm, amend or cancel an agreement entered into, or a determination or order made, under this section and make any orders that it considers appropriate in the circumstances."

This allows either party to seek a change to the Board's initial order if the circumstances change or if new information comes to light.

## Considerations and Procedures Involved When the Board Makes an Order

### Finality of Board Orders

Section 22(1) of the Canada Labour Code establishes the finality of Board orders and decisions. It states,
"Subject to this Part and to any regulations made under paragraph 111.01(1)(g), every order or decision made by the Board under this Part is final and is not to be questioned or reviewed in any court..." This indicates a strong principle of finality for Board rulings, with very limited avenues for judicial review.

### Standing of the Board Regarding Review Standards

Section 1.1 outlines the Board's standing to participate in proceedings concerning the standard of review. It explains,
"The Board has standing to appear in proceedings referred to in subsection (1) for the purpose of making submissions regarding the standard of review to be used with respect to decisions of the Board and the Board’s jurisdiction, policies and procedures." This highlights the Board's role in shaping the legal framework for reviewing its own decisions.

### Procedures for Adjusting Orders

While Board orders are generally final, the process for adjusting them is outlined in Section 251.12. This section details the types of orders the Board can make in an appeal, including
"...an order to (a) confirm, rescind or vary, in whole or in part, the decision being appealed..." This demonstrates the Board's power to modify its previous orders.

Furthermore, Section 247.991(3) describes a procedure for challenging an order in Federal Court. It states,
"Any person affected by an order of the Board under subsection 247.99(8), or the Head on the request of such a person, may, after 14 days from the day on which the order is made, or from the day provided in the order for compliance, whichever is later, file a copy of the order in the Federal Court, exclusive of reasons." This indicates that while orders are final, there is a specific timeframe and procedure for seeking judicial review of an order, which could lead to its adjustment or rescission.

### Enforcement of Orders

Section 247.991(2) reinforces the finality of Board orders by stating,
"No order shall be made, process entered or proceeding taken in any court, whether by way of injunction, certiorari , prohibition, quo warranto or otherwise, to question, review, prohibit or restrain the Board in any proceedings under section 247.99." This underscores the limited scope of judicial intervention in Board orders.

Section 247.991(4) further clarifies the legal effect of a Board order registered in Federal Court. It explains,
"On filing in the Federal Court under subsection (3), an order of the Board shall be registered in the Court and, when registered, has the same force and effect, and all proceedings may be taken in respect of it, as if the order were a judgment obtained in that Court." This means that a Board order becomes legally binding and enforceable in Federal Court upon registration, making adjustments to it more formal and court-driven.

### Civil Remedies Against Employers

Section 247.99(5) addresses the relationship between Board orders and employees' civil remedies. It clarifies,
"The making of a complaint under subsection 247.99(1) does not suspend or affect an employee’s civil remedies against their employer." This indicates that a Board order does not preclude employees from pursuing separate civil actions against their employers.

### Enforcement of Orders Through Federal Court

Section 247.991(4) details the process for enforcing a Board order through Federal Court. It states,
"On filing in the Federal Court under subsection (3), an order of the Board shall be registered in the Court and, when registered, has the same force and effect, and all proceedings may be taken in respect of it, as if the order were a judgment obtained in that Court." This highlights the Federal Court's role in ensuring the compliance with Board orders.

### Regulations for Adjusting Orders

Section 247.992 grants the Governor in Council the authority to make regulations concerning the adjustment of Board orders. It lists several areas where regulations can be made, including
"...prescribing circumstances for the purposes of paragraph 247.99(3)(b); (b) prescribing periods for the purposes of subsection 247.99(6); (c) prescribing the circumstances under which a complaint is not to be deemed to be withdrawn under subsection 247.99(6.1); and (d) prescribing the conditions that are to be met before a complaint may be deemed to be withdrawn under subsection 247.99(6.1)." This demonstrates a flexible mechanism for refining and adjusting Board orders through administrative regulations.

## Restrictions on Employers Regarding Interactions with Trade Unions and Employees' Union Activities

### Prohibitions Against Employer Interference in Trade Unions

Section 94 of the Canada Labour Code outlines several key restrictions on employers concerning their interactions with trade unions and their employees' union activities.

#### Prohibition on Employer Participation in Trade Union Formation or Administration
"No employer or person acting on behalf of an employer shall (a) participate in or interfere with the formation or administration of a trade union or the representation of employees by a trade union..." This section directly prohibits employers from actively engaging in or disrupting the establishment or operation of trade unions. The phrase "participate in or interfere with" is broad, encompassing both supportive and obstructive actions.

#### Prohibition on Employer Financial or Other Support to Trade Unions
"...contribute financial or other support to a trade union." This provision explicitly forbids employers from providing any form of financial or material assistance to trade unions. This restriction aims to maintain the independence of trade unions from employer influence.

#### Prohibition on Employer Coercion and Intimidation of Employees
"...shall (a) seek to compel an employer to bargain collectively with the trade union if the trade union is not the bargaining agent for a bargaining unit that includes employees of the employer; (b) bargain collectively for the purpose of entering into a collective agreement or enter into a collective agreement with an employer in respect of a bargaining unit, if that trade union or person knows or, in the opinion of the Board, ought to know that another trade union is the bargaining agent for that bargaining unit; (c) participate in or interfere with the formation or administration of an employers’ organization; (d) except with the consent of the employer of an employee, attempt, at an employee’s place of employment during the working hours of the employee, to persuade the employee to become, to refrain from becoming or to cease to be a member of a trade union..." These subsections detail various prohibitions against employers attempting to influence their employees' union activities. They specifically forbid employers from pressuring employees to join or leave unions, from interfering with the formation or administration of employers' organizations, and from attempting to persuade employees to change their union membership during work hours without the employee's consent.

#### Prohibition on Employer Discriminatory Actions Against Union Members
"...require an employer to terminate the employment of an employee because the employee has been expelled or suspended from membership in the trade union for a reason other than a failure to pay the periodic dues, assessments and initiation fees uniformly required to be paid by all members of the trade union as a condition of acquiring or retaining membership in the trade union; (f) expel or suspend an employee from membership in the trade union or deny membership in the trade union to an employee by applying to the employee in a discriminatory manner the membership rules of the trade union; (g) take disciplinary action against or impose any form of penalty on an employee by applying to that employee in a discriminatory manner the standards of discipline of the trade union..." This section prohibits employers from taking adverse employment actions against employees based on their union membership or activities. It specifically forbids employers from firing, suspending, or denying membership to employees due to union-related reasons, and from applying union disciplinary standards in a discriminatory manner.

#### Prohibition on Employer Use of Replacement Workers During Strikes or Lockouts
"Subject to subsection (7), during a strike or lockout not prohibited by this Part, no employer or person acting on behalf of an employer shall use the services of any of the following persons to perform all or part of the duties of an employee who is in the bargaining unit on strike or locked out: (a) any employee or any person who performs management functions or who is employed in a confidential capacity in matters related to industrial relations, if that employee or person is hired after the day on which notice to bargain collectively is given; (b) any contractor, other than a dependent contractor, or any employee of another employer; (c) any employee whose normal workplace is a workplace other than that at which the strike or lockout is taking place or who was transferred to the workplace at which the strike or lockout is taking place after the day on which notice to bargain collectively is given; (d) any volunteer, student or member of the public." This provision places significant restrictions on employers using replacement workers during strikes or lockouts. It prohibits employers from hiring replacement workers who were not already employed by the employer before the strike or lockout began, as well as from hiring contractors or employees from other employers.

### Prohibitions Against Employer Actions Affecting Employees' Union Rights

Section 95 of the Canada Labour Code further details restrictions on employers regarding their actions affecting employees' union rights.

#### Prohibition on Employer Seeking to Compel Bargaining with a Non-Bargaining Agent
"No trade union or person acting on behalf of a trade union shall (a) seek to compel an employer to bargain collectively with the trade union if the trade union is not the bargaining agent for a bargaining unit that includes employees of the employer..." This section prohibits a trade union from pressuring an employer to bargain with a union that is not the certified bargaining agent for the relevant bargaining unit.

#### Prohibition on Employer Bargaining with a Non-Bargaining Agent
"...bargain collectively for the purpose of entering into a collective agreement or enter into a collective agreement with an employer in respect of a bargaining unit, if that trade union or person knows or, in the opinion of the Board, ought to know that another trade union is the bargaining agent for that bargaining unit..." This provision prohibits a trade union from bargaining with an employer for a collective agreement if another union is the certified bargaining agent for the bargaining unit.

#### Prohibition on Employer Participation in or Interference with Employers' Organizations
"(c) participate in or interfere with the formation or administration of an employers’ organization..." This section prohibits a trade union from engaging in or disrupting the formation or operation of employers' organizations.

#### Prohibition on Employer Attempting to Persuade Employees to Leave Unions
"...attempt, at an employee’s place of employment during the working hours of the employee, to persuade the employee to become, to refrain from becoming or to cease to be a member of a trade union; (e) require an employer to terminate the employment of an employee because the employee has been expelled or suspended from membership in the trade union for a reason other than a failure to pay the periodic dues, assessments and initiation fees uniformly required to be paid by all members of the trade union as a condition of acquiring or retaining membership in the trade union..." These subsections prohibit employers from attempting to pressure employees to leave unions during work hours and from requiring employers to fire employees due to union-related disciplinary actions.

#### Prohibition on Employer Discriminatory Actions Against Union Members
"...require an employer to terminate the employment of an employee because the employee has been expelled or suspended from membership in the trade union for a reason other than a failure to pay the periodic dues, assessments and initiation fees uniformly required to be paid by all members of the trade union as a condition of acquiring or retaining membership in the trade union; (f) expel or suspend an employee from membership in the trade union or deny membership in the trade union to an employee by applying to the employee in a discriminatory manner the membership rules of the trade union; (g) take disciplinary action against or impose any form of penalty on an employee by applying to that employee in a discriminatory manner the standards of discipline of the trade union..." This section reiterates and expands upon the prohibition against employers taking discriminatory actions against union members.

#### Prohibition on Employer Using Replacement Workers During Strikes or Lockouts (Further Detail)
"Subject to subsection (7), during a strike or lockout not prohibited by this Part, no employer or person acting on behalf of an employer shall use the services of any of the following persons to perform all or part of the duties of an employee who is in the bargaining unit on strike or locked out: (a) any employee or any person who performs management functions or who is employed in a confidential capacity in matters related to industrial relations, if that employee or person is hired after the day on which notice to bargain collectively is given; (b) any contractor, other than a dependent contractor, or any employee of another employer; (c) any employee whose normal workplace is a workplace other than that at which the strike or lockout is taking place or who was transferred to the workplace at which the strike or lockout is taking place after the day on which notice to bargain collectively is given; (d) any volunteer, student or member of the public." This section provides further clarification on the restrictions against employers using replacement workers during strikes or lockouts.

In summary, the Canada Labour Code imposes significant restrictions on employers regarding their interactions with trade unions and their employees' union activities. These restrictions aim to protect employees' rights to organize and bargain collectively, and to prevent employers from interfering with or coercing employees in their union-related endeavors.

## Prohibited Actions for Trade Unions and Their Representatives Under the Canada Labour Code

### Section 95: Prohibitions Relating to Trade Unions

Section 95 of the Canada Labour Code outlines a comprehensive list of prohibited actions for trade unions and their representatives. These prohibitions aim to prevent undue influence, coercion, and interference in the formation and administration of trade unions, as well as in collective bargaining processes.

#### Compelling Collective Bargaining
"No trade union or person acting on behalf of a trade union shall (a) seek to compel an employer to bargain collectively with the trade union if the trade union is not the bargaining agent for a bargaining unit that includes employees of the employer..."

This prohibition directly addresses the issue of unions attempting to force employers into bargaining situations where they are not the recognized bargaining agent. The section clarifies that a union cannot demand collective bargaining unless it is the legitimate bargaining representative for the relevant bargaining unit.

#### Bargaining Without Recognition
"(b) bargain collectively for the purpose of entering into a collective agreement or enter into a collective agreement with an employer in respect of a bargaining unit, if that trade union or person knows or, in the opinion of the Board, ought to know that another trade union is the bargaining agent for that bargaining unit..."

This prohibition further reinforces the principle of recognizing the legitimate bargaining agent. It states that a union cannot engage in collective bargaining or enter into a collective agreement if it is aware or should be aware that another union is already the recognized bargaining representative for the bargaining unit.

#### Interference in Employers' Organizations
"(c) participate in or interfere with the formation or administration of an employers’ organization..."

This prohibition aims to prevent unions from disrupting or influencing the activities of employers' organizations. It explicitly forbids unions from getting involved in the formation or management of such organizations.

#### Persuading Employees During Work Hours
"...except with the consent of the employer of an employee, attempt, at an employee’s place of employment during the working hours of the employee, to persuade the employee to become, to refrain from becoming or to cease to be a member of a trade union..."

This prohibition addresses the issue of unions attempting to recruit or discourage union membership while employees are on the clock. It states that such persuasion is prohibited unless the employer has given their consent.

#### Requiring Employer Termination for Union Membership
"...require an employer to terminate the employment of an employee because the employee has been expelled or suspended from membership in the trade union for a reason other than a failure to pay the periodic dues, assessments and initiation fees uniformly required to be paid by all members of the trade union as a condition of acquiring or retaining membership in the trade union..."

This prohibition prevents unions from pressuring employers to fire employees based on union disciplinary actions. It clarifies that an employer cannot terminate an employee solely because they have been expelled or suspended from union membership for reasons other than financial obligations.

#### Expelling or Suspending Employees Discriminatorily
"...expel or suspend an employee from membership in the trade union or deny membership in the trade union to an employee by applying to the employee in a discriminatory manner the membership rules of the trade union..."

This prohibition addresses the issue of unions applying their membership rules in a discriminatory manner. It states that unions cannot expel, suspend, or deny membership to employees based on discriminatory application of their rules.

#### Taking Disciplinary Action Discriminatorily
"...take disciplinary action against or impose any form of penalty on an employee by applying to that employee in a discriminatory manner the standards of discipline of the trade union..."

This prohibition prevents unions from imposing disciplinary actions on employees in a discriminatory manner. It clarifies that unions cannot apply their disciplinary standards unfairly to individual employees.

#### Discriminating Against Persons Based on Union Membership

individual_results.question: What is the procedure for filing a complaint under the Canada Labour Code, and what are the key requirements that must be met?
individual_results.answer:
## Procedure for Filing a Complaint Under the Canada Labour Code

### Before You File a Complaint

The initial step before submitting a complaint is to consider whether you are eligible and within the required timeframe. The documents outline this process in detail.
"If you are a unionized employee covered by a collective agreement, which provides for third party resolution provisions, you must first contact your union representative to discuss: the issue, and how it might be addressed In most instances, the Labour Program is not authorized to handle your complaint which may be rejected." This indicates that for unionized employees with third-party resolution processes, the first step is to engage with their union representative. The Labour Program may not be the appropriate avenue for such complaints.

### Eligibility and Timelines

There are specific eligibility criteria and timelines for filing a complaint. The documents detail these for monetary, non-monetary, and unjust dismissal complaints.
"You must file your monetary complaint within 6 months from the last day your employer was required to pay you." This clearly states the six-month limitation for filing complaints related to unpaid wages and other monetary amounts.
"You must file your non-monetary complaint within 6 months from the day you were aware of the issue." This specifies the six-month timeframe for complaints not involving monetary amounts, such as not receiving a response to a flexible work arrangement request.
"You must file your unjust dismissal complaint within 90 days from the date of dismissal." This sets a tighter 90-day deadline for complaints concerning unjust dismissal. Additionally, it outlines the eligibility requirements for filing such a complaint, including having been dismissed, having at least 12 consecutive months of employment, not being covered by a collective agreement, and not being a manager.

### Complete the Complaint Form

The next step is to meticulously complete the complaint form. While the exact form is not provided in the documents, the text indicates its importance.

"Complete the complaint form" is listed as the fourth step in the overall complaint filing process. This implies that a specific form must be filled out with all the necessary details of your complaint.

### Provide Records

Supporting documentation is crucial for a successful complaint. The documents specify the types of records that should be provided.
"If relevant to your complaint allegations, you should provide:  pay stubs  employment contracts, and  employee records or receipts..." This lists the essential financial and contractual documents that should accompany your complaint.
"**Note:** For complaints related to wages or other amounts owed, you should only provide documents covering a period of 24 months prior to the complaint." This provides a specific timeframe for wage-related documentation.
"If your employer provided the reasons for your  dismissal in writing, you should provide a copy of that letter." This highlights the importance of any written communication from your employer regarding your dismissal.

### Submit Your Complaint

The final step is to formally submit your complaint to the Labour Program. The documents provide instructions on how to do this.

"Submit your complaint" is listed as the sixth step in the overall complaint filing process. The text also mentions that you should keep the Labour Program updated on any changes in your contact information and respond to their correspondence within the noted timelines to avoid your complaint being abandoned.

### After You File a Complaint

The documents also outline the process that follows the submission of your complaint.
"The Labour Program will accept and investigate your complaint if filed within 6 months from the last day your employer was required to pay you..." This reiterates the time limit for monetary complaints and confirms that the Labour Program will investigate valid complaints.
"After you file a complaint, the Labour Program may write to you about  your complaint asking for you to provide information or answer questions within certain timelines." This indicates that the Labour Program may request further information from you during their investigation.
"If an agreement is not reached, at your request, the Labour Program may refer the complaint to the Canada Industrial Relations Board (the “Board”)." This explains the next step if the Labour Program's attempt at settlement fails.

individual_results.answer:
## Process for Handling a Complaint Made Under Section 97 of the Canada Labour Code

### Initial Filing and Time Limit

Section 97 of the Canada Labour Code outlines the process for making a complaint to the Board. It states,
"Subject to subsections (2) to (5), any person or organization may make a complaint in writing to the Board that (a) an employer, a person acting on behalf of an employer, a trade union, a person acting on behalf of a trade union or an employee has contravened or failed to comply with subsection 24(4) or 34(6) or section 37, 47.3, 50, 69, 87.5 or 87.6, subsection 87.7(2) or section 94, 95 or 96.1; or (b) any person has failed to comply with section 96." This indicates that any individual or organization can submit a written complaint to the Board detailing a violation of various sections of the Code.

The section also specifies a time limit for filing a complaint:
"Subject to subsections (4) and (5), a complaint pursuant to subsection (1) must be made to the Board not later than ninety days after the date on which the complainant knew, or in the opinion of the Board ought to have known, of the action or circumstances giving rise to the complaint." This means that a complaint must be submitted to the Board within ninety days of becoming aware of the alleged violation.

### Board's Role in Complaint Resolution

Section 98 details the Board's powers and duties upon receipt of a complaint. It states,
"Subject to subsection (3), on receipt of a complaint made under section 97, the Board may assist the parties to the complaint to settle the complaint and shall, where it decides not to so assist the parties or the complaint is not settled within a period considered by the Board to be reasonable in the circumstances, determine the complaint." This highlights the Board's initial role as a facilitator, attempting to help the parties reach a resolution. However, if settlement is not achieved within a reasonable timeframe, the Board has the authority to make a determination on the complaint.

### Factors Influencing the Board's Decision

Several factors influence the Board's decision to assist parties or determine the complaint.

#### Reasonable Timeframe for Settlement

The Board considers whether a reasonable timeframe has been allowed for the parties to settle the complaint. It states,
"...or the complaint is not settled within a period considered by the Board to be reasonable in the circumstances..." This suggests that the Board will assess the efforts made by the parties to reach a settlement and whether a sufficient amount of time has passed.

#### Referral to Collective Agreement

Section 98(3) outlines a situation where the Board may refuse to determine a complaint. It states,
"The Board may refuse to determine any complaint made pursuant to section 97 in respect of a matter that, in the opinion of the Board, could be referred by the complainant pursuant to a collective agreement to an arbitrator or arbitration board." This indicates that if the complaint falls under a matter that is already subject to a collective agreement and can be addressed through arbitration, the Board may decline to make a determination.

#### Burden of Proof

Section 98(4) clarifies the burden of proof when a complaint is made in writing pursuant to section 97. It states,
"Where a complaint is made in writing pursuant to section 97 in respect of an alleged failure by an employer or any person acting on behalf of an employer to comply with subsection 94(3), the written complaint is itself evidence that such failure actually occurred and, if any party to the complaint proceedings alleges that such failure did not occur, the burden of proof thereof is on that party." This means that the written complaint serves as initial evidence of the alleged violation, and any party disputing the violation bears the responsibility of proving that it did not occur.

#### Failure to Comply with Collective Agreement

Section 99.1 of the Canada Labour Code addresses the Board's power to certify a trade union even without majority support under certain circumstances. It states,
"The Board may certify a trade union despite a lack of evidence of majority support if (a) the employer has failed to comply with section 94; and (b) the Board is of the opinion that, but for the unfair labour practice, the trade union could reasonably have been expected to have had the support of a majority of the employees in the unit." This implies that if an employer has failed to comply with a collective agreement, the Board may certify a trade union even without majority support, as it believes that the union would have had majority support had the employer complied.

#### Other Means of Resolution

Section 97(1)(a)(iv) addresses the rejection of a complaint when other means of resolution are available. It states,
"A complaint may be rejected if it is determined that other means are available to the complainant." This indicates that the Board may reject a complaint if the complainant has other avenues for resolving the issue, such as a provincial Privacy Commissioner or the Canada Industrial Relations Board. The Board will assess whether these other means are appropriate for resolving the complaint.

individual_results.question: What can the Board do if it determines that a party to a complaint has contravened or failed to comply with certain provisions of the Canada Labour Code?
individual_results.answer:
## Board Actions Upon Finding a Contravention

### Section 134: Board Orders

Section 134 outlines the Board's powers when it determines an employer has contravened section 147. It states:
"If, under subsection 133(5), the Board determines that an employer has contravened section 147, the Board may, by order, require the employer to cease contravening that section and may, if applicable, by order, require the employer to (a) permit any employee who has been affected by the contravention to return to the duties of their employment; (b) reinstate any former employee affected by the contravention; (c) pay to any employee or former employee affected by the contravention compensation not exceeding the sum that, in the Board’s opinion, is equivalent to the remuneration that would, but for the contravention, have been paid by the employer to the employee or former employee; and (d) rescind any disciplinary action taken in respect of, and pay compensation to any employee affected by, the contravention, not exceeding the sum that, in the Board’s opinion, is equivalent to any financial or other penalty imposed on the employee by the employer."

This section details the specific orders the Board can issue. It can order the employer to stop the contravention, reinstate affected employees, pay compensation, and rescind disciplinary actions. The Board's power is exercised through "order," which carries the force of law.

### Section 133: Complaints When Action Against Employees: Complaint to Board

Section 133 describes the process for filing a complaint with the Board when an employer has taken action against an employee in contravention of section 147. It mentions the Board's potential actions:
"On receipt of a complaint made under this section, the Board may assist the parties to the complaint to settle the complaint and shall, if it decides not to so assist the parties or the complaint is not settled within a period considered by the Board to be reasonable in the circumstances, hear and determine the complaint."

This indicates that the Board has the power to facilitate settlement of the complaint and, if unsuccessful, to formally hear and determine the complaint. The Board's determination can lead to the orders outlined in Section 134.

### Section 98: Unfair Practices: Duty and power of the Board

Section 98 reiterates the Board's powers upon receiving a complaint of a contravention of section 147:
"...on receipt of a complaint made under section 97, the Board may assist the parties to the complaint to settle the complaint and shall, where it decides not to so assist the parties or the complaint is not settled within a period considered by the Board to be reasonable in the circumstances, determine the complaint."

This section is very similar to Section 133, emphasizing the Board's ability to assist in settlement and, if that fails, to formally determine the complaint and issue orders as per Section 134.

In summary, if the Board determines that a party to a complaint has contravened or failed to comply with certain provisions of the Canada Labour Code, it can issue orders requiring the employer to cease the contravention, reinstate employees, pay compensation, rescind disciplinary actions, and formally determine the complaint, leading to the enforcement of the Code's provisions.

individual_results.question: Under what circumstances can the Board certify a trade union even if there is no evidence that it has the support of a majority of employees?
individual_results.answer:
## Certification of Bargaining Agents Without Majority Support

### Section 28: Duty to certify trade union
"The Board shall, subject to this Part, certify a trade union as the bargaining agent for a bargaining unit if the Board (a) has received from the trade union an application for certification as the bargaining agent for a unit; (b) has determined the unit that constitutes a unit appropriate for collective bargaining; and (c) is satisfied that, as of the date of the filing of the application or of any other date that the Board considers appropriate, a majority of the employees in the unit wish to have the trade union represent them as their bargaining agent."

This section outlines the general duty of the Board to certify a trade union. However, it explicitly states a condition for certification:
"...a majority of the employees in the unit wish to have the trade union represent them as their bargaining agent." This indicates that a majority of employees must support the union for certification to occur.

### Section 29: Representation vote
"The Board may, in any case, for the purpose of satisfying itself as to whether employees in a unit wish to have a particular trade union represent them as their bargaining agent, order that a representation vote be taken among the employees in the unit."

This section details the Board's power to order a representation vote to determine whether a union has majority support. It states that the Board can order a vote
"...for the purpose of satisfying itself as to whether employees in a unit wish to have a particular trade union represent them as their bargaining agent..." This implies that the Board will only certify a union if the vote demonstrates majority support.

### Section 30: Conduct of vote
"Where the Board orders that a representation vote be taken among employees in a unit, the Board shall (a) determine the employees that are eligible to vote; and (b) make such arrangements and give such directions as the Board considers necessary for the proper conduct of the representation vote, including the preparation of ballots, the method of casting and counting ballots and the custody and sealing of ballot boxes."

This section further elaborates on the Board's role in conducting a representation vote. It specifies the steps the Board must take to ensure the vote is conducted properly. The focus remains on determining whether a majority of employees support the union.

### Section 31: Result of representation vote
"Section 31 (1) Subject to subsection (2), the Board shall determine the result of a representation vote on the basis of the ballots cast by the majority of employees voting."

This section clarifies how the Board determines the outcome of a representation vote. It states that the Board will base its determination
"...the ballots cast by the majority of employees voting." This reinforces the requirement for majority support for certification.

### Section 25: Application for Certification: Where certification prohibited
"Notwithstanding anything in this Part, where the Board is satisfied that a trade union is so dominated or influenced by an employer that the fitness of the trade union to represent employees of the employer for the purpose of collective bargaining is impaired, the Board shall not certify the trade union as the bargaining agent for any unit comprised of employees of the employer and any collective agreement between the trade union and the employer that applies to any such employees shall be deemed not to be a collective agreement for the purposes of this Part."

This section presents a specific circumstance where the Board can deny certification even without majority support. It states that if the Board is convinced that a trade union is
"...so dominated or influenced by an employer that the fitness of the trade union to represent employees of the employer for the purpose of collective bargaining is impaired..." it will not certify the union. This indicates that the Board can override majority support if it deems the union's independence compromised.

### Section 29: Representation vote
"(2) If a trade union applies for certification as the bargaining agent for a unit in respect of which no other trade union is the bargaining agent, and the Board is satisfied that not less than 35% and not more than 50% of the employees in the unit are members of the trade union, the Board shall order that a representation vote be taken among the employees in the unit."

This subsection addresses a situation where the union has a significant, but not yet majority, membership. It states that if the Board is satisfied that between 35% and 50% of the employees are members, it will order a representation vote. This suggests that the Board might order a vote even without majority support to further assess the union's standing.

### Section 30: Conduct of vote
"(3) Where the Board is satisfied that a trade union has an established practice of admitting persons to membership without regard to the eligibility requirements of its charter, constitution or by-laws, the Board may disregard those requirements in determining whether a person is a member of a trade union."

This subsection provides another scenario where the Board can deviate from strict membership requirements. It states that if a union has a lax membership policy, the Board can disregard the union's eligibility rules when determining whether a person is a member. This could potentially lead to certification even without majority support if the union's membership is inflated.

In summary, the Board can certify a trade union even if there is no evidence of majority employee support under specific circumstances. These circumstances include when the Board is convinced that the union is unduly influenced by an employer, when the union has a significant but not yet majority membership, or when the union has a lax membership policy. However, the general rule remains that the Board will only certify a union if it is satisfied that a majority of employees wish to have the union represent them.
