individual_results.question: What are the consequences for employers, trade unions, and individuals who declare or cause a lockout or strike contrary to the regulations in the Canada Labour Code?
individual_results.answer:
## Consequences for Employers, Trade Unions, and Individuals Who Declare or Cause a Lockout or Strike Contrary to the Canada Labour Code

### Offences and Punishment for Lockout and Strike

#### Employers
"Every employer who declares or causes a lockout contrary to this Part is guilty of an offence and liable on summary conviction to a fine not exceeding one thousand dollars for each day that the lockout continues." This section clearly outlines the financial penalty for employers who declare or cause a lockout in violation of the Canada Labour Code. The fine is per day the lockout persists, indicating a cumulative consequence.
"Every person who, on behalf of an employer, declares or causes a lockout contrary to this Part is guilty of an offence and liable on summary conviction to a fine not exceeding ten thousand dollars." This expands the liability to individuals acting on behalf of the employer. The fine is significantly higher than that for the employer directly, suggesting a greater degree of responsibility for those facilitating the lockout.

#### Trade Unions
"Every trade union that declares or authorizes a strike contrary to this Part is guilty of an offence and liable on summary conviction to a fine not exceeding one thousand dollars for each day that the strike continues." This section details the financial penalty for trade unions who declare or authorize a strike in contravention of the Canada Labour Code. The fine is also per day the strike continues, indicating a cumulative consequence.
"Every officer or representative of a trade union who declares or authorizes a strike contrary to this Part is guilty of an offence and liable on summary conviction to a fine not exceeding ten thousand dollars." Similar to employers, this section extends the liability to individuals acting on behalf of the trade union. The fine is substantially higher than that for the trade union itself, highlighting the significant responsibility of union officials.

#### Individuals Participating in Strike or Lockout
"Every person who, on behalf of an employer, declares or causes a lockout contrary to this Part is guilty of an offence and liable on summary conviction to a fine not exceeding ten thousand dollars." This section specifies the penalty for individuals acting on behalf of an employer in declaring or causing a lockout.
"Every trade union that declares or authorizes a strike contrary to this Part is guilty of an offence and liable on summary conviction to a fine not exceeding one thousand dollars for each day that the strike continues." This section specifies the penalty for trade unions who declare or authorize a strike contrary to the Canada Labour Code.

### Declarations and Prohibitions

#### Employer Application for Declaration of Unlawful Strike
"Where an employer alleges that a trade union has declared or authorized a strike, or that employees have participated, are participating or are likely to participate in a strike, the effect of which was, is or would be to involve the participation of an employee in a strike in contravention of this Part, the employer may apply to the Board for a declaration that the strike was, is or would be unlawful." This section outlines the process for an employer to seek a declaration from the Board that a strike is unlawful. The Board will consider representations from both the employer and the trade union before making such a declaration.

#### Board Order Regarding Unlawful Strike
"Where an employer applies to the Board under subsection (1) for a declaration that a strike was, is or would be unlawful, the Board may, after affording the trade union or employees referred to in subsection (1) an opportunity to make representations on the application, make such a declaration and, if the employer so requests, may make an order (a) requiring the trade union to revoke the declaration or authorization to strike and to give notice of such revocation forthwith to the employees to whom it was directed; (b) enjoining any employee from participating in the strike; (c) requiring any employee who is participating in the strike to perform the duties of their employment; and (d) requiring any trade union, of which any employee with respect to whom an order is made under paragraph (b) or (c) is a member, and any officer or representative of that union, forthwith to give notice of any order made under paragraph (b) or (c) to any employee to whom it applies." This section details the types of orders the Board may issue upon declaring a strike unlawful. These orders can include requiring the union to revoke the strike authorization, enjoining employees from participating, requiring employees to return to work, and mandating the union to notify its members and officers of the order.

#### Board Declaration Regarding Immediate Danger to Public Safety
"If, in determining an application made under subsection (4) or referral made under subsection (5), the Board is of the opinion that a strike or lockout could pose an immediate and serious danger to the safety or health of the public, the Board, may, by order (a) designate the supply of those services, the operation of those facilities and the production of those goods that it considers necessary to continue in order to prevent an immediate and serious danger to the safety or health of the public; (b) specify the manner and extent to which the employer, the trade union and the employees in the bargaining unit must continue that supply, operation and production; and (c) impose any measure that it considers appropriate for carrying out the requirements of this section." This section addresses situations where a strike or lockout could pose an immediate danger to public safety. The Board has the power to issue an order requiring the continuation of essential services and specifying the manner in which this must be done.

#### Board Review of Agreement or Determination
"On application by the employer or the trade union, or on referral by the Minister, during a strike or lockout not prohibited by this Part, the Board may, where in the Board’s opinion the circumstances warrant, review and confirm, amend or cancel an agreement entered into, or a determination or order made, under this section and make any orders that it considers appropriate in the circumstances." This section allows the Board to review and modify agreements or orders made under this section, particularly if the circumstances warrant it.

#### Binding Method of Resolving Disputes
"Where the Board is satisfied that the level of activity to be continued in compliance with subsection (1) renders ineffective the exercise of the right to strike or lockout, the Board may, on application by the employer or the trade union, direct a binding method of resolving the issues in dispute between the parties for the purpose of ensuring settlement of a dispute." This section provides the Board with the power to direct a binding method of dispute resolution if the level of activity required to prevent public safety risks renders the right to strike or lockout ineffective.

individual_results.question: What are the consequences for an individual who fails to comply with a requirement to attend, produce documents, take an oath, or answer questions from certain authorities under the Canada Labour Code?
individual_results.answer:
## Offences and Punishment: Failure to Act

### Section 102: General Offences
"Every person who (a) being required to attend to give evidence pursuant to paragraph 16(a), fails, without valid excuse, to attend accordingly, (b) being commanded to produce, pursuant to paragraph 16(a), any document or thing in their possession or under their control, fails to produce the document or thing, (c) refuses to be sworn or to affirm, as the case may be, after being required to do so pursuant to paragraph 16(a), or (d) refuses to answer any proper question put to them, pursuant to paragraph 16(a), by the Board, a conciliation board, a conciliation commissioner, an arbitrator or an arbitration board, is guilty of an offence and liable on summary conviction to a fine not exceeding four hundred dollars."

This section of the Canada Labour Code outlines the specific offences for individuals who fail to comply with requirements from various authorities. It details four distinct actions that constitute an offence: failing to attend to give evidence without a valid excuse, failing to produce documents or things when commanded, refusing to take an oath, or refusing to answer proper questions. The consequence for committing any of these offences is a fine "not exceeding four hundred dollars" upon summary conviction.

### Section 290: Failure to Act
"A person or a department that neither pays a penalty imposed under this Part nor requests a review or an appeal in the specified time is considered to have committed the violation and is liable for the penalty."

This section addresses the consequence of failing to act upon a penalty imposed under the Canada Labour Code. It states that if a person or department does not pay a penalty or request a review or appeal within the specified timeframe, they are considered to have committed the violation and are liable for the penalty. This highlights the importance of timely action when faced with a penalty.

### Section 259: Failure to Comply with Order | Imprisonment Precluded in Certain Cases
"An employer that fails to comply with an order of a convicting court made under section 258 is guilty of an offence punishable on summary conviction and liable to a fine of not more than $1,000 for each day during which the failure continues."

This section specifically addresses the consequences for employers who fail to comply with an order issued by a convicting court. It states that such a failure is an offence punishable on summary conviction and carries a fine of
"...not more than $1,000 for each day during which the failure continues." This indicates that the penalty for non-compliance is cumulative, increasing daily.

### Section 259.1: Imprisonment Precluded in Certain Cases
"Where a person is convicted of an offence under this Part punishable on summary conviction, no imprisonment may be imposed as punishment for the offence or in default of payment of any fine imposed as punishment."

This subsection clarifies that imprisonment is not a possible punishment for offences punishable on summary conviction under this Part, even in default of paying a fine. This is a significant limitation on the potential penalties for such offences.

### Section 259.2: Recovery of Penalties
"(2) Where a person is convicted of an offence under this Part and the fine that is imposed is not paid when required, the prosecutor may, by filing the conviction, enter as a judgment the amount of the fine and costs, if any, in a superior court of the province in which the trial was held, and the judgment is enforceable against the person in the same manner as if it were a judgment rendered against the person in that court in civil proceedings."

This subsection outlines the process for recovering unpaid penalties. It states that if a person is convicted of an offence and fails to pay the fine when required, the prosecutor can enter the fine and costs as a judgment in a superior court of the province where the trial was held. This judgment is then enforceable against the person in the same way as a judgment rendered in civil proceedings.

individual_results.question: Who can bring a prosecution for an offence under this Part of the Canada Labour Code (PART I - Industrial Relations) and under what conditions can their actions be considered as having been done by the organization itself?
individual_results.answer:
## Who Can Bring a Prosecution for an Offence Under Part I of the Canada Labour Code?

### Entities Authorized to Bring Prosecution

Section 103(1) of the Canada Labour Code explicitly states:
"A prosecution for an offence under this Part may be brought against and in the name of an employers’ organization, a trade union or a council of trade unions." This indicates that a wide range of organizations, representing either employers or employees, have the legal standing to initiate a prosecution for violations of Part I of the Canada Labour Code.

### Conditions for Actions to Be Considered as Having Been Done by the Organization Itself

Section 103(2) clarifies the conditions under which the actions of an officer or agent of an organization can be attributed to the organization itself for the purpose of a prosecution. It states:
"For the purpose of a prosecution under subsection (1), (a) an employers’ organization, trade union or council of trade unions shall be deemed to be a person; and (b) any act or thing done or omitted to be done by an officer or agent of an employers’ organization, trade union or council of trade unions within the scope of their authority to act on behalf of the employers’ organization, trade union or council of trade unions shall be deemed to be an act or thing done or omitted to be done by the employers’ organization, trade union or council of trade unions."

This passage is crucial because it establishes that for a prosecution to be validly brought against an organization, the actions of its representatives must be considered as having been done by the organization itself. This is achieved by deeming the organization a "person" for the purposes of the prosecution and by stating that any act or omission by an officer or agent acting within their authority is to be attributed to the organization. This ensures that the organization is held accountable for the actions of its representatives.

individual_results.question: What is required to institute a prosecution for an offence under this Part of the Canada Labour Code (PART I - Industrial Relations)?
individual_results.answer:
## Requirements for Instituting a Prosecution under Part I of the Canada Labour Code

### Consent of the Board
"Except with the consent in writing of the Board, no prosecution shall be instituted in respect of an offence under this Part." This section clearly states the primary requirement for instituting a prosecution: the prior written consent of the Board. This provision indicates a level of oversight and control by the Board over the initiation of prosecutions, suggesting a desire to ensure that such actions are warranted and in the public interest.

### Consent of the Minister
"No proceeding against a director of a corporation in respect of an offence under this Part shall be instituted except with the consent of the Minister." This subsection introduces a specific exception to the general requirement of Board consent. It mandates the Minister's consent for any prosecution against a director of a corporation. This provision likely aims to provide a safeguard against politically motivated or overly aggressive prosecutions targeting corporate directors.

### Prosecution Against Employers’ Organizations, Trade Unions and Councils of Trade Unions
"(1) A prosecution for an offence under this Part may be brought against and in the name of an employers’ organization, a trade union or a council of trade unions." This section outlines the possibility of prosecuting entities other than individual employers. It states that a prosecution can be brought against an employers’ organization, trade union, or council of trade unions, with the prosecution being conducted in their name. This provision allows for the holding of these organizations accountable for offences committed by their officers or agents.
"(2) For the purpose of a prosecution under subsection (1), (a) an employers’ organization, trade union or council of trade unions shall be deemed to be a person; and (b) any act or thing done or omitted to be done by an officer or agent of an employers’ organization, trade union or council of trade unions within the scope of their authority to act on behalf of the employers’ organization, trade union or council of trade unions shall be deemed to be an act or thing done or omitted to be done by the employers’ organization, trade union or council of trade unions." This subsection clarifies the legal standing of these organizations for the purpose of prosecution. It deems them "persons" and holds their officers and agents accountable for their actions within the scope of their authority.

### Other Requirements
"Every person who (a) being required to attend to give evidence pursuant to paragraph 16(a), fails, without valid excuse, to attend accordingly, (b) being commanded to produce, pursuant to paragraph 16(a), any document or thing in their possession or under their control, fails to produce the document or thing, (c) refuses to be sworn or to affirm, as the case may be, after being required to do so pursuant to paragraph 16(a), or (d) refuses to answer any proper question put to them, pursuant to paragraph 16(a), by the Board, a conciliation board, a conciliation commissioner, an arbitrator or an arbitration board, is guilty of an offence and liable on summary conviction to a fine not exceeding four hundred dollars." This section details additional requirements for instituting a prosecution. It lists various offences that can lead to a summary conviction and a fine, including failing to attend to give evidence, failing to produce documents, refusing to swear, or refusing to answer questions.

individual_results.question: Under what circumstances can a mediator be appointed to assist in settling a labour dispute, and what actions can they take?
individual_results.answer:
## Appointment of a Mediator

### Circumstances for Appointment

A mediator can be appointed to assist in settling a labour dispute under two primary circumstances, as outlined in the Canada Labour Code:

1. **Minister's Initiative or Request:
"The Minister, on request or on the Minister’s own initiative, may, where the Minister deems it expedient, at any time appoint a mediator to confer with the parties to a dispute or difference and endeavour to assist them in settling..." This section clearly states that the Minister has the authority to appoint a mediator either upon request from the parties involved in the dispute or based on their own assessment of the situation. The Minister's decision is guided by what they deem "expedient" for resolving the labour issue.

2. **Request from Parties or the Minister:
"At the request of the parties or the Minister, a mediator appointed pursuant to subsection (1) may make recommendations for settlement of the dispute or the difference." This further clarifies the avenues for mediator appointment. The parties themselves can request a mediator, or the Minister can initiate the appointment based on their own judgment or a request from the parties.

### Actions a Mediator Can Take

Once appointed, a mediator undertakes specific actions to facilitate the resolution of the labour dispute. These actions are detailed in Section 105(1) and (2) of the Canada Labour Code, as well as in the Labour-Reports-10_2 document.

1. **Conferring with Parties and Endeavouring to Assist:
"The Minister, on request or on the Minister’s own initiative, may, where the Minister deems it expedient, at any time appoint a mediator to confer with the parties to a dispute or difference and endeavour to assist them in settling..." This action involves the mediator engaging in discussions with the representatives of the disputing parties. Their primary goal is to
"endeavour to assist them in settling the dispute or the difference." (no source found for the quotation) This involves understanding the perspectives of each side and exploring potential areas of agreement.

2. **Making Recommendations for Settlement:
"At the request of the parties or the Minister, a mediator appointed pursuant to subsection (1) may make recommendations for settlement of the dispute or the difference." This action allows the mediator to propose potential solutions to the parties. These recommendations are not binding but serve as a starting point for further negotiation and potential agreement.

The Labour-Reports-10_2 document elaborates on the mediator's role, stating,
"The mediator will structure the discussions, organize information, help the parties express their concerns and point out opportunities for agreement. The mediator helps the parties talk to each other, examine their positions, achieve understanding, explore creative solutions and create a joint resolution." This highlights the mediator's active facilitation role in guiding the parties towards a mutually acceptable outcome. The mediator remains neutral and does not impose a decision, but rather assists the parties in reaching their own resolution.

individual_results.question: Under what circumstances can the Minister initiate inquiries into industrial relations matters?
individual_results.answer:
## Minister's Authority to Initiate Inquiries

### General Circumstances for Inquiry Initiation

The Minister possesses broad authority to initiate inquiries into industrial relations matters. This authority can be exercised "on application or on the Minister’s own initiative," as stated in Section 106 of the Canada Labour Code. This indicates that the Minister is not solely reliant on a formal request to commence an inquiry.

Furthermore, the Minister can initiate inquiries "where the Minister deems it expedient," suggesting a discretionary power based on the Minister's assessment of the situation. This discretion allows the Minister to proactively address issues impacting industrial relations.

### Specific Scenarios for Inquiry Initiation

Section 107 elaborates on the Minister's power to initiate inquiries in situations where it is
"...likely to maintain or secure industrial peace and to promote conditions favourable to the settlement of industrial disputes or differences..." This highlights a key objective of the Minister's inquiry power: to foster a stable and productive industrial environment.

Section 12.07 also outlines specific measures the Minister may take, including
"...request the Governor in Council to have an inquiry held under section 12.08..." This demonstrates a pathway for the Minister to formally request a more structured inquiry process.

Additionally, Section 106 explicitly states that the Minister
"...may, where the Minister deems it expedient, make any inquiries that the Minister considers advisable regarding matters that may affect industrial relations." This reinforces the Minister's wide-ranging power to investigate any issue deemed relevant to industrial relations.

### Minister's Role in Directing the Board

Section 107 further details the Minister's ability to direct the Board to undertake inquiries. It states,
"...to those ends the Minister may refer any question to the Board or direct the Board to do such things as the Minister deems necessary." This indicates that the Minister can delegate the responsibility of conducting inquiries to the Board when appropriate.

In summary, the Minister can initiate inquiries into industrial relations matters under a variety of circumstances, including on their own initiative, in situations where it is deemed expedient to maintain industrial peace, or by formally requesting an inquiry through the Governor in Council. The Minister also has the power to direct the Board to conduct inquiries as necessary.

individual_results.question: What is the role of an Industrial Inquiry Commission in the event of a labour dispute or difference between an employer and employees, and how does it report its findings?
individual_results.answer:
## The Role of an Industrial Inquiry Commission in Labour Disputes

### Appointment and Investigation
"Pursuant to section 106 or where, in any industry, a dispute or difference between any employer and employees exists or is apprehended, the Minister may appoint a commission to be designated as an Industrial Inquiry Commission and to which the Minister shall refer the matter under consideration for investigation and report to the Minister." This section clearly outlines the role of an Industrial Inquiry Commission. It is appointed by the Minister either pursuant to section 106 (which is not detailed in the provided documents) or when a labour dispute or difference is present or anticipated. The Minister then refers the matter to the Commission for investigation, with the Commission tasked with preparing a report for the Minister.

### Functions and Report
"Forthwith on its appointment, an Industrial Inquiry Commission (a) shall inquire into the matters referred to it by the Minister and endeavour to carry out its terms of reference; and (b) where the Commission is inquiring into a dispute or difference between any employer and employees and a settlement of the dispute or difference is not effected during the inquiry, shall make its report and recommendations to the Minister within fourteen days after its appointment or within such longer period as the Minister may allow." This passage details the Commission's immediate actions upon appointment. It is responsible for investigating the matters referred to it and attempting to resolve the dispute. If a settlement is not reached within fourteen days (or a longer period allowed by the Minister), the Commission must submit its report and recommendations to the Minister.
"On receipt of a report of an Industrial Inquiry Commission relating to any dispute or difference between any employer and employees, the Minister shall (a) furnish a copy of the report to each employer and trade union involved in the dispute or difference; and (b) publish the report in such manner as the Minister considers advisable." This section explains how the Minister disseminates the Commission's findings. Upon receiving the report, the Minister is obligated to provide a copy to all employers and trade unions involved in the dispute and to publish the report in a manner deemed appropriate by the Minister. This ensures transparency and allows all parties to be informed of the Commission's conclusions and recommendations.

individual_results.question: What can the Minister do if it is in the public interest that employees in a bargaining unit be given the opportunity to accept or reject the employer's last offer, and what are the potential consequences of a favourable vote by the employees?
individual_results.answer:
## Minister's Intervention in Collective Bargaining: Public Interest and Vote Outcomes

### Minister's Authority to Order a Vote

The Minister possesses the authority to order a vote on an employer's last offer if it is deemed to be in the public interest. This power is outlined in Section 108.1(1) of the Canada Labour Code.
"Where notice to bargain collectively has been given under this Part, and the Minister is of the opinion that it is in the public interest that the employees in the affected bargaining unit be given the opportunity to accept or reject the offer of the employer last received by the trade union in respect of all matters remaining in dispute between the parties, the Minister may (a) on such terms and conditions as the Minister considers appropriate, direct that a vote of the employees in the bargaining unit to accept or reject the offer be held as soon as possible; and (b) designate the Board, or any other person or body, to be in charge of conducting that vote."

This section explicitly states that the Minister can direct a vote "if it is in the public interest." The Minister also has the discretion to set the terms and conditions of the vote and to designate the body responsible for its conduct.

### Consequences of a Favourable Vote

The Canada Labour Code details the potential consequences of a favourable vote by the employees on the employer's last offer.
"Where the majority of the employees participating in the vote accept the employer’s last offer, (a) the parties are bound by that offer and shall, without delay, enter into a collective agreement that incorporates the terms of that offer; and (b) any lockout or strike not prohibited by this Part that is in progress when the Board or other person or body in charge of conducting the vote notifies the parties in writing of the employees’ acceptance shall cease forthwith."

According to Section 108.1(3), if a majority of employees vote to accept the employer's last offer, the parties are legally obligated to enter into a collective agreement that reflects those terms without delay. Furthermore, any ongoing lockout or strike that was not prohibited by the Part will immediately end upon notification of the employees' acceptance. This demonstrates the significant impact the Minister's intervention and a favourable vote can have on the collective bargaining process.

individual_results.question: Under what conditions can a trade union's authorized representative be granted access to employees living in isolated locations on an employer's premises or those of another person?
individual_results.answer:
## Conditions for Trade Union Access to Employees in Isolated Locations

### Application Process and Board Determination
"Where the Board receives from a trade union an application for an order granting an authorized representative of the trade union access to employees living in an isolated location on premises owned or controlled by their employer or by any other person, the Board may make an order granting the authorized representative of the trade union designated in the order access to the employees on the premises of their employer or such other person, as the case may be, that are designated in the order if the Board determines that access to the employees (a) would be impracticable unless permitted on premises owned or controlled by their employer or by such other person; and (b) is reasonably required for purposes relating to soliciting union memberships, the negotiation or administration of a collective agreement, the processing of a grievance or the provision of a union service to employees." This section outlines the initial step for a trade union to request access. The Board reviews the application and makes a determination based on two key factors: first, whether access would be
"...impracticable unless permitted on premises owned or controlled by their employer or by such other person..." and second, whether access is
"...reasonably required for purposes relating to soliciting union memberships, the negotiation or administration of a collective agreement, the processing of a grievance or the provision of a union service to employees."

### Reasonableness Requirement

The Board's determination hinges on the "reasonableness" of the access request. The text specifies that access is
"...reasonably required for purposes relating to soliciting union memberships, the negotiation or administration of a collective agreement, the processing of a grievance or the provision of a union service to employees." This indicates that the Board will consider whether the union's need for access falls within these legitimate union activities.

### Impracticability Condition

Another condition for granting access is
"...unless permitted on premises owned or controlled by their employer or by such other person..." This suggests that if it would be "impracticable" for the union representative to reach the employees without permission from the employer or another property owner, the Board may grant access.

### Order Contents
"The Board shall, in every order made under subsection (1), specify the method of access to the employees, the times at which access is permitted and the periods of its duration."  This clarifies that any order granting access must detail the specifics of how the union representative will be able to reach the employees, including the permitted times and the length of the access period.

### Protection of Privacy and Safety
"...the Board may (a) provide each employee with the opportunity to refuse the giving of their name and address to the representative of the trade union that the Board authorizes and, if the employee does not so refuse, may transmit that name and address to the authorized representative; or (b) transmit the information that the union wishes to communicate to the employees in the manner it considers appropriate." This section addresses the protection of employee privacy and safety. The Board can either offer employees the option to refuse their contact information or directly transmit the information to the union representative in a manner deemed appropriate.

individual_results.question: Under what circumstances can a trade union request that an employer provide employee contact information to facilitate communication, and what protections are in place for employees?
individual_results.answer:
## Trade Union Request for Employee Contact Information and Employee Protections

### Circumstances for Trade Union Request

A trade union can request an employer to provide employee contact information through an application to the Board. The Board may, by order, require the employer to furnish the union with the names and addresses of employees whose normal workplace is not on premises owned or controlled by their employer. This request is specifically for the purpose of facilitating communication with those employees. The Board can then authorize the trade union to communicate with these employees
"...by electronic means or otherwise, if the Board is of the opinion that such communication is required for purposes relating to soliciting trade union memberships, the negotiation or administration of a collective agreement, the processing of a grievance or the provision of a trade union service to employees."

### Protections for Employees

Several protections are in place for employees when a trade union requests their contact information.

#### Board Oversight and Order Requirements

The Board has significant oversight in this process. Any order made under subsection (1)(a) must specify the method of communication, the times of day and the periods during which the communication is authorized, and the conditions that must be met to ensure the protection of the privacy and the safety of affected employees and to prevent the abusive use of information.

#### Employee Refusal and Board Transmission

If the Board believes that the privacy and safety of affected employees cannot otherwise be protected, it may provide each employee with the opportunity to refuse the giving of their name and address to the representative of the trade union that the Board authorizes. If the employee does not so refuse, the Board may transmit that name and address to the authorized representative. This ensures that employees have a choice regarding whether or not to share their contact information.

#### Protection of Names and Addresses

The names and addresses of employees provided under subsection (1) shall not be used
"...unless it is for a purpose consistent with this section." This limits the use of the provided information to the specific purposes outlined in the section, such as soliciting union memberships or negotiating collective agreements.

#### Employer Transmission via Electronic Systems

The Board may also include a requirement that the employer, in accordance with any terms and conditions that the Board establishes, transmit the information that the union wishes to communicate to the employees by means of any electronic communications system that the employer uses to communicate with the employees. This provides an alternative method of communication that respects employee privacy.

#### Confidentiality Requests

Employees may request that their identity be kept confidential from their employer during the investigation of a monetary or non-monetary complaint. However, this may limit the possibility of facilitating and expediting the handling of their complaint, causing delays. Confidentiality cannot be kept if
"...the disclosure is necessary for the purposes of a prosecution the disclosure is in the public interest, or the Labour Program determines that the disclosure is necessary for the investigation of the complaint to be carried out and you consent to the disclosure in writing." If an employee refuses to provide consent after being requested to do so in writing, the Labour Program may deem the complaint to be withdrawn.

## Obligations of Trade Unions and Employers' Organizations Regarding Financial Statements

### Disclosure of Financial Statements

#### Upon Request
"Every trade union and every employers’ organization shall, forthwith on the request of any of its members, provide the member, free of charge, with a copy of a financial statement of its affairs to the end of the last fiscal year, certified to be a true copy by its president and treasurer or by its president and any other officer responsible for the handling and administration of its funds." The provision is "forthwith" and "free of charge," emphasizing the immediate and cost-free nature of this disclosure. The statement must be "certified to be a true copy" by designated officers, ensuring its accuracy.

#### Content of Financial Statements
"Any financial statement provided under subsection (1) shall contain information in sufficient detail to disclose accurately the financial condition and operations of the trade union or employers’ organization for the fiscal year for which it was prepared." This subsection specifies the required level of detail for financial statements. They must provide
"...information in sufficient detail to disclose accurately the financial condition and operations..." of the organization for the preceding fiscal year. This ensures transparency and allows members to understand the organization's financial health and activities.

### Board Intervention for Non-Compliance

#### Complaint Process
"The Board, on the complaint of any member of a trade union or employers’ organization that it has failed to comply with subsection (1), may make an order requiring the trade union or employers’ organization to file with the Board, within the time set out in the order, a statement in such form and with such particulars as the Board may determine." This section details the mechanism for the Board to intervene when organizations fail to provide financial statements. A complaint from a member triggers the Board's authority to issue an order compelling the organization to file a statement. The order specifies the required format and level of detail.

#### Board Order for Provision of Statements
"The Board may make an order requiring a trade union or employers’ organization to provide a copy of a statement filed under subsection (3) to such members of the trade union or employers’ organization as the Board in its discretion directs." This subsection grants the Board further power to order the provision of financial statements to members. The Board has discretion over which members receive the statements, allowing for targeted disclosure if deemed appropriate.

individual_results.question: What type of regulations can the Governor in Council make according to section 111 of the Canada Labour Code?
individual_results.answer:
## Regulations under Section 111 of the Canada Labour Code

### General Powers of the Governor in Council

Section 111 of the Canada Labour Code grants the Governor in Council broad powers to make regulations. It states:
"The Governor in Council may make regulations (a) prescribing to or by whom and in what manner any notice, request or report that may be given or made to or received by the Minister shall be given, made or received; (b) prescribing in what form and manner any notice or report that is authorized or required to be given or sent by the Minister, a conciliation commissioner, a conciliation board or an Industrial Inquiry Commission shall be given or sent and what shall constitute sufficient service of such notice or report on the person to whom it is given or sent; (c) designating, with respect to any notice or request authorized or required to be given or sent by the Minister, the officer who may give or send the notice or request on behalf of the Minister; (d) prescribing the form and content of a notice to commence collective bargaining; (e) prescribing the form and content of a notice under section 71 and prescribing any additional information that is to be furnished with such a notice; (f) prescribing the form and content of a notice under section 87.2 and prescribing any additional information that is to be furnished with such a notice; (g) prescribing a time limit for the purposes of subsection 99.01(1), as well as rules respecting the Board’s jurisdiction, and the validity of a decision or order made by it, after the time limit; (h) [Repealed, 1998, c. 26, s. 51] (i) prescribing the form and content of any written request to the Minister under subsection 57(2) or (4) and prescribing any additional information that is to be furnished with such a request; (j) prescribing the manner in which and the time within which a copy of an order or decision referred to in section 59 shall be filed with the Minister; (k) prescribing the circumstances in which copies of orders and decisions filed with the Minister pursuant to section 59 may be examined by members of the public and the fees, if any, to be charged for providing copies thereof; and (l) prescribing the manner in which a report of a conciliation commissioner or a conciliation board may be released by the Minister to the parties to a dispute pursuant to paragraph 77(a)."

This section outlines a wide array of regulatory powers. The Governor in Council can establish procedures for communications with the Minister, specify formats for notices and reports, designate officers to send notices, prescribe the content of notices for collective bargaining and other purposes, set time limits for certain proceedings, and govern the public access to orders and decisions.

### Administrative Monetary Penalties

Subsection 111.01 specifically details regulations concerning administrative monetary penalties. It states:
"The Governor in Council may make regulations establishing an administrative monetary penalties scheme for the purpose of promoting compliance with subsections 94(4) and (6), including regulations (a) designating as a violation the contravention of subsection 94(4) or (6); (b) respecting the administrative monetary penalties that may be imposed for a violation, including in relation to (i) the amount, or range of amounts, of the administrative monetary penalties that may be imposed on employers or classes of employers, (ii) the factors to be taken into account in imposing an administrative monetary penalty, (iii) the payment of administrative monetary penalties that have been imposed, and (iv) the recovery, as a debt, of unpaid administrative monetary penalties; (c) respecting the persons or classes of persons who are considered a party to the violation and the amount, or range of amounts, of the administrative monetary penalties for which they are liable; (d) respecting what constitutes sufficient proof that a violation was committed; (e) respecting the powers, duties and functions of the Board and of any person or class of persons who may exercise powers or perform duties or functions with respect to the scheme, including the designation of such persons or classes of persons by the Board; (f) respecting the proceedings in respect of a violation, including in relation to (i) commencing the proceedings, (ii) the defences that may be available in respect of a violation, and (iii) the circumstances in which the proceedings may be brought to an end; and (g) respecting reviews or appeals of any orders or decisions in the proceedings."

This subsection empowers the Governor in Council to create a system for imposing administrative monetary penalties to encourage compliance with certain provisions of the Canada Labour Code. The regulations would cover aspects such as defining violations, determining penalty amounts, procedures for payment and recovery, identifying liable parties, establishing proof of violation, outlining the powers of the Board, and governing the proceedings for addressing violations.

### Delegation of Powers

Section 111.1 addresses the power of the Minister to delegate certain regulatory powers. It states:
"The Minister may delegate to the head of the Federal Mediation and Conciliation Service his or her powers of appointment under this Act."

This provision allows the Minister to transfer specific regulatory responsibilities to the head of the Federal Mediation and Conciliation Service. In this instance, the Minister can delegate the power to make regulations concerning the appointment of individuals to various bodies established under the Canada Labour Code.

individual_results.question: Who can the Minister delegate his or her powers of appointment under the Act to?
individual_results.answer:
## Delegation of Appointment Powers by the Minister

### General Delegation to Qualified Persons

The Minister has the power to delegate their appointment powers to "any qualified person or class of persons." This delegation is subject to any terms and conditions specified by the Minister.
"Subject to any terms and conditions specified by the Minister, the Minister may delegate to any qualified person or class of persons any of the powers, duties or functions the Minister is authorized to exercise or perform for the purposes of this Part."

This broad delegation allows the Minister to assign their appointment responsibilities to various individuals or groups, provided they meet the qualifications set by the Minister.

### Delegation to Provincial Bodies

The Minister can also enter into an agreement with any province or provincial body to delegate their appointment powers to a person employed by that province or provincial body. This delegation is subject to the approval of the Governor in Council.
"Subject to subsection (3), the Minister may, with the approval of the Governor in Council, enter into an agreement with any province or any provincial body specifying the terms and conditions under which the Minister may delegate to a person employed by that province or provincial body the powers, duties or functions that the Minister or the Head is authorized to exercise or perform for the purposes of this Part."

This provision facilitates collaboration with provincial entities in the appointment process, allowing the Minister to assign their powers to individuals within the provincial government.

### Delegation to the Head

The Head also has the power to delegate their appointment powers to "any qualified person or class of persons." This delegation is also subject to any terms and conditions specified by the Head.
"Subject to any terms and conditions specified by the Minister, the Head may delegate to any qualified person or class of persons any of the powers the Head is authorized to exercise or any of the duties or functions the Head is authorized to perform for the purposes of this Part. The Head may make the delegation subject to any terms and conditions that the Head considers appropriate."

This mirrors the Minister's delegation power, extending it to the Head of the Board.

### Certificate of Authority

When powers, duties, or functions have been delegated, the Minister or the Head may provide the person to whom the delegation was made with a certificate of authority. This certificate must be shown to anyone who asks to see it when exercising those delegated powers.
"The Minister may provide any person to whom powers, duties or functions have been delegated under subsection (1), or under an agreement entered into under subsection (2), with a certificate of authority and, when exercising those powers or performing those duties or functions, that person shall show the certificate to any person who asks to see it."

This certificate serves as proof of the delegation and authorizes the person to exercise the delegated powers.

### Limitation of Liability

A person to whom powers, duties, or functions have been delegated is not personally liable for anything done or omitted to be done by them in good faith in the actual or purported exercise of those powers or performance of those duties or functions.
"A person to whom powers, duties or functions have been delegated under subsection (1) or (1.1), or under an agreement entered into under subsection (2), is not personally liable for anything done or omitted to be done by them in good faith in the actual or purported exercise of those powers or performance of those duties or functions."

This provision protects the delegate from personal liability for actions taken while exercising the delegated powers.

individual_results.question: What is the evidentiary status of documents purporting to be orders or decisions of the Board or certificates from the Minister or an official of the Federal Mediation and Conciliation Service in a court of law?
individual_results.answer:
## Evidentiary Status of Documents Purporting to be Orders or Decisions and Certificates

### Documents Purporting to be Orders or Decisions of the Board

#### General Admissibility
"Any document purporting to contain or to be a copy of any order or decision of the Board and purporting to be signed by a member of the Board is admissible in any court in evidence without proof of the signature or official character of the person appearing to have signed the document and without further proof thereof." This section clearly establishes the evidentiary status of documents claiming to be orders or decisions of the Board. It states that such documents are admissible in court as evidence
"...without proof of the signature or official character of the person appearing to have signed the document and without further proof thereof." This means that the court will accept the document as evidence simply because it "purports to contain or to be a copy" of an order or decision and
"...to be signed by a member of the Board..." The document does not need to have its signature or official character independently verified.

#### Further Explanation

The quote emphasizes the relaxed evidentiary standard applied to such documents. The court does not require additional proof of the signature or the official capacity of the person who signed the document. This provision likely aims to streamline legal proceedings by allowing the use of readily available copies of orders and decisions without the need for extensive authentication procedures.

### Certificates from the Minister or an Official of the Federal Mediation and Conciliation Service

#### General Admissibility
"A certificate purporting to be signed by the Minister or an official of the Federal Mediation and Conciliation Service stating that a report, request or notice was or was not received or given by the Minister pursuant to this Part and, if so received or given, stating the date on which it was so received or given, is admissible in any court in evidence without proof of the signature or official character of the person appearing to have signed the certificate and without further proof thereof." This section similarly grants admissibility to certificates issued by the Minister or an official of the Federal Mediation and Conciliation Service. It specifies that such certificates, "purporting to be signed" by the designated individuals and stating the receipt or delivery of a report, request, or notice, are admissible in court as evidence
"...without proof of the signature or official character of the person appearing to have signed the certificate and without further proof thereof."

#### Further Explanation

The evidentiary status of these certificates mirrors that of the documents purporting to be orders or decisions. The court will accept the certificate as evidence based on its "purporting to be signed" by the Minister or an official of the Federal Mediation and Conciliation Service and its stated information regarding the receipt or delivery of a document. No further proof of the signature or official capacity of the person who signed the certificate is required. This provision likely serves to facilitate the tracking and verification of communications between the Minister and the Federal Mediation and Conciliation Service.

## Effect of Defect in Form or Technical Irregularity on a Proceeding under Part I of the Canada Labour Code

### Section 114: No Proceeding Invalid Due to Defect in Form

#### Summary
Section 114 of the Canada Labour Code explicitly states that a defect in form or a technical irregularity does not invalidate a proceeding under Part I. This provision ensures that proceedings are not dismissed or rendered void based on minor procedural flaws.

#### Analysis
The section clearly articulates the consequence of such defects:
"No proceeding under this Part is invalid by reason only of a defect in form or a technical irregularity." This means that even if a proceeding contains a minor procedural error, it will not be deemed invalid. The focus remains on the substantive issues being addressed in the proceeding.

### Section 113: Late Report Not Invalid

#### Summary
While not directly addressing defects in form, Section 113 provides a related principle. It clarifies that a failure of a conciliation officer, commissioner, or board to report to the Minister within a specified timeframe does not invalidate the proceeding or terminate their authority. This suggests a degree of flexibility in procedural adherence, where minor delays do not necessarily jeopardize the progress of the proceeding.

#### Analysis
The section states,
"The failure of a conciliation officer, conciliation commissioner or conciliation board to report to the Minister within a period limited by this Part does not invalidate the proceeding or terminate the authority of the conciliation officer, conciliation commissioner or conciliation board." This indicates that procedural timelines are not rigidly enforced to the point of invalidating proceedings due to minor reporting delays. The emphasis is on the overall progress and authority of the conciliation body.

In essence, both Section 113 and Section 114 contribute to a procedural flexibility within Part I of the Canada Labour Code. Section 114 directly addresses defects in form, stating they are not invalidating, while Section 113 provides a related principle by clarifying that minor reporting delays do not jeopardize the proceeding. These provisions ensure that proceedings are not dismissed based on minor procedural imperfections.

individual_results.question: What is required of each party to a collective agreement immediately after it is executed?
individual_results.answer:
## Obligations of Parties to a Collective Agreement Immediately After Execution

### Filing of Orders and Decisions

Section 59 of the Canada Labour Code outlines the obligation of each party to a collective agreement to file any orders or decisions made by an arbitrator or arbitration board with the Minister.
"A copy of every order or decision of an arbitrator or arbitration board shall be filed with the Minister by the arbitrator or arbitration board chairperson and shall be available to the public in circumstances prescribed by the Governor in Council."

This requirement ensures transparency and public access to the rulings made by arbitrators and arbitration boards, which are integral to the enforcement of collective agreements.

### Implementation of the Determination

Section 79(1) addresses the agreement between an employer and a bargaining agent to refer any matter concerning the renewal or revision of a collective agreement to a person or body for final and binding determination.
"Despite any other provision of this Part, an employer and a bargaining agent may agree in writing, as part of a collective agreement or otherwise, to refer any matter respecting the renewal or revision of a collective agreement or the entering into of a new collective agreement to a person or body for final and binding determination."

This agreement suspends the right to strike or lockout and constitutes a commitment to implement the determination. This means that once a binding determination is reached, both parties are obligated to adhere to its terms.

### Application of the Federal Public Sector Labour Relations Act

Section 47.1 details the application of the Federal Public Sector Labour Relations Act to any terms and conditions of employment continued or resumed in force after a deletion or severance.
"(b) the Federal Public Sector Labour Relations Act applies in all respects to the interpretation and application of any term or condition continued or resumed by paragraph (a); (c) on application by the corporation or business, as employer, or the bargaining agent for those employees, made during the period beginning on the one hundred and twentieth day and ending on the one hundred and fiftieth day after the date of the deletion or severance, the Board shall make an order determining (i) whether the employees of the corporation or business who are represented by the bargaining agent constitute one or more units appropriate for collective bargaining, and (ii) which trade union shall be the bargaining agent for the employees in each such unit; (d) where the Board makes the determinations under paragraph (c), the corporation or business, as employer, or the bargaining agent may, by notice, require the other to commence collective bargaining under this Act for the purpose of entering into a collective agreement; and (e) this Part, other than section 80, applies in respect of a notice given under paragraph (d)."

This provision clarifies that the Federal Public Sector Labour Relations Act governs the interpretation and application of any terms and conditions of employment that are carried over or reinstated after a change in the employer's structure. This ensures consistency and predictability in the application of labour relations law.

### Collective Bargaining Requirements

Section 48 outlines the obligation of the bargaining agent to commence collective bargaining for the purpose of entering into a collective agreement when the Board has certified a bargaining agent and no collective agreement is in force.
"Where the Board has certified a bargaining agent for a bargaining unit and no collective agreement binding on the employees in the bargaining unit is in force, the bargaining agent may, by notice, require the employer of those employees, or the employer may, by notice, require the bargaining agent to commence collective bargaining for the purpose of entering into a collective agreement."

This requirement ensures that collective bargaining is initiated promptly after a bargaining agent is certified and a collective agreement is not yet in effect. This process is essential for establishing a legally binding agreement between the employer and the bargaining agent.

"The members of an Industrial Inquiry Commission, the members of a conciliation board and every person not employed in the federal public administration who acts as a conciliation officer or conciliation commissioner or who functions under this Part in any other capacity at the request of the Minister, except as an arbitrator or arbitration board chairperson, shall be paid such remuneration and expenses as may be fixed by the Governor in Council by regulation or by order."

### Section 118: Witness Fees and Expenses

This indicates that the witness fee is based on the standard rates applicable to witnesses in civil court proceedings within the relevant province. The provision applies to anyone

"...entitled to be paid by the employer at the employee’s regular rate of wages for the time spent at the proceeding that would otherwise have been time at work." This means that the employee is compensated for the time they spend at the proceeding, which would have otherwise been considered regular work time. The payment is made at their "regular rate of wages," ensuring that they are not financially disadvantaged by their attendance as a witness.

individual_results.question: Who is protected from being required to give evidence in civil actions or proceedings, and what type of information are they protected from disclosing?
individual_results.answer:
## Individuals Protected from Giving Evidence in Civil Actions

### Individuals Generally Not Required to Give Evidence

Section 119(1) of the Canada Labour Code states,
"No member of a conciliation board or no conciliation officer, conciliation commissioner, officer or employee employed in the federal public administration or person appointed by the Board or the Minister under this Part shall be required to give evidence in any civil action, suit or other proceeding respecting information obtained in the discharge of their duties under this Part." This provision broadly protects individuals holding specific roles within the conciliation and administrative tribunals system, as well as those appointed to assist the Board. The protection extends to information gathered while performing their duties under this Part of the Canada Labour Code.

Section 119.1 further clarifies this protection by stating,
"For greater certainty, the following may not be disclosed without the consent of the person who made them: (a) notes or draft orders or decisions of the Board or any of its members, of an external adjudicator or of an arbitrator or arbitration board chairperson appointed by the Minister under this Part; and (b) notes or draft reports of persons appointed by the Minister under this Part to assist in resolving disputes or differences, or of persons authorized or designated by the Board to assist in resolving complaints or issues in dispute before the Board." This section explicitly protects specific types of information from disclosure without consent, including internal Board documents and reports from appointed individuals.

### Individuals Not Required to Give Evidence in Civil Actions or Proceedings Respecting Information Obtained in the Discharge of Their Duties Under This Part

Section 119(1.1) expands on this protection by stating,
"No member of the Board or no external adjudicator shall be required to give evidence in any civil action, suit or other proceeding respecting information obtained in the discharge of their duties under this Act." This provision extends the protection to Board members and external adjudicators, ensuring they are not compelled to testify in civil actions regarding information obtained while performing their duties under the Canada Labour Code.

Section 119(2) further clarifies this by stating,
"Neither the Chief Administrator nor an employee of the Administrative Tribunals Support Service of Canada shall be required to give evidence in any civil action, suit or other proceeding respecting information obtained in the discharge of their duties in providing services to the Board." This protection extends to the Chief Administrator and employees of the Administrative Tribunals Support Service of Canada, ensuring they are not required to give evidence in civil actions regarding information obtained while providing services to the Board.

### Individuals Not Required to Give Evidence in Civil Actions or Proceedings Respecting Information Obtained in the Discharge of Their Duties Under This Part

Section 119(3) provides additional protection by stating,
"No person to whom powers, duties or functions have been delegated under subsection 140(1) or (1.1), or under an agreement entered into under subsection 140(2), and no person who has accompanied or assisted that person in exercising those powers or performing those duties or functions may be required to give testimony in civil or administrative proceedings, other than proceedings under this Part, with regard to information obtained in exercising those powers or performing those duties or functions, except with the written permission of the Head, in which case subsection (5) does not apply to restrict the disclosure of the information." This provision protects individuals who have been delegated powers or functions under specific agreements, as well as those who have assisted in exercising those powers or performing those duties. The protection extends to information obtained while performing these delegated powers or functions, except with the written permission of the Head.

Section 119(4) further clarifies this protection by stating,
"Subject to subsection (4), the Head, an external adjudicator or a member of the Board who is admitted to a work place under the powers conferred by section 141 — or a person who is admitted to a work place under the powers conferred by section 141 that are delegated to them under subsection 140(1.1) or under an agreement entered into under subsection 140(2) — and any person accompanying them, shall not disclose to any person any information obtained in the work place by the Head, external adjudicator or member or person with regard to any secret process or trade secret, except for the purposes of this Part or as required by law." This provision protects individuals who have been admitted to a workplace under specific delegated powers, as well as those who have accompanied them, from disclosing information obtained while performing those delegated powers, except for the purposes of this Part or as required by law.

### Types of Information Protected from Disclosure

The individuals protected from giving evidence are shielded from disclosing a wide range of information obtained while performing their duties under this Part of the Canada Labour Code. This includes:

*   Notes or draft orders or decisions of the Board or any of its members, of an external adjudicator or of an arbitrator or arbitration board chairperson appointed by the Minister under this Part.
*   Notes or draft reports of persons appointed by the Minister under this Part to assist in resolving disputes or differences, or of persons authorized or designated by the Board to assist in resolving complaints or issues in dispute before the Board.
*   Information obtained while performing delegated powers or functions under specific agreements.
*   Information obtained while admitted to a workplace under specific delegated powers, as well as those who have accompanied them, regarding secret processes or trade secrets, except for the purposes of this Part or as required by law.

In essence, the Canada Labour Code provides broad protection to individuals holding specific roles within the conciliation and administrative tribunals system, as well as those appointed to assist the Board, from being required to give evidence in civil actions or proceedings respecting information obtained while performing their duties under this Part. The types of information protected from disclosure are extensive, encompassing internal Board documents, reports from appointed individuals, information obtained while performing delegated powers, and information regarding secret processes or trade secrets.

individual_results.question: What is the purpose of an agreement that can be made between the Government of Canada and a provincial government under the Canada Labour Code?
individual_results.answer:
## Purpose of Agreements Between the Government of Canada and Provincial Governments

### Administration of Provincial Legislation by Federal Officers
"Where this Part and legislation enacted by the legislature of a province are substantially uniform, the Minister may, on behalf of the Government of Canada, with the approval of the Governor in Council, enter into an agreement with the government of the province to provide for the administration of the legislation of the province by officers and employees employed in the federal public administration."

This section outlines the primary purpose of an agreement that can be made between the Government of Canada and a provincial government under the Canada Labour Code. It states that when provincial legislation is substantially similar to federal legislation, the Minister can enter into an agreement with the provincial government to allow federal officers and employees to administer that provincial legislation. This arrangement aims to streamline the administrative process and potentially reduce duplication of effort.

### Administration by Canada or Provincial Government
"An agreement made pursuant to subsection (1) in respect of the administration of any legislation of a province may provide (a) for the administration by Canada of the legislation of the province with respect to any particular work, undertaking or business; (b) that the Minister may, on behalf of the province, exercise the powers conferred or perform the duties imposed under the legislation of the province; (c) that the members of the Board, or officers and employees employed in the federal public administration, may exercise the powers conferred or perform the duties imposed under the legislation of the province; and (d) for payment by the government of the province to the Government of Canada for expenses incurred by the Government of Canada in the administration of the legislation of the province."

This subsection elaborates on the potential provisions of such an agreement. It specifies that the agreement can authorize Canada to administer the provincial legislation for specific work, undertakings, or businesses. Alternatively, it can empower the Minister to act on behalf of the province, or allow Board members or federal public administration officers to exercise provincial powers. Furthermore, it addresses the financial aspect, stating that the provincial government can compensate the federal government for expenses incurred in administering the provincial legislation.

### Exercise of Provincial Powers by Federal Officials
"Where an agreement has been entered into between the Government of Canada and the government of a province in respect of any legislation of the province, the Minister, the members of the Board and any officers or employees employed in the federal public administration may, if the legislation so provides and the Governor in Council so orders, exercise the powers and perform the duties specified in the legislation or agreement."

This final subsection clarifies the practical implications of such an agreement. It states that once an agreement is in place, federal officials can exercise the powers and perform the duties outlined in the provincial legislation or the agreement itself, provided the legislation permits and the Governor in Council approves. This provision ensures that federal authorities can effectively administer provincial legislation when it is substantially uniform with federal law.

## Circumstances for Directing Application of Part I of the Canada Labour Code

### General Authority of the Governor in Council

The Governor in Council possesses the authority to direct the application of Part I of the Canada Labour Code through regulation. This power is explicitly stated in Section 158 of the Canada Labour Code:
"The Governor in Council may, by regulation, direct that this Part applies in respect of any employment, or any class or classes of employment, on or in connection with a federal work, undertaking or business set out in the regulation that is, or is part of, a corporation that is an agent of Her Majesty in right of a province, including a corporation whose activities are regulated, in whole or in part, under the Nuclear Safety and Control Act..."

This broad directive allows the Governor in Council to tailor the application of Part I to specific contexts, particularly those involving federal work, undertakings, or businesses that are agents of a province and subject to the Nuclear Safety and Control Act.

### Specific Circumstances: Provincial Crown Corporations

Section 265 of the Canada Labour Code elaborates on one such circumstance:
"The Governor in Council may by regulation direct that this Part applies in respect of any employment, or any class or classes of employment, on or in connection with a work or undertaking set out in the regulation that is, or is part of, a corporation that is an agent of Her Majesty in right of a province and whose activities are regulated, in whole or in part, pursuant to the Nuclear Safety and Control Act..."

This section specifically addresses the application of Part I to provincial Crown corporations that are agents of a province and regulated under the Nuclear Safety and Control Act. It mirrors the general authority outlined in Section 158 but focuses on this particular type of entity.

### Exclusion from Application

Conversely, Section 266 of the Canada Labour Code also grants the Governor in Council the authority to exclude certain employment from the application of Part I through regulation:
"(1) The Governor in Council may by regulation exclude, in whole or in part, from the application of any of the provisions of this Part any employment, or any class or classes of employment, on or in connection with a work or undertaking set out in the regulation whose activities are regulated, in whole or in part, pursuant to the Nuclear Safety and Control Act..."

This provision provides the Governor in Council with the power to create exceptions to the general application of Part I, again with a specific focus on provincial Crown corporations regulated under the Nuclear Safety and Control Act.

### Application to Federal Work, Undertakings, and Businesses

Section 4 of the Canada Labour Code outlines the general application of Part I:
"This Part applies in respect of employees who are employed on or in connection with the operation of any federal work, undertaking or business, in respect of the employers of all such employees in their relations with those employees and in respect of trade unions and employers’ organizations composed of those employees or employers."

This section establishes the baseline application of Part I to employees working on or in connection with federal work, undertakings, or businesses, as well as to the employers and trade unions involved in those operations. The Governor in Council's power to direct application through regulation then allows for further tailoring of this baseline to specific situations, such as those involving provincial Crown corporations regulated under the Nuclear Safety and Control Act.

The ability to incorporate provincial laws through regulation further strengthens the connection between this regulatory power and employment in the nuclear sector. It allows for the harmonization of certain labour laws between the federal and provincial levels within this industry, potentially creating a more consistent and predictable labour environment.

In essence, section 121.2 of the Canada Labour Code empowers the Governor in Council to adapt the general Canada Labour Code provisions to the specific needs and regulations of the nuclear sector through targeted regulatory exclusions and the incorporation of provincial laws.
