individual_results.question: What happens to a collective agreement and a bargaining agent when a new regulation is made under the Canada Labour Code that applies to the employees represented by the bargaining agent?
individual_results.answer:
## Effect of Certification on Collective Agreements and Bargaining Agents

### Section 36(1) of the Canada Labour Code
"Where a trade union is certified as the bargaining agent for a bargaining unit, (a) the trade union so certified has exclusive authority to bargain collectively on behalf of the employees in the bargaining unit; (b) the certification of any trade union that was previously certified as the bargaining agent for any employees in the bargaining unit is deemed to be revoked to the extent that the certification relates to those employees; (c) the trade union so certified is substituted as a party to any collective agreement that affects any employees in the bargaining unit, to the extent that the collective agreement relates to those employees, in the place of the bargaining agent named in the collective agreement or any successor thereto; and (d) the trade union so certified is deemed to be the bargaining agent for the purposes of paragraph 50(b)."

This section directly addresses the impact of a new certification on existing collective agreements and bargaining agents. When a new union is certified, the previous certification is revoked to the extent it relates to those employees. The newly certified union is then substituted as a party to any existing collective agreement that covers those employees. This means the new union takes over the exclusive authority to bargain collectively on behalf of those employees, and it becomes the primary party responsible for renewing or revising the collective agreement.

### Section 56 of the Canada Labour Code
"A collective agreement entered into between a bargaining agent and an employer in respect of a bargaining unit is, subject to and for the purposes of this Part, binding on the bargaining agent, every employee in the bargaining unit and the employer."

This section clarifies the binding nature of collective agreements. It states that any collective agreement reached between a bargaining agent and an employer is binding on the bargaining agent, every employee in the bargaining unit, and the employer. This is a crucial point because it ensures that the new certification effectively transfers the responsibility for bargaining to the newly certified union, and the existing collective agreement is now binding on that union.

### Section 24(1) of the Canada Labour Code
"A trade union seeking to be certified as the bargaining agent for a unit that the trade union considers constitutes a unit appropriate for collective bargaining may, subject to this section and any regulations made by the Board under paragraph 15(e), apply to the Board for certification as the bargaining agent for the unit."

This section outlines the process for a new union to seek certification. It states that a trade union can apply to the Board for certification as the bargaining agent for a unit it considers appropriate for collective bargaining. This application can be made at various times, depending on the status of the existing collective agreement.

### Section 24(2) of the Canada Labour Code
"Subject to subsection (3), an application by a trade union for certification as the bargaining agent for a unit may be made (a) where no collective agreement applicable to the unit is in force and no trade union has been certified under this Part as the bargaining agent for the unit, at any time; (b) where no collective agreement applicable to the unit is in force but a trade union has been certified under this Part as the bargaining agent for the unit, after the expiration of twelve months from the date of that certification or, with the consent of the Board, at any earlier time; (c) where a collective agreement applicable to the unit is in force and is for a term of not more than three years, only after the commencement of the last three months of its operation; and (d) where a collective agreement applicable to the unit is in force and is for a term of more than three years, only after the commencement of the thirty-fourth month of its operation and before the commencement of the thirty-seventh month of its operation and, thereafter, only (i) during the three month period immediately preceding the end of each year that the collective agreement continues to operate after the third year of its operation, and (ii) after the commencement of the last three months of its operation."

This section provides further details on when a new union can apply for certification. It specifies that an application can be made at any time if there is no existing collective agreement or no previously certified union. If there is an existing collective agreement, an application can be made after twelve months from the date of the previous certification, or earlier with the Board's consent. It also outlines specific timeframes for applications based on the remaining term of the existing collective agreement.

### Section 24(3) of the Canada Labour Code
"An application for certification under subsection (2) in respect of a unit must not, except with the consent of the Board, be made during a strike or lockout that is not prohibited by this Part and that involves employees in the unit."

This section prohibits new certification applications during certain types of industrial action. It states that an application cannot be made during a strike or lockout that is not prohibited by the Part and that involves employees in the unit, unless the Board consents.

### Section 24(4) of the Canada Labour Code
"Where an application by a trade union for certification as the bargaining agent for a unit is made in accordance with this section, no employer of employees in the unit shall, after notification that the application has been made, alter the rates of pay, any other term or condition of employment or any right or privilege of such employees until (a) the application has been withdrawn by the trade union or dismissed by the Board, or (b) thirty days have elapsed after the day on which the Board certifies the trade union as the bargaining agent for the unit, except pursuant to a collective agreement or with the consent of the Board."

This section outlines the employer's obligations during the certification process. It states that employers cannot alter employees' terms and conditions of employment after being notified of the application until the application is withdrawn, dismissed, or the Board certifies the new union. Exceptions are made for changes pursuant to a collective agreement or with the Board's consent.

### Section 24(5) of the Canada Labour Code
"An employer representative shall be deemed to be an employer for the purposes of this Part and, by virtue of having been appointed under this section, has the power to, and shall, discharge all the duties and responsibilities of an employer under this Part on behalf of all the employers of the employees in the bargaining unit, including the power to enter into a collective agreement on behalf of those employers."

This section clarifies the role of the employer representative. It states that the employer representative is deemed to be an employer for the purposes of this Part and has the authority to enter into a collective agreement on behalf of all employers in the bargaining unit.

### Section 56 of the Canada Labour Code
"A collective agreement entered into between a bargaining agent and an employer in respect of a bargaining unit is, subject to and for the purposes of this Part, binding on the bargaining agent, every employee in the bargaining unit and the employer."

This section reiterates the binding nature of collective agreements. It emphasizes that any collective agreement reached between a bargaining agent and an employer is binding on the bargaining agent, every employee in the bargaining unit, and the employer. This is a crucial point because it ensures that the new certification effectively transfers the responsibility for bargaining to the newly certified union, and the existing collective agreement is now binding on that union.

### Section 36(1) of the Canada Labour Code
"Where a trade union is certified as the bargaining agent for a bargaining unit, (a) the trade union so certified has exclusive authority to bargain collectively on behalf of the employees in the bargaining unit; (b) the certification of any trade union that was previously certified as the bargaining agent for any employees in the bargaining unit is deemed to be revoked to the extent that the certification relates to those employees; (c) the trade union so certified is substituted as a party to any collective agreement that affects any employees in the bargaining unit, to the extent that the collective agreement relates to those employees, in the place of the bargaining agent named in the collective agreement or any successor thereto; and (d) the trade union so certified is deemed to be the bargaining agent for the purposes of paragraph 50(b)."

This section directly addresses the effect of certification on existing collective agreements and bargaining agents. When a new union is certified, the previous certification is revoked to the extent it relates to those employees. The newly certified union is then substituted as a party to any existing collective agreement that covers those employees. This means the new union takes over the exclusive authority to bargain collectively on behalf of those employees, and it becomes the primary party responsible for renewing or revising the collective agreement.

### Section 36(2) of the Canada Labour Code
"Subsection (2) does not apply to a trade union certified as a result of an application made under section 24.1."

This section provides an exception to the rule regarding the substitution of the new union as a party to the collective agreement. It states that this exception does not apply to a trade union certified as a result of an application made under section 24.1.

individual_results.question: What is the primary goal of preventive measures in the workplace according to the Canada Labour Code?
individual_results.answer:
## Primary Goal of Preventive Measures in the Workplace

### Section 122.2: Preventive Measures

#### The Hierarchical Approach
"Preventive measures should consist first of the elimination of hazards, then the reduction of hazards and finally, the provision of personal protective equipment, clothing, devices or materials, all with the goal of ensuring the health and safety of employees."

This passage from Section 122.2 outlines the hierarchical approach to preventive measures in the workplace. It emphasizes that the most effective preventive measures are those that eliminate hazards altogether. If elimination is not feasible, the next step is to reduce the hazards. Finally, personal protective equipment (PPE) is provided as a last resort to protect employees from remaining risks. The overarching goal of all preventive measures is "ensuring the health and safety of employees."

### Section 122.1: Purpose of Part

#### Broad Prevention Objective
"The purpose of this Part is to prevent accidents, occurrences of harassment and violence and physical or psychological injuries and illnesses arising out of, linked with or occurring in the course of employment to which this Part applies."

This section, which defines the overall purpose of Part II of the Canada Labour Code, directly addresses the goal of preventive measures. It states that the primary objective is to
"...prevent accidents, occurrences of harassment and violence and physical or psychological injuries and illnesses..." This broad preventive aim encompasses all aspects of workplace health and safety, from physical dangers to psychological harm.

### Section 122.21(1): Head of Compliance and Enforcement

#### Role of the Head
"The Minister may designate a person as Head of Compliance and Enforcement."

While this section focuses on the role of the Head of Compliance and Enforcement, it indirectly supports the goal of preventive measures. The Head is responsible for ensuring compliance with the Code's preventive requirements, including the implementation of hazard elimination and reduction strategies.

### Section 122.2: Further Preventive Measures

#### Specific Preventive Measures
"Preventive measures should consist first of the elimination of hazards, then the reduction of hazards and finally, the provision of personal protective equipment, clothing, devices or materials, all with the goal of ensuring the health and safety of employees."

This reiterates the hierarchical approach to preventive measures, emphasizing the importance of hazard elimination and reduction as the primary goals. It also acknowledges the role of PPE as a supplementary measure. The ultimate aim of all preventive measures is to "ensuring the health and safety of employees."

In summary, the primary goal of preventive measures in the workplace according to the Canada Labour Code is to prevent accidents, occurrences of harassment and violence, and physical or psychological injuries and illnesses. This is achieved through a hierarchical approach that prioritizes hazard elimination and reduction, followed by the provision of PPE as a last resort. The overarching aim is to ensure the health and safety of all employees.

individual_results.question: How must employers provide direction, notice, information, instruction, or training to employees who have a condition that impairs their ability to receive information through standard communication methods?
individual_results.answer:
## Communication with Employees Having Special Needs

### Methods of Communication

Section 122.3(1) of the Canada Labour Code outlines the methods employers must use to provide direction, notice, information, instruction, or training to employees with special needs. It states:
"An employee with a special need shall be given any direction, notice, information, instruction or training that is required to be given to employees under this Part by any method of communication that readily permits the employee to receive it, including braille, large print, audio tape, computer disk, sign language and verbal communication."

This section emphasizes the requirement for employers to utilize a variety of communication methods to ensure that all employees can access necessary information. It specifically lists several examples, including
"...braille, large print, audio tape, computer disk, sign language and verbal communication." This demonstrates a proactive approach to accommodating employees with different abilities.

### Defining Special Needs

Section 122.3(2) provides a definition of what constitutes a "special need" for communication purposes:
"For the purposes of this section, an employee has a special need if the employee is affected by a condition that impairs their ability to receive any direction, notice, information, instruction or training given by a method that would otherwise be sufficient under this Part."

This definition clarifies that an employee has a special need if their condition
"...impairs their ability to receive any direction, notice, information, instruction or training given by a method that would otherwise be sufficient under this Part." This ensures that employers are required to adapt their communication methods only when necessary to accommodate specific impairments.

In essence, employers must provide direction, notice, information, instruction, or training to employees with special needs using any method of communication that "readily permits the employee to receive it." The Code provides a comprehensive list of such methods and a clear definition of what constitutes a "special need" to guide employers in their communication practices.

## Scope of Part II of the Canada Labour Code (Occupational Health and Safety)

### Types of Employment Subject to Part II

Part II of the Canada Labour Code applies to a wide range of employment situations.

#### Employment on or in Connection with Federal Work, Undertaking or Business
"Notwithstanding any other Act of Parliament or any regulations thereunder, this Part applies to and in respect of employment (a) on or in connection with the operation of any federal work, undertaking or business other than a work, undertaking or business of a local or private nature in Yukon, the Northwest Territories or Nunavut..."

This section clearly states that Part II applies to employment directly related to the operation of any federal work, undertaking, or business. It specifically excludes employment within local or private ventures in the territories.

#### Employment by a Corporation Established for Federal Government Functions
"...by a corporation established to perform any function or duty on behalf of the Government of Canada..."

This provision extends Part II's applicability to employment within corporations specifically created to carry out functions or duties for the federal government.

#### Employment by a Canadian Carrier Acting as an Agent of Her Majesty in Right of a Province
"...by a Canadian carrier, as defined in section 2 of the Telecommunications Act , that is an agent of Her Majesty in right of a province."

Part II also covers employment by Canadian carriers that are acting as agents of the federal government in right of a province.

#### Employment within the Federal Public Administration
"This Part applies to the federal public administration and to persons employed in the federal public administration to the extent provided for under Part 3 of the Federal Public Sector Labour Relations Act..."

This section explicitly states that Part II applies to employment within the federal public administration, with further details provided in Part 3 of the Federal Public Sector Labour Relations Act.

#### Employment Under the Public Service Employment Act
"This Part applies to persons appointed under subsection 128(1) of the Public Service Employment Act , other than persons appointed by a person holding the recognized position of Leader of the Opposition in the Senate or Leader of the Opposition in the House of Commons, and to their employer."

Part II also applies to individuals appointed under the Public Service Employment Act, with a specific exclusion for those appointed by the Leaders of the Opposition.

#### Activities Performed for an Employer to Which Part II Applies
"This Part applies to any person who is not an employee but who performs for an employer to which this Part applies activities whose primary purpose is to enable the person to acquire knowledge or experience, and to the employer, as if that person were an employee of the employer, and every provision of this Part must be read accordingly."

This provision broadens the scope to include individuals who are not formal employees but are performing activities for an employer to which Part II applies, with the intent of gaining knowledge or experience.

### Entities Subject to Part II

Part II applies to various entities, including federal works, undertakings, businesses, corporations established for federal government functions, Canadian carriers acting as agents of Her Majesty in right of a province, the federal public administration, and employers to which Part II applies.

individual_results.question: Who bears the burden of proof in a proceeding to determine if a person is an employee of an employer under the Canada Labour Code?
individual_results.answer:
## Burden of Proof in Determining Employee Status

### General Rule

According to Section 167.2 of the Canada Labour Code, the burden of proof rests on the employer when they allege that a person is not their employee. This means that if an employer claims that a worker is an independent contractor, they must present sufficient evidence to support that claim.
"If, in any proceeding under this Part other than a prosecution, or in any proceeding under Part IV in respect of a violation that is related to this Part, an employer alleges that a person is not their employee, the burden of proof is on the employer."

This statement clearly establishes the employer's responsibility to prove that a worker is not an employee. The presumption of employee status, as outlined in Section 167.01, further reinforces this burden.

### Exceptions

Section 167.1 of the Canada Labour Code prohibits an employer from treating an employee as if they were not their employee. This exception does not alter the general rule regarding the burden of proof. It simply clarifies that an employer cannot attempt to deny employee status without providing evidence to the contrary.

### Presumption of Employee Status

Section 167.01(1) states that
"A person who is paid remuneration by an employer is presumed to be their employee unless the contrary is proved by the employer." This presumption is a significant factor in determining employee status. It places the onus on the employer to demonstrate that a worker is an independent contractor.
"A person who is paid remuneration by an employer is presumed to be their employee unless the contrary is proved by the employer."

This presumption is consistently reiterated throughout the documents, emphasizing the employer's burden of proof.

### Additional Considerations

Section 167.2 further clarifies the burden of proof in proceedings other than prosecutions. It states that "the burden of proof is on the employer." This applies to any proceeding under Part IV of the Canada Labour Code that is related to a violation of this Part.
"If, in any proceeding under this Part other than a prosecution, or in any proceeding under Part IV in respect of a violation that is related to this Part, an employer alleges that a person is not their employee, the burden of proof is on the employer."

This provision reinforces the employer's responsibility to prove that a worker is not an employee in all relevant proceedings.

## General Responsibility of an Employer for Employee Health and Safety

### Section 124: General Duty of Employer

#### Summary
Section 124 of the Canada Labour Code establishes the fundamental responsibility of every employer to protect the health and safety of all employees. This section is presented as a broad, overarching duty.

#### Analysis
The text states,
"Every employer shall ensure that the health and safety at work of every person employed by the employer is protected." This quote directly addresses the general responsibility of an employer. The phrase
"...ensure that the health and safety at work of every person employed by the employer is protected." is a clear and concise articulation of this duty. It emphasizes the employer's proactive obligation to create and maintain a safe working environment for all employees. The use of the word "ensure" highlights the required level of commitment and action from the employer.

### Section 125: Specific Duties of Employer

#### Summary
Section 125 expands upon the general duty outlined in Section 124 by detailing a wide range of specific responsibilities that an employer must fulfill to safeguard employee health and safety.

#### Analysis
This section lists numerous duties, covering aspects from building standards and safety equipment to hazard identification, information provision, and emergency preparedness. It begins with the broad statement,
"Without restricting the generality of section 124, every employer shall, in respect of every work place controlled by the employer and, in respect of every work activity carried out by an employee in a work place that is not controlled by the employer, to the extent that the employer controls the activity, (a) ensure that all permanent and temporary buildings and structures meet the prescribed standards..." This quote reinforces the general duty by providing concrete examples of what that duty entails. It specifies areas such as building standards, safety equipment, hazard identification, information provision, and emergency preparedness.

Furthermore, the text emphasizes the employer's responsibility to provide information to employees, stating,
"(e) [Repealed, 2018, c. 22, s. 3] (f) if the information referred to in any of subparagraphs (d)(i) to (iii) is made available in electronic form, ensure that employees receive appropriate training to enable them to have access to the information and, on the request of an employee, make a printed copy of the information available..." This highlights the employer's obligation to ensure employees have access to relevant health and safety information.

The section also details duties related to hazard prevention, such as investigating accidents, maintaining records, and implementing safety codes. It further specifies responsibilities concerning personal protective equipment, emergency measures, and the provision of necessary facilities. The concluding part of Section 125 underscores the employer's role in fostering a culture of safety by ensuring employees are trained, informed, and empowered to protect their own health and safety.

individual_results.question: What are the primary responsibilities of an employer in relation to managing and controlling hazardous substances in the workplace?
individual_results.answer:
## Employer Responsibilities for Managing and Controlling Hazardous Substances

### General Responsibilities for Hazardous Substances

Employers bear significant responsibility for managing and controlling hazardous substances in the workplace. This encompasses a wide range of duties aimed at protecting employee health and safety.

#### Controlling Concentrations of Hazardous Substances
"...ensure that concentrations of hazardous substances in the work place are controlled in accordance with prescribed standards..."

This primary responsibility requires employers to actively manage the levels of hazardous substances present in the workplace. They must implement measures to keep these concentrations within acceptable limits, as defined by relevant safety standards. This could involve ventilation systems, engineering controls, or other methods to minimize exposure.

#### Storage and Handling of Hazardous Substances

Employers are also tasked with ensuring that all hazardous substances are stored and handled in a manner that prevents accidents and exposure.
"...ensure that all hazardous substances in the work place are stored and handled in the manner prescribed..."

This duty necessitates adherence to specific regulations and guidelines for the storage and handling of hazardous materials. This includes proper labeling, containment, and segregation to prevent spills, leaks, and unintended contact.

#### Identification of Hazardous Substances

Employers must ensure that all hazardous substances present in the workplace are clearly identified.
"...ensure that all hazardous substances in the work place, other than hazardous products, are identified in the manner prescribed..."

This involves implementing systems for labeling and documenting hazardous substances, making this information readily accessible to employees. This allows employees to understand the potential risks associated with the substances they may be exposed to.

#### Safety Data Sheets (SDS)

Employers are legally obligated to make Safety Data Sheets (SDS) available to all employees who may be exposed to hazardous products.
"...subject to the Hazardous Materials Information Review Act , make available to every employee, in the prescribed manner, a safety data sheet for each hazardous product to which the employee may be exposed that meets the requirements set out in the regulations made under subsection 15(1) of the Hazardous Products Act..."

SDS provide comprehensive information about the hazards of a substance, including its physical and chemical properties, health effects, safe handling procedures, and emergency measures. Making SDS readily available empowers employees to make informed decisions about their safety.

#### Exposure Investigation and Assessment

When employees may be exposed to hazardous substances, employers must investigate and assess the level of exposure.
"...where employees may be exposed to hazardous substances, investigate and assess the exposure in the manner prescribed, with the assistance of the work place committee or the health and safety representative..."

This involves conducting monitoring and evaluations to determine the extent of employee exposure. This information is crucial for implementing appropriate control measures.

#### Record Keeping and Employee Exposure Records

Employers are required to maintain detailed records of employee exposure to hazardous substances.
"...ensure that all records of exposure to hazardous substances are kept and maintained in the prescribed manner and that personal records of exposure are made available to the affected employees."

These records are essential for tracking employee health and safety over time and for identifying potential trends or issues. Providing employees with their personal exposure records promotes transparency and allows them to understand their own potential risks.

### Additional Employer Responsibilities

Beyond the specific duties related to hazardous substances, employers have broader responsibilities for workplace safety and health.

#### Hazardous Materials Information Review Act

Employers must comply with the Hazardous Materials Information Review Act, which governs the labeling and SDS requirements for hazardous products.
"...subject to the Hazardous Materials Information Review Act , ensure that each hazardous product in the work place or each container in the work place in which a hazardous product is contained has affixed to it, printed on it, attached to it or otherwise applied to it a label that meets the prescribed requirements..."

This act ensures that employees have access to the necessary information about the hazards of the substances they may be exposed to.

#### Work Place Committee and Health and Safety Representative Involvement

Employers must involve the work place committee and the health and safety representative in the management and control of hazardous substances.
"...investigate and assess the exposure in the manner prescribed, with the assistance of the work place committee or the health and safety representative..."

This collaborative approach leverages the expertise of these representatives to ensure that control measures are effective and meet the needs of employees.

#### Program for Hazard Prevention

Employers are required to develop, implement, and monitor a program for the prevention of hazards in the workplace.
"...develop, implement and monitor, in consultation with the policy committee or, if there is no policy committee, with the work place committee or the health and safety representative, a prescribed program for the prevention of hazards in the work place appropriate to its size and the nature of the hazards in it that also provides for the education of employees in health and safety matters..."

This program should address all types of workplace hazards, including those related to hazardous substances, and should include employee education components.

#### Consultation and Reporting

Employers must consult with the work place committee and the health and safety representative on the implementation and monitoring of hazard prevention programs and must respond to their recommendations in writing within thirty days.
"...consult with the work place committee or the health and safety representative on the implementation and monitoring of programs developed in consultation with the policy committee."

This ensures that all stakeholders are involved in the decision-making process and that control measures are effective.

individual_results.question: What are the responsibilities of an employer and a medical professional regarding the disclosure and confidentiality of information about hazardous products in emergency situations?
individual_results.answer:
## Employer and Medical Professional Responsibilities Regarding Hazardous Product Information in Emergencies

### Employer Responsibilities

#### Providing Information in Emergencies
"(e) subject to the Hazardous Materials Information Review Act , make available to every employee, in the prescribed manner, a safety data sheet for each hazardous product to which the employee may be exposed that meets the requirements set out in the regulations made under subsection 15(1) of the Hazardous Products Act ; (f) where employees may be exposed to hazardous substances, investigate and assess the exposure in the manner prescribed, with the assistance of the work place committee or the health and safety representative; and (g) ensure that all records of exposure to hazardous substances are kept and maintained in the prescribed manner and that personal records of exposure are made available to the affected employees." This section of the Canada Labour Code outlines the employer's broad responsibilities regarding hazardous products, including making safety data sheets (SDS) available to employees. Crucially, it also mandates that employers provide information to medical professionals in emergencies. The employer is required to
"...provide, in respect of any hazardous product to which an employee may be exposed, as soon as is practicable in the circumstances, any information that is included in the safety data sheet that is in the employer’s possession for the hazardous product to any physician or other prescribed medical professional who requests that information for the purpose of making a medical diagnosis of, or rendering medical treatment to, an employee in an emergency." This provision directly addresses the disclosure of hazardous product information in emergency situations.

#### Maintaining Confidentiality of Information Provided
"Any physician or other prescribed medical professional to whom information is provided by an employer pursuant to subsection (1) shall keep confidential any information specified by the employer as being confidential, except for the purpose for which it is provided." This subsection clarifies the medical professional's responsibility regarding the confidentiality of information received from the employer in emergencies. It states that the medical professional must maintain confidentiality for the specified information, except when it is necessary for the medical diagnosis or treatment of the injured employee. This ensures that sensitive information is protected while still allowing for appropriate medical care.

### Medical Professional Responsibilities

#### Requesting Information in Emergencies

The Canada Labour Code does not explicitly detail the medical professional's responsibilities regarding the disclosure of information in emergencies beyond the right to request it. However, the provision stating that the employer must provide information "as soon as is practicable in the circumstances" implies that the medical professional has the right to request the relevant information from the employer.

#### Maintaining Confidentiality of Information Received
"Any physician or other prescribed medical professional to whom information is provided by an employer pursuant to subsection (1) shall keep confidential any information specified by the employer as being confidential, except for the purpose for which it is provided." This subsection directly addresses the medical professional's obligation to maintain confidentiality of information received from the employer in emergency situations. The confidentiality is maintained
"...except for the purpose for which it is provided." meaning the medical professional can share the information with other medical professionals involved in the emergency care of the employee.

In summary, employers have a primary responsibility to ensure that hazardous product information, including SDS, is readily available to employees and to provide this information to medical professionals in emergency situations. Medical professionals, in turn, have the responsibility to request the necessary information from the employer and to maintain the confidentiality of any information the employer designates as confidential, except for the purpose of providing medical care to the injured employee.

### Hazardous Substances Management

Employers in coal mines bear significant responsibilities regarding the management of hazardous substances. This includes ensuring that concentrations of hazardous substances are controlled according to prescribed standards.
"...ensure that concentrations of hazardous substances in the work place are controlled in accordance with prescribed standards..."

This responsibility extends to the proper storage and handling of all hazardous substances.
"...ensure that all hazardous substances in the work place are stored and handled in the manner prescribed..."

Furthermore, employers must identify all hazardous substances in the workplace in the manner prescribed.
"...ensure that all hazardous substances in the work place, other than hazardous products, are identified in the manner prescribed..."

For hazardous products, employers are required to affix labels meeting prescribed requirements.
"...ensure that each hazardous product in the work place or each container in the work place in which a hazardous product is contained has affixed to it, printed on it, attached to it or otherwise applied to it a label that meets the prescribed requirements..."

Employers are also obligated to make safety data sheets (SDS) available to every employee who may be exposed to hazardous products.
"...make available to every employee, in the prescribed manner, a safety data sheet for each hazardous product to which the employee may be exposed that meets the requirements set out in the regulations made under subsection 15(1) of the Hazardous Products Act..."

Finally, when employees may be exposed to hazardous substances, employers must investigate and assess the exposure with the assistance of the workplace committee or the health and safety representative.
"...where employees may be exposed to hazardous substances, investigate and assess the exposure in the manner prescribed, with the assistance of the work place committee or the health and safety representative..."

All records of exposure to hazardous substances must be kept and maintained in the prescribed manner, and personal records of exposure must be made available to affected employees.
"...ensure that all records of exposure to hazardous substances are kept and maintained in the prescribed manner and that personal records of exposure are made available to the affected employees."

### Coal Mine Specific Requirements

Beyond general hazardous substances management, employers in coal mines have additional specific duties.

#### Plans and Procedures

Employers must submit plans and procedures relating to any activity for which the submission is prescribed to the Coal Mining Safety Commission for approval.
"...submit to the Coal Mining Safety Commission for approval, in the form and manner and at the time prescribed, plans and procedures relating to that activity and carry out the activity in conformity with plans and procedures as approved."

Employers are prohibited from requiring or permitting the use of any mining method, machinery, or equipment in respect of which no prescribed safety standards are applicable unless the use thereof has been approved.
"No employer shall require or permit the use in a coal mine of any mining method, machinery or equipment in respect of which no prescribed safety standards are applicable unless the use thereof has been approved pursuant to paragraph 137.2(2)(a)."

#### Searches for Prohibited Substances

Employers in coal mines are required to conduct personal searches of all persons entering underground portions of the mine who are not employed there, and a proportion of employees employed in the underground portions of the mine, to prevent the introduction of alcohol, smoking materials, and drugs.
"...require every person entering an underground portion of the mine who is not employed there to submit to a personal search conducted in the prescribed manner; and (b) require a proportion, not less than the prescribed proportion, of employees employed in the underground portions of the mine to submit to personal searches conducted in the prescribed manner."

#### Inspections and Tests

Employers must permit inspections and tests to be carried out on behalf of the employees, in any part of the mine and on any machinery or equipment therein, in the prescribed manner and at intervals not greater than the prescribed interval.
"...permit inspections and tests to be carried out on behalf of the employees, in any part of the mine and on any machinery or equipment therein, in the prescribed manner and at intervals not greater than the prescribed interval..."

### Emergency Information Provision

Employers are responsible for providing employees with emergency information regarding hazardous products.
"...provide, in respect of any hazardous product to which an employee may be exposed, as soon as is practicable in the circumstances, any information that is included in the safety data sheet that is in the employer’s possession for the hazardous product to any physician or other prescribed medical professional who requests that information for the purpose of making a medical diagnosis of, or rendering medical treatment to, an employee in an emergency."

This information must be provided to any physician or other prescribed medical professional who requests it for emergency medical treatment.
"...provide, in respect of any hazardous product to which an employee may be exposed, as soon as is practicable in the circumstances, any information that is included in the safety data sheet that is in the employer’s possession for the hazardous product to any physician or other prescribed medical professional who requests that information for the purpose of making a medical diagnosis of, or rendering medical treatment to, an employee in an emergency."

### Record Keeping and Confidentiality

Employers must maintain records of exposure to hazardous substances and make personal records of exposure available to affected employees.
"...ensure that all records of exposure to hazardous substances are kept and maintained in the prescribed manner and that personal records of exposure are made available to the affected employees."

Any physician or other prescribed medical professional who receives information from an employer must keep any information specified by the employer as being confidential, except for the purpose for which it is provided.
"Any physician or other prescribed medical professional to whom information is provided by an employer pursuant to subsection (1) shall keep confidential any information specified by the employer as being confidential, except for the purpose for which it is provided."

individual_results.question: What is an employer prohibited from doing to an employee in terms of their employment status?
individual_results.answer:
## Employer Prohibition on Employment Status Treatment

### Misclassification of Employees
"Employers are prohibited from treating an employee as if they were not their employee. A person who is paid remuneration by an employer is presumed to be their employee unless the contrary is proved by the employer." This statement establishes a fundamental prohibition against misclassifying employees. An employer cannot deny an employee their rights and protections simply by labeling them as something other than an employee.

### Disciplinary Action Related to Employee Rights
"No employer shall dismiss, suspend, lay off or demote an employee, impose a financial or other penalty on an employee, or refuse to pay an employee remuneration in respect of any period that the employee would, but for the exercise of the employee’s rights under this Part, have worked, or take any disciplinary action against or threaten to take any such action against an employee because the employee (a) has testified or is about to testify in a proceeding taken or an inquiry held under this Part; (b) has provided information to a person engaged in the performance of duties under this Part regarding the conditions of work affecting the health or safety of the employee or of any other employee of the employer; or (c) has acted in accordance with this Part or has sought the enforcement of any of the provisions of this Part." This section details specific disciplinary actions that are prohibited against employees who exercise their rights under the Canada Labour Code. An employer cannot retaliate against an employee for testifying in a proceeding, providing safety information, or acting in accordance with the Code.

### Prohibition on Interference with Trade Unions
"No employer or person acting on behalf of an employer shall (a) participate in or interfere with the formation or administration of a trade union or the representation of employees by a trade union; or (b) contribute financial or other support to a trade union." This prohibition directly addresses employer interference with trade unions. An employer cannot actively participate in or disrupt the formation or administration of a union, nor can they provide financial or other support to a union.

### Prohibition on Refusal to Work if Danger
"Subject to this section, an employee may refuse to use or operate a machine or thing, to work in a place or to perform an activity, if the employee while at work has reasonable cause to believe that (a) the use or operation of the machine or thing constitutes a danger to the employee or to another employee; (b) a condition exists in the place that constitutes a danger to the employee; or (c) the performance of the activity constitutes a danger to the employee or to another employee." While this section allows an employee to refuse work if it poses a danger, it also prohibits an employer from retaliating against an employee for exercising this right.

### Prohibition on Replacement Workers During Strikes or Lockouts
"Subject to subsection (7), during a strike or lockout not prohibited by this Part, no employer or person acting on behalf of an employer shall use the services of any of the following persons to perform all or part of the duties of an employee who is in the bargaining unit on strike or locked out: (a) any employee or any person who performs management functions or who is employed in a confidential capacity in matters related to industrial relations, if that employee or person is hired after the day on which notice to bargain collectively is given; (b) any contractor, other than a dependent contractor, or any employee of another employer; (c) any employee whose normal workplace is a workplace other than that at which the strike or lockout is taking place or who was transferred to the workplace at which the strike or lockout is taking place after the day on which notice to bargain collectively is given; (d) any volunteer, student or member of the public." This section prohibits employers from using replacement workers during strikes or lockouts. This is a key protection for striking employees, preventing employers from undermining their efforts by hiring temporary replacements.

### Prohibition on Disciplinary Action for Exercising Employee Rights
"No employer shall dismiss, suspend, lay off or demote an employee, impose a financial or other penalty on an employee, or refuse to pay an employee remuneration in respect of any period that the employee would, but for the exercise of the employee’s rights under this Part, have worked, or take any disciplinary action against or threaten to take any such action against an employee because the employee (a) has testified or is about to testify in a proceeding taken or an inquiry held under this Part; (b) has provided information to a person engaged in the performance of duties under this Part regarding the conditions of work affecting the health or safety of the employee or of any other employee of the employer; or (c) has acted in accordance with this Part or has sought the enforcement of any of the provisions of this Part." This reiterates the prohibition on disciplinary action taken against employees who exercise their rights under the Code.

individual_results.question: What are the general responsibilities of an employee in ensuring health and safety in the workplace according to the Canada Labour Code?
individual_results.answer:
## General Responsibilities of an Employee in Ensuring Health and Safety

### Use of Safety Materials and Equipment
"...use all safety materials, equipment, devices, and clothing that are provided by the employer and are intended to protect employees..."

This section clearly outlines a fundamental responsibility of every employee. It mandates the proper utilization of all safety provisions supplied by the employer. This includes wearing appropriate personal protective equipment (PPE), using safety tools and devices as instructed, and adhering to safety procedures related to these materials. The emphasis is on actively engaging with and benefiting from the safety resources made available.

### Following Safety Procedures and Instructions
"...follow procedures relating to the health and safety of employees..."
"...follow all instructions provided by the employer concerning the health and safety of employees..."

These two points reinforce the employee's obligation to adhere to established safety protocols and directives. Employers are responsible for creating and communicating these procedures, and employees are required to follow them without question. This includes specific work practices, emergency procedures, and the safe operation of equipment. The emphasis is on compliance with safety guidelines as a core part of the job.

### Taking Reasonable Precautions
"...take all reasonable and necessary precautions to ensure the health and safety of the employee, the other employees and any person likely to be affected by the employee’s acts or omissions..."

This responsibility extends beyond simply following instructions. It requires employees to proactively consider the potential safety implications of their actions and to take steps to mitigate risks for themselves and others. This involves being aware of hazards, communicating concerns, and making safe choices in their work. The phrase "reasonable and necessary precautions" highlights the expectation of a proactive and thoughtful approach to safety.

### Reporting Hazards and Incidents
"...report to the employer any thing or circumstance that is likely to be hazardous to employees or any other person in the workplace..."
"...report to the employer all work-related accidents, occupational diseases, or other hazardous occurrences that have caused injury to you or any other person..."

Employees have a crucial role in identifying and communicating potential safety risks. They are obligated to promptly report any conditions or circumstances that could pose a threat to their own safety or the safety of others. This includes hazards they observe, near misses, and any incidents that result in injury or illness. This reporting mechanism is essential for enabling employers to address risks and prevent future harm.

### Cooperation with Safety Initiatives
"...co-operate with any person carrying out a duty or function required by the Code..."
"...cooperate with the policy and work place committees or the health and safety representative..."

This responsibility emphasizes the importance of teamwork and collaboration in maintaining a safe workplace. Employees are expected to actively support and participate in any safety initiatives undertaken by the employer or safety committees. This includes providing information, assisting with investigations, and adhering to recommendations made by safety representatives. Cooperation is seen as a vital element of a shared commitment to health and safety.

### Compliance with Directions
"...comply with every oral or written direction given by a health and safety officer or an appeals officer..."
"...respond in writing to a health and safety officer's direction or report when requested to do so by the health and safety officer..."

Employees must adhere to any safety-related directions issued by designated safety officials. This includes responding to inquiries, providing information, and implementing corrective actions as instructed. Compliance with these directions is a direct demonstration of the employee's commitment to workplace safety.

individual_results.question: What are the rules regarding the handling of wreckage, articles, or things related to a workplace incident where an employee is killed or seriously injured?
individual_results.answer:
## Handling Wreckage, Articles, or Things Related to a Workplace Incident

### General Prohibition on Interference
"Subject to subsection (2), if an employee is killed or seriously injured in a work place, no person shall, unless authorized to do so by the Head, remove or in any way interfere with or disturb any wreckage, article or thing related to the incident except to the extent necessary to (a) save a life, prevent injury or relieve human suffering in the vicinity; (b) maintain an essential public service; or (c) prevent unnecessary damage to or loss of property."

This section of the Canada Labour Code establishes a general prohibition against tampering with wreckage, articles, or things related to a workplace incident resulting in death or serious injury. The exception is limited to actions strictly necessary to
"...save a life, prevent injury or relieve human suffering in the vicinity; (b) maintain an essential public service; or (c) prevent unnecessary damage to or loss of property." This highlights the priority of immediate safety and essential services over potentially hindering an investigation.

### Exceptions to the Prohibition
"No authorization referred to in subsection (1) is required where an employee is killed or seriously injured by an accident or incident involving (a) an aircraft, a vessel, rolling stock or a pipeline, if the accident or incident is being investigated under the Aeronautics Act , the Canada Shipping Act, 2001 or the Canadian Transportation Accident Investigation and Safety Board Act ; or (b) a motor vehicle on a public highway."

This subsection outlines specific exceptions to the general prohibition. It states that no authorization is needed to handle wreckage, articles, or things related to an incident involving certain modes of transportation (aircraft, vessels, rolling stock, pipelines) if the incident is being investigated under specific federal acts. Similarly, it applies to incidents involving motor vehicles on public highways. This exception is likely due to the existence of separate, specialized investigative bodies and procedures for these types of incidents.

### Additional Exception for Certain Accidents
"Exception (2) No authorization referred to in subsection (1) is required where an employee is killed or seriously injured by an accident or incident involving (a) an aircraft, a vessel, rolling stock or a pipeline, if the accident or incident is being investigated under the Aeronautics Act , the Canada Shipping Act, 2001 or the Canadian Transportation Accident Investigation and Safety Board Act ; or (b) a motor vehicle on a public highway."

This is a repetition of the previous exception, reinforcing the rule that no authorization is needed to handle wreckage, articles, or things related to incidents involving certain modes of transportation if they are being investigated under specific federal acts.

individual_results.question: What steps should an employee take if they believe there has been a contravention of the Part of the Canada Labour Code related to workplace safety and health, or if they believe there is likely to be an accident, injury or illness arising out of their employment?

## Steps for Reporting Workplace Safety and Health Concerns

### Reporting a Contravention of Part II of the Canada Labour Code

The Canada Labour Code grants employees significant rights to address workplace safety and health concerns. If an employee believes there has been a contravention of Part II of the Code, they should follow a specific reporting procedure.
"...employee may, if otherwise entitled to under this section, continue the refusal and the employee shall without delay report the circumstances of the matter to the employer and to the work place committee or the health and safety representative." This passage directly addresses the situation where an employee believes there is a contravention. It states that if an employee has a reasonable cause to believe a danger is not a normal condition of employment, they can continue their refusal to work and must immediately report the circumstances to the employer and the relevant health and safety committee or representative.

### Reporting a Likely Accident, Injury, or Illness

Employees also have the right to report situations they believe are likely to result in an accident, injury, or illness. The Canada Labour Code outlines several avenues for employees to make such reports.
"...report to the employer any thing or circumstance that is likely to be hazardous to employees or any other person in the workplace..." This section explicitly instructs employees to report any condition they believe is hazardous. This proactive reporting is crucial for preventing future incidents.
"...report to the employer all work-related accidents, occupational diseases, or other hazardous occurrences that have caused injury to you or any other person..." This passage details the requirement for employees to report any work-related accidents, occupational diseases, or other hazardous occurrences that have caused injury. This reporting is essential for investigation and preventative measures.
"...report to the employer any situation you believe to be a contravention of Part II of the Code by the employer, another employee, or any other person..." This section reiterates the employee's right and responsibility to report any situation they believe is a contravention of Part II of the Code. This reporting is vital for ensuring compliance with workplace safety and health regulations.

### Utilizing the Internal Complaint Resolution Process

The Canada Labour Code also provides an internal complaint resolution process for addressing workplace safety and health concerns.
"The provisions of the Code are designed to strengthen employers' and employees' self-reliance in dealing with occupational health and safety issues and thereby making workplaces safer." This statement highlights the Code's emphasis on empowering workplace parties to address safety concerns internally.
"Part II of the Code also provides for employee participation through the use of an internal complaint resolution process." This passage specifically mentions the internal complaint resolution process as a mechanism for employee participation in identifying and correcting workplace safety and health issues. Employees can utilize this process to raise concerns and seek resolution.

## Steps an Employee Can Take if They Have Reasonable Cause to Believe a Danger Exists

### Right to Refuse Dangerous Work

The Canada Labour Code grants employees the right to refuse to work if they have reasonable cause to believe that using a machine or working in a place poses a danger to themselves or another employee. This right is outlined in Section 128(1) of the Code.
"Subject to this section, an employee may refuse to use or operate a machine or thing, to work in a place or to perform an activity, if the employee while at work has reasonable cause to believe that (a) the use or operation of the machine or thing constitutes a danger to the employee or to another employee; (b) a condition exists in the place that constitutes a danger to the employee; or (c) the performance of the activity constitutes a danger to the employee or to another employee."

This section clearly states the conditions under which an employee can refuse to work. The employee must have "reasonable cause to believe" that the situation presents a danger. This means there must be a legitimate and well-founded concern about the potential for harm.

### Internal Complaint Resolution Process

Employees also have the right to participate in identifying and correcting work-related health and safety concerns through the Internal Complaint Resolution Process (ICRP). This process allows employees to raise concerns and have them addressed by the employer.
"As health and safety representatives or workplace health and safety committee or policy health and safety committee members, employees have the right to participate in identifying and correcting work-related health and safety concerns."

This right is further elaborated upon in the document "905-1-IPG-059". It states that employees can raise concerns through the ICRP and that the employer must take corrective action if a danger is substantiated.

### Reporting to Employer and Workplace Committees

If an employee has reasonable cause to believe a danger exists, they should report this to their employer and/or the relevant workplace health and safety committees.
"...is informed that the employee may not discontinue the use or operation of a machine or thing or cease to work in a place or perform an activity shall not, while the ship or aircraft on which the employee is employed is in operation, refuse under this section to use or operate the machine or thing, work in that place or perform that activity."

This passage indicates that if an employee is informed that a danger exists but the employer does not intend to take immediate action, the employee can still refuse to work under the right to refuse dangerous work. However, they must follow the proper procedure for exercising this right.

### Employer's Responsibilities

The employer has a responsibility to investigate any concerns raised by employees and to take immediate action to protect employees from any identified dangers.
"If, following its investigation, the employer agrees that a danger exists, the employer shall take immediate action to protect employees from the danger. The employer shall inform the work place committee or the health and safety representative of the matter and the action taken to resolve it."

This section emphasizes the employer's obligation to address any concerns raised by employees and to implement preventative measures to ensure employee safety.

individual_results.question: What happens to an employee's pay and benefits during a work stoppage due to certain provisions of the Canada Labour Code, and under what conditions might they have to repay those wages or benefits?
individual_results.answer:
## Employee Pay and Benefits During a Work Stoppage

### Rights Unaffected During a Strike or Lockout

The Canada Labour Code outlines specific provisions regarding employee pay and benefits during a work stoppage, such as a strike or lockout. Section 87.5(1) states,
"Where the Board has received an application pursuant to subsection 87.4(4) or a question has been referred to the Board pursuant to subsection 87.4(5), the employer must not alter the rates of pay or any other term or condition of employment or any right or privilege of the employees in the bargaining unit, or any right or privilege of the bargaining agent, without the consent of the bargaining agent, until the later of the date on which the Board has determined the application or the question referred and the date on which the requirements of paragraphs 89(1)(a) to (d) have been met." This provision is crucial because it ensures that employees' existing pay and benefits remain in effect during a work stoppage, provided the bargaining agent consents to any changes.

### Continuation of Services and Rights

Furthermore, Section 87.5(2) clarifies that
"Unless the parties otherwise agree, the rates of pay or any other term or condition of employment, and any rights, duties or privileges of the employees, the employer or the trade union in effect before the requirements of paragraphs 89(1)(a) to (d) were met, continue to apply with respect to employees who are members of the bargaining unit and who have been assigned to maintain services, facilities and production pursuant to section 87.4." This means that employees who are required to maintain essential services during a work stoppage continue to receive their regular pay and benefits, unless the parties specifically agree otherwise.

### Reinstatement After a Strike or Lockout

The Canada Labour Code also guarantees the reinstatement of employees after a work stoppage. Section 87.6(1) declares,
"At the end of a strike or lockout not prohibited by this Part, the employer must reinstate employees in the bargaining unit who were on strike or locked out, in preference to any other person." This provision protects employees from being replaced upon the conclusion of a work stoppage.

## Conditions for Potential Wage or Benefit Repayment

### Unauthorized Deductions

The Canada Labour Code addresses situations where an employee might have to repay wages or benefits due to unauthorized deductions. Section 6.3(1) states,
"Your employer can only deduct traffic tickets and fines from your wages if you provide a written authorization." This highlights that any deductions beyond those legally required must be based on the employee's explicit written consent. If an employer makes unauthorized deductions, the Labour Program may find that the employer owes the employee those amounts.

### Wage Recovery from an Employer

The Labour Program has the authority to recover unpaid wages from an employer. Section 6.5(1) outlines this process:
"The Labour Program may find that your employer does not owe you wages or other amounts under the Code. In this case, you (and your employer):  will receive the Labour Program’s findings in  writing, and may receive a Notice of Unfounded Complaint, which:           advises that your employer is in compliance, including the reasons why, and provides you with the opportunity to request a review..." If the Labour Program finds that an employer owes an employee wages, it will first request the employer to voluntarily pay those wages. If the employer does not comply, the Labour Program may issue a Payment Order to the employer or the director of the corporation to collect the unpaid wages.

### Director's Liability

In cases where wage recovery from an employer is unlikely or impossible, the Labour Program may hold the corporation's directors liable for the amounts employers owe to employees during their time as director. Section 6.5(3) explains this:
"Sometimes, wage recovery from an employer is unlikely or impossible. In this case, the Labour Program may hold the corporation’s directors liable for amounts employers owe to employees during their time as director. Corporate directors are jointly and individually liable for employees’ wages and other amounts to which employees are entitled, up to a limit equivalent to 6 months’ wages." This provision provides a mechanism for ensuring that employees receive their wages even if the corporation is unable to pay.

individual_results.question: What are the circumstances under which the Head may decide not to investigate an employee's refusal to work due to a potential danger, and what happens to the employee's refusal in such cases?
individual_results.answer:
## Circumstances Under Which the Head May Decide Not to Investigate

### Situations Where the Head Declines Investigation

Section 129(1) of the Canada Labour Code outlines the circumstances under which the Head may decide not to investigate an employee's refusal to work due to a potential danger. These situations are:
"(a) the matter is one that could more appropriately be dealt with, initially or completely, by means of a procedure provided for under Part I or III or under another Act of Parliament; (b) the matter is trivial, frivolous or vexatious; or (c) the continued refusal by the employee under 128(15) is in bad faith."

This indicates that the Head may decline an investigation if the issue is better addressed through another established process within the Canada Labour Code or other federal legislation. Additionally, the Head may deem the matter "trivial, frivolous or vexatious" and therefore not warrant an investigation. Finally, the Head may refuse to investigate if the employee's continued refusal is considered "in bad faith," suggesting a lack of genuine concern for safety.

### Consequences of the Head's Decision Not to Investigate

Section 129(1.1) details what happens to the employee's refusal when the Head decides not to investigate.
"If the Head does not proceed with an investigation, the Head shall inform the employer and the employee in writing, as soon as feasible, of that decision. The employer shall then inform in writing, as the case may be, the members of the work place committee who were designated under subsection 128(10) or the health and safety representative and the person who is designated by the employer under that subsection of the Head’s decision."

This means that if the Head declines an investigation, they must promptly notify both the employer and the employee of their decision in writing. The employer is then obligated to inform the relevant safety and health representatives of this decision.

Section 129(1.2) further clarifies the employee's rights after the Head's decision not to investigate.
"On being informed of the Head’s decision not to proceed with an investigation, the employee is no longer entitled to continue their refusal under subsection 128(15)."

This is a crucial point. The employee loses their right to continue their refusal to work based on the potential danger once the Head decides not to investigate.

### Employee's Refusal During Investigation

Section 129(1.3) addresses the employee's right to continue their refusal *during* an investigation.
"If the Head proceeds with an investigation, the employee may continue to refuse, for the duration of the investigation, to use or operate the machine or thing, to work in the place or to perform the activity that may constitute a danger."

This indicates that the employee retains their right to refuse to work while the Head is conducting an investigation into their refusal.

### Persons Present During Investigation

Section 129(1.4) specifies who may be present during the Head's investigation.
"If the Head proceeds with an investigation, the Head may do so in the presence of the employer, the employee and one other person who is (a) an employee member of the work place committee; (b) the health and safety representative; or (c) if a person mentioned in paragraph (a) or (b) is not available, another employee from the work place who is designated by the employee."

This outlines the potential attendees of the investigation, including representatives from the safety and health committee or the health and safety representative, as well as another employee designated by the employee.

### Head's Decision After Investigation

Section 129(4) details the Head's decision following the investigation.
"The Head shall, on completion of an investigation made under subsection (1), make one of the decisions referred to in paragraphs 128(13)(a) to (c) and shall immediately give written notification of the decision to the employer and the employee."

This means that after the investigation, the Head will make one of three decisions: agree that a danger exists, agree that a danger exists but consider that the circumstances provided for in paragraph (2)(a) or (b) apply, or determine that a danger does not exist. The Head must then inform both the employer and the employee of this decision in writing.

### Continuation of Work After Head's Decision

Section 129(5) explains what happens to the employee's refusal after the Head's decision.
"If the employee has exercised their right under subsection (1.3), the employer may, during the investigation and until the Head has issued a decision, require that the employee concerned remain at a safe location near the place in respect of which the investigation is being made or assign the employee reasonable alternative work, and shall not assign any other employee to use or operate the machine or thing, work in that place or perform the activity referred to in subsection (1) unless (a) the other employee is qualified for the work; (b) the other employee has been advised of the refusal of the employee concerned and of the reasons for the refusal; and (c) the employer is satisfied on reasonable grounds that the other employee will not be put in danger."

This indicates that the employer may require the employee to remain in a safe location or assign them alternative work during the investigation. However, the employer cannot assign another employee to perform the refused work unless they are qualified, have been informed of the original employee's refusal and reasons, and the employer is reasonably certain the other employee will not be put in danger.

### Appeal Process

Section 129(7) outlines the appeal process if the Head makes a decision that the danger does not exist.
"If the Head makes a decision referred to in paragraph 128(13)(b) or (c), the employee is not entitled under section 128 or this section to continue to refuse to use or operate the machine or thing, work in that place or perform that activity, but the employee, or a person designated by the employee for the purpose, may appeal the decision, in writing, to the Board within 10 days after receiving notice of the decision."

This means that if the Head decides that a danger does not exist, the employee cannot continue their refusal to work based on that potential danger. However, the employee or a designated person may appeal this decision in writing to the Board within 10 days of receiving notice.

individual_results.question: Under what circumstances can employees be excluded from the application of certain health and safety provisions in the Canada Labour Code?
individual_results.answer:
## Exclusion from Application of Certain Health and Safety Provisions

### Section 159(1) of the Canada Labour Code
"The Governor in Council may by regulation exclude, in whole or in part, from the application of any of the provisions of this Part any employment, or any class or classes of employment, on or in connection with a work or undertaking set out in the regulation whose activities are regulated, in whole or in part, pursuant to the Nuclear Safety and Control Act..."

This section outlines the mechanism by which employees can be excluded from the application of certain health and safety provisions. It grants the Governor in Council the authority to create regulations that specifically exclude certain types of employment from the Code's requirements. This exclusion can be either complete ("in whole") or partial ("in part"). The regulation can apply to specific jobs, job categories, or even entire work projects that are already subject to the Nuclear Safety and Control Act.

### Section 266(1) of the Canada Labour Code
"The Governor in Council may by regulation exclude, in whole or in part, from the application of any of the provisions of this Part any employment, or any class or classes of employment, on or in connection with a work or undertaking set out in the regulation whose activities are regulated, in whole or in part, pursuant to the Nuclear Safety and Control Act..."

This section reiterates the same exclusion power granted to the Governor in Council under Section 159(1). It emphasizes that this exclusion can be broad or narrow, and can apply to various types of employment that are already regulated by the Nuclear Safety and Control Act.

### Section 266(2) of the Canada Labour Code
"On the recommendation of the Minister after consultation with the Canadian Nuclear Safety Commission, the Governor in Council may make regulations relating to occupational safety and health in relation to employment that is subject to a regulation made pursuant to subsection (1)."

This subsection provides further detail on the process for creating exclusions through regulation. It states that the Governor in Council can issue regulations concerning occupational safety and health in relation to employment that is already regulated by the Nuclear Safety and Control Act. This regulation can be made following a recommendation from the Minister after consulting with the Canadian Nuclear Safety Commission. This suggests that exclusions can be tailored to the specific safety requirements of the nuclear industry.

individual_results.question: Can compliance or non-compliance with the provisions of this Part affect an employee's right to compensation for employment injury or illness under other statutes?
individual_results.answer:
## Section 131: Internal Complaint Resolution Process: Compensation under other laws not precluded

### Analysis of Section 131

Section 131 of the Canada Labour Code directly addresses the question of whether compliance or non-compliance with the provisions of this Part can affect an employee's right to compensation under other statutes. The section explicitly states:
"The fact that an employer or employee has complied with or failed to comply with any of the provisions of this Part may not be construed as affecting any right of an employee to compensation under any statute relating to compensation for employment injury or illness, or as affecting any liability or obligation of any employer or employee under any such statute."

This quote is a clear and unambiguous answer to the question. It asserts that whether an employer or employee adheres to the rules outlined in this Part has no bearing on an employee's entitlement to compensation under other laws governing employment injury or illness. The section further clarifies that this non-interference extends to any liability or obligation of either party under those other statutes.

In essence, Section 131 provides a safeguard, ensuring that an employee's right to compensation under separate compensation statutes remains unaffected by any actions or inactions related to the provisions of this Part. It establishes a principle of separation between the rules of this Part and the rules of other compensation statutes.
