individual_results.question: What are the steps an employee who is pregnant or nursing must take if they believe continuing their current job functions may pose a risk to their health or to that of the fetus or child?
individual_results.answer:
## Steps for Pregnant or Nursing Employees Concerned About Job Risks

### Ceasing to Perform Job

#### Initial Consultation with Healthcare Practitioner
"On being informed of the cessation, the employer, with the consent of the employee, shall notify the work place committee or the health and safety representative." This indicates that upon informing the employer of their concern, the employer is obligated to notify relevant workplace representatives. However, the employee's first step is to consult with a healthcare practitioner.
"The employee must consult with a , as defined in section 166, of her choice as soon as possible to establish whether continuing any of her current job functions poses a risk to her health or to that of the foetus or child." This passage explicitly states that the employee must consult with a healthcare practitioner to determine if their current job functions pose a risk. The healthcare practitioner will assess the situation and provide a certificate.

#### Providing a Certificate
"As an employee who is pregnant or nursing, you are entitled to an unpaid maternity-related leave of absence during the period from the beginning of the pregnancy to the end of the 24th week following the birth. To take this leave, you must provide your employer with a certificate from a health care practitioner." This section details the process for taking unpaid maternity leave, which is triggered by a healthcare practitioner's certificate.
"Section 132 (1) In addition to the rights conferred by section 128 and subject to this section, an employee who is pregnant or nursing may cease to perform her job if she believes that, by reason of the pregnancy or nursing, continuing any of her current job functions may pose a risk to her health or to that of the foetus or child." This passage reiterates the employee's right to cease performing their job if they have health concerns, and it specifies the requirement of a healthcare practitioner's certificate.

#### Employer's Options
"For the period during which the employee does not perform her job under subsection (1), the employer may, in consultation with the employee, reassign her to another job that would not pose a risk to her health or to that of the foetus or child." This passage outlines the employer's responsibility to consider a reassignment if the employee ceases performing their job due to health concerns. The reassignment should not pose a risk to the employee's health or that of the fetus or child.
"The onus is on the employer to show that a modification of job functions or a reassignment that would avoid the activities or conditions indicated in the certificate issued under subsection 204(2) is not reasonably practicable." This passage clarifies the employer's burden of proof when denying a reassignment. They must demonstrate that a modification or reassignment that would eliminate the risk is not reasonably practicable.

### Maternity-Related Reassignment and Leave (Unpaid)
"Where a reassignment or a job modification is not reasonably practicable, you may take an unpaid leave of absence for the duration of the risks as indicated in the medical certificate." This indicates that if a reassignment is not feasible, the employee can take an unpaid leave of absence for the duration of the health risks identified by the healthcare practitioner.
"...pregnant or nursing, you are entitled to an unpaid maternity-related leave of absence during the period from the beginning of the pregnancy to the end of the 24th week following the birth." This passage specifies the entitlement to unpaid maternity leave, which begins at the start of the pregnancy and ends 24 weeks after the birth.
"...you must provide your employer with a certificate from a health care practitioner. This certificate must indicate that you are unable to work by reason of the pregnancy or nursing, and the duration of the inability." This passage details the requirement for a healthcare practitioner's certificate to take unpaid maternity leave. The certificate must state the inability to work due to pregnancy or nursing and the length of that inability.

### Maternity Leave (Unpaid)
"As a pregnant employee, you are entitled to up to 17 weeks of maternity leave." This passage states the entitlement to up to 17 weeks of maternity leave.
"You can take this leave any time during the period that:  begins 13 weeks before the expected date of birth, and ends 17 weeks after the actual birth date..." This passage specifies the timeframe for taking maternity leave.
"You must provide your employer with a certificate from a health care practitioner confirming that you are pregnant. You must also give your employer written notice at least 4 weeks before starting your leave. This notice must advise your employer of the length of the leave." This passage details the requirements for taking maternity leave, including a healthcare practitioner's certificate and written notice.
"If your child was not born during the 17 weeks of your maternity leave, the maternity leave is extended until the date of the birth." This passage clarifies that maternity leave is extended if the child is not born within the initial 17-week period.
"As a pregnant employee, you are not obligated to take maternity leave unless your employer can show that you are unable to perform an essential function of your job." This passage states that maternity leave is not mandatory unless the employer can demonstrate that the employee is unable to perform an essential function of their job.
"The Code does not provide for paid maternity leave." This passage clarifies that paid maternity leave is not provided under the Canada Labour Code.

individual_results.question: What is the process for an employee to make a complaint if they believe their employer has taken action against them in contravention of section 147, and what is the role of the Board in handling such complaints?
individual_results.answer:
## Process for an Employee to Make a Complaint Regarding Contravention of Section 147

### Filing a Complaint with the Board

Section 133(1) of the Canada Labour Code outlines the process for an employee to file a complaint with the Board if they believe their employer has taken action against them in contravention of section 147. It states:
"An employee, or a person designated by the employee for the purpose, who alleges that an employer has taken action against the employee in contravention of section 147 may, subject to subsection (3), make a complaint in writing to the Board of the alleged contravention."

This indicates that the complaint must be in writing and directed to the Board. Section 133(2) specifies the timeframe for making such a complaint:
"The complaint shall be made to the Board not later than ninety days after the date on which the complainant knew, or in the Board’s opinion ought to have known, of the action or circumstances giving rise to the complaint."

This sets a deadline for filing the complaint, which is ninety days from when the employee becomes aware of the action taken against them.

### The Role of the Board in Handling Complaints

Section 133(4) clarifies that a complaint made under this section cannot be referred to arbitration or adjudication, even if an agreement to the contrary exists. This highlights the Board's exclusive jurisdiction over such complaints.
"Notwithstanding any law or agreement to the contrary, a complaint made under this section may not be referred by an employee to arbitration or adjudication."

Section 133(5) details the Board's potential actions upon receiving a complaint. It states:
"On receipt of a complaint made under this section, the Board may assist the parties to the complaint to settle the complaint and shall, if it decides not to so assist the parties or the complaint is not settled within a period considered by the Board to be reasonable in the circumstances, hear and determine the complaint."

This reveals that the Board initially attempts to facilitate settlement between the parties. If settlement is not reached within a reasonable timeframe, the Board will conduct a hearing to determine the merits of the complaint.

Section 133(6) further explains the evidentiary role of the complaint itself:
"A complaint made under this section in respect of the exercise of a right under section 128 or 129 is itself evidence that the contravention actually occurred and, if a party to the complaint proceedings alleges that the contravention did not occur, the burden of proof is on that party."

This means that the complaint serves as prima facie evidence of the contravention. If the employer denies the contravention, the employer bears the burden of proving that it did not occur.

### Outcomes of Board Complaints

Section 134(1) outlines the remedies the Board may order if it finds an employer has contravened section 147. It states:
"If, under subsection 133(5), the Board determines that an employer has contravened section 147, the Board may, by order, require the employer to cease contravening that section and may, if applicable, by order, require the employer to (a) permit any employee who has been affected by the contravention to return to the duties of their employment; (b) reinstate any former employee affected by the contravention; (c) pay to any employee or former employee affected by the contravention compensation not exceeding the sum that, in the Board’s opinion, is equivalent to the remuneration that would, but for the contravention, have been paid by the employer to the employee or former employee; and (d) rescind any disciplinary action taken in respect of, and pay compensation to any employee affected by, the contravention, not exceeding the sum that, in the Board’s opinion, is equivalent to any financial or other penalty imposed on the employee by the employer."

This indicates that the Board has broad powers to order corrective action, including reinstatement, compensation, and rescission of disciplinary measures.

## Section 4 of the Regulations: What Constitutes a Complaint Under Subsection 127.1(1) of the Act?

Section 4 of the Regulations addresses questions concerning section 4 of the Regulations. Question 1 asks:
"What is meant by “a complaint under subsection 127.1(1) of  the Act” in section 4 of the Regulations?"

The Guidance provided in this IPG clarifies the meaning of a complaint under subsection 127.1(1) of the Act:
"In this IPG, the term “complaint” refers to an  allegation by you, as an employee, that your employer has failed to fulfill  their duties under the Code or the  Regulations relating to a notice of an occurrence of harassment and violence."

This definition is crucial for understanding the scope of the complaint process. It specifies that a complaint is an assertion by an employee that their employer has not met their obligations under the Code or the Regulations in response to a harassment and violence notice.

### The Amended Internal Complaint Resolution Process (ICRP)

Section 4 further details the amended ICRP that an employee must follow if they believe their employer has failed to comply with the Code or Regulations when responding to a harassment and violence notice.
"If you experience an occurrence of harassment and violence, you must first  submit a “notice of an occurrence” to your employer or designated recipient. If  you believe your employer or designated recipient has failed to comply with the Code or  Regulations when responding to this notice, you must  follow the amended Internal Complaint Resolution Process (ICRP) that came into  force in 2021, outlined below..."

The ICRP involves several steps:

1.  The employee notifies their supervisor or the person designated in the HVP Policy of the contravention.
2.  The employee attempts to resolve the complaint with their supervisor or the designated person as soon as possible.
3.  If the complaint is unresolved, the employee can refer the complaint to the Labour Program.

However, the Labour Program's role is limited to hearing and determining the complaint, not to resolving it directly.

### The Board's Role in Handling Complaints

Section 133(5) reiterates the Board's role in assisting parties to settle complaints and, if unsuccessful, hearing and determining them.
"On receipt of a complaint made under this section, the Board may assist the parties to the complaint to settle the complaint and shall, if it decides not to so assist the parties or the complaint is not settled within a period considered by the Board to be reasonable in the circumstances, hear and determine the complaint."

This emphasizes the Board's function as a neutral third party to facilitate resolution and, if necessary, to make a binding determination on the complaint.

individual_results.question: What actions can the Board require an employer to take if it determines that the employer has contravened section 147 of the Canada Labour Code?
individual_results.answer:
## Board Orders for Contravention of Section 147

### Section 134(1) - Board Orders for Contravention
"If, under subsection 133(5), the Board determines that an employer has contravened section 147, the Board may, by order, require the employer to cease contravening that section and may, if applicable, by order, require the employer to (a) permit any employee who has been affected by the contravention to return to the duties of their employment; (b) reinstate any former employee affected by the contravention; (c) pay to any employee or former employee affected by the contravention compensation not exceeding the sum that, in the Board’s opinion, is equivalent to the remuneration that would, but for the contravention, have been paid by the employer to the employee or former employee; and (d) rescind any disciplinary action taken in respect of, and pay compensation to any employee affected by, the contravention, not exceeding the sum that, in the Board’s opinion, is equivalent to any financial or other penalty imposed on the employee by the employer."

This section of the Canada Labour Code outlines the specific actions the Board can order an employer to take if it finds a contravention of section 147. Section 147 prohibits employers from taking disciplinary action against employees because they have testified or are about to testify in a proceeding under this Part, have provided information to someone performing duties under this Part regarding health or safety conditions, or have acted in accordance with this Part or sought enforcement of its provisions.

The Board's orders are comprehensive. Firstly, it can order the employer to "cease contravening that section." Secondly, it can order the employer to
"...permit any employee who has been affected by the contravention to return to the duties of their employment..." and to "reinstate any former employee affected by the contravention." These orders aim to rectify the unfair disciplinary action taken against the employee.

Furthermore, the Board can order the employer to
"...pay to any employee or former employee affected by the contravention compensation not exceeding the sum that, in the Board’s opinion, is equivalent to the remuneration that would, but for the contravention, have been paid by the employer to the employee or former employee..." This compensation is intended to make up for the lost wages or other financial benefits the employee would have received had the disciplinary action not occurred.

Finally, the Board can order the employer to
"...rescind any disciplinary action taken in respect of, and pay compensation to any employee affected by, the contravention, not exceeding the sum that, in the Board’s opinion, is equivalent to any financial or other penalty imposed on the employee by the employer." This order ensures that any previous disciplinary action is reversed and that the employee is compensated for any financial penalties they were subjected to.

### Section 134(2) - Enforcement of Orders
"Any person affected by an order of the Board under subsection (1), or the Head on the request of such a person, may, after 14 days from the day on which the order is made, or from the day provided in the order for compliance, whichever is later, file in the Federal Court a copy of the order, exclusive of reasons."

This section details how the Board's orders can be enforced. It states that any person impacted by an order, or the Head of the Labour Program upon request, can file a copy of the order in Federal Court. This action initiates the process of ensuring the employer complies with the Board's requirements.

### Section 134(3) - Registration of Orders
"On filing in the Federal Court under subsection (2), an order of the Board shall be registered in the Court and, when registered, has the same force and effect, and all proceedings may be taken in respect of it, as if the order were a judgment obtained in that Court."

This section explains the legal effect of registering the Board's order in Federal Court. Upon registration, the order gains the same legal force as a judgment obtained in that Court. This means that the employer is legally obligated to comply with the Board's order, and any legal proceedings can be taken in respect of the order as if it were a judgment.

individual_results.question: What are the main responsibilities of a policy health and safety committee that an employer is required to establish under the Canada Labour Code?
individual_results.answer:
## Main Responsibilities of a Policy Health and Safety Committee

### Section 134.1(4) - Duties of Policy Committee

Section 134.1(4) of the Canada Labour Code outlines the primary duties of a policy health and safety committee that an employer is required to establish under the Code. These duties are comprehensive and cover a wide range of aspects related to occupational health and safety.

#### Development of Health and Safety Policies and Programs
"A policy committee (a) shall participate in the development of health and safety policies and programs..." This responsibility highlights the committee's crucial role in shaping the overall health and safety framework within the workplace. The committee is not merely a recipient of policies but an active contributor to their creation and implementation.

#### Consideration and Resolution of Health and Safety Matters
"...shall consider and expeditiously dispose of matters concerning health and safety raised by members of the committee or referred to it by a work place committee or a health and safety representative..." This duty emphasizes the committee's function as a forum for addressing health and safety concerns. It is tasked with reviewing and resolving issues brought forward by its members or those referred to it by other health and safety bodies within the workplace.

#### Participation in Hazard Prevention and Education Programs
"...shall participate in the development and monitoring of a program for the prevention of hazards in the work place that also provides for the education of employees in health and safety matters..." This responsibility underscores the committee's involvement in proactive hazard prevention efforts. It contributes to the creation and oversight of programs designed to identify and mitigate workplace risks, while also ensuring that employees are adequately educated on health and safety practices.

#### Participation in Inquiries, Investigations, Studies, and Inspections
"...shall participate to the extent that it considers necessary in inquiries, investigations, studies and inspections pertaining to occupational health and safety..." This duty highlights the committee's role in supporting and contributing to investigations and assessments related to occupational health and safety. It can provide input, participate in analyses, and offer recommendations based on its knowledge of the workplace.

#### Participation in Personal Protective Equipment Programs
"...shall participate in the development and monitoring of a program for the provision of personal protective equipment, clothing, devices or materials..." This responsibility indicates the committee's involvement in ensuring that employees have access to the necessary personal protective equipment. It contributes to the creation and oversight of programs designed to provide and maintain this essential safety gear.

#### Cooperation with the Head

"shall cooperate with the Head" This duty emphasizes the committee's collaborative relationship with the employer's leadership. It is expected to work constructively with the employer to achieve common health and safety goals.

#### Monitoring Data on Work Accidents, Injuries, and Health Hazards
"...shall monitor data on work accidents, injuries and health hazards..." This responsibility highlights the committee's role in tracking and analyzing workplace safety data. It contributes to the identification of trends, the evaluation of program effectiveness, and the development of targeted interventions.

#### Participation in Planning and Implementation of Changes
"...shall participate in the planning of the implementation and in the implementation of changes that might affect occupational health and safety, including work processes and procedures." This duty underscores the committee's involvement in adapting workplace practices to improve health and safety. It contributes to the planning and execution of changes that address identified risks and enhance overall safety.

### Section 134.1(5) - Information Requests
"A policy committee may request from an employer any information that the committee considers necessary to identify existing or potential hazards with respect to materials, processes, equipment or activities in any of the employer’s work places." This provision grants the committee the right to request information from the employer to better understand and address workplace hazards. It ensures that the committee has access to the data it needs to effectively fulfill its duties.

individual_results.question: What are the requirements for the composition of a policy committee or a work place committee in terms of employee representation and selection?
individual_results.answer:
## Composition Requirements for Policy and Workplace Committees

### Employee Representation

#### General Requirement
"Subject to this section, a policy committee or a work place committee shall consist of at least two persons and at least half of the members shall be employees who (a) do not exercise managerial functions; and (b) subject to any regulations made under subsection 135.2(1), have been selected by (i) the employees, if the employees are not represented by a trade union, or (ii) the trade union representing employees, in consultation with any employees who are not so represented." This section establishes the fundamental requirement for both policy and workplace committees: a minimum of two members, with at least half being employees who do not hold managerial roles.

#### Employee Selection Process

The selection process for employee members varies depending on whether employees are represented by a trade union. If employees are not represented by a trade union, they are responsible for selecting the employee members. However, if employees are represented by a trade union, the trade union is responsible for the selection, but must consult with any employees who are not represented by a trade union. This ensures that all employees have a voice in the committee's composition.

#### Exceptions
"Despite subsection (1) and if provided in a collective agreement or other agreement, the members of a policy committee may include persons who are not employees." This subsection provides an exception for policy committees, allowing for the inclusion of non-employee members if stipulated in a collective agreement or other agreement.

#### Workplace Committee Exception
"If there is no policy committee, a work place committee may, when dealing with an issue that would have come within the responsibilities of a policy committee, select two additional members. Unless otherwise provided in a collective agreement or other agreement, one of the additional members shall be an employee who meets the criteria set out in paragraphs (1)(a) and (b)." This subsection outlines an exception for workplace committees, allowing them to select two additional members if they are addressing an issue typically handled by a policy committee. At least one of these additional members must be an employee who meets the criteria outlined in paragraphs (1)(a) and (b).

### Chairperson Selection
"A committee shall have two chairpersons selected from among the committee members. One of the chairpersons shall be selected by the employee members and the other shall be selected by the employer members." This section details the process for selecting the two chairpersons of each committee. One chairperson is chosen by the employee members, while the other is chosen by the employer members. This ensures that both employee and employer perspectives are represented in the committee's leadership.

### Alternate Members
"The employer and employees may select alternate members to serve as replacements for members selected by them who are unable to perform their functions. Alternate members for employee members shall meet the criteria set out in paragraphs (1)(a) and (b)." This section allows for the selection of alternate members to cover for those who are unable to fulfill their committee duties. Alternate employee members must meet the same criteria as the regular employee members.

### Committee Rules of Procedure
"Subject to subsections 134.1(7) and 135(10) and any regulations made under subsection 135.2(1), a committee shall establish its own rules of procedure in respect of the terms of office, not exceeding two years, of its members and the time, place and frequency of regular meetings of the committee and may establish any rules of procedure for its operation that it considers advisable." This section mandates that each committee establish its own rules of procedure. These rules can cover various aspects of the committee's operation, including the term length of its members, the schedule of its meetings, and any other operational guidelines deemed necessary.

individual_results.question: What are the rules surrounding the provision of information that could reveal the identity of a person involved in workplace harassment and violence to a policy committee or a workplace committee?
individual_results.answer:
## Rules Regarding Provision of Information Likely to Reveal Identity

### Section 135.11(1) of the Canada Labour Code
"Neither the Head nor an employer shall, without the person’s consent, provide, under this Part, a health and safety representative with any information that is likely to reveal the identity of a person who was involved in an occurrence of harassment and violence in the work place. A health and safety representative shall not have access to that information without the person’s consent."

This section of the Canada Labour Code establishes a clear rule regarding the provision of information that could identify a person involved in workplace harassment and violence to a policy committee or a workplace committee. It states that neither the Head nor an employer can provide such information without the individual's consent. This provision is directly applicable to both policy committees and workplace committees, as it applies to any health and safety representative, which includes members of these committees.

### Section 135.11(2) of the Canada Labour Code
"Subsection (1) does not apply with respect to (a) information provided under section 128 or 129 or a direction or report relating to the application of those sections; or (b) a decision, reasons or a direction referred to in subsection 146.1(2)."

This subsection provides two exceptions to the rule outlined in section 135.11(1). The first exception states that the rule does not apply to information provided under sections 128 or 129, or to any direction or report relating to the application of those sections. The second exception applies to decisions, reasons, or directions referred to in subsection 146.1(2). These exceptions clarify that the consent requirement does not extend to certain types of information that are already subject to different rules or processes.

### Section 136.1(1) of the Canada Labour Code
"Neither the Head nor an employer shall, without the person’s consent, provide, under this Part, a health and safety representative with any information that is likely to reveal the identity of a person who was involved in an occurrence of harassment and violence in the work place. A health and safety representative shall not have access to that information without the person’s consent."

This section of the Canada Labour Code reiterates the rule established in section 135.11(1) and applies it specifically to health and safety representatives. It emphasizes that consent is required before providing any information that could identify a person involved in workplace harassment and violence to a health and safety representative, which includes members of policy committees and workplace committees.

individual_results.question: What are the primary responsibilities of a health and safety representative in a workplace with fewer than 20 employees, and how are they selected?
individual_results.answer:
## Primary Responsibilities of a Health and Safety Representative in a Small Workplace

### Selection Process

The selection of a health and safety representative in a workplace with fewer than 20 employees is a specific process outlined in Section 136 of the Canada Labour Code. It states:
"The health and safety representative for a work place shall be selected as follows: (a) the employees at the work place who do not exercise managerial functions shall select from among those employees the person to be appointed; or (b) if those employees are represented by a trade union, the trade union shall select the person to be appointed, in consultation with any employees who are not so represented, and subject to any regulations made under subsection (11)."

This indicates that if employees are not represented by a trade union, they directly select the representative from among themselves. However, if employees are represented by a trade union, the trade union is responsible for the selection, but must consult with any employees who are not represented by the union. The selected representative's name must then be advised to the employer in writing.

### Core Responsibilities

Section 136 further details the primary responsibilities of a health and safety representative in a small workplace. These responsibilities are quite comprehensive and cover a wide range of health and safety matters.

#### General Duties
"A health and safety representative, in respect of the work place for which the representative is appointed, (a) shall consider and expeditiously dispose of complaints relating to the health and safety of employees; (b) shall ensure that adequate records are maintained pertaining to work accidents, injuries, health hazards and the disposition of complaints related to the health and safety of employees and regularly monitor data relating to those accidents, injuries, hazards and complaints; (c) shall meet with the employer as necessary to address health and safety matters; (d) shall participate in the implementation and monitoring of the program referred to in paragraph 134.1(4)(c); (e) where the program referred to in paragraph 134.1(4)(c) does not cover certain hazards unique to that work place, shall participate in the development, implementation and monitoring of a program for the prevention of those hazards that also provides for the education of employees in health and safety matters related to those hazards; (f) where there is no policy committee, shall participate in the development, implementation and monitoring of a program for the prevention of hazards in the work place that also provides for the education of employees in health and safety matters; (g) shall participate in all of the inquiries, investigations, studies and inspections pertaining to the health and safety of employees, including any consultations that may be necessary with persons who are professionally or technically qualified to advise the representative on those matters; (h) shall cooperate with the Head; (i) shall participate in the implementation of changes that may affect occupational health and safety, including work processes and procedures and, where there is no policy committee, shall participate in the planning of the implementation of those changes; (j) shall inspect each month all or part of the work place, so that every part of the work place is inspected at least once each year; (k) shall participate in the development of health and safety policies and programs; (l) shall assist the employer in investigating and assessing the exposure of employees to hazardous substances; and (m) shall participate in the implementation and monitoring of a program for the provision of personal protective equipment, clothing, devices or materials and, where there is no policy committee, shall participate in the development of the program."

This list highlights the representative's role in addressing employee concerns, maintaining safety records, communicating with the employer, participating in safety programs and inspections, and contributing to the development of safety policies. The monthly workplace inspection is a particularly noteworthy responsibility, ensuring consistent safety oversight.

#### Specific Investigative and Consultation Duties

Further responsibilities are outlined in Section 136(5) and (6).
"Despite paragraph (5)(g), a health and safety representative shall not participate in an investigation, other than an investigation under section 128 or 129, relating to an occurrence of harassment and violence in the work place." This clarifies a limitation on the representative's involvement in specific types of investigations.
"A health and safety representative, in respect of the work place for which the representative is appointed, may request from an employer any information that the representative considers necessary to identify existing or potential hazards with respect to materials, processes, equipment or activities." This grants the representative the right to request information from the employer to proactively identify and address potential safety issues.

#### Access to Information and Time Allocation

Section 136(7) and (8) address the representative's access to information and time allocation.
"A health and safety representative, in respect of the work place for which the representative is appointed, shall have full access to all of the government and employer reports, studies and tests relating to the health and safety of employees, or to the parts of those reports, studies and tests that relate to the health and safety of employees, but shall not have access to the medical records of any person except with the person’s consent." This ensures the representative has comprehensive access to relevant safety data.
"A health and safety representative is entitled to take the time required, during their regular working hours, (a) to perform any of the representative’s functions; and (b) for the purposes of preparation and travel, as authorized by both chairpersons of the policy committee or, if there is no policy committee, as authorized by the employer." This guarantees the representative adequate time to fulfill their duties during regular working hours.

In summary, the primary responsibilities of a health and safety representative in a workplace with fewer than 20 employees are broad and encompass addressing employee concerns, maintaining safety records, communicating with the employer, participating in safety programs and inspections, contributing to safety policies, assisting with hazard investigations, and ensuring access to relevant safety information. The selection process is straightforward, allowing employees to directly choose their representative if not represented by a union, or the union to select if they are represented.

individual_results.question: Under what conditions can the identity of a person involved in a workplace harassment and violence incident be revealed to a health and safety representative?
individual_results.answer:
## Conditions for Revealing Identity to a Health and Safety Representative

### General Requirement for Consent
"Neither the Head nor an employer shall, without the person’s consent, provide, under this Part, a health and safety representative with any information that is likely to reveal the identity of a person who was involved in an occurrence of harassment and violence in the work place." This section of the Canada Labour Code establishes a fundamental principle: the identity of a person involved in a workplace harassment and violence incident cannot be disclosed to a health and safety representative without their explicit consent. This requirement is designed to protect the privacy and safety of individuals who have experienced or been accused of engaging in such incidents.

### Exceptions to the Consent Requirement

The Canada Labour Code outlines specific exceptions to the general consent requirement. These exceptions are narrowly defined and relate to particular types of information or circumstances.

#### Information Provided Under Sections 128 or 129
"Subsection (1) does not apply with respect to (a) information provided under section 128 or 129 or a direction or report relating to the application of those sections..." This exception applies to information shared under specific provisions of the Canada Labour Code. Sections 128 and 129 deal with the role of health and safety representatives in investigations and the information they are entitled to receive. Therefore, information provided under these sections can be shared with a health and safety representative without the consent of the individual involved.

#### Decisions, Reasons, or Directions Referred to in Subsection 146.1(2)
"(b) a decision, reasons or a direction referred to in subsection 146.1(2)." This exception pertains to decisions, reasons, or directions made by the Minister of Labour or the Labour Program Labour Affairs Officers. Such information can be shared with a health and safety representative without the consent of the individual involved.

### Employer's Responsibility to Obtain Consent
"For each person involved, the employer may obtain consent  for all disclosures at the same time, as long as this is made clear to the  person involved, or may obtain each consent separately so that the person  involved can pick and choose which consent to grant." This passage emphasizes the employer's obligation to obtain consent from all individuals involved before disclosing their identities to a health and safety representative. It also provides flexibility in how consent can be obtained, allowing for either a single consent form covering all disclosures or separate consent forms for each disclosure.

### Employer's Documentation of Consent
"...it is recommended  the employer obtain consent in writing; a template “consent form” is found at Appendix B." This recommendation underscores the importance of documenting consent in writing. A consent form serves as evidence that the individual involved has provided their permission for their identity to be disclosed to a health and safety representative.

### Redaction of Information
"If a person involved consents to their identity being  disclosed to the CP, but not to one or more recipients of the CP’s report, (as  discussed in section 11.4), the employer must redact this information from the  report before forwarding it to the specific recipient(s)." This provision addresses situations where consent is given to one recipient of a report but not to others. In such cases, the employer is required to redact the information that was not consented to before sharing the report with the other recipients.

individual_results.question: Under what circumstances may an employer need to establish multiple workplace health and safety committees or appoint multiple health and safety representatives?
individual_results.answer:
## Circumstances Requiring Multiple Workplace Health and Safety Committees or Representatives

### Employer Controlling Multiple Workplaces
"...sections 135 and 136, if an employer controls more than one work place or the size or nature of the operations of the employer or those of the work place precludes the effective functioning of a single work place committee or health and safety representative, as the case may be, for those work places, the employer shall, subject to the approval or in accordance with the direction of the Head, establish or appoint in accordance with section 135 or 136, as the case may be, a work place committee or health and safety representative for the work places that are specified in the approval or direction."

This section explicitly states that an employer may need to establish multiple committees or appoint multiple representatives when they control more than one workplace. The reasoning provided is that the size or nature of the operations of the employer or the individual workplaces may make a single committee or representative ineffective. This suggests that a larger organization with diverse operations might benefit from having separate committees or representatives for different work areas to ensure adequate attention to specific health and safety concerns.

### Employer Operations or Workplaces Precluding Effective Functioning of a Single Committee or Representative
"...sections 135 and 136, if an employer controls more than one work place or the size or nature of the operations of the employer or those of the work place precludes the effective functioning of a single work place committee or health and safety representative, as the case may be, for those work places, the employer shall, subject to the approval or in accordance with the direction of the Head, establish or appoint in accordance with section 135 or 136, as the case may be, a work place committee or health and safety representative for the work places that are specified in the approval or direction."

This reiterates the circumstance where multiple committees or representatives might be necessary. It expands on the initial point by including the size or nature of the operations of the employer or the individual workplaces as potential factors. The text indicates that if the operations are too large or diverse, or if the nature of the workplaces makes a single committee or representative unable to function effectively, the employer must establish multiple committees or appoint multiple representatives. This implies that the complexity of the employer's operations can necessitate a more decentralized approach to health and safety representation.

### Employer Agreement with Employees for Multiple Committees or Representatives
"If, under a collective agreement or any other agreement between an employer and the employer’s employees, a committee of persons has been appointed and the committee has, in the opinion of the Head, a responsibility for matters relating to health and safety in the work place to such an extent that a work place committee established under subsection (1) for that work place would not be necessary, (a) at an employer’s request, the Head may, in writing, exempt the employer from the requirements of subsection (1) in respect of that work place; (b) the committee of persons that has been appointed for the work place has, in addition to any rights, functions, powers, privileges and obligations under the agreement, the same rights, functions, powers, privileges and obligations as a work place committee under this Part; and (c) the committee of persons so appointed is, for the purposes of this Part, deemed to be a work place committee established under subsection (1) and all rights and obligations of employers and employees under this Part and the provisions of this Part respecting a work place committee apply, with any modifications that the circumstances require..."

This section addresses a scenario where an employer and employees have already established a committee with sufficient responsibility. It allows the employer to seek an exemption from the requirement to establish a separate committee if the existing committee effectively addresses health and safety matters. Furthermore, it clarifies that such an existing committee will have the same rights and obligations as a newly established committee under the Canada Labour Code. This suggests that employers and employees can agree to a more flexible approach to health and safety representation, potentially utilizing multiple committees or representatives based on the specific needs of different workplaces.

individual_results.question: What is the purpose of the Coal Mining Safety Commission and how is it structured?
individual_results.answer:
## Purpose of the Coal Mining Safety Commission

### Ensuring Coal Mine Health and Safety

The primary purpose of the Coal Mining Safety Commission is to "protect the health and safety of employees" in coal mines. This is explicitly stated in Section 137.2(1) of the Canada Labour Code, which outlines the Commission's authority to
"...approve in writing, with or without modification, plans or procedures submitted in accordance with paragraph 125.3(1)(d)." This approval process is designed to ensure that mining methods, machinery, and equipment used in coal mines meet prescribed safety standards.

### Approving Plans and Procedures

The Commission plays a crucial role in reviewing and approving plans and procedures related to coal mine safety. Section 137.2(1) details this function, stating that the Commission can approve plans and procedures submitted in accordance with Section 125.3(1)(d). This approval can be granted with or without modifications, allowing the Commission to suggest improvements to enhance safety.

### Approving Non-Standard Methods and Equipment

The Commission also has the authority to approve the use of mining methods, machinery, or equipment that do not meet prescribed safety standards, but only if the Commission believes that
"...protection of the health and safety of employees would not thereby be diminished..." This provision, found in Section 137.2(2), allows for flexibility in the adoption of new technologies or methods, provided that safety is not compromised.

### Exemptions and Substitutions

Furthermore, the Commission can grant exemptions from compliance with certain regulations or substitute them with other provisions, subject to the approval of the Minister. This power, detailed in Section 137.2(3), allows the Commission to tailor regulations to the specific conditions of coal mines.

### Recommendations for Amendments

The Commission can also make recommendations to the Minister for amending or revoking any provision of the regulations applicable to coal mines or for adding any provision thereto. This proactive role ensures that the regulations remain current and effective in protecting coal mine workers.

## Structure of the Coal Mining Safety Commission

### Composition of the Commission

The Coal Mining Safety Commission is composed of "not more than five members" to be appointed by the Minister "to hold office during pleasure." This is outlined in Section 137.1(1) of the Canada Labour Code.

### Chairperson and Representatives

The Commission has a chairperson, who is designated by the Minister. The other members are
"...equally representative of the non-supervisory employees employed in coal mines and of the employers of those employees." This structure ensures that the Commission considers the perspectives of both workers and employers when making decisions related to safety.

### Alternate Chairperson

The Minister may also appoint an alternate chairperson to act in the absence or incapacity of the chairperson. This provision, found in Section 137.1(2.1), ensures continuity in the Commission's operations.

### Selection and Tenure of Members

The manner of selection of the members of the Commission, other than the chairperson and an alternate chairperson, and the term of office of the members of the Commission shall be "such as may be prescribed." This allows for flexibility in the appointment process and the length of service of the members.

### Quorum

A quorum of the Commission consists of the chairperson or alternate chairperson, one member representative of non-supervisory employees, and one member representative of employers. This ensures that the Commission has a sufficient number of members present to conduct its business.

### Ineligibility

Certain individuals are ineligible to be appointed to the Commission or as alternate chairperson. This includes those who have delegated powers, duties, or functions under other agreements.

### Remuneration and Expenses

The members of the Commission, including an alternate chairperson, shall be paid the remuneration that may be fixed by the Governor in Council, and any reasonable travel and living expenses incurred while performing their functions away from their ordinary place of residence, subject to the approval of the Treasury Board.

### By-laws and Staff Assistance

The Commission may make by-laws for the conduct of its activities, subject to the approval of the Minister. The Minister may also make available to the Commission such staff and other assistance as are necessary for the proper conduct of its activities.

### Annual Report and Immunity

The Commission shall submit an annual report to the Minister of its activities during the year. No member of the Commission and no person designated by the Commission pursuant to Section 137.2(1) or (2) is personally liable for anything done or omitted to be done in good faith under Section 137.2.

individual_results.question: What is the primary goal that the Commission considers when approving plans, procedures, methods, machinery, and equipment in coal mines, or when granting exemptions and substitutions for regulatory provisions?
individual_results.answer:
## Primary Goal of the Commission in Approving Plans, Procedures, and Equipment

### Approval of Plans, Procedures, Methods, Machinery, and Equipment

The primary goal that the Commission considers when approving plans, procedures, methods, machinery, and equipment in coal mines, or when granting exemptions and substitutions for regulatory provisions is the **protection of the health and safety of employees**. This is explicitly stated in several sections of the Canada Labour Code.

Section 137.2(1) states:
"The Commission or persons designated by the Commission for the purposes of this subsection may approve in writing, with or without modification, plans or procedures submitted in accordance with paragraph 125.3(1)(d)." This indicates that the Commission's approval process is centered around ensuring that the submitted plans and procedures will not diminish the health and safety of employees.

Section 137.2(2) further elaborates on this goal:
"On the application of an employer, the Commission or persons designated by the Commission for the purposes of this subsection may, if, in the opinion of the Commission or those persons, protection of the health and safety of employees would not thereby be diminished..." followed by two options for approval. The first option is to approve the use of mining methods, machinery, or equipment that do not meet prescribed safety standards, provided that it would not diminish employee health and safety. The second option is to approve the use of such equipment for a specified time and subject to specified conditions, again with the caveat that it would not diminish employee health and safety. This demonstrates that the Commission's approval is contingent upon ensuring the well-being of employees.

### Exemptions and Substitutions for Regulatory Provisions

The Commission also prioritizes employee health and safety when granting exemptions and substitutions for regulatory provisions.

Section 137.2(3) outlines the Commission's authority to grant exemptions and substitutions:
"On the application of an employer, the Commission may, if in its opinion protection of the health and safety of employees would not thereby be diminished, by order, (a) exempt the employer from compliance with any provision of the regulations in the operation of coal mines controlled by the employer, subject to any conditions contained in the order; or (b) substitute for any provision of the regulations, so far as it applies to coal mines controlled by the employer, another provision having substantially the same purpose and effect." This section clearly indicates that the Commission will only grant exemptions or substitutions if it determines that employee health and safety will not be compromised.

Section 137.2(4) further reinforces this commitment:
"The Commission may make recommendations to the Minister for amending or revoking any provision of the regulations applicable to coal mines or for adding any provision thereto." This power to recommend amendments allows the Commission to proactively address any potential threats to employee health and safety by updating or adding regulations as needed.

In summary, the Commission consistently considers the **protection of the health and safety of employees** as its primary goal when approving plans, procedures, methods, machinery, and equipment in coal mines, or when granting exemptions and substitutions for regulatory provisions. This overarching principle guides all of the Commission's decisions and recommendations.

individual_results.question: What actions can the Minister take to promote and ensure occupational health and safety in employment to which the Part applies?
individual_results.answer:
## Minister's Actions to Promote and Ensure Occupational Health and Safety

### Special Committees

The Minister has the authority to establish special committees to provide assistance and advice on occupational health and safety matters. This allows for focused expertise and input on specific issues.
"The Minister may appoint committees of persons to assist or advise the Minister on any matter that the Minister considers advisable concerning occupational health and safety related to employment to which this Part applies." This quote directly states the Minister's power to create these committees, highlighting their role in supporting the Minister's efforts to improve workplace safety.

### Inquiries

The Minister can initiate inquiries into occupational health and safety concerns within federally regulated workplaces. These inquiries can be conducted by one or more individuals appointed by the Minister.
"The Minister may cause an inquiry to be made into and concerning occupational health and safety in any employment to which this Part applies and may appoint one or more persons to hold the inquiry." This passage clearly outlines the Minister's ability to order investigations into safety issues, ensuring a thorough understanding of the problems and potential solutions.

### Research

The Minister can undertake research into the causes of and methods for preventing employment injury and occupational illness. This research can be conducted independently or in collaboration with other government departments, agencies, or even provincial or organizational research efforts.
"The Minister may undertake research into the cause of and the means of preventing employment injury and occupational illness and may, where the Minister deems it appropriate, undertake such research in cooperation with any department or agency of the Government of Canada or with any or all provinces or with any organization undertaking similar research." This quote emphasizes the Minister's proactive approach to occupational health and safety through research, allowing for evidence-based interventions.

### Publication of Information

The Minister can disseminate the findings of any research conducted under subsection (4) and compile, prepare, and distribute data or information related to employee health and safety. This ensures that relevant knowledge is shared widely.
"The Minister may publish the results of any research undertaken under subsection (4) and compile, prepare and disseminate data or information bearing on health or safety of employees obtained from that research or otherwise." This passage highlights the Minister's commitment to transparency and knowledge sharing by making research findings accessible.

### Occupational Safety and Health Programs

The Minister can implement programs to reduce or prevent employment injury and occupational illness. These programs can be undertaken independently or in partnership with other government bodies, provinces, or organizations.
"The Minister may undertake programs to reduce or prevent employment injury and occupational illness and may, where the Minister deems it appropriate, undertake those programs in cooperation with any department or agency of the Government of Canada or with any or all provinces or any organization undertaking similar programs." This quote underscores the Minister's role in actively promoting workplace safety through the development and execution of preventative programs.

### Medical Surveillance and Examination Programs

The Minister can establish medical surveillance and examination programs to monitor the health of employees and identify potential risks early on.
"The Minister may undertake programs to reduce or prevent employment injury and occupational illness and may, where the Minister deems it appropriate, undertake those programs in cooperation with any department or agency of the Government of Canada or with any or all provinces or any organization undertaking similar programs." This passage, while part of a broader section on occupational safety and health programs, specifically mentions the Minister's ability to initiate medical surveillance and examination programs.

### Information, Training, and Supervision

The Minister can ensure that employees receive the necessary information, training, and supervision to perform their jobs safely. This includes providing an appropriate understanding of work safety procedures, knowledge of safe use of tools and equipment, and awareness of known or foreseeable workplace hazards.
"As an employer, you must ensure that employees have the necessary information, training, and supervision to perform their work safely. This includes:  an appropriate understanding of overall work safety procedures knowledge of the safe use of workplace tools and equipment awareness of known or foreseeable workplace hazards (whenever possible) training sessions should include documentation..." This quote, from a section outlining employer responsibilities, indirectly reflects the Minister's role in establishing the framework and expectations for providing this essential support to employees.

### Employer Investigations

The Minister can mandate that employers properly investigate employee complaints, including refusals to work, and accidents and injuries. This ensures accountability and allows for the identification and correction of safety issues.
"Under Part II of the Canada Labour Code, employers are required to protect the health and safety of employees at work, by ensuring that employee complaints, including refusals to work, and accidents and injuries are properly investigated." This passage directly states the Minister's power to require employers to conduct thorough investigations into safety concerns.

### Inspections

The Minister can require regular inspections of workplaces to identify and address occupational health and safety hazards before they lead to injuries.
"Regular inspections help ensure that occupational health and safety hazards are addressed before they result in possible injuries. Part II of the Canada Labour Code requires the health and safety committee/representative to carry out monthly inspections in the workplace in whole or in part." This quote highlights the Minister's ability to implement a system of regular workplace inspections to proactively prevent accidents.

individual_results.question: What is the role of the Minister in relation to medical surveillance, examination programs, and reporting on harassment and violence in workplaces under the Canada Labour Code?
individual_results.answer:
## The Minister's Role in Medical Surveillance, Examination Programs, and Reporting on Harassment and Violence

### Medical Surveillance and Examination Programs

The Minister plays a significant role in establishing and overseeing medical surveillance and examination programs within federally regulated workplaces under the Canada Labour Code.
"The Minister may undertake medical surveillance and examination programs with respect to occupational health and safety and may, if the Minister considers it appropriate, undertake those programs in cooperation with any department or agency of the Government of Canada or with any or all of the provinces or any organization undertaking similar programs." This passage clearly outlines the Minister's authority to initiate and collaborate on medical surveillance programs. It highlights the flexibility the Minister has to act independently or in partnership with other governmental bodies and organizations.

Furthermore, the Minister has the power to appoint medical practitioners to carry out these programs.
"The Minister may appoint any medical practitioner qualified in occupational medicine to undertake the medical surveillance and examination programs." This indicates the Minister's direct involvement in selecting the professionals responsible for conducting the medical surveillance and examinations.

### Administration: Special Committees

The Minister also has the authority to establish special committees to provide assistance or advice on occupational health and safety matters.
"The Minister may appoint committees of persons to assist or advise the Minister on any matter that the Minister considers advisable concerning occupational health and safety related to employment to which this Part applies." This passage emphasizes the Minister's power to create advisory bodies to support their work in promoting workplace health and safety.

### Administration: Annual Report on Harassment and Violence

The Minister is mandated to produce and publish an annual report detailing statistical data on harassment and violence in workplaces covered by the Canada Labour Code.
"The Minister shall prepare and publish an annual report that contains statistical data relating to harassment and violence in work places to which this Part applies. The report shall not contain any information that is likely to reveal the identity of a person who was involved in an occurrence of harassment and violence." This passage explicitly states the Minister's responsibility for compiling and disseminating this crucial information. It also includes a privacy safeguard to prevent the disclosure of individuals involved in harassment and violence incidents.

The annual report must categorize the statistical data according to prohibited grounds of discrimination under the Canadian Human Rights Act.
"The statistical data contained in the report shall include information that is categorized according to prohibited grounds of discrimination under the Canadian Human Rights Act..." This ensures that the data collected is analyzed and presented in a way that highlights potential patterns of discrimination contributing to harassment and violence.

Finally, the Minister is required to conduct a review of the harassment and violence provisions of this Part every five years and report on the findings to Parliament.
"Five years after the day on which this section comes into force and every five years after that, the Minister shall commence a review of the provisions of this Part relating to harassment and violence. At the conclusion of the review, the Minister shall prepare a report on the review." This passage details the Minister's ongoing commitment to evaluating the effectiveness of the harassment and violence provisions and to informing Parliament of the results. The report must be tabled in both Houses of Parliament within fifteen days of its completion.

individual_results.question: Who can the Minister and the Head delegate their powers, duties, or functions to, and under what conditions?
individual_results.answer:
## Delegation of Powers, Duties, or Functions by the Minister and the Head

### Minister's Delegation Powers

#### To Whom the Minister Can Delegate
"Subject to any terms and conditions specified by the Minister, the Head may delegate to any qualified person or class of persons any of the powers the Head is authorized to exercise or any of the duties or functions the Head is authorized to perform for the purposes of this Part." This section clearly states that the Minister has the authority to delegate their powers, duties, or functions to "any qualified person or class of persons." The phrase "qualified person or class of persons" indicates that there are criteria that must be met for someone to be eligible for such a delegation.

#### Conditions Governing the Minister's Delegation
"The Head may make the delegation subject to any terms and conditions that the Head considers appropriate." While this section refers to the Head's delegation powers, it is relevant to the Minister's as well. It highlights that the Minister can impose specific terms and conditions on any delegation they make. These terms and conditions are at the Minister's discretion and can be tailored to the specific delegation being made.

### Head's Delegation Powers

#### To Whom the Head Can Delegate
"Subject to any terms and conditions specified by the Minister, the Head may delegate to any qualified person or class of persons any of the powers the Head is authorized to exercise or any of the duties or functions the Head is authorized to perform for the purposes of this Part." This section mirrors the Minister's delegation powers, stating that the Head can delegate their powers, duties, or functions to "any qualified person or class of persons," subject to any terms and conditions set by the Minister.

#### Conditions Governing the Head's Delegation
"The Head may make the delegation subject to any terms and conditions that the Head considers appropriate." This condition is identical to the one governing the Minister's delegation powers, emphasizing the Head's discretion in setting terms and conditions for any delegation they make.

#### Delegation to Specific Entities
"...the Head may delegate to any qualified person or class of persons any of the powers the Head is authorized to exercise or any of the duties or functions the Head is authorized to perform for the purposes of this Part." This statement is broad, indicating that the Head can delegate to individuals or groups who meet the "qualified person or class of persons" criteria. It does not specify any limitations on the type of entity to whom the Head can delegate.

#### Delegation to Provincial Bodies
"Subject to subsection (3), the Minister may, with the approval of the Governor in Council, enter into an agreement with any province or any provincial body specifying the terms and conditions under which the Minister may delegate to a person employed by that province or provincial body the powers, duties or functions that the Minister or the Head is authorized to exercise or perform for the purposes of this Part." This section outlines a specific condition for the Minister's delegation powers: the need for approval from the Governor in Council and an agreement with the relevant province or provincial body. This agreement must detail the terms and conditions under which the Minister can delegate to a person employed by that province or provincial body.

#### Delegation to Persons in Connection with Federal Work
"The Head may, at any reasonable time, enter on any place used in connection with a federal work, undertaking or business for the purpose of making an inspection authorized under subsection (2), and may, for that purpose, question any employee apart from his employer." While this section pertains to the Head's inspection powers, it is relevant to delegation as it implies that the Head can delegate inspection authority to any qualified person or class of persons who are present at a federal work, undertaking, or business.

#### Delegation to Persons in Carrying Out Duties
"The Head may, in carrying out the Head’s duties and functions, be accompanied or assisted by any persons that the Head considers necessary." This section indicates that the Head can delegate assistance in carrying out their duties to any persons they deem necessary.

#### Delegation to Persons in Obtaining Information
"(c.1) require any employer that provides benefits to its employees under a long-term disability plan that must be insured in accordance with subsection 239.2(1) to furnish proof that the plan is insured in accordance with that subsection; (d) require an employee to make full disclosure, production and delivery to the Head of all records, documents, statements, writings, books, papers, extracts therefrom or copies thereof or of other information, either orally or in writing, that are in the possession or under the control of the employee and that in any way relate to the wages, hours of work or conditions of his employment..." These sections describe the Head's powers to require information from employers and employees. The Head can delegate the power to require such information to any qualified person or class of persons.

#### Delegation to Persons in Responding to Complaints
"(e) require any party to a complaint made under subsection 240(1) to make or furnish full and correct statements, either orally or in writing, in such form as may be required, respecting the circumstances of the dismissal in respect of which the complaint was made." This section outlines the Head's power to require statements from parties to complaints. The Head can delegate this power to any qualified person or class of persons.

#### Delegation to Persons in Carrying Out Inspection
"The Head may, in carrying out the Head’s duties and functions, be accompanied or assisted by any persons that the Head considers necessary." This section reiterates the Head's ability to delegate assistance in carrying out their duties, which could include delegating inspection authority.

#### Delegation to Persons in Testimony
"No person to whom powers, duties or functions have been delegated under subsection (1), and no person who has accompanied or assisted such a person or the Head in carrying out their duties and functions, shall be required to give testimony in any civil suit or civil proceedings, or in any proceeding under section 242, with regard to information obtained in carrying out those..." This section clarifies that persons to whom delegation has been granted, and those who assisted in carrying out those delegated powers, are exempt from being required to give testimony in civil suits or proceedings regarding information obtained in exercising those delegated powers.

#### Delegation to Persons in Providing Certificates of Authority
"The Minister may provide any person to whom powers, duties or functions have been delegated under subsection (1), or under an agreement entered into under subsection (2), with a certificate of authority and, when exercising those powers or performing those duties or functions, that person shall show the certificate to any person who asks to see it." This section states that the Minister can provide a certificate of authority to persons to whom delegation has been granted, and they must present this certificate upon request.

#### Limitation of Liability for Delegated Powers
"A person to whom powers, duties or functions have been delegated under subsection (1) or (1.1), or under an agreement entered into under subsection (2), is not personally liable for anything done or omitted to be done by them in good faith in the actual or purported exercise of those powers or performance of those duties or functions." This section provides a limitation on liability for delegated powers, stating that a person to whom delegation has been granted is not personally liable for any actions taken by them in good faith in exercising those delegated powers.

#### Duty of Her Majesty
"Despite subsection (5), and for greater certainty, Her Majesty in right of Canada is not relieved of any civil liability to which Her Majesty in right of Canada may otherwise be subject." This section clarifies that despite the limitation of liability for delegated powers, Her Majesty in right of Canada is not relieved of any other civil liabilities.

individual_results.question: What are the powers and responsibilities of the Head in carrying out duties related to workplace health and safety, particularly in terms of entering workplaces, conducting examinations, and issuing directions?
individual_results.answer:
## Powers and Responsibilities of the Head in Workplace Health and Safety

### Entering Workplaces and Conducting Examinations

The Head possesses extensive powers to enter workplaces and conduct examinations related to workplace health and safety. Section 141(1) states,
"Subject to section 143.2, the Head may, in carrying out the Head’s duties and at any reasonable time, enter any work place controlled by an employer and, in respect of any work place, may (a) conduct examinations, tests, inquiries, investigations and inspections or direct the employer to conduct them; (b) take or remove for analysis, samples of any material or substance or any biological, chemical or physical agent..." This indicates the Head has the authority to enter any workplace and undertake a wide range of health and safety related activities, including conducting examinations, tests, inquiries, investigations, and inspections. Furthermore, the Head can direct the employer to carry out these same activities.

Section 141.1(1) elaborates on these powers, stating,
"Subject to section 143.2, the Head may, in carrying out the Head’s duties and at any reasonable time, enter any work place controlled by an employer and, in respect of any work place, may (a) conduct examinations, tests, inquiries, investigations and inspections or direct the employer to conduct them; (b) take or remove for analysis, samples of any material or substance or any biological, chemical or physical agent; (c) be accompanied or assisted by any person and bring any equipment that the Head deems necessary to carry out the Head’s duties; (d) take or remove, for testing, material or equipment if there is no reasonable alternative to doing so; (e) take photographs and make sketches; (f) direct the employer to ensure that any place or thing specified by the Head not be disturbed for a reasonable period pending an examination, test, inquiry, investigation or inspection in relation to the place or thing; (g) direct any person not to disturb any place or thing specified by the Head for a reasonable period pending an examination, test, inquiry, investigation or inspection in relation to the place or thing; (h) direct the employer to produce documents and information relating to the health and safety of the employer’s employees or the safety of the work place and to permit the Head to examine and make copies of or take extracts from those documents and that information; (i) direct the employer or an employee to make or provide statements, in the form and manner that the Head may specify, respecting working conditions and material and equipment that affect the health or safety of employees; (j) direct the employer or an employee or a person designated by either of them to accompany the Head while the Head, is in the work place; and (k) meet with any person in private or, at the request of the person, in the presence of the person’s legal counsel or union representative." This section further details the Head's ability to conduct examinations, take samples, bring necessary equipment, direct the employer to maintain undisturbed areas, take photographs, direct the employer to produce documents, and even meet with individuals in private or with legal counsel present.

### Issuing Directions

The Head also has the power to issue directions related to workplace health and safety. Section 141(1)(g) states,
"...direct any person not to disturb any place or thing specified by the Head for a reasonable period pending an examination, test, inquiry, investigation or inspection in relation to the place or thing..." This demonstrates the Head's ability to issue orders to prevent interference with areas under examination. Section 141(2) further clarifies this power, stating,
"The Head may issue a direction under subsection (1) whether or not the Head is in the work place at the time the direction is issued." This indicates that the Head can issue directions remotely as well as in person.

### Investigation of Workplace Deaths and Accidents

The Head is responsible for investigating workplace deaths and accidents. Section 141(3) states,
"The Head shall investigate every death of an employee that occurred in the work place or while the employee was working, or that was the result of an injury that occurred in the work place or while the employee was working." This highlights the Head's duty to thoroughly investigate all workplace fatalities and injuries. Section 141(4) adds to this responsibility by stating,
"If the death results from a motor vehicle accident on a public road, as part of the investigation the Head shall obtain a copy of any police report as soon as possible after the accident." This specifies an additional action the Head must take in the event of a workplace-related motor vehicle accident.

### Reporting Findings

Following an investigation, the Head is required to report their findings. Section 141(6) states,
"Within 10 days after completing a written report on the findings of an inquiry or investigation, the Head shall provide the employer and the work place committee or the health and safety representative with a copy of the report." This indicates the Head's obligation to provide a written report of their investigation to relevant parties within a specified timeframe.
