## Section 141.1: Exercise of Powers in Relation to Health and Safety: Inspections

### Presence During Inspection

#### Requirement for Specific Representatives
"If the Head conducts an inspection of the work place at the work place, it shall be done in the presence of (a) an employee member and an employer member of the work place committee; or (b) the health and safety representative and a person designated by the employer."

This section clearly outlines who must be present when the Head conducts an inspection. It provides two options: either an employee member and an employer member of the workplace committee, or the health and safety representative and a person designated by the employer. This requirement ensures that the inspection is conducted with the involvement of representatives from both the employee and employer sides, promoting transparency and collaboration.

#### Inspection Not to be Delayed
"The Head may proceed with an inspection in the absence of any person mentioned in subsection (1) if that person chooses not to be present."

This subsection clarifies that the Head is not obligated to wait for the presence of all the specified representatives if they choose not to attend. The Head can proceed with the inspection even if one or more of the representatives are absent. This provision allows for flexibility in scheduling inspections while still ensuring that the inspection is conducted with the involvement of relevant workplace representatives.

individual_results.question: Who is required to give all reasonable assistance in a workplace to enable certain individuals to exercise their powers or perform their duties under the Canada Labour Code?
individual_results.answer:
## Section 142: Duty to Assist in a Workplace

### Individuals Required to Provide Assistance

Section 142 of the Canada Labour Code outlines the individuals who are required to give all reasonable assistance in a workplace. It specifies two primary categories of people who have this duty:

#### The Person in Charge and All Employees
"The person in charge of a work place and every person employed at, or in connection with, a work place shall give all reasonable assistance to (a) the Head to enable him or her to exercise his or her powers or to perform his or her duties or functions under this Part..."

This passage clearly states that the person in charge of a workplace, along with every employee working there, is obligated to provide all reasonable assistance to the Head. The Head is defined as the person in charge of the workplace, as indicated by the preceding phrase. This duty extends to enabling the Head to exercise their powers and perform their duties under the Canada Labour Code.

#### External Adjudicators and Board Members
"(a.1) an external adjudicator and a member of the Board to enable them to, in accordance with subsection 12.001(2) or 14(5), exercise or perform the powers, duties or functions conferred on the Board by this Part; and (b) every person to whom powers, duties or functions have been delegated under subsection 140(1) or (1.1), or under an agreement entered into under subsection 140(2), who is exercising those powers or performing those duties or functions."

This section further clarifies the duty to assist by including external adjudicators and Board members. It states that they are entitled to "all reasonable assistance" to enable them to exercise or perform the powers, duties, or functions conferred on the Board by this Part. Additionally, it extends this duty to any person to whom powers, duties, or functions have been delegated under specific subsections, and who is currently exercising those powers or performing those duties. This ensures that all individuals authorized to exercise powers or perform duties under the Canada Labour Code receive the necessary support from those in charge and all employees.

individual_results.question: What are the consequences and prohibitions related to interfering with the exercise of powers and duties under Part of the Canada Labour Code (PART II - Occupational Health and Safety), and providing information to authorities?
individual_results.answer:
## Consequences and Prohibitions Related to Interfering with Powers and Duties and Providing Information

### Section 143: Obstruction and False Statements | Provision of Information

#### Prohibitions Against Obstruction and False Statements
"No person shall obstruct or hinder, or make a false or misleading statement either orally or in writing to (a) the Head in the exercise of his or her powers, or in the performance of his or her duties or functions, under this Part; (a.1) an external adjudicator or a member of the Board in the exercise or performance, in accordance with subsection 12.001(2) or 14(5), of the powers, duties or functions conferred on the Board by this Part; or (b) any person to whom powers, duties or functions have been delegated under subsection 140(1) or (1.1), or under an agreement entered into under subsection 140(2), who is exercising those powers or performing those duties or functions."

This section clearly outlines prohibitions against interfering with the exercise of powers and duties under Part II of the Canada Labour Code. Furthermore, it prohibits making "false or misleading statements" to these individuals. This prohibition is broad, encompassing both oral and written communications. This provision is crucial for ensuring that authorities have access to the necessary information to carry out their occupational health and safety duties effectively. ### Section 141: Exercise of Powers in Relation to Health and Safety: Inspections

This comprehensive set of powers ensures that the Head has the necessary tools to effectively carry out occupational health and safety inspections and address any concerns that may arise.

#### Directions and Reporting Requirements

This subsection clarifies that the Head can issue directions during inspections even if they are not physically present at the workplace. This flexibility allows for timely interventions and ensures that the Head can effectively guide the employer in addressing any identified hazards or concerns.

individual_results.question: What are the general rules regarding the disclosure of information obtained by certain individuals, such as the Head, external adjudicators, members of the Board, and others, in the exercise of their powers or performance of their duties under the Canada Labour Code?
individual_results.answer:
## General Rules Regarding Disclosure of Information

### Preclusion of Testimony in Civil or Administrative Proceedings
"No person to whom powers, duties or functions have been delegated under subsection 140(1) or (1.1), or under an agreement entered into under subsection 140(2), and no person who has accompanied or assisted that person in exercising those powers or performing those duties or functions may be required to give testimony in civil or administrative proceedings, other than proceedings under this Part, with regard to information obtained in exercising those powers or performing those duties or functions, except with the written permission of the Head, in which case subsection (5) does not apply to restrict the disclosure of the information."

This section of the Canada Labour Code establishes a general rule precluding testimony in civil or administrative proceedings for certain individuals. It states that anyone delegated powers, duties, or functions under specific subsections of the Code, or who assisted such individuals, cannot be compelled to testify about information obtained while exercising those powers or performing those duties. This rule is subject to the Head's written permission, in which case the restriction on disclosure under subsection (5) does not apply.

### Non-Disclosure of Information by Specific Individuals
"...the Head, an external adjudicator or a member of the Board who is admitted to a work place under the powers conferred by section 141 — or a person who is admitted to a work place under the powers conferred by section 141 that are delegated to them under subsection 140(1.1) or under an agreement entered into under subsection 140(2) — and any person accompanying them, shall not disclose to any person any information obtained in the work place by the Head, external adjudicator or member or person with regard to any secret process or trade secret, except for the purposes of this Part or as required by law."

This rule further restricts the disclosure of information by specific individuals. It prohibits the Head, external adjudicators, members of the Board, and any accompanying persons from disclosing information obtained while working in a workplace to any other person, except for the purposes of this Part or as required by law. This provision aims to protect confidential business information.

### Privileged Information
"All information that, under the Hazardous Materials Information Review Act , an employer is exempt from disclosing under this Act or the Hazardous Products Act and that is obtained in a work place under section 141 is privileged and, notwithstanding the Access to Information Act or any other Act or law, shall not be disclosed to any other person except for the purposes of this Part."

This section clarifies the status of certain information as privileged. It states that any information that an employer is exempt from disclosing under the Hazardous Materials Information Review Act or the Hazardous Products Act, and that is obtained in a workplace under section 141, is privileged and shall not be disclosed to any other person except for the purposes of this Part. This privilege is applicable regardless of other disclosure requirements under the Access to Information Act or other laws.

### Information Not to be Published
"No person shall, except for the purposes of this Part or for the purposes of a prosecution under this Part or unless the Head is satisfied that the publication or disclosure is in the interest of occupational health and safety or the public interest, publish or disclose any information obtained as a result of activities carried out under section 141."

This rule prohibits the general publication or disclosure of information obtained while working in a workplace under section 141. It allows for such publication or disclosure only for the purposes of this Part, for the purposes of a prosecution under this Part, or if the Head is satisfied that the publication or disclosure is in the interest of occupational health and safety or the public interest. This provision balances the need for transparency with the protection of confidential information.

individual_results.question: What actions can the Head take if they believe a provision of the Part is being or has been contravened, and what are the requirements for documenting and communicating these actions?
individual_results.answer:
## Head's Actions Upon Belief of Contravention

### Actions the Head Can Take

The Head possesses several actions they can undertake if they believe a provision of the Part is being or has been contravened. These actions are outlined in Section 271 and Section 286 of the Canada Labour Code.

#### Establishing Notices of Violation
"The Head may (a) establish the form of notices of violation..." This indicates that the Head has the authority to define the format and content of notices issued when a contravention is suspected. This ensures consistency and clarity in communicating violations.

#### Designating Issuers of Notices
"(b) designate persons, or classes of persons, who are authorized to issue notices of violation..." This power allows the Head to delegate the responsibility of issuing notices to specific individuals or groups. This can streamline the enforcement process and ensure that notices are issued by qualified personnel.

#### Establishing Short-Form Descriptions for Violations
"...and (c) establish a short-form description for each violation to be used in notices of violation." This action facilitates efficient communication by providing concise labels for different types of violations. This aids in tracking and categorizing contraventions.

#### Presenting Evidence and Representations to the Board
"The Head may, in an appeal, present evidence and make representations to the Board." While this action is specifically within the context of an appeal, it highlights the Head's ability to provide information and arguments to the Board regarding a potential contravention.

#### Inspecting and Examining Records
"...the Head may (a) inspect and examine all books, payrolls and other records of an employer that relate to the wages, hours of work or conditions of employment affecting any employee..." This power allows the Head to gather evidence of a contravention by reviewing relevant employer records.

#### Requiring Statements and Information
"...require any employer to make or furnish full and correct statements, either orally or in writing, in such form as may be required, respecting the wages paid to all or any of his employees, and the hours of work and conditions of their employment..." This action enables the Head to obtain detailed information from employers regarding potential violations.

#### Requiring Disclosure of Records
"...employee to make full disclosure, production and delivery to the Head of all records, documents, statements, writings, books, papers, extracts therefrom or copies thereof or of other information, either orally or in writing, that are in the possession or under the control of the employee and that in any way relate to the wages, hours of work or conditions of his employment..." This power allows the Head to obtain information from employees that may shed light on a contravention.

#### Requiring Statements from Parties to Complaints
"...require any party to a complaint made under subsection 240(1) to make or furnish full and correct statements, either orally or in writing, in such form as may be required, respecting the circumstances of the dismissal in respect of which the complaint was made." This action allows the Head to gather information from parties involved in dismissal complaints that may indicate a contravention.

#### Entering Premises for Inspection
"The Head may, at any reasonable time, enter on any place used in connection with a federal work, undertaking or business for the purpose of making an inspection authorized under subsection (2), and may, for that purpose, question any employee apart from his employer." This power enables the Head to conduct on-site inspections to gather evidence of a contravention.

#### Requiring Reasonable Assistance
"The person in charge of any federal work, undertaking or business and every person employed in it or in connection with its operation shall give the Head all reasonable assistance to enable the Head to carry out the Head’s duties and functions under this Part or the regulations." This requirement ensures that employers and their employees cooperate with the Head's investigations into potential contraventions.

### Requirements for Documenting and Communicating These Actions

The documents do not explicitly detail the formal requirements for documenting and communicating these actions. However, Section 286 outlines the Head's obligations in communicating an appeal.

#### Informing the Head in Writing
"The Board shall inform the Head in writing when an appeal is brought under subsection 285(1) and provide the Head with a copy of the request for appeal." This requirement emphasizes the importance of written communication when an appeal is initiated.

#### Providing Copies of Documents
"The Head shall, on request of the Board, provide to the Board a copy of any document that the Head relied on for the purpose of making the decision being appealed." This requirement highlights the need for documentation to support any actions taken.
"The Board shall, on request of the Head, provide to the Head a copy of any document that is filed with the Board in the appeal." This reciprocal requirement ensures that the Head has access to all relevant documentation pertaining to the appeal.

#### Establishing Notice of Violation Form
"The Head may (a) establish the form of notices of violation..." This action implies a requirement to document the content of each notice issued.

#### Designating Issuers of Notices
"(b) designate persons, or classes of persons, who are authorized to issue notices of violation..." This action suggests a need to document the authorization process for issuing notices.

#### Establishing Short-Form Descriptions for Violations
"...and (c) establish a short-form description for each violation to be used in notices of violation." This action indicates a requirement to document the standardized descriptions for each violation.

In summary, the Head has a range of powers to address suspected contraventions of the Part, including establishing violation notices, designating issuers, inspecting records, requiring statements, and presenting evidence to the Board. While the documents do not specify formal documentation requirements, they emphasize the importance of written communication, providing copies of relevant documents, and establishing standardized formats for notices and descriptions.

## Powers, Duties, and Functions of the Board under the Canada Labour Code

### Section 84: Powers of Board

#### Conciliation Procedures
"A conciliation commissioner or a conciliation board (a) may determine their own procedure; (b) has, in relation to any proceeding before them, the powers conferred on the Board, in relation to any proceeding before the Board, by paragraphs 16(a), (b), (c), (f) and (h); and (c) may authorize any person to do anything described in paragraph 16(b) or (f) that the conciliation commissioner or conciliation board may do and to report to the conciliation commissioner or conciliation board thereon."

This section outlines the broad powers of a conciliation commissioner or board. It grants them autonomy in determining their own procedures while also explicitly conferring upon them the powers already held by the Board under specific paragraphs of Section 16. This ensures consistency in the Board's authority across different types of proceedings. Furthermore, it allows for the delegation of certain powers to other individuals or entities who can then report back to the conciliation commissioner or board.

### Section 15.1: General Power to Assist Parties

#### Assistance in Resolving Disputes
"(1) The Board, any member of the Board or any external adjudicator — or an employee of the Administrative Tribunals Support Service of Canada who is authorized by the Board — may, if the parties agree, assist the parties in resolving any issues in dispute at any stage of a proceeding and by any means that the Board considers appropriate, without prejudice to the Board’s power to determine issues that have not been settled."

This section details the Board's general power to assist parties in resolving disputes. It states that the Board, its members, external adjudicators, or authorized employees of the Administrative Tribunals Support Service of Canada can provide assistance if the parties consent. This assistance can be provided through any means the Board deems appropriate, as long as it does not limit the Board's authority to make final decisions on unresolved issues.

#### Declaratory Opinions
"(2) The Board, on application by an employer or a trade union, may give declaratory opinions."

This subsection specifies another function of the Board: the ability to issue declaratory opinions. This power is exercised upon application from an employer or a trade union, allowing the Board to provide its interpretation of the application of the Canada Labour Code to a particular situation.

### Section 15: Regulations

#### General Power to Make Regulations
"The Board may make regulations of general application respecting (a) the establishment of rules of procedure for its pre-hearing proceedings and hearings; (a.1) the use of means of telecommunication that permit the parties and the Board or its members to communicate simultaneously for pre-hearing conferences, hearings and Board meetings; (b) the determination of units appropriate for collective bargaining; (c) the certification of trade unions as bargaining agents for bargaining units; (d) the conduct of representation votes; (e) the specification of the period of time after which the Board may receive an application from a trade union for certification as the bargaining agent for a unit where the Board has refused an application from the trade union for certification in respect of the same or substantially the same unit; (f) the specification of the period of time after which the Board may receive an application from an employee for revocation of a trade union’s certification as the bargaining agent for a unit where the Board has refused an application for revocation in respect of the same unit; (g) the hearing or determination of any application, complaint, question, dispute, difference or appeal that may be made or referred to the Board; (g.1) an expeditious procedure and matters that may be determined under that procedure; (h) the forms to be used in respect of any proceeding that may come before the Board; (i) the time within which and the circumstances under which the Board may exercise its powers under section 18; (j) any inquiry that the Board may make under subsection 34(2); (k) the form in which and the period during which evidence and information may be presented to the Board in connection with any proceeding that may come before it; (l) the specification of the time within which and the parties or persons to whom notices and other documents shall be sent and the circumstances in which such notices or other documents shall be deemed to have been given or received by the Board or any party or person; (m) the determination of the form in which and the period during which evidence as to (i) the membership of any employees in a trade union, (ii) any objection by employees to the certification of a trade union, or (iii) any signification by employees that they no longer wish to be represented by a trade union shall be presented to the Board on an application made to it pursuant to this Part; (n) the criteria for determining whether an employee is a member of a trade union; (o) the circumstances in which evidence referred to in paragraph (m) may be received by the Board as evidence that any employees wish or do not wish to have a particular trade union represent them as their bargaining agent, including the circumstances in which the evidence so received by the Board may not be made public by the Board; (o.1) the conditions for valid strike or lockout votes; (p) the authority of any person to act on behalf of the Board and the matters and things to be done and the action to be taken by that person, including the authority of an employee of the Administrative Tribunals Support Service of Canada to make decisions on uncontested applications or questions; (p.1) the manner and criteria for selecting external adjudicators; and (q) any other matters and things that may be incidental or conducive to the proper performance of the duties of the Board under this Act."

This section grants the Board extensive rulemaking authority. It allows the Board to create regulations of general application covering a wide range of procedural and operational aspects of its work. These regulations can address everything from pre-hearing procedures and telecommunication methods to the determination of bargaining units and the conduct of representation votes. This power ensures the Board can adapt its processes to meet evolving needs and promote efficiency.

### Section 21: Exercise of Powers, Duties and Functions
"The Board shall exercise the powers and perform the duties and functions that are conferred or imposed on it by this Act..."

This section provides a general statement of the Board's obligation to exercise its powers and perform its duties. It clarifies that these powers and duties are derived from the Canada Labour Code itself and the regulations established by the Board under its rulemaking authority. This ensures that the Board's actions are always within the scope of its legal mandate.

### Section 16: Determination without oral hearing

#### Deciding Questions Arising in Proceedings
"(q) to decide any question that may arise in a proceeding under Part II, III or IV."

This section explicitly states the Board's power to decide any questions that may arise in proceedings under specific parts of the Canada Labour Code. This broad power ensures the Board can resolve any legal or procedural issues that come before it, facilitating the efficient conduct of its proceedings.

## Appeal of a Direction Issued by the Head

### Status of a Direction During an Appeal
"Unless otherwise ordered by the Board on application by the employer, employee or trade union, an appeal of a direction does not operate as a stay of the direction." This passage directly addresses the status of a direction while an appeal is pending. It clarifies that filing an appeal does not automatically halt the direction from being enforced. However, the Board has the authority to issue a stay of the direction upon request.

### Requirements for Making an Appeal

### Who Can Appeal?
"An employer, employee or trade union that feels aggrieved by a direction issued by the Head under this Part may appeal the direction to the Board, in writing, within 30 days after the day on which the direction was issued or confirmed in writing." This section outlines the parties eligible to appeal a direction. It specifies that any employer, employee, or trade union who believes they have been negatively impacted by a direction issued by the Head can file an appeal.

### How to Make an Appeal?
"...an appeal of a direction does not operate as a stay of the direction." This statement indicates that the appeal must be submitted in writing. The deadline for filing an appeal is within 30 days after the direction was issued or confirmed in writing.

### Information Required for the Appeal
"The Board shall inform the Head in writing when an appeal is brought under subsection 129(7) or section 146 and provide him or her with a copy of the request for appeal." This passage details the notification process for an appeal. The Board is obligated to inform the Head when an appeal is filed and to provide the Head with a copy of the appeal request.
"The Head shall, on request of the Board, provide to the Board a copy of any document that the Head relied on for the purpose of making the decision or issuing the direction being appealed." This section outlines the Head's obligation to provide relevant documentation to the Board upon request. The Head must furnish any documents they used to arrive at the direction being appealed.
"The Board shall, on request of the Head, provide to the Head a copy of any document that is filed with the Board in the appeal." This passage specifies the Board's responsibility to provide the Head with a copy of any documents submitted to the Board as part of the appeal.
"The Head may, in an appeal, present evidence and make representations to the Board." This statement confirms the Head's right to participate in the appeal process by presenting evidence and making arguments to the Board.

## Appeals of Decisions and Directions: Inquiry by the Board

### Section 146.1: Inquiry by the Board
"If an appeal is brought under subsection 129(7) or section 146, the Board shall, in a summary way and without delay, inquire into the circumstances of the decision or direction, as the case may be, and the reasons for it and may (a) vary, rescind or confirm the decision or direction; and (b) issue any direction that the Board considers appropriate under subsection 145(2) or (2.1)."

This section details the immediate action the Board takes upon receiving an appeal. It states that the Board will conduct a "summary way and without delay" inquiry into the appeal's circumstances and the rationale behind the original decision or direction. The Board then has several options: it can "vary, rescind or confirm" the original decision or direction, or it can issue a new direction that it deems appropriate under specific provisions of the Canada Labour Code. This indicates the Board's power to review and potentially overturn or modify decisions made by the Head.

### Section 146.5: Wages for Board Proceedings
"An employee who is a party to a proceeding under subsection 146.1(1) and who attends at the proceeding, or any employee who has been summoned by the Board to attend at such a proceeding and who attends, is entitled to be paid by the employer at the employee’s regular rate of wages for the time spent at the proceeding that would otherwise have been time at work."

This section addresses the compensation of employees who participate in Board proceedings related to appeals. It clarifies that such employees are entitled to be paid their regular rate of wages for the time they spend at the proceeding, which would otherwise have been considered time at work. This ensures that employees are not financially penalized for participating in the appeal process.

individual_results.question: What protection does the Canada Labour Code offer to employees who exercise their rights or provide information related to workplace health and safety?
individual_results.answer:
## Protection for Employees Exercising Health and Safety Rights

### Right to Refuse Dangerous Work

The Canada Labour Code explicitly grants employees the right to refuse to work if they have a reasonable belief that their workplace presents a danger to them or another employee. This right is protected by the Code, provided employees follow the proper procedure.
"You have the right to refuse to work if you have reasonable cause to believe that:  your workplace presents a danger to you the use or operation of a machine or apparatus presents a danger to you or to another employee, and  the performance of an activity constitutes a danger to you or to another employee..."

This protection is crucial for ensuring employee safety. It allows workers to protect themselves from imminent hazards without fear of reprisal.

### Anti-reprisal Protection for Concerted Activity

The Canada Labour Code also offers anti-reprisal protection for employees who exercise their rights or provide information related to workplace health and safety through concerted activity. This means that employers are prohibited from retaliating against employees who engage in collective efforts to address health and safety concerns.
"**Anti-reprisal protection for  concerted activity** Studies  show that many workers are unlikely to speak out about problems in the  workplace if they do not have access to collective voice mechanisms because  they fear reprisal."

This protection is vital for encouraging employees to speak up about safety issues without fear of negative consequences. It empowers workers to collectively advocate for a safer work environment.

### Right to Know

Employees have the right to be informed of known or foreseeable hazards in the workplace and to be provided with the information, instructions, training, and supervision necessary to protect their health and safety.
"You have the right to be informed of known or foreseeable hazards in the workplace and to be provided with the information, instructions, training, and supervision necessary to protect your health and safety."

This right to know is fundamental to preventing workplace accidents and injuries. It ensures that employees are aware of the risks they face and are equipped to protect themselves.

### Right to Participate

Employees have the right to participate in identifying and correcting work-related health and safety concerns. This participation can occur through health and safety representatives, workplace health and safety committees, or policy health and safety committees.
"As health and safety representatives or workplace health and safety committee or policy health and safety committee members, employees have the right to participate in identifying and correcting work-related health and safety concerns."

This right to participate is essential for fostering a collaborative approach to workplace health and safety. It ensures that employees have a voice in shaping a safer work environment.

### Reporting Obligations and Protection

The Canada Labour Code requires employees to report any thing or circumstance in a workplace that is likely to be hazardous to the health or safety of the employee, or that of other persons granted access to the workplace by the employer. Employees who make such reports are protected from reprisal.
"...report to the employer any thing or circumstance in a work place that is likely to be hazardous to the health or safety of the employee, or that of the other employees or other persons granted access to the work place by the employer..."

This reporting obligation and protection are crucial for ensuring that workplace hazards are identified and addressed promptly. It encourages employees to speak up about safety concerns without fear of retaliation.

individual_results.question: What are the potential consequences for a person who contravenes a provision of Part of the Canada Labour Code related to health and safety, and how do these consequences vary depending on the circumstances of the contravention?
individual_results.answer:
## Consequences for Contravention of Health and Safety Provisions

### General Offences

Section 101 of the Canada Labour Code outlines the general offences for persons who contravene provisions of Part II, excluding sections 50, 94, or 95. It states:
"Subject to section 100, every person other than an employer or a trade union who contravenes or fails to comply with any provision of this Part other than section 50, 94 or 95 is guilty of an offence and liable on summary conviction to a fine not exceeding one thousand dollars."

This indicates that a general contravention of health and safety provisions can result in a fine of up to one thousand dollars upon summary conviction.

Section 273 further elaborates on the general offences, stating:
"Every person or department that contravenes or fails to comply with a provision, direction, order or condition designated by regulations made under paragraph 270(1)(a) commits a violation and is liable to a penalty of an amount to be determined in accordance with the regulations."

This provision reinforces the general offence and specifies that the penalty will be determined by the regulations, allowing for flexibility in setting the fine amount.

### Offences Related to Death or Serious Injury

Section 148(1) details the potential consequences for a person whose contravention of Part II results in the death of, serious illness of, or serious injury to an employee. It specifies:
"Every person who contravenes a provision of this Part the direct result of which is the death of, serious illness of or serious injury to an employee is guilty of an offence and liable (a) on conviction on indictment, to a fine of not more than $1,000,000 or to imprisonment for a term of not more than two years, or to both; or (b) on summary conviction, to a fine of not more than..."

This section highlights a significant escalation in the potential consequences. If a contravention directly leads to death, serious illness, or serious injury, the penalties are substantially higher. On indictment, the fine can be up to one million dollars or imprisonment for up to two years, or both. On summary conviction, the fine can be up to one hundred thousand dollars.

### Offences Related to Wilful Contravention

Section 148(3) addresses the offence of wilfully contravening a provision of Part II knowing that the contravention is likely to cause death, serious illness, or serious injury to an employee. It states:
"Every person who wilfully contravenes a provision of this Part knowing that the contravention is likely to cause the death of, serious illness of or serious injury to an employee is guilty of an offence and liable (a) on conviction on indictment, to a fine of not more than $1,000,000 or to imprisonment for a term of not more than two years, or to both; or (b) on summary conviction, to a fine of not more than $1,000,000."

This provision further increases the severity of the penalties for a contravention that is knowingly likely to cause serious harm. The penalties are the same as those outlined in Section 148(1) for contraventions resulting in death, serious illness, or serious injury.

### Offences Related to Refusal to Work

Section 4_1 of the Canada Labour Code outlines the rights of employees, including the right to refuse to work if they have reasonable cause to believe that their workplace presents a danger. It states:
"You have the right to refuse to work if you have reasonable cause to believe that:  your workplace presents a danger to you the use or operation of a machine or apparatus presents a danger to you or to another employee, and  the performance of an activity constitutes a danger to you or to another employee..."

While this section doesn't explicitly detail the consequences for a person who contravenes a health and safety provision by creating a dangerous workplace, it implies that such a contravention could lead to an employee's right to refuse to work. However, it does not specify penalties for the person who created the dangerous situation.

### Defence for Due Care and Diligence

Section 148(4) provides a defence for a person prosecuted for a contravention of Part II, except for certain paragraphs. It states:
"On a prosecution of a person for a contravention of any provision of this Part, except paragraphs 125(1)(c), (z.10) and (z.11), it is a defence for the person to prove that the person exercised due care and diligence to avoid the contravention."

This defence allows a person to avoid a conviction if they can demonstrate that they took reasonable steps to prevent the contravention. However, it does not alter the potential penalties for a wilful contravention or one resulting in serious harm.

### Additional Considerations

Section 148(5) addresses the application of regulations made under subsection 157(1.1) in relation to health and safety matters. It states:
"For the purposes of this section, if regulations are made under subsection 157(1.1) in relation to health or safety matters referred to in a paragraph of any of sections 125 to 126 by which a standard or other thing is to be prescribed, that standard or other thing is deemed to be prescribed within the meaning of that paragraph."

This provision clarifies how regulations made under specific circumstances are treated for the purposes of the offences outlined in Section 148. It ensures that such regulations are considered as prescribed standards when assessing contraventions.

individual_results.question: Who can be held liable and prosecuted for an offence under this Part of the Canada Labour Code (PART II - Occupational Health and Safety), and what are the conditions for instituting proceedings?
individual_results.answer:
## Liability and Prosecution for Offences under Part II of the Canada Labour Code

### Who Can Be Held Liable?

Section 274 of the Canada Labour Code outlines who can be held liable for an offence committed by a corporation or a department. It states:
"If a corporation or a department commits a violation, any of the following persons who directed, authorized, assented to, acquiesced in or participated in the commission of the violation is a party to the violation and is liable to a penalty of an amount to be determined in accordance with the regulations, whether or not the corporation or department has been proceeded against in accordance with this Part: (a) any officer, director, agent or mandatary of the corporation; (b) any senior official in the department; or (c) any other person exercising managerial or supervisory functions in the corporation or department."

This section broadens the scope of liability beyond just the corporation or department itself. It identifies various individuals within the organization who can be held responsible for the violation, including officers, directors, agents, senior officials, and any other person with managerial or supervisory roles. The liability is assessed based on their involvement in directing, authorizing, consenting to, acquiescing in, or participating in the commission of the violation.

### Conditions for Instituting Proceedings

Section 148 of the Canada Labour Code details the conditions for instituting proceedings against a person who contravenes a provision of Part II. It outlines the potential penalties:
"Section 148 (1) Subject to this section, every person who contravenes a provision of this Part is guilty of an offence and liable (a) on conviction on indictment, to a fine of not more than $1,000,000 or to imprisonment for a term of not more than two years, or to both; or (b) on summary conviction, to a fine of not more than $100,000."

This section establishes that any person who violates a provision of Part II is guilty of an offence and can be prosecuted. The penalties vary depending on the type of conviction: indictment carries a fine of up to \$1,000,000 or imprisonment for up to two years, or both, while summary conviction results in a fine of up to \$100,000.

Section 148 also addresses more serious contraventions resulting in death, serious illness, or serious injury to an employee. It states:
"(2) Every person who contravenes a provision of this Part the direct result of which is the death of, serious illness of or serious injury to an employee is guilty of an offence and liable (a) on conviction on indictment, to a fine of not more than $1,000,000 or to imprisonment for a term of not more than two years, or to both; or (b) on summary conviction, to a fine of not more than $1,000,000."

This section specifies that if a contravention directly leads to death, serious illness, or serious injury, the penalties are significantly increased, with indictment carrying a fine of up to \$1,000,000 or imprisonment for up to two years, or both.

Furthermore, Section 148(3) addresses wilful contraventions:
"(3) Every person who wilfully contravenes a provision of this Part knowing that the contravention is likely to cause the death of, serious illness of or serious injury to an employee is guilty of an offence and liable (a) on conviction on indictment, to a fine of not more than $1,000,000 or to imprisonment for a term of not more than two years, or to both; or (b) on summary conviction, to a fine of not more than $1,000,000."

This section clarifies that a wilful contravention, where the person knows it is likely to cause serious harm, carries the same severe penalties as a contravention that directly results in death, serious illness, or serious injury.

Finally, Section 148(4) provides a defence for certain contraventions:
"(4) On a prosecution of a person for a contravention of any provision of this Part, except paragraphs 125(1)(c), (z.10) and (z.11), it is a defence for the person to prove that the person exercised due care and diligence to avoid the contravention. However, no person is liable to imprisonment on conviction for an offence under any of paragraphs 125(1)(c), (z.10) and (z.11)."

This section states that a person can argue they exercised due care and diligence to avoid the contravention as a defence, except in specific cases outlined in paragraphs 125(1)(c), (z.10), and (z.11). Importantly, no imprisonment is possible for offences under these specific paragraphs.

individual_results.question: What can the Head do to prevent or address contraventions of this Part of the Canada Labour Code (PART II - Occupational Health and Safety)?
individual_results.answer:
## Preventing and Addressing Contraventions of Part II of the Canada Labour Code

### Section 145: Special Safety Measures: Direction to terminate contravention

Section 145 outlines the Head's authority to prevent or address contraventions of Part II. It states,
"If the Head is of the opinion that a provision of this Part is being contravened or has recently been contravened, the Head may direct the employer or employee concerned, or both, to (a) terminate the contravention within the time that the officer may specify; and (b) take steps, as specified by the Head and within the time that the Head may specify, to ensure that the contravention does not continue or re-occur."

This section provides the Head with a direct mechanism to stop ongoing violations. The Head can issue a command to cease the contravention within a specified timeframe and to implement measures to prevent its recurrence. The Head can also issue directions to take specific steps to correct the hazard or condition that is causing the contravention.

### Section 145(2): Dangerous Situations — direction to employer

Section 145(2) details the Head's power to issue directions to employers when a situation poses a danger to employees. It states,
"If the Head considers that the use or operation of a machine or thing, a condition in a place or the performance of an activity constitutes a danger to an employee while at work, (a) the Head shall notify the employer of the danger and issue directions in writing to the employer directing the employer, immediately or within the period that the Head specifies, to take measures to (i) correct the hazard or condition or alter the activity that constitutes the danger, or (ii) protect any person from the danger; and (b) the Head may, if the Head considers that the danger or the hazard, condition or activity that constitutes the danger cannot otherwise be corrected, altered or protected against immediately, issue a direction in writing to the employer directing that the place, machine, thing or activity in respect of which the direction is issued not be used, operated or performed, as the case may be, until the Head’s directions are complied with, but nothing in this paragraph prevents the doing of anything necessary for the proper compliance with the direction."

This section empowers the Head to issue immediate orders to employers to address dangerous situations. The Head must notify the employer of the danger and direct them to take steps to correct the hazard or protect employees. If the danger cannot be immediately addressed, the Head can order the cessation of the dangerous activity until the necessary measures are taken.

### Section 145(2.1): Dangerous Situations — direction to employee

Section 145(2.1) extends the Head's authority to issue directions to employees when their actions pose a danger to themselves or others. It states,
"If the Head considers that the use or operation of a machine or thing by an employee, a condition in a place or the performance of an activity by an employee constitutes a danger to the employee or to another employee, the Head shall, in addition to the directions issued under paragraph (2)(a), issue a direction in writing to the employee to discontinue the use, operation or activity or cease to work in that place until the employer has complied with the directions issued under that paragraph."

This section allows the Head to order employees to stop dangerous activities if they are creating a risk. In addition to directing the employer to correct the hazard, the Head can issue a direct order to the employee to cease the dangerous behavior until the employer takes the necessary corrective actions.

### Section 145(3): Posting notice of danger

Section 145(3) mandates that when the Head issues a direction under paragraph (2)(a), a notice of danger must be posted. It states,
"If the Head issues a direction under paragraph (2)(a), the Head shall affix or cause to be affixed to or near the place, machine or thing in respect of which the direction is issued, or in the area in which the activity in respect of which the direction is issued is performed, a notice of danger in the form and containing the information that the Head may specify, and no person shall remove the notice unless authorized to do so by the Head."

This provision ensures that employees are clearly warned of the danger before the dangerous activity is resumed. The notice must be prominently displayed and cannot be removed without the Head's permission.

### Section 145(4): Cessation of use

Section 145(4) clarifies that if the Head issues a direction under paragraph (2)(b), the employer must immediately stop the dangerous activity. It states,
"If the Head issues a direction under paragraph (2)(b) in respect of a place, machine, thing or activity, the employer shall cause the use of the place, the use or operation of the machine or thing or the performance of the activity to be discontinued, and no person shall use or operate the machine or thing, work in that place or perform the activity until the measures directed by the Head have been taken."

This section reinforces the Head's power to order the immediate cessation of a dangerous activity. The employer is required to stop the activity and prevent anyone from resuming it until the Head's directions are followed.

### Section 145(5): Copies of directions and reports

Section 145(5) requires employers to distribute any directions or reports issued by the Head. It states,
"If the Head issues a direction in writing under subsection (1) or (2) or makes a report in writing to an employer on any matter under this Part, the employer shall without delay (a) cause a copy or copies of the direction or report to be posted in a conspicuous place accessible to every employee; (b) give a copy of the direction or report to the policy committee and a copy to the work place committee or the health and safety representative."

This provision ensures that all employees are informed of any directions or reports issued by the Head. The employer must post the direction or report in a visible location and provide copies to relevant committees.

### Section 145(6): Copy to person who made complaint

Section 145(6) mandates that the Head must provide a copy of any direction or report issued following a complaint to the person who made the complaint. It states,
"If the Head issues a direction under subsection (1), (2) or (2.1) or makes a report referred to in subsection (5) in respect of an investigation made by the Head following a complaint, the Head shall immediately provide a copy of the direction or report to each person, if any, whose complaint led to the investigation."

This provision ensures that the person who raised the complaint is kept informed of the Head's actions in response to their concern.

### Section 145(7): Copy to employer

Section 145(7) requires the Head to provide a copy of any direction issued to an employee to the employee's employer. It states,
"If the Head issues a direction to an employee under subsection (1) or (2.1), the Head shall immediately provide a copy of the direction to the employee’s employer."

This provision keeps the employer informed of any directions issued to their employees regarding dangerous situations.

### Section 145(8): Response to direction or report

Section 145(8) allows the Head to request a written response from the employer or employee to any direction or report issued. It states,
"If the Head issues a direction under subsection (1), (2) or (2.1) or makes a report referred to in subsection (5), the Head may require the employer or the employee to whom the direction is issued or to whom the report relates to respond in writing to the direction or report, within the time that the Head may specify. The employer or employee shall provide a copy of the response to the policy committee and a copy to the work place committee or the health and safety representative."

This provision allows the Head to seek clarification or confirmation of compliance with any directions issued. The response must be shared with relevant committees.

### Section 290

individual_results.question: How can the Head require a person to provide information for the purposes of this Part of the Canada Labour Code (PART II - Occupational Health and Safety), and what type of evidence can be used to prove that the information was not provided?
individual_results.answer:
## How the Head Can Require Information and Evidence of Non-Provision

### Method of Requiring Information

Section 155(1) of the Canada Labour Code outlines the process by which the Head can require a person to provide information. It states:
"If a person is required to provide information for the purposes of this Part, the Head may require the information to be provided by a notice to that effect served personally or sent by registered mail addressed to the latest known address of the person, and the person shall comply with the notice within such reasonable time as is specified in it."

This indicates that the Head can issue a formal notice to the person requesting the information. This notice can be served either in person or by registered mail to the person's last known address. The notice must specify a reasonable timeframe within which the information must be provided.

### Evidence of Non-Provision

Section 155(2) details the type of evidence that can be used to prove that the information was not provided. It states:
"A certificate purporting to be signed by the Head or by a person authorized by the Head, (a) certifying that a notice was sent by registered mail to the person to whom it was addressed, accompanied by an identified post office certificate of the registration and a true copy of the notice, and (b) certifying that the information has not been provided as requested in the notice sent by the Head, is evidence of the facts set out therein without proof of the signature or official character of the person by whom the certificate purports to be signed."

This section specifies that a certificate, either signed by the Head or an authorized person, can serve as evidence of non-provision. This certificate must include two key elements: first, a certification that a notice was sent by registered mail to the person, accompanied by proof of registration and a true copy of the notice; and second, a certification that the information was not provided as requested in the notice. The certificate is considered evidence of these facts without needing further proof of the signature or official capacity of the person who signed it.

## Status of Board Orders and Decisions

### Finality of Board Orders and Decisions

Section 243(1) of the Canada Labour Code explicitly states that
"Every order of the Board is final and shall not be questioned or reviewed in any court." This indicates a strong finality to the orders and decisions issued by the Board under Part II. The provision further clarifies this by stating that
"No order shall be made, process entered or proceeding taken in any court, whether by way of injunction, certiorari , prohibition, quo warranto or otherwise, to question, review, prohibit or restrain the Board in any proceedings under section 242." This reinforces the lack of avenues for judicial review of Board orders.

Section 156(1) reiterates this finality, asserting that
"Every order or decision made or direction issued by the Board under this Part is final and shall not be questioned or reviewed in any court." This repetition emphasizes the lack of judicial recourse for challenging Board decisions.

### Exceptions to Finality

While Board orders and decisions are generally final and not subject to court review, there is a limited exception outlined in Section 22(1). This section states,
"Subject to this Part and to any regulations made under paragraph 111.01(1)(g), every order or decision made by the Board under this Part is final and is not to be questioned or reviewed in any court, except in accordance with the Federal Courts Act on the grounds referred to in paragraph 18.1(4)(a), (b) or (e) of that Act." This exception allows for judicial review only on very specific grounds as outlined in the Federal Courts Act. These grounds include, but are not limited to, jurisdiction of the Board, exceeding its jurisdiction, or a failure to exercise its jurisdiction.

### Board Standing to Appear in Proceedings

Section 146.1(1) addresses the Board's standing to appear in court proceedings. It states,
"If an appeal is brought under subsection 129(7) or section 146, the Board shall, in a summary way and without delay, inquire into the circumstances of the decision or direction, as the case may be, and the reasons for it and may (a) vary, rescind or confirm the decision or direction; and (b) issue any direction that the Board considers appropriate under subsection 145(2) or (2.1)." This indicates that the Board has the authority to actively participate in court proceedings related to its orders and decisions, including the power to modify, overturn, or reaffirm its own decisions.

individual_results.question: What is the purpose of the regulations that can be made under section 157 of the Canada Labour Code, and who is responsible for making them?
individual_results.answer:
## Purpose of Regulations under Section 157 of the Canada Labour Code

### General Authority for Regulations
"...the Governor in Council may make regulations (a) prescribing anything that by this Part is to be prescribed..." This statement from Section 157(1)(a) establishes the broad authority of the Governor in Council to create regulations under this part of the Canada Labour Code. It indicates that the regulations can cover any matter that is deemed necessary to carry out the provisions of the Part.

### Specific Areas Covered by Regulations

Section 157(1) further details the specific areas that regulations can address. These include:
"...defining the expressions “harassment” and “violence” for the purposes of this Part..."
"...restricting or prohibiting any activity or thing that any provision of this Part contemplates being the subject of regulations..."
"...prescribing the method for calculating and determining the regular rate of wages for the purpose of section 146.5..."
"...respecting such other matters or things as are necessary to carry out the provisions of this Part."

These points illustrate the wide scope of the regulatory power granted to the Governor in Council. Regulations can clarify definitions, prohibit certain actions, establish calculation methods for wages, and address any other issues deemed necessary for the effective implementation of the Canada Labour Code.

### Responsibilities for Making Regulations
"Regulations of the Governor in Council under subsection (1) or (1.1) in respect of occupational safety and health of employees employed (a) on ships, trains or aircraft, while in operation, shall be made on the recommendation of the Minister and the Minister of Transport..." This passage from Section 157(3) clearly identifies the responsible parties for making regulations concerning occupational safety and health. It states that such regulations must be made
"...on the recommendation of the Minister and the Minister of Transport..." This indicates a collaborative process involving the relevant federal ministers.

Furthermore, Section 157(3)(b) specifies the recommendation process for regulations related to oil and gas exploration and production:

"...any employers of the employees described in paragraph (b)..." This ensures that the Part also governs the relationship between federal employers and their employees.

"...any corporation established to perform any function or duty on behalf of the Government of Canada other than a department as defined in the Financial Administration Act..." This broadens the scope to encompass various entities working on behalf of the federal government.

Finally, the section specifies that Part I applies
"...to or in respect of any Canadian carrier, as defined in section 2 of the Telecommunications Act , that is an agent of Her Majesty in right of a province." This includes carriers acting as agents for the federal government in provincial jurisdictions.

In essence, Section 167 serves to establish the comprehensive applicability of Part I of the Act to a wide range of federal government activities, employers, and related entities, ensuring that the provisions of this Part govern employment relationships within these contexts.

## Canada Labour Code and Interactions with Other Laws, Customs, Contracts, or Collective Agreements

### General Applicability and Precedence of the Canada Labour Code

The Canada Labour Code establishes a framework for labour relations and employee rights. However, its application is not absolute. Section 168(1) of the Code explicitly states that
"This Part and all regulations made under this Part apply notwithstanding any other law or any custom, contract or arrangement..." This indicates that the Code takes precedence over other legal instruments, customs, contracts, or collective agreements when it comes to determining employee rights and benefits.

However, this precedence is qualified. The Code continues by stating,
"...but nothing in this Part shall be construed as affecting any rights or benefits of an employee under any law, custom, contract or arrangement that are more favourable to the employee than his rights or benefits under this Part." This crucial caveat ensures that employees are not disadvantaged by the Code's application if they already possess more beneficial rights or benefits under other agreements.

### Collective Agreements and the Canada Labour Code

The Canada Labour Code has a significant interaction with collective agreements. Section 69(1) defines "collective agreement" within the context of the Part, including various terms related to employment processes. Furthermore, the Code acknowledges the role of collective agreements in shaping employee rights and benefits.

Section 168(1) reiterates the Code's applicability
"...notwithstanding any other law or any custom, contract or arrangement..." but it also makes an exception for collective agreements that provide employees with more favourable terms.
"...nothing in this Part shall be construed as affecting any rights or benefits of an employee under any law, custom, contract or arrangement that are more favourable to the employee than his rights or benefits under this Part." This demonstrates that the Code respects collective agreements that offer employees better conditions than those mandated by the Code itself.

Moreover, the Code outlines specific provisions for collective agreements in certain contexts. Section 168(1)(1) addresses situations where a collective agreement confers on employees rights and benefits
"...at least as favourable as those conferred by those respective Divisions in respect of length of leave, rates of pay and qualifying periods for benefits..." In such cases, the settlement of disagreements is governed exclusively by the collective agreement. This highlights the Code's recognition of the autonomy of collective bargaining in establishing employee terms and conditions.

### Other Laws, Customs, and Contracts

While the Code generally takes precedence, it does not entirely disregard other legal instruments, customs, or contracts. Section 168(1) states that the Code applies "notwithstanding any other law." This implies that other laws may still apply to certain aspects of employment, even when the Code is the primary governing framework.

The Code also acknowledges the existence of customs and contracts. Section 168(1) explicitly states that the Code applies
"...notwithstanding any other law or any custom, contract or arrangement..." This indicates that other legal instruments may still be relevant in specific situations, but the Code's provisions will generally prevail.

### Sector-Based Approaches and Collective Agreements

The Labour Reports provide further insights into the interaction between the Canada Labour Code and other legal instruments through sector-based approaches. For instance, the report discusses the Status of the Artist Act, which allows for the recognition and certification of artists' associations with the exclusive right to represent their members in collective bargaining. This demonstrates how specific legislation can complement the broader framework of the Canada Labour Code to address the unique needs of particular sectors.

The report also mentions Quebec's Act Respecting Collective Agreement Decrees, which provides the government with the power to order that a collective agreement binding on all employers and employees in a specified sector. This illustrates how provincial legislation can interact with the federal Canada Labour Code to establish minimum standards for employment conditions.

In summary, the Canada Labour Code generally takes precedence over other laws, customs, contracts, or collective agreements when it comes to determining employee rights and benefits. However, it makes exceptions for collective agreements that offer employees more favourable terms and acknowledges the role of other legal instruments in specific contexts. The Code interacts with other legal frameworks, such as sector-based legislation and provincial collective agreement decrees, to address the unique needs of different industries and regions.

individual_results.question: What are the standard hours of work for an employee under the Canada Labour Code, and are there any exceptions or alternative arrangements that can be made?
individual_results.answer:
## Standard Hours of Work Under the Canada Labour Code

### General Standard Hours
"Section 169 (1) Except as otherwise provided by or under this Division (a) the standard hours of work of an employee shall not exceed eight hours in a day and forty hours in a week; and (b) no employer shall cause or permit an employee to work longer hours than eight hours in any day or forty hours in any week." This section of the Canada Labour Code clearly establishes the general standard hours of work for an employee: a maximum of eight hours per day and forty hours per week. It also prohibits employers from requiring employees to work more than these limits.

### Exceptions and Alternative Arrangements

#### Averaging Hours
"Where the nature of the work in an industrial establishment necessitates irregular distribution of the hours of work of an employee, the hours of work in a day and the hours of work in a week may be calculated, in such manner and in such circumstances as may be prescribed by the regulations, as an average for a period of two or more weeks." This passage introduces the concept of averaging hours. Averaging allows for a more flexible work schedule when the work demands are not consistent throughout the week. The standard hours are then calculated as an average over a period of two or more weeks.

#### Modified Work Schedules
"Modified work schedules may provide you and your employer with greater flexibility in the workplace as they allow employees to work outside the standard hours of work. Examples of modified work schedules include:   compressed work weeks flexible hours of work   Note: you can also request modified work schedules under the right to request flexible work arrangements. For more information, please consult the Flexible Work Arrangements web page." This section details modified work schedules as an alternative arrangement. These schedules allow employees to work outside the standard hours, such as compressed work weeks or flexible hours. Employees can also request modified work schedules under the right to request flexible work arrangements.
"If you have a modified work schedule:   your standard hours of work for a period of 2 or more weeks cannot exceed an average of 40 hours in a week  the maximum hours for the same period cannot exceed an average of 48 hours in a week your employer must pay overtime when  your daily or weekly hours exceed those established under the modified work schedule." This further elaborates on the limitations of modified work schedules. While the average standard hours can be higher than 40 hours per week, the maximum hours for any given period cannot exceed 48 hours per week. Employers are also required to pay overtime when an employee's daily or weekly hours exceed those established under the modified work schedule.
"If you are a student intern, your employer may establish a modified work schedule with your approval. This schedule can exceed 8 hours per day and 40 hours per week. However, it cannot exceed 40 hours per week averaged over a period of 2 or more weeks." This passage specifically addresses modified work schedules for student interns. These schedules can exceed 8 hours per day and 40 hours per week, but the average standard hours over a period of two or more weeks cannot exceed 40 hours per week.

#### Excess Hour Permits and Averaging Plans
"The maximum hours of work in a week can be exceeded in exceptional circumstances. For example, the maximum hours of work can be exceeded:  under an excess hour permit  for emergency work under an averaging plan under a modified work schedule..." individual_results.question: Under what circumstances can an employer postpone or cancel an employee's break or require an employee to work without the standard rest period?
individual_results.answer:
## Postponement or Cancellation of Breaks and Modification of Rest Periods

### Circumstances for Postponement or Cancellation of Breaks

An employer may postpone or cancel an employee's break under very specific and unforeseen circumstances. Section 169.2(2) of the Canada Labour Code outlines these conditions:
"An employer may postpone or cancel the break set out in subsection (1) if it is necessary for the employee to work in order to deal with a situation that the employer could not have reasonably foreseen and that presents or could reasonably be expected to present an imminent or serious (a) threat to the life, health or safety of any person; (b) threat of damage to or loss of property; or (c) threat of serious interference with the ordinary working of the employer’s industrial establishment."

This section clearly states that the postponement or cancellation of a break is permissible only when the situation is "unforeseen" and poses a
"...threat to the life, health or safety of any person; (b) threat of damage to or loss of property; or (c) threat of serious interference with the ordinary working of the employer’s industrial establishment." The employer must demonstrate that the situation was not reasonably anticipated and presents a significant and immediate risk.

### Circumstances for Requiring Additional Work Without Standard Rest Periods

An employer may require an employee to work additional hours without the standard rest period if it is necessary to deal with an "unforeseen" situation that poses a
"...threat to the life, health or safety of any person; (b) threat of damage to or loss of property; or (c) threat of serious interference with the ordinary working of the employer’s industrial establishment." This is further elaborated in Section 169.2(2):
"Despite subsection (1), an employer may require that an employee work additional hours to their scheduled work periods or shifts which would result in them having a rest period of fewer than eight consecutive hours between their work periods or shifts if it is necessary for the employee to work in order to deal with a situation that the employer could not have reasonably foreseen and that presents or could reasonably be expected to present an imminent or serious (a) threat to the life, health or safety of any person; (b) threat of damage to or loss of property; or (c) threat of serious interference with the ordinary working of the employer’s industrial establishment."

This provision indicates that even if the employee would end up with a rest period shorter than the standard eight hours, the employer can require additional work if it is essential to address an "unforeseen" and "imminent or serious" threat. The employer must again demonstrate that the situation was not reasonably anticipated.

## Conditions for Establishing, Modifying, or Cancelling a Work Schedule Exceeding Standard Hours

### Collective Agreement

#### General Conditions
"An employer may, in respect of one or more employees subject to a collective agreement, establish, modify or cancel a work schedule under which the hours exceed the maximum set out in section 171 or in regulations made under section 175 if (a) the average hours of work for a period of two or more weeks does not exceed forty-eight hours a week; and (b) the schedule, or its modification or cancellation, is agreed to in writing by the employer and the trade union." This section outlines the primary condition for an employer to establish, modify, or cancel a work schedule exceeding standard hours when a collective agreement is in place. It specifies that the average hours of work for a period of two or more weeks must not exceed forty-eight hours per week, and the schedule must be agreed upon in writing by both the employer and the trade union.

#### Specific Conditions for One or More Employees
"Subject to subsection (3), an employer may, in respect of one or more employees not subject to a collective agreement, establish, modify or cancel a work schedule under which the hours exceed the maximum set out in section 171 or in regulations made under section 175 if (a) the average hours of work for a period of two or more weeks does not exceed forty-eight hours a week; and (b) the schedule, or its modification or cancellation, has been approved (i) in the case of one employee’s schedule, in writing by that employee, or (ii) in the case of more than one employee’s schedule, by at least 70% of the affected employees." This subsection details the conditions for an employer to establish, modify, or cancel a work schedule exceeding standard hours when no collective agreement exists. It mirrors the conditions for collective agreements regarding average hours but introduces a requirement for approval from at least 70% of the affected employees for schedules involving more than one employee. For a single employee's schedule, approval must be in writing from that employee.

### Non-Collective Agreement
"Where a work schedule is to be established, modified or cancelled pursuant to subsection (2), the employer shall post a notice of the new schedule, or of its modification or cancellation, in readily accessible places where it is likely to be seen by the affected employees, for at least thirty days before the new schedule or its modification or cancellation takes effect." This section mandates that employers must provide advance notice of any changes to a work schedule exceeding standard hours. The notice must be posted in a visible location at least thirty days before the new schedule takes effect.

### Exceptions
"Subsection (3) does not apply to the establishment, modification or cancellation of one employee’s work schedule that results from a request made under subsection 177.1(1)." This subsection specifies an exception to the notice requirement. If a change to a work schedule exceeding standard hours is requested by an employee under subsection 177.1(1), the employer is not required to post a notice.
"...does not apply in respect of a work period or shift that an employee refuses to work under subsection (2)." This subsection clarifies that the notice requirement does not apply to a work period or shift that an employee refuses to work under subsection (2).
"(7) This section does not apply to employees who are employed under the terms of a collective agreement that specifies an alternate time frame for providing the work schedule or provides that this section does not apply to those employees." This subsection reiterates the exception for employees covered by a collective agreement that has a different timeframe for providing the work schedule or explicitly excludes this section's application to those employees.
