individual_results.question: What is the general rule regarding the maximum number of hours an employee can work in a week under the Canada Labour Code?
individual_results.answer:
## General Rule Regarding Maximum Hours of Work

### Section 171(1) of the Canada Labour Code
"An employee may be employed in excess of the standard hours of work but, subject to sections 172, 176 and 177, and to any regulations made pursuant to section 175, the total hours that may be worked by any employee in any week shall not exceed forty-eight hours in a week or such fewer total number of hours as may be prescribed by the regulations as maximum working hours in the industrial establishment in or in connection with the operation of which the employee is employed."

This section of the Canada Labour Code establishes the general rule for the maximum number of hours an employee can work in a week. It states that while an employee can be employed for more than the standard hours, the total number of hours worked in a week cannot exceed forty-eight hours, unless otherwise specified by regulations. This sets the baseline for most federally regulated workplaces.

### Section 171(2) and Averaging
"Subsection 169(2) applies in the computation of the maximum hours of work in a week prescribed under this section."

This subsection clarifies that the rules for averaging hours of work, as outlined in Part III of the Canada Labour Code, apply to the computation of the maximum hours of work in a week. This means that in certain circumstances, the standard forty-eight-hour limit can be exceeded if the average hours worked over a period of two or more weeks do not exceed forty-eight hours per week.

### Section 172 and Emergency Work
"In case of emergency, such as an accident or essential work on equipment, an employer may exceed the maximum hours of work without a permit. The employer must submit a report to the Head and if applicable to a trade union representing affected employees, within 15 days of the end of the month in which the employee(s) worked emergency hours. The report must include the:  nature of the emergency number of employees working in excess of the maximum hours, and number of additional hours each employee worked..."

This section addresses the exception to the general rule regarding maximum hours of work. It allows employers to exceed the forty-eight-hour limit in case of emergency work without a permit. However, it mandates that the employer submit a report to the Head and, if applicable, to a trade union, within 15 days of the end of the month in which the emergency hours were worked. This report must detail the nature of the emergency, the number of employees working in excess of the maximum hours, and the number of additional hours each employee worked.

### Section 173 and Averaging
"**Averaging** In some establishments, the nature of work necessitates irregular hours of work due to seasonal or other factors. This means that as an employee, you may be subject to:   scheduled hours that vary from time to time, or no regularly scheduled hours  If this applies to you, your employer may average your hours of work over a period of 2 or more weeks. As such, standard and maximum hours would be calculated across a period of 2 or more weeks rather than on a daily or weekly basis."

This section further elaborates on the averaging provision. It explains that in certain workplaces with irregular hours, employers may average an employee's hours of work over a period of two or more weeks. This means that the maximum hours of work per week are calculated based on the average hours worked over that period, rather than on a daily or weekly basis.

### Section 174 and Maximum Hours for Certain Classes of Employees
"Regulations set out exemptions from or modifications to what maximum hours of work is for certain classes of employees:  drivers in the trucking industry (Motor Vehicle Operators Hours of Work Regulations) employees on ships in the East Coast and Great Lakes shipping industry (East Coast and Great Lakes Shipping Employees Hours of Work Regulations, 1985) and the West Coast shipping industry (West Coast Shipping Employees Hours of Work Regulations) running trades employees in the railway industry (Railway Running-Trades Employees Hours of Work Regulations) the commission salespersons in the broadcasting industry (Broadcasting Industry Commission Salesmen Hours of Work Regulations), and the commission-paid salespeople in the banking industry (Banking Industry Commission-paid Salespeople Hours of Work Regulations)..."

This section lists specific exemptions or modifications to the general maximum hours rule for certain classes of employees. These include drivers in the trucking industry, employees on ships in the East Coast and Great Lakes shipping industry, employees on ships in the West Coast shipping industry, running trades employees in the railway industry, commission salespersons in the broadcasting industry, and commission-paid salespeople in the banking industry. These exemptions are detailed in specific regulations.

individual_results.answer:
## Conditions for Establishing, Modifying, or Cancelling Work Schedules Exceeding Maximum Hours

### Collective Agreement

#### General Conditions
"An employer may, in respect of one or more employees subject to a collective agreement, establish, modify or cancel a work schedule under which the hours exceed the maximum set out in section 171 or in regulations made under section 175 if (a) the average hours of work for a period of two or more weeks does not exceed forty-eight hours a week; and (b) the schedule, or its modification or cancellation, is agreed to in writing by the employer and the trade union."

This section outlines the primary condition under which an employer can establish, modify, or cancel a work schedule exceeding the standard maximum. It specifies that this is permissible only if the average hours worked over a period of two or more weeks do not exceed forty-eight hours. Furthermore, it mandates that such changes must be agreed upon in writing by both the employer and the trade union. This collaborative requirement ensures that any deviation from the standard maximum is mutually consented to.

#### Additional Conditions for One Employee's Schedule
"Subject to subsection (3), an employer may, in respect of one or more employees not subject to a collective agreement, establish, modify or cancel a work schedule under which the hours exceed the maximum set out in section 171 or in regulations made under section 175 if (a) the average hours of work for a period of two or more weeks does not exceed forty-eight hours a week; and (b) the schedule, or its modification or cancellation, has been approved (i) in the case of one employee’s schedule, in writing by that employee, or (ii) in the case of more than one employee’s schedule, by at least 70% of the affected employees."

This subsection details the additional conditions that apply when an employer is not bound by a collective agreement but still wishes to establish, modify, or cancel a work schedule exceeding the standard maximum. It reiterates the average hours constraint of not exceeding forty-eight hours per week over a two-week period. However, it introduces a requirement for approval. For a single employee's schedule, this approval must be in writing from that employee. For a schedule affecting more than one employee, it must be approved by at least seventy percent of the affected employees. This approval mechanism ensures that any schedule exceeding the standard maximum has the support of a significant portion of the workforce.

### Modified Work Schedule

#### General Conditions
"Modified work schedules may provide you and your employer with greater flexibility in the workplace as they allow employees to work outside the standard hours of work. Examples of modified work schedules include:   compressed work weeks flexible hours of work   Note: you can also request modified work schedules under the right to request flexible work arrangements. For more information, please consult the Flexible Work Arrangements web page.  If you have a modified work schedule:   your standard hours of work for a period of 2 or more weeks cannot exceed an average of 40 hours in a week  the maximum hours for the same period cannot exceed an average of 48 hours in a week your employer must pay overtime when  your daily or weekly hours exceed those established under the modified work schedule."

This section introduces the concept of modified work schedules as a way to exceed the standard maximum hours. It explains that these schedules offer flexibility and can allow employees to work outside the standard hours. It then lays out the conditions under which a modified work schedule can exceed the standard maximum. It states that the average hours worked over a period of two or more weeks cannot exceed forty hours per week, and the maximum hours for the same period cannot exceed forty-eight hours per week. Additionally, it specifies that overtime must be paid when daily or weekly hours exceed those established under the modified work schedule.

#### Additional Conditions for One Employee's Schedule
"For employees covered and not covered by a collective agreement, employers must post a notice of the new, revised or cancelled schedule at least 30 days before the schedule starts."

This subsection provides an additional requirement for establishing, modifying, or cancelling a modified work schedule for one employee. It mandates that employers must post a notice of the new, revised, or cancelled schedule at least thirty days before the schedule takes effect. This notice ensures that affected employees are informed of any changes to their work schedule in advance.

#### Exception
"Subsection (3) does not apply to the establishment, modification or cancellation of one employee’s work schedule that results from a request made under subsection 177.1(1)."

This subsection introduces an exception to the thirty-day posting requirement. It states that this requirement does not apply to the establishment, modification, or cancellation of one employee's work schedule that results from a request made under subsection 177.1(1). This exception likely pertains to requests made under emergency work provisions, where the schedule change is necessary to prevent serious interference with operations.

### Other Circumstances

#### Emergency Work
"The maximum hours of work in a week specified in or prescribed under section 171, established pursuant to section 172 or prescribed by regulations made under section 175 may be exceeded, but only to the extent necessary to prevent serious interference with the ordinary working of the industrial establishment affected, in cases of (a) accident to machinery, equipment, plant or persons; (b) urgent and essential work to be done to machinery, equipment or plant; or (c) other unforeseen or unpreventable circumstances."

This section addresses situations where the maximum hours can be exceeded due to unforeseen circumstances. It states that the maximum hours can be exceeded, but only to the extent necessary to prevent serious interference with the ordinary working of the industrial establishment affected. It then lists specific cases where this is permissible: accidents, urgent and essential work, and other unforeseen or unpreventable circumstances.

#### Reporting Additional Work
"Where the maximum hours of work in an industrial establishment have been exceeded under the authority of subsection (1), the employer shall report in writing to the Head, and also to the trade union if the affected employees are subject to a collective agreement, within 15 days after the end of the month in which the maximum was exceeded, stating the nature of the circumstances in which the maximum was exceeded, the number of employees who worked in excess of the maximum and the number of additional hours each of them worked."

This subsection outlines the reporting requirements when the maximum hours have been exceeded due to emergency work. It mandates that the employer must report in writing to the Head and the trade union (if applicable) within fifteen days of the end of the month in which the maximum was exceeded. The report must detail the circumstances leading to the excess hours, the number of employees who worked over the maximum, and the number of additional hours each of them worked. This reporting requirement ensures transparency and accountability when the maximum hours are exceeded.

individual_results.question: What is the process and implications for an employer if a work schedule is established, modified, or cancelled and a vote is requested by affected employees to determine approval of the change?
individual_results.answer:
## Process and Implications of a Work Schedule Vote

### Requesting a Vote

#### Section 172.1(1)
"If a work schedule is established, modified or cancelled under subsection 170(2) or 172(2), any affected employee may, within ninety days after the new schedule or its modification or cancellation takes effect, request that the Head conduct a vote to determine whether seventy per cent of the affected employees approve the new schedule or its modification or cancellation."
This section outlines the initial step in the voting process. It states that any employee affected by a new, modified, or cancelled work schedule can request a vote within ninety days of the change taking effect. This right to request a vote is a key component of the collective agreement process, allowing employees to have a say in changes to their work schedules.

#### Section 172.1(2)
"If a request is made under subsection (1), the Head must conduct a secret vote to determine the percentage of the affected employees that approves the new schedule or the modification or cancellation."
Following a request for a vote, the Head is obligated to conduct a secret vote. This ensures confidentiality and prevents any undue influence on the voting process. The purpose of the vote is to determine if at least seventy percent of the affected employees approve of the new work schedule.

#### Section 172.1(3)
"A request made under subsection (1), the ballots and any other documents relating to the vote are confidential and shall not be given to the employer."
This section emphasizes the confidentiality of the voting process. It explicitly states that all ballots and related documents are confidential and cannot be disclosed to the employer. This protects the privacy of the employees' votes and prevents any potential retaliation.

#### Section 172.1(4)
"The Head must count the ballots in the presence of a representative chosen by the affected employees and a representative chosen by the employer."
To ensure transparency and fairness, the Head is required to count the ballots in the presence of representatives chosen by both the affected employees and the employer. This allows both sides to observe the counting process and verify its accuracy.

#### Section 172.1(5)
"The Head must inform the employer, by written notice, of the result."
After the vote is conducted and the results are tallied, the Head must promptly inform the employer of the outcome in writing. This ensures that the employer is aware of the employees' approval of the new work schedule.

### Implications of a Vote

#### Section 172.1(6)
"If the result of the vote indicates that less than 70% of the affected employees approve the new schedule or its modification or cancellation, the employer must comply with the result of the vote within 30 days after being informed of that result by the Head."
This section details the employer's obligation if the vote fails to achieve the required seventy percent approval. It states that the employer must comply with the vote's result within thirty days of being informed of the outcome. This means the employer must revert to the previous work schedule or make further modifications based on the employees' preference.

#### Section 172.1(7)
"The Governor in Council may make regulations respecting the conduct of votes under this section."
This section grants the Governor in Council the authority to create regulations governing the conduct of votes under this section. These regulations could address various aspects of the voting process, such as the timing of the vote, the method of voting, and the roles of the Head and the representatives.

#### Section 172.1(8)
"The Statutory Instruments Act does not apply in respect of the written notice given by the Head to the employer under subsection (5)."
This section clarifies that the Statutory Instruments Act does not apply to the written notice provided by the Head to the employer regarding the vote's result. This likely means that the notice is exempt from certain requirements or procedures outlined in the Statutory Instruments Act.

In summary, the process for a work schedule vote involves an employee requesting a vote within ninety days of a new schedule taking effect, the Head conducting a secret vote, the vote being kept confidential, the ballots being counted with representatives present, the Head informing the employer of the result, and the employer complying with the vote's outcome within thirty days if less than seventy percent approval is obtained. The implications for the employer are that they are legally bound to adhere to the employees' preference if the vote fails to reach the required threshold.

individual_results.answer:
## Requirements for Scheduling Rest Days for Employees According to the Canada Labour Code

### Section 173 of the Canada Labour Code
"Except as may be otherwise prescribed by the regulations, hours of work in a week shall be so scheduled and actually worked that each employee has at least one full day of rest in the week, and, wherever practicable, Sunday shall be the normal day of rest in the week."

This section of the Canada Labour Code establishes the fundamental requirement for scheduling rest days. It mandates that every employee must have at least one full day of rest per week. Furthermore, it suggests that Sunday should be the standard day of rest, but acknowledges that this may not always be feasible. The phrase "so scheduled and actually worked" emphasizes that the work schedule must be structured to ensure this rest day is consistently provided.

### Section 169.1 of the Canada Labour Code
"(1) Every employee is entitled to and shall be granted an unpaid break of at least 30 minutes during every period of five consecutive hours of work. If the employer requires the employee to be at their disposal during the break period, the employee must be paid for the break."

While this section primarily addresses breaks, it indirectly supports the requirement for rest days. The provision for a 30-minute unpaid break during every five consecutive hours of work contributes to the overall well-being of employees and can be considered part of ensuring adequate rest throughout the workday.

### Section 169.2 of the Canada Labour Code
"(1) Every employee is entitled to and shall be granted a rest period of at least eight consecutive hours between work periods or shifts."

This section explicitly states the requirement for a rest period of at least eight consecutive hours between work periods or shifts. This is a crucial component of ensuring employees have sufficient time to recover from work and maintain their health and safety. The exception provided in subsection (2) allows employers to require additional hours to achieve a rest period of fewer than eight consecutive hours in specific, unforeseen circumstances, such as imminent threats to life, health, safety, property, or serious interference with business operations.

individual_results.question: What are the requirements for an employer to provide an employee's work schedule, and what are the consequences for an employee who refuses to work a scheduled period or shift?
individual_results.answer:
## Employer Requirements for Providing Work Schedules

### Notice of Work Schedule
"The employer shall provide an employee with their work schedule in writing at least 96 hours before the start of the employee’s first work period or shift under that schedule." This section clearly outlines the employer's obligation to provide a work schedule to employees with a minimum of 96 hours' notice. The notice must be in writing.

### Exceptions to the Notice Requirement
"Subject to subsection (3), an employee may refuse to work any work period or shift in their schedule that starts within 96 hours from the time that the schedule is provided to them." This subsection establishes an exception to the 96-hour notice requirement. An employee has the right to refuse a scheduled period or shift if it begins within 96 hours of the schedule being provided.

### Situations Where Refusal is Not Permitted
"An employee shall not refuse to work a work period or shift if it is necessary for them to work in order to deal with a situation that the employer could not have reasonably foreseen and that presents or could reasonably be expected to present an imminent or serious (a) threat to the life, health or safety of any person; (b) threat of damage to or loss of property; or (c) threat of serious interference with the ordinary working of the employer’s industrial establishment." This subsection specifies circumstances where an employee's refusal to work a scheduled period or shift is not permitted. These circumstances involve imminent or serious threats to human life, health or safety, property, or the normal operation of the employer's business.

### Modification of Work Schedule Following Request
"Subsection (1) does not apply to a change to an employee’s work schedule following a request made under subsection 177.1(1)." This subsection clarifies that the 96-hour notice requirement does not apply to changes to an employee's work schedule that occur after a request has been made under section 177.1(1).

## Consequences for an Employee Who Refuses to Work a Scheduled Period or Shift

### Employer's Prohibition Against Retaliation
"An employer shall not dismiss, suspend, lay off, demote or discipline an employee because the employee has refused to work a work period or shift under subsection (2) or take such a refusal into account in any decision to promote or train the employee." This section prohibits employers from taking adverse employment actions against an employee who refuses to work a scheduled period or shift within the 96-hour notice period. The refusal cannot be considered in decisions regarding promotion or training.

### Non-Application of Subsection 196(4)
"Subsection 196(4) does not apply in respect of a work period or shift that an employee refuses to work under subsection (2)." This subsection states that subsection 196(4) does not apply when an employee refuses to work a scheduled period or shift within the 96-hour notice period.

### Non-Application to Collective Agreements
"This section does not apply to employees who are employed under the terms of a collective agreement that specifies an alternate time frame for providing the work schedule or provides that this section does not apply to those employees." This subsection clarifies that this section does not apply to employees covered by a collective agreement that has a different timeframe for providing work schedules or explicitly excludes such employees from the 96-hour notice requirement.

## Conditions for Employer Written Notice of Work Schedule Changes

### General Notice Requirements
"The employer shall provide an employee with their work schedule in writing at least 96 hours before the start of the employee’s first work period or shift under that schedule." This section establishes the standard requirement for employers to provide employees with their work schedules in writing with a minimum of 96 hours' notice. This ensures employees have adequate time to plan their personal lives and make necessary arrangements.

### Exceptions to the 96-Hour Notice

Several exceptions exist to the standard 96-hour notice requirement.

#### Unforeseen Emergencies
"Subject to subsection (3), an employee may refuse to work any work period or shift in their schedule that starts within 96 hours from the time that the schedule is provided to them." This exception allows employees to refuse work periods or shifts scheduled within 96 hours of receiving the schedule, unless certain conditions are met.
"An employee shall not refuse to work a work period or shift if it is necessary for them to work in order to deal with a situation that the employer could not have reasonably foreseen and that presents or could reasonably be expected to present an imminent or serious (a) threat to the life, health or safety of any person; (b) threat of damage to or loss of property; or (c) threat of serious interference with the ordinary working of the employer’s industrial establishment." This further clarifies the emergency exceptions. An employee cannot refuse work if it is necessary to address an unforeseen imminent or serious threat to life, health, safety, property, or the normal operation of the employer's business.

#### Changes Following Employee Request
"Subsection (1) does not apply to a change to an employee’s work schedule following a request made under subsection 177.1(1)." This exception states that if an employee makes a request for a change to their work schedule, the employer is not required to provide the standard 96-hour notice.

#### Dismissal, Suspension, Layoff, Demotion, or Discipline
"An employer shall not dismiss, suspend, lay off, demote or discipline an employee because the employee has refused to work a work period or shift under subsection (2) or take such a refusal into account in any decision to promote or train the employee." This provision protects employees who refuse work periods or shifts within the 96-hour notice window from adverse employment actions.

#### Collective Agreements
"This section does not apply to employees who are employed under the terms of a collective agreement that specifies an alternate time frame for providing the work schedule or provides that this section does not apply to those employees." This exception applies when a collective agreement establishes a different timeframe for providing work schedules or explicitly states that this section does not apply to those employees.

### Notice for Shift Changes and Additions
"If an employer changes a period or shift during which an employee is due to work or adds another work period or shift to the employee’s schedule, the employer shall give the employee written notice of the change or addition at least 24 hours before (a) in the case of a change, the employee’s original work period or shift is to begin or, if the work period or shift that results from the change is to begin earlier than the original work period or shift, before the period or shift that results from the change is to begin; and (b) in the case of an addition, the work period or shift that was added is to begin." This section outlines the 24-hour notice requirement for shift changes and additions. The notice must be provided at least 24 hours before the change or addition is to take effect.

#### Exceptions to the 24-Hour Notice
"Subsection (1) does not apply if the change to or addition of a work period or shift is necessary to deal with a situation that the employer could not have reasonably foreseen and that presents or could reasonably be expected to present an imminent or serious (a) threat to the life, health or safety of any person; (b) threat of damage to or loss of property; or (c) threat of serious interference with the ordinary working of the employer’s industrial establishment." This exception mirrors the emergency exceptions for standard work schedule changes, allowing for less than 24 hours' notice when necessary to address an unforeseen imminent or serious threat.

This exception applies when an employee makes a request for a change to their work schedule, in which case the employer is not required to provide the standard 24-hour notice.

individual_results.question: What are the two options available to an employee who is required or permitted to work overtime under the Canada Labour Code?
individual_results.answer:
## Overtime Pay or Time Off

### Right to Refuse Overtime

The Canada Labour Code grants employees the right to refuse overtime under certain circumstances. Section 174.1(1) states,
"Subject to subsections (2) and (3), an employee may refuse to work the overtime requested by the employer in order to carry out the employee’s family responsibilities referred to in paragraph 206.6(1)(b) or (c)." This directly addresses the question by outlining one option available to an employee facing overtime requests.

### Overtime Pay or Time Off

Section 174(1) details the two options available to an employee who is required or permitted to work overtime:
"(a) be paid for the overtime at a rate of wages not less than one and one-half times their regular rate of wages; or (b) be granted not less than one and one-half hours of time off with pay for each hour of overtime worked, subject to subsections (2) to (5)."

This passage explicitly lays out the two alternatives: overtime pay at a premium rate or compensatory time off with pay. It further elaborates on the conditions under which an employee is entitled to time off, stating,
"An employee is entitled to time off for overtime worked only if, (a) at their request, they and the employer enter into an agreement in writing providing for the taking of time off, subject to paragraph (b) and subsections (3) to (5), on a date or dates agreed on by them and the employer; and (b) the time off is taken within a period of three months after the end of the pay period in which the overtime was worked, or within any longer period set out in (i) if the employee is subject to a collective agreement, the collective agreement, or (ii) if the employee is not subject to a collective agreement, the agreement referred to in paragraph (a) or any other agreement in writing entered into by them and the employer." This provides further detail on the process and timeframe for receiving compensatory time off.

individual_results.question: Under what conditions can an employee refuse to work overtime requested by their employer, and what protections do they have against reprisals for making such a refusal?
individual_results.answer:
## Conditions for Refusing Overtime and Protections Against Reprisals

### Conditions for Refusing Overtime

An employee has the right to refuse overtime to fulfill family responsibilities related to the health or care of family members, or the education of family members under 18 years of age. However, this refusal is subject to certain conditions.
"...an employee may refuse to work the overtime requested by the employer in order to carry out the employee’s family responsibilities referred to in paragraph 206.6(1)(b) or (c)." This statement directly addresses the core condition for refusing overtime. It clarifies that the right to refuse is specifically tied to family responsibilities.

Furthermore, an employee can only refuse overtime if they have taken reasonable steps to address those family responsibilities in some other way.
"An employee may refuse to work overtime only if (a) they have taken reasonable steps to carry out their family responsibility by other means, so as to enable them to work overtime; and (b) even though the steps referred to in paragraph (a) have been taken, they are still required to carry out that responsibility during the period of the overtime." This passage emphasizes the requirement of making reasonable efforts to resolve family matters before resorting to refusing overtime. It also states that even after reasonable steps have been taken, the employee must still be required to fulfill those family responsibilities during the overtime period to justify the refusal.

There is also an exception to the right to refuse overtime. An employee cannot refuse overtime if it is necessary due to a situation that their employer could not reasonably anticipate and that presents or could reasonably be expected to present an imminent or serious threat.
"An employee is not to refuse to work overtime if it is necessary for them to work overtime to deal with a situation that the employer could not have reasonably foreseen and that presents or could reasonably be expected to present an imminent or serious (a) threat to the life, health or safety of any person; (b) threat of damage to or loss of property; or (c) threat of serious interference with the ordinary working of the employer’s industrial establishment." This exception outlines specific, serious circumstances where refusing overtime would not be permissible.

### Protections Against Reprisals for Refusing Overtime

Employees who refuse overtime under the specified conditions are protected from reprisals from their employer.
"An employer shall not dismiss, suspend, lay off, demote or discipline an employee because the employee has refused to work overtime under subsection (1) or take such a refusal into account in any decision to promote or train the employee." This provision explicitly prohibits employers from taking adverse actions against employees who legitimately refuse overtime to meet family responsibilities. It covers a range of potential reprisals, including dismissal, suspension, demotion, and disciplinary measures, as well as consideration of the refusal in promotion or training decisions.

The Canada Labour Code further reinforces this protection by stating that an employer cannot take a refusal to work overtime into account in any decision to promote or train the employee. This ensures that employees who exercise their right to refuse overtime are not penalized in their career advancement opportunities.

individual_results.question: Under what circumstances can the Governor in Council make regulations modifying or exempting certain classes of employees from the application of this Division of the Canada Labour Code?
individual_results.answer:
## Circumstances for Governor in Council Regulations Modifying or Exempting Employees

### Exclusion from Application of Provisions of this Part

The Governor in Council possesses the authority to make regulations that modify or exempt certain classes of employees from the application of this Division of the Canada Labour Code. This power is explicitly stated in Section 121.2(1):
"The Governor in Council may by regulation exclude, in whole or in part, from the application of any of the provisions of this Part any employment, or any class or classes of employment, on or in connection with a work or undertaking set out in the regulation whose activities are regulated, in whole or in part, pursuant to the Nuclear Safety and Control Act..."

This section outlines a broad power to exclude specific employment or classes of employment from the Division's provisions. The exclusion can be "in whole or in part," indicating flexibility in the scope of the exemption. The regulation can apply to any employment or any class of employment
"...on or in connection with a work or undertaking set out in the regulation whose activities are regulated, in whole or in part, pursuant to the Nuclear Safety and Control Act..." This suggests a specific context for such exclusions, relating to activities regulated under the Nuclear Safety and Control Act.

### Regulations Incorporating Provincial Laws

The Governor in Council can also make regulations that incorporate provincial laws, potentially modifying or exempting certain classes of employees. This is detailed in Section 121.3(3):
"A regulation made under subsection (2) incorporating by reference, in whole or in part, an Act of the legislature of a province or an instrument made under such an Act may incorporate the Act or instrument as amended to a certain date or from time to time."

This provision allows for the integration of provincial labour laws into federal regulations. If a provincial law modifies or exempts certain classes of employees, the federal regulation can incorporate that provincial law, thereby extending the modification or exemption to the federal employment covered by the regulation.

### Regulations Relating to Labour Standards in Relation to Employment Subject to Nuclear Safety Act

Furthermore, the Governor in Council can make regulations relating to labour standards in relation to employment subject to the Nuclear Safety and Control Act. This power is outlined in Section 121.2(2):
"On the recommendation of the Minister, the Governor in Council may make regulations respecting any matter relating to industrial relations, including the prevention of a work stoppage or the continuation or resumption of operations, in relation to employment that is subject to a regulation made pursuant to subsection (1)."

This regulation-making power is triggered by the Minister's recommendation and specifically addresses labour standards in connection with employment regulated under the Nuclear Safety and Control Act. These regulations could potentially modify or exempt certain classes of employees from the application of this Division of the Canada Labour Code, depending on the specific labour standards addressed.

### Regulations Applying Generally or to Specific Classes of Employment

The Governor in Council can also make regulations that apply generally to all employment subject to a regulation made pursuant to subsection (1) or to any class or classes of employment that are subject to such a regulation. This is explained in Section 121.3(4):
"A regulation made under subsection (2) may apply (a) generally, with respect to all employment that is subject to a regulation made pursuant to subsection (1); or (b) to any class or classes of employment that are subject to a regulation made pursuant to subsection (1)."

This provision provides flexibility in the scope of the regulation, allowing for either a broad application to all regulated employment or a more targeted application to specific classes of employment.

### Administration and Enforcement

The administration and enforcement of regulations made under subsection (2), incorporating provincial laws, are also subject to regulation. This is detailed in Section 121.3(5):
"A regulation made under subsection (2) incorporating an Act or instrument shall, after consultation by the Minister with the appropriate provincial minister, be administered and enforced by the person or authority that is responsible for the administration and enforcement of the Act or instrument."

This ensures that the enforcement of regulations incorporating provincial laws is aligned with the existing provincial administrative structures.

individual_results.question: Under what conditions can an employer or employer's organization apply for a permit to have employees work beyond the maximum hours of work specified in the Canada Labour Code?
individual_results.answer:
## Conditions for Applying for an Excess Hours Permit

### General Conditions

An employer or employer's organization can apply for a permit to have employees work beyond the maximum hours of work specified in the Canada Labour Code under specific conditions. These conditions are outlined in Section 176(1) of the Canada Labour Code and further elaborated upon in CLC-176 and LABOUR-STANDARDS-4_5.

#### Exceptional Circumstances

The primary condition for obtaining an excess hours permit is the existence of
"...exceptional circumstances exist that justify the working of additional hours..." This means that the additional hours are necessary due to unforeseen or urgent situations.

>
"On the application of an employer or an employer’s organization, the Head, having regard to the conditions of employment in any industrial establishment and the welfare of the employees, may, by a permit in writing, authorize hours to be worked by any class of employees set out in the permit in excess of the maximum hours of work specified in or prescribed under section 171, established under section 172 or prescribed by regulations made under section 175."

This quote directly states the fundamental requirement: exceptional circumstances must exist to justify the permit. The Head of Compliance and Enforcement (Head) will consider the conditions of employment and the welfare of employees when deciding whether to grant the permit.

#### Notice Requirements

In addition to exceptional circumstances, the employer must meet specific notice requirements.

>
"No permit may be issued under subsection (1) unless the applicant has satisfied the Head (a) that exceptional circumstances exist that justify the working of additional hours; (b) that the employer had posted a notice of the application for the permit, for at least 30 days before its proposed effective date, in places readily accessible to the affected class of employees where they were likely to see it; and (c) that the employer had informed the trade union in writing of the application for the permit, if those employees are represented by a trade union."

This passage details the mandatory posting of notice. The notice must be displayed in accessible locations for at least 30 days before the permit's intended start date. Furthermore, if the employees are represented by a trade union, the employer must inform the union in writing of the application.

#### Advance Application

Employers are generally required to apply for an excess hours permit with sufficient advance notice.

>
"The employer must normally apply 60 days in advance of the proposed effective date of the excess hours permit."

This indicates a 60-day advance application requirement. However, LABOUR-STANDARDS-4_5 mentions an exception:

>
"Federally regulated employers may use the application form available on the Government of Canada web site to apply for a permit."

This suggests that the 60-day advance application may not be strictly enforced for employers using the online application form.

### Additional Considerations

### Day of Rest Requirement

The permit may also exempt the employer from the 'day of rest' requirement.

>
"The permit may also exempt the employer from the "day of rest" requirement."

This indicates a potential exemption from the mandatory day of rest.

### Overtime Obligations

Obtaining an excess hours permit does not relieve the employer from the obligation to pay overtime.

>
"Obtaining a permit does not exempt the employer from the obligation to pay overtime. The employer must report in writing to the Head within 15 days after the permit expires or at another date specified in the permit. The report must show the number of:  employees who worked more than 48 hours in a week, and additional hours in a week each employee worked..."

This passage explicitly states that overtime must still be paid. The employer is required to report the number of employees working over 48 hours in a week and the additional hours each employee worked within 15 days of the permit's expiration.

individual_results.question: Under what conditions can the maximum hours of work in a week be exceeded in an industrial establishment, and what are the employer's obligations in such cases?
individual_results.answer:
## Conditions for Exceeding Maximum Hours of Work

### Emergency Work
"In case of emergency, such as an accident or essential work on equipment, an employer may exceed the maximum hours of work without a permit." This indicates that the primary condition for exceeding the maximum hours is an unforeseen and critical situation requiring immediate attention. The employer is permitted to exceed the limit in these specific circumstances.

### Averaging
"In some establishments, the nature of work necessitates irregular hours of work due to seasonal or other factors. This means that as an employee, you may be subject to:   scheduled hours that vary from time to time, or no regularly scheduled hours  If this applies to you, your employer may average your hours of work over a period of 2 or more weeks. As such, standard and maximum hours would be calculated across a period of 2 or more weeks rather than on a daily or weekly basis." This section outlines the concept of averaging hours. When work is irregular, employers can calculate the maximum hours over a longer period (two or more weeks) rather than on a daily or weekly basis. This allows for flexibility in scheduling while still adhering to the overall maximum hours.

### Excess Hour Permit
"The maximum hours of work in a week specified in or prescribed under section 171, established pursuant to section 172 or prescribed by regulations made under section 175 may be exceeded, but only to the extent necessary to prevent serious interference with the ordinary working of the industrial establishment affected, in cases of (a) accident to machinery, equipment, plant or persons; (b) urgent and essential work to be done to machinery, equipment or plant; or (c) other unforeseen or unpreventable circumstances." This passage details further conditions under which the maximum hours can be exceeded. These are limited to situations that are
"...necessary to prevent serious interference with the ordinary working of the industrial establishment affected..." specifically mentioning accidents, urgent essential work, and other unforeseen circumstances.

### Employer Obligations in Cases of Excess Hours

### Reporting Additional Work
"Where the maximum hours of work in an industrial establishment have been exceeded under the authority of subsection (1), the employer shall report in writing to the Head, and also to the trade union if the affected employees are subject to a collective agreement, within 15 days after the end of the month in which the maximum was exceeded, stating the nature of the circumstances in which the maximum was exceeded, the number of employees who worked in excess of the maximum and the number of additional hours each of them worked." This section clearly states the employer's obligation to report any instances where the maximum hours have been exceeded. The report must be submitted within 15 days of the end of the month in which the excess hours occurred and must include details about the circumstances, the number of employees working over the limit, and the number of additional hours each worked. The report is to be sent to both the Head and the trade union, if applicable.

### Posting Notice
"Where a work schedule is to be established, modified or cancelled pursuant to subsection (2), the employer shall post a notice of the new schedule, or of its modification or cancellation, in readily accessible places where it is likely to be seen by the affected employees, for at least thirty days before the new schedule or its modification or cancellation takes effect." While not directly addressing exceeding maximum hours, this obligation to post notice is relevant to any changes in work schedules, including those involving excess hours. It ensures that affected employees are informed of any modifications.

### Collective Agreement Requirements
"Section 172 (1) An employer may, in respect of one or more employees subject to a collective agreement, establish, modify or cancel a work schedule under which the hours exceed the maximum set out in section 171 or in regulations made under section 175 if (a) the average hours of work for a period of two or more weeks does not exceed forty-eight hours a week; and (b) the schedule, or its modification or cancellation, is agreed to in writing by the employer and the trade union." This passage highlights that exceeding maximum hours under a collective agreement requires written agreement from both the employer and the trade union, provided the average hours over a two-week period do not exceed forty-eight hours.

### Other Employer Obligations
"Section 177 (1) The maximum hours of work in a week specified in or prescribed under section 171, established pursuant to section 172 or prescribed by regulations made under section 175 may be exceeded, but only to the extent necessary to prevent serious interference with the ordinary working of the industrial establishment affected, in cases of (a) accident to machinery, equipment, plant or persons; (b) urgent and essential work to be done to machinery, equipment or plant; or (c) other unforeseen or unpreventable circumstances." This section reiterates the conditions for exceeding maximum hours and reinforces the employer's obligation to report such instances.

individual_results.question: What are the steps an employee must take and considerations they must keep in mind when requesting a change to their terms and conditions of employment from their employer?
individual_results.answer:
## Steps an Employee Must Take When Requesting a Change to Terms and Conditions of Employment

### Submitting a Written Request

The first step an employee must take is to submit their request to their employer in writing. This is a mandatory requirement outlined in Section 177.1(2) of the Canada Labour Code. The written request must include specific information.
"The request shall be made in writing and shall include (a) the employee’s name; (b) the date on which the request is made; (c) a description of the change to the terms and conditions of employment that is requested; (d) the date on which the change would take effect and, if the change is intended to be temporary, the date on which the change would cease to have effect; (e) an explanation of the effect that, in the employee’s opinion, the requested change would have on the employer and the manner in which, in the employee’s opinion, the employer could manage that effect; and (f) any information that may be prescribed by regulation."

This detailed information ensures the employer understands the specific changes being requested and the employee's rationale behind them.

### Employer's Decision and Notice

Once the employee submits their written request, the employer has 30 days to respond. The employer must make one of four possible decisions in writing.
"An employer to whom a request is made shall make one of the following decisions: (a) grant the request; (b) offer to grant the request in part or to make an alternative change to the terms and conditions of employment; or (c) refuse the request on one or more of the following grounds..."

The employer's decision must be communicated to the employee in writing within 30 days. If the request is refused, the employer must provide written reasons for doing so.
"The notice in respect of a decision made under paragraph (3)(b) or (c) shall include written reasons for refusing the requested change or for not granting a part of it."

### Considerations for the Employee

Several considerations are important for an employee when making a request for a change to their terms and conditions of employment.

#### Timing

Employees must have completed six consecutive months of continuous employment with their employer before making such a request. This is a prerequisite stated in Section 177.1(1).

#### Specificity of the Request

The request must be detailed and clearly articulate the specific changes being sought. This includes the number of hours, work schedule, location of work, and any other relevant terms and conditions. The employee should also explain the potential impact of the requested change on the employer and how the employer could manage that impact.

#### Employer's Grounds for Refusal

Employees should be aware of the potential grounds on which an employer may refuse a request. These include additional costs, negative impacts on work quality or customer demand, inability to reorganize work or hire additional employees, insufficient work available, and any other grounds prescribed by regulation.

#### Protections Against Reprisals

Employees are protected from reprisals for making a written request for a flexible work arrangement. Employers are prohibited from taking the request into account in any decision to promote or train the employee, or threatening to take such actions.
"An employer shall not dismiss, suspend, lay off, demote or discipline an employee because the employee has made a request under subsection (1) or take such a request into account in any decision to promote or train the employee."

### Submitting a Request to the Labour Program's Head of Compliance and Enforcement

Employers may also request a waiver of certain requirements by completing the form “Notice to the Head of Compliance and Enforcement of a group termination of employment and Request for waiver under the Canada Labour Code - Part III (ESDC-LAB1197)”. This form can be used to provide notice to the Labour Program’s Head of Compliance and Enforcement and/or make an application to the Minister of Labour for a waiver of specific requirements.

individual_results.question: What is the general rule regarding the minimum wage that an employer must pay to each employee under the Canada Labour Code?
individual_results.answer:
## General Rule Regarding Minimum Wage

### Minimum Hourly Rate
"Section 178 (1) Subject to subsections (2) to (5), an employer shall pay to each employee a wage at a minimum hourly rate that is not less than the rate that is determined in accordance with section 178.1." This passage directly states the fundamental rule: an employer must pay an employee a minimum hourly rate that is at least the rate determined by the provisions in section 178.1. This section details the process for calculating the federal minimum wage, which is adjusted annually based on the Consumer Price Index.

### Minimum Wage for Non-Hourly Pay
"Where the wages of an employee are computed and paid on a basis other than time or on a combined basis of time and some other basis, the Minister may, by order, (a) fix a standard basis of work to which a minimum wage on a basis other than time may be applied; and (b) fix a minimum rate of wage that in the opinion of the Minister is the equivalent of (i) the minimum rate determined in accordance with subsection (2), if that minimum rate is higher than or equal to the minimum rate determined in accordance with section 178.1, or (ii) the minimum rate determined in accordance with section 178.1, if that minimum rate is higher than the minimum rate determined in accordance with subsection (2)." This section addresses situations where employees are paid on a basis other than an hourly rate, such as annual salaries or mileage rates. It clarifies that the Minister has the authority to establish an equivalent minimum wage rate for these types of compensation structures.

### Minimum Wage for Employees Under 18 Years of Age
"Note: On June 12, 2023, the Canada  Labour Code , Part III (Code) and the Canada  Labour Standards Regulations were amended to raise the minimum age of employment from 17 to 18.   However, a transitional provision set in the Code allows  employees who are 17 years of age prior to June 12, 2023, to be considered  as if they are 18 years of age, and may keep their employment if they:   remain employed by the same employer, and remain in  the same position..." This note provides specific information regarding the minimum wage for employees under 18 years of age. It explains that the minimum age of employment was raised to 18, but a transitional provision allows 17-year-olds who remain employed by the same employer and in the same position to continue working at the minimum wage.

### Minimum Wage for Employees Not Paid Hourly
"If your employer does not pay you on an hourly basis, you must receive at least the equivalent of the minimum wage. Where the basis of your pay is not time (for example, you may be paid an  annual salary or in accordance with a mileage rate), the Minister of Labour may  fix a rate that is equivalent to at least the minimum wage. This rate is  determined by dividing the amount of salary you received (excluding any  vacation pay, general holiday pay, and overtime pay) by the number of hours  worked you performed." This passage reiterates the general rule that non-hourly paid employees must receive at least the equivalent of the minimum wage. It further explains the method for calculating this equivalent rate when the pay is not based on time.

individual_results.question: How is the minimum hourly rate for employees adjusted in Canada, and what is the basis for this adjustment?
individual_results.answer:
## Minimum Hourly Rate Adjustment in Canada

### Current Approach and Basis for Adjustment

The minimum hourly rate in Canada is adjusted annually based on the Consumer Price Index (CPI). This adjustment is outlined in section 178 of Part III of the Canada Labour Code.
"On April 1 of each year after the year in which this section comes into force, the minimum hourly rate is to be adjusted to the rate, rounded up to the nearest $0.05, that is equal to the product of (a) as the case may be, (i) in respect of April 1 of the year after the year in which this section comes into force, $15, or (ii) in respect of April 1 of each subsequent year, the rate that is determined in accordance with this section on April 1 of the preceding year, and (b) the ratio that the Consumer Price Index for the preceding calendar year bears to the Consumer Price Index for the calendar year before that preceding calendar year."

This mechanism ensures that the federal minimum wage keeps pace with inflation, maintaining its relevance across the country. The CPI is used as the basis for this adjustment because it reflects the average change in prices paid by urban consumers for a basket of goods and services.

### Historical Approach and Current Implementation

Historically, the minimum wage rate was specified in the Code and then adjusted by the Governor in Council through regulation. However, the current approach, adopted in 1996, links the federal minimum wage to provincial and territorial rates.
"The current  approach, adopted in 1996, is set out in section 178 of Part III. Section 178 establishes  the federal  minimum wage as the "minimum hourly rate fixed,  from time to time, by or under an Act of the legislature of the province where  the employee is usually employed and that is generally applicable regardless of  occupation, status or work..."

This "pegged" approach means that the federal minimum wage will automatically adjust when provincial and territorial minimum wages change. This ensures that the federal rate remains competitive and reflects the cost of living in different regions of the country.

### Exceptions and Considerations

While the federal minimum wage is adjusted annually, there are some exceptions and considerations. For example, the minimum wage for employees under 18 years of age is subject to different rules.
"Note: On June 12, 2023, the Canada  Labour Code , Part III (Code) and the Canada  Labour Standards Regulations were amended to raise the minimum age of employment from 17 to 18.   However, a transitional provision set in the Code allows  employees who are 17 years of age prior to June 12, 2023, to be considered  as if they are 18 years of age, and may keep their employment if they:   remain employed by the same employer, and remain in  the same position..."

Additionally, the Governor in Council has the authority to adjust the minimum wage rate for a province if no such rate has been fixed, but this authority has never been used.

individual_results.question: What conditions must an employer meet in order to employ a person under the age of 18?
individual_results.answer:
## Conditions for Employing a Person Under 18 Years of Age

### General Conditions

An employer may employ a person under the age of 18 years only if they meet specific conditions outlined in the Canada Labour Code and the Canada Labour Standards Regulations.

#### Provincial Law
"An employer may employ a person under the age of 18 years only (a) in an occupation specified by the regulations; and (b) subject to the conditions fixed by the regulations for employment in that occupation." This section of the Canada Labour Code establishes that the employment of a minor is subject to regulations specific to the occupation. Employers must adhere to these regulations.

#### Health and Safety
"...the work in which the person is to be employed (i) is not carried on underground in a mine, (ii) would not cause them to be employed in or enter a place that they are prohibited from entering under the Explosives Regulations, 2013 , (iii) is not work as a nuclear energy worker as defined in the Nuclear Safety and Control Act , (iv) is not work that they are prohibited from doing under the Canada Shipping Act, 2001 by reason of their age, and (v) is not likely to be injurious to their health or to endanger their safety." This condition details several restrictions on the types of work minors can perform. It explicitly prohibits work underground in a mine, work in prohibited places, work as a nuclear energy worker, work prohibited by the Canada Shipping Act due to age, and work likely to be injurious to their health or endanger their safety.

#### School Attendance

individual_results.question: What types of regulations can the Governor in Council make to carry out the purposes and provisions of this Division of the Canada Labour Code?
individual_results.answer:
## Regulations Made by the Governor in Council

### General Powers of Regulation

The Governor in Council possesses broad powers to make regulations to achieve the objectives and provisions of this Division of the Canada Labour Code. Section 264(1) states:
"The Governor in Council may make regulations for carrying out the purposes of this Part and, without restricting the generality of the foregoing, may make regulations (a) requiring employers to keep records of wages, vacations, holidays and overtime of employees and of other particulars relevant to the purposes of this Part or any Division thereof..."

This passage establishes the foundational power of the Governor in Council to enact regulations. The phrase "for carrying out the purposes of this Part" indicates that these regulations are intended to implement and advance the goals outlined in the Division. The subsequent list of examples further elaborates on the types of regulations that can be made.

### Specific Types of Regulations

Section 264(1) provides a detailed breakdown of the specific types of regulations the Governor in Council can enact. These include:

#### Record Keeping Requirements
"(a) requiring employers to keep records of wages, vacations, holidays and overtime of employees and of other particulars relevant to the purposes of this Part or any Division thereof; (a.1) requiring employers to keep records relevant to the purposes of this Part in respect of persons who are excluded under subsection 167(1.2) from the application of all or any of this Part; (a.2) respecting the information that an employer must provide to the Head for the purpose of establishing that the performance of activities referred to in subsection 167(1.2) fulfils the requirements of a program referred to in that subsection, and the circumstances in which an employer must provide it; (a.3) specifying the circumstances in which a person who performs activities referred to in subsection 167(1.2) must provide to an employer the information referred to in paragraph (a.2); (a.4) for the purpose of subsection 167(1.2), specifying or describing secondary or post-secondary educational institutions, vocational schools, or equivalent educational institutions outside Canada..."

This section outlines regulations concerning the documentation employers must maintain. This includes detailed records of employee compensation, time off, and other relevant information. It also addresses specific scenarios, such as those involving exclusions from the application of this Part and those related to educational institutions outside Canada.

#### Designation of Industrial Establishments
"(b) designating any branch, section or other division of any federal work, undertaking or business as an industrial establishment for the purposes of this Part or any Division thereof; (b.1) extending the application of this Part, in the manner and to the extent provided for in the regulations, to any class of persons..."

This regulation allows the Governor in Council to designate specific workplaces as "industrial establishments." This designation can be used to broaden the application of this Division to certain groups of people working in those establishments.

#### Governance of Record Production and Inspection
"(c) governing the production and inspection of records required to be kept by employers..."

This regulation provides the framework for how employers must produce and how the Minister or their representatives can inspect the records they are required to keep.

#### Wage Calculation and Determination
"(d) for calculating and determining wages received by an employee in respect of his employment, including the monetary value of remuneration other than money and, for the purposes of any provision or provisions of this Part specified in the regulations, the regular rate of wages of employees; (e) for calculating and determining the regular rate of wages, on an hourly basis, of employees who are paid on any basis of time other than hourly or who are not paid solely on a basis of time; (e.1) respecting the calculation and payment of the wages and other amounts to which an employee whose wages are paid on a commission basis, on a salary plus commission basis or on any other basis other than time is entitled to under Divisions V, VII, VIII, X and XI..."

This section details regulations for calculating and determining employee wages. It covers various payment structures, including hourly, commission-based, and salary-plus-commission arrangements.

#### Maximum Working Hours
"(f) prescribing the maximum number of hours that may elapse between the commencement and termination of the working day of any employee..."

This regulation sets a limit on the maximum number of consecutive hours an employee can work.

#### Notification to Employees
"(g) [Repealed, 2018, c. 27, s. 505] (h) requiring an employer in any industrial establishment to notify employees, by the publication of such notices, in such manner as may be prescribed, of (i) the provisions of this Part or any regulation or order made under this Part, (ii) the particulars of hours of work, including the hours at which shifts change, (iii) the particulars of rest periods and meal periods, and (iv) other matters related to hours and conditions of work of employees..."

This regulation mandates that employers provide employees with clear information regarding their working hours, rest periods, and other relevant conditions of employment.

#### Payment of Wages
"(i) providing for the payment of any wages of an employee to the Head or to another person in the event that the employee cannot be found or in any other case; (i.1) providing for the application of any provisions of this Part or of the regulations made under this Part to persons and, in relation to those persons, employers who are otherwise excluded under subsection 167(1.2) from the application of this Part and adapting those provisions for the purpose of applying them to those persons and those employers..."

This regulation outlines procedures for the payment of wages when an employee cannot be located or in other exceptional circumstances. It also addresses the application of this Division's provisions to individuals and employers who are otherwise excluded from its application.

#### Establishment of Consultative Committees
"(j) providing for the establishment of consultative or advisory committees to advise the Minister on any matters arising in relation to the administration of this Part; (j.1) prescribing the circumstances and conditions for the purposes of subsection 251.01(3); (j.2) prescribing the circumstances under which a complaint is not to be rejected under paragraph 251.05(1)(c); (j.3) prescribing the conditions that are to be met before a complaint may be rejected under paragraph 251.05(1)(c); (j.4) prescribing periods for the purposes of subsection 251.05(1.1); and (j.5) [Repealed, 2020, c. 12, s. 4] (k) for any other matter or purpose that under this Part is required or permitted to be prescribed by regulation."

This regulation allows the Governor in Council to create committees to provide advice to the Minister on matters related to the administration of this Division. It also covers specific aspects of complaint handling and time limits.

### Incorporation of Documents

Section 264(2) further clarifies the power of the Governor in Council to make regulations by incorporating external documents. It states:
"A regulation made under paragraph (1)(a.4) that incorporates by reference, in whole or in part, a document may incorporate the document, regardless of its source, as it exists on..."

This passage explains that regulations can refer to existing documents, and these documents are incorporated into the regulation as they existed at the time the regulation was made. This allows the Governor in Council to leverage existing frameworks and guidelines when enacting new regulations.

## Medical Breaks for Medical Reasons

### Unpaid Breaks for Medical Reasons
"Subject to the regulations, every employee is entitled to and shall be granted any unpaid breaks that are necessary for medical reasons." This section of the Canada Labour Code clearly states that employees are entitled to unpaid breaks when medically necessary. The reference to "regulations" indicates that the specifics of these breaks may be further defined by subsequent rules.

### Certificate Requirements
"On written request by the employer, the employee must provide a certificate issued by a health care practitioner setting out the length and frequency of the breaks needed for medical reasons and any additional information that may be prescribed by regulation." This subsection outlines the employer's right to request a medical certificate. The certificate must detail the duration and frequency of the breaks required for medical reasons, along with any other information specified in the regulations. This ensures that the breaks are genuinely medically necessary.

## Nursing Breaks

### Unpaid Breaks for Nursing
"...every employee who is nursing is entitled to and shall be granted any unpaid breaks necessary for them to nurse or to express breast milk." This section specifically grants nursing mothers unpaid breaks as needed for nursing or expressing breast milk. The language is straightforward, ensuring that nursing employees have the necessary time for this essential aspect of their caregiving responsibilities.

### Certificate Requirements for Nursing Breaks
"On written request by the employer, the employee must provide a certificate issued by a health care practitioner setting out the length and frequency of the breaks needed for medical reasons and any additional information that may be prescribed by regulation." Similar to medical breaks, employers can request a medical certificate for nursing breaks. This certificate must detail the length and frequency of the breaks required for nursing, along with any other information specified in the regulations.

## Additional Considerations

### Regulations
"The Governor in Council may make regulations (a) modifying the provisions of sections 181.1 or 181.2 for the purpose of the application of this Division to any class of employees; (b) exempting any class of employees from the application of section 181.1 or 181.2; (c) respecting the breaks set out in subsection 181.1(1) and section 181.2, including circumstances in which those breaks cannot be taken; and (d) respecting additional information to be included in a certificate required under subsection 181.1(2)." This section grants the Governor in Council the authority to create regulations that further clarify and modify the provisions regarding medical and nursing breaks. individual_results.question: What constitutes a year of employment for an employee in terms of continuous employment with one employer?
individual_results.answer:
## Defining a Year of Employment for Continuous Employment

### Continuous Employment and the Definition of a Year

The Canada Labour Code, specifically Division IV on Annual Vacations, defines a year of employment for the purposes of continuous employment in the context of annual vacations. It states,
"Section 189 (1) Despite the lease or transfer of a work, undertaking or business, or any part of a work, undertaking or business, from one employer to another employer by sale, merger or otherwise, the employment of the employee, before and after the lease or transfer, who is employed in or in connection with the operation of that work, undertaking or business, is, for the purposes of this Division, deemed to be continuous with one employer if the work, undertaking or business (a) is a federal work, undertaking or business; or (b) becomes a federal work, undertaking or business due to the lease or transfer."

This section clarifies that for continuous employment, the employee's employment before and after a lease or transfer of a business is considered continuous with one employer if the work, undertaking, or business is either a federal one or becomes one due to the lease or transfer. This implies that a year of employment is considered continuous if the employee's work is with the same federal employer throughout the year, even if the employer undergoes a lease or transfer.

### Calculation of Continuous Employment Period

Further details on the calculation of continuous employment are provided in Section 189(1.3):
"For greater certainty, if an employer’s work, undertaking or business becomes a federal work, undertaking or business due to a change in its activities, for the purposes of this Division, an employee’s period of continuous employment by the employer includes any period in which the work, undertaking or business in or in connection with the operation of which the employee is employed was not a federal work, undertaking or business."

This subsection explains that if an employer's work becomes federal due to a change in its activities, the employee's continuous employment period includes any period where the work was not federal. This means that a year of employment is considered continuous even if the employer's status changes during the year.

### Exceptions to Continuous Employment

However, there are exceptions to the rule of continuous employment. Section 189(1.2) states,
"Subsections (1) and (1.1) do not apply if the employee’s first day of employment by the second employer is more than 13 weeks after the day that is the earlier of (a) the employee’s last day of employment by the first employer; and (b) the day on which the federal work, undertaking or business is transferred or the first day the second employer carries out the federal work, undertaking or business, as the case may be."

This exception indicates that if there is a gap of more than 13 weeks between the employee's last day of employment by the first employer and their first day of employment by the second employer, the continuous employment period is not considered continuous. This means that a year of employment is not considered continuous if there is a significant break between employers.

### Employer Obligations Regarding Annual Vacations

Section 188 outlines the employer's obligations regarding annual vacations upon termination of employment. It states,
"When an employee ceases to be employed, the employer shall pay to the employee within 30 days after the day on which the employee ceases to be employed (a) any vacation pay then owing by the employer to the employee under this Division in respect of any prior completed year of employment; and (b) the applicable percentage, under section 184.01, of the wages of the employee during any part of the completed portion of their year of employment in respect of which vacation pay has not been paid to them."

This section emphasizes that for any prior completed year of employment, the employer must pay any outstanding vacation pay within 30 days of the employee's termination. This reinforces the concept of a year of employment as a continuous period for vacation entitlement.

individual_results.question: What are the minimum vacation entitlements for employees in Canada under the Labour Code, and how is vacation pay calculated?
individual_results.answer:
## Minimum Vacation Entitlements in Canada

### Entitlement Based on Years of Employment

According to Section 184 of the Canada Labour Code, employees are entitled to a minimum vacation with vacation pay based on their years of continuous employment with the same employer. The minimum vacation entitlement is as follows:
"...at least two weeks if they have completed at least one year of employment; (b) at least three weeks if they have completed at least five consecutive years of employment with the same employer; and (c) at least four weeks if they have completed at least 10 consecutive years of employment with the same employer."

This clearly outlines a progressive increase in vacation entitlement as an employee accumulates more years of service.

### Vacation Pay Calculation

The vacation pay is calculated as a percentage of the gross wages earned during the "year of employment" for which the vacation is granted. The percentage is determined by the number of weeks of vacation entitlement:
"An employee is entitled to vacation pay equal to: (a) 4% of their wages during the year of employment in respect of which they are entitled to the vacation; (b) 6% of their wages during the year of employment in respect of which they are entitled to the vacation, if they have completed at least five consecutive years of employment with the same employer; and (c) 8% of their wages during the year of employment in respect of which they are entitled to the vacation, if they have completed at least 10 consecutive years of employment with the same employer."

This indicates a tiered vacation pay rate, with a higher percentage applied to employees with longer tenures. For instance, an employee with at least one year of employment receives 4% of their gross wages as vacation pay for two weeks of vacation. This percentage increases to 6% for employees with at least five consecutive years of employment and further to 8% for those with at least ten consecutive years of employment.

## Additional Considerations

The documents also mention that vacation pay is typically paid within 14 days before the vacation begins, but can be paid during or immediately following the vacation period if that is not practical. Additionally, employees can agree with their employer to split their vacation time into more than one period, subject to the employer's approval.
