## Employee Responsibilities Regarding Maternity-Related Leave

### Notifying the Employer

#### Initial Notification for Maternity Leave
"An employee who is pregnant or nursing is entitled to and shall be granted a leave of absence during the period from the beginning of the pregnancy to the end of the twenty-fourth week following the birth, if she provides the employer with a certificate issued by a health care practitioner of her choice indicating that she is unable to work by reason of the pregnancy or nursing and indicating the duration of that inability." This section clearly outlines the employee's initial responsibility: to provide the employer with a medical certificate from a healthcare practitioner. This certificate must state the reason for the inability to work (pregnancy or nursing) and the duration of that inability. This notification must occur during the specified period, from the beginning of the pregnancy to the end of the twenty-fourth week following the birth.

#### Notification for Interruption of Maternity Leave
"An employee who intends to interrupt their maternity or parental leave in order to return to work as a result of the hospitalization of his or her child shall provide the employer with a notice in writing of the interruption as soon as possible." This passage details the employee's obligation to inform the employer of any interruption to their maternity leave due to the hospitalization of their child. This notification must be in writing and provided to the employer as soon as reasonably possible.

#### Notification for Resumption of Maternity Leave
"An employee who intends to return to their maternity or parental leave after an interruption shall, as soon as possible, advise the employer in writing of the date on which the maternity or parental leave is to resume." This section specifies the employee's responsibility to inform the employer of their intention to resume their maternity leave after an interruption. This notification must be in writing and provided to the employer as soon as reasonably possible.

"An employee whose job functions have been modified, who has been reassigned or who is on a leave of absence shall give at least two weeks’ notice in writing to the employer of any change in the duration of the risk or in the inability as indicated in the certificate issued by a health care practitioner, unless there is a valid reason why that notice cannot be given, and the notice must be accompanied by a new certificate." #### Medical Certificate for Change in Risk or Inability During Leave
"An employee whose job functions have been modified, who has been reassigned or who is on a leave of absence shall give at least two weeks’ notice in writing to the employer of any change in the duration of the risk or in the inability as indicated in the certificate issued by a health care practitioner, unless there is a valid reason why that notice cannot be given, and the notice must be accompanied by a new certificate." ## Maternity Leave Entitlements and Extensions

### Entitlement to Leave
"Every employee is entitled to and shall be granted a leave of absence from employment of up to 17 weeks, which leave may begin not earlier than 13 weeks prior to the estimated date of her confinement and end not later than 17 weeks following the actual date of her confinement, if the employee provides her employer with a certificate of a health care practitioner certifying that she is pregnant." This section of the Canada Labour Code clearly states the initial entitlement to maternity leave. The leave can begin up to 13 weeks before the estimated due date and end up to 17 weeks after the actual birth date, provided the employee submits a medical certificate confirming her pregnancy.

Furthermore, the code specifies the requirement for a medical certificate:
"This certificate must indicate that you are unable to work by reason of the pregnancy or nursing, and the duration of the inability." This ensures that the leave is medically justified.

### Extension of Leave

The maternity leave can be extended under specific circumstances.

#### Extension Due to Hospitalization
"If, during the period of 17 weeks following the date of confinement, the child who was born is hospitalized, the period is extended by the number of weeks during which the child is hospitalized." This subsection details an extension of the leave if the newborn child requires hospitalization. The extension is equal to the duration of the child's hospital stay.

#### Extension Due to Inability to Perform Essential Functions
"A pregnant employee who is unable to perform an essential function of her job and for whom no appropriate alternative job is available may be required to take a leave of absence from employment only for such time as she is unable to perform that essential function." This section outlines another potential extension. If a pregnant employee is medically unable to perform an essential function of her job and no suitable alternative position exists, she can take leave only for the duration of her inability to perform that function.

#### Limitation on Extension
"An extension under subsection (2) must not result in the period being longer than 52 weeks." This subsection places a limit on the total length of the extended leave. Even with hospitalizations or medical inabilities, the total maternity leave period cannot exceed 52 weeks.

### Employee's Duty to Inform Employer
"An employee whose job functions have been modified, who has been reassigned or who is on a leave of absence shall give at least two weeks’ notice in writing to the employer of any change in the duration of the risk or in the inability as indicated in the certificate issued by a health care practitioner, unless there is a valid reason why that notice cannot be given, and the notice must be accompanied by a new certificate." This section emphasizes the employee's responsibility to inform the employer of any changes to the duration of the medical certificate-supported inability to work. This ensures that the employer is aware of any extensions or modifications to the leave.

## Purpose of Parental Leave under Section 206.1 of the Canada Labour Code

### Entitlement to Leave
"Subject to subsections (2) and (3), every employee is entitled to and shall be granted a leave of absence from employment of up to 63 weeks to care for a newborn child of the employee or a child who is in the care of the employee for the purpose of adoption under the laws governing adoption in the province in which the employee resides."

This section clearly states the primary purpose of the leave provided under section 206.1: to care for a newborn child or a child who is in the employee's care for the purpose of adoption. The maximum duration of this leave is 63 weeks, with potential extensions under certain circumstances.

### Qualifying Life Events

Several life events qualify an employee for this parental leave. These are detailed in subsection (2):
"The leave of absence granted under this section may only be taken during the 78-week period beginning (a) in the case of a new-born child of the employee, at the option of the employee, on the day the child is born or comes into the actual care of the employee; and (b) in the case of an adoption, on the day the child comes into the actual care of the employee."

This indicates that an employee is eligible for parental leave starting on the day the newborn child comes into their care or on the day the child is adopted into their care. The total leave period is 78 weeks, which can be taken within a 78-week window beginning on the qualifying event.

### Extension of Period
"The period referred to in subsection (2) is extended by the number of weeks during which the employee is on leave under any of sections 206.3 to 206.5 and 206.9, is absent due to a reason referred to in subsection 239(1) or 239.1(1) or is on leave under any of paragraphs 247.5(1)(a), (b) and (d) to (g)."

The leave period can be extended if the employee takes other types of leave concurrently or is absent for other qualifying reasons. This extension is calculated by adding the number of weeks the employee is on other types of leave or absent for other reasons to the initial 78-week period.

### Extension for Hospitalized Child
"If the child referred to in subsection (1) is hospitalized during the period referred to in subsection (2), the period is extended by the number of weeks during which the child is hospitalized."

If the newborn child or adopted child is hospitalized during the parental leave period, the leave is extended by the number of weeks the child remains hospitalized.

### Limitation on Aggregate Leave
"The aggregate amount of leave that may be taken by more than one employee under this section in respect of the same birth or adoption shall not exceed 71 weeks, but the amount of leave that may be taken by one employee under this section in respect of the same birth or adoption shall not exceed 63 weeks."

There is a limit on the total amount of leave that can be taken by multiple employees for the same birth or adoption. This limit is 71 weeks for all employees combined, but each individual employee is limited to 63 weeks of leave.

individual_results.question: What is the purpose of the leave of absence provided for in the CLC, and under what conditions can an employee take this leave?
individual_results.answer:
## Purpose of Leave of Absence in the Canada Labour Code

### General Purpose

The leave of absence provided for in the Canada Labour Code (CLC) serves multiple purposes. Primarily, it allows employees to take time off work for various personal reasons, including illness, family responsibilities, education, urgent personal matters, and civic duties. Additionally, it specifically addresses the needs of members of the Reserve Force, granting them leave to participate in military operations, training, and other activities.

### Conditions for Taking Leave

#### General Conditions

According to Section 206.6(1) of the CLC,
"Every employee is entitled to and shall be granted a leave of absence from employment of up to five days in every calendar year for (a) [Repealed, 2021, c. 27, s. 6] (b) carrying out responsibilities related to the health or care of any of their family members; (c) carrying out responsibilities related to the education of any of their family members who are under 18 years of age; (d) addressing any urgent matter concerning themselves or their family members; (e) attending their citizenship ceremony under the Citizenship Act ; and (f) any other reason prescribed by regulation." This indicates that all employees are generally entitled to up to five days of leave per year for a wide range of personal obligations.

Section 247.5(1) further elaborates on the leave of absence for Reserve Force members. It states,
"An employee who is a member of the reserve force and has completed at least three consecutive months of continuous employment with an employer — or a shorter period that is prescribed for a class of employees to which the employee belongs — is entitled to and shall be granted a leave of absence from employment to take part in the following operations or activities: (a) an operation in Canada or abroad — including preparation, training, rest or travel from or to the employee’s residence — that is designated by the Minister of National Defence; (b) an activity set out in the regulations; (c) Canadian Armed Forces military skills training; (d) training that they are ordered to take under paragraph 33(2)(a) of the National Defence Act ; (e) duties that they are called out on service to perform under paragraph 33(2)(b) of the National Defence Act ; (f) service in aid of a civil power for which they are called out under section 275 of the National Defence Act ; or (g) treatment, recovery or rehabilitation in respect of a physical or mental health problem that results from service in an operation or activity referred to in this subsection." This specifies that Reserve Force members are entitled to leave for a variety of military-related activities, contingent on meeting the minimum employment period requirement.

#### Conditions for Reserve Force Leave

Section 247.5(1.1) sets a maximum limit on the total leave that can be taken by a Reserve Force member within a 60-month period:
"Leaves taken by an employee under paragraphs (1)(a) to (d) can total no more than an aggregate of 24 months in any 60-month period." This cap is in place to prevent excessive absences from civilian employment.

Section 247.5(4) provides an exception to the leave entitlement for Reserve Force members. It states,
"Despite subsection (1), an employee is not entitled to a leave of absence under this Division if, in the opinion of the Head, it would adversely affect public health or safety or would cause undue hardship to the employer if the employee, as an individual or as a member of a class of employees, were to take leave." This exception allows the Head of National Defence to deny leave if it would negatively impact public safety or create significant difficulties for the employer.

#### Conditions for Personal Leave

Section 206.6(2) outlines the conditions for taking personal leave for employees who have completed three consecutive months of continuous employment:
"If the employee has completed three consecutive months of continuous employment with the employer, the employee is entitled to the first three days of the leave with pay at their regular rate of wages for their normal hours of work, and such pay shall for all purposes be considered to be wages." This indicates that personal leave is initially paid for employees with at least three months of continuous service.

Section 206.6(3) clarifies the flexibility of taking personal leave:
"The leave of absence may be taken in one or more periods. The employer may require that each period of leave be of not less than one day’s duration." This allows employees to take leave in segments, with a minimum duration of one day per segment, subject to the employer's requirements.

Section 206.6(4) mandates that the employer may request documentation to support the reasons for the leave:
"The employer may, in writing and no later than 15 days after an employee’s return to work, request that the employee provide documentation to support the reasons for the leave. The employee shall provide that documentation only if it is reasonably practicable for them to obtain and provide it." This ensures that the employer has a basis for approving the leave request.

## Leave of Absence for Family Members of Critically Ill Individuals - Section 206.4

### Circumstances Entitling Leave

Section 206.4 outlines the circumstances under which an employee is entitled to a leave of absence from employment to care for or support a critically ill child or a critically ill adult. The section begins by defining key terms: "critically ill adult," "critically ill child," "family member," and "support," stating that these terms have the same meaning as those in the regulations made under the Employment Insurance Act, subject to those regulations. It also clarifies that "week" has the same meaning as in subsection 206.3(1).

The entitlement to leave is triggered by a health care practitioner issuing a certificate that meets specific requirements. For a critically ill child, the certificate must state that the child is critically ill and requires the care or support of one or more of their family members, and it must set out the period during which the child requires that care or support.

Similarly, for a critically ill adult, the certificate must state that the adult is critically ill and requires the care or support of one or more of their family members, and it must set out the period during which the adult requires that care or support.

### Maximum Duration of Leave

Section 206.4 specifies the maximum duration of leave available to family members of critically ill individuals. For a critically ill child, the maximum leave is up to 37 weeks. For a critically ill adult, the maximum leave is up to 17 weeks.

The section further details the period during which the employee may take leave. It states that the period begins on the first day of the week in which either of the following falls: (i) the day on which the first certificate is issued in respect of the child or adult, as the case may be, that meets the requirements of subsection (2) or (2.1), or (ii) if the leave begins before the day on which the certificate is issued, the day from which the health care practitioner certifies that the child or adult, as the case may be, is critically ill; and (b) ends on the last day of the week in which either of the following occurs: (i) the child or adult, as the case may be, dies, or (ii) the expiry of 52 weeks following the first day of the week referred to in paragraph (a).

However, the section also includes limitations on the aggregate leave that may be taken by employees under this section during the period referred to in subsection (4). It states that the aggregate amount of leave that may be taken by employees under this section during the period referred to in subsection (4) must not exceed (a) in respect of the same critically ill child, 37 weeks; or (b) in respect of the same critically ill adult, 17 weeks. This means that even if multiple employees are family members of the same critically ill child or adult, the total leave taken by all of them cannot exceed these maximum durations.

## Leave of Absence Under Section 206.5 of the Canada Labour Code

### Circumstances Entitling an Employee to Leave

Section 206.5 of the Canada Labour Code outlines the circumstances under which an employee is entitled to a leave of absence. It specifically addresses leave related to the death or disappearance of a child.
"Every employee is entitled to and shall be granted a leave of absence from employment of up to 156 weeks if the employee is the parent of a child who has died and it is probable, considering the circumstances, that the child died as a result of a crime."

This passage clearly states that an employee is entitled to a leave of absence of up to 156 weeks if they are the parent of a child who has died and it is probable that the child's death was the result of a crime.
"Every employee is entitled to and shall be granted a leave of absence from employment of up to 156 weeks if the employee is the parent of a child who has disappeared and it is probable, considering the circumstances, that the child disappeared as a result of a crime."

Similarly, the section also grants a leave of absence of up to 156 weeks if the employee is the parent of a child who has disappeared and it is probable that the child's disappearance was the result of a crime.

The section further clarifies an exception:
"An employee is not entitled to a leave of absence if they are charged with the crime."

This exception indicates that an employee facing criminal charges related to the child's death or disappearance is not eligible for the leave.

### Maximum Duration of Such Leave

The maximum duration of such leave is specified in the section:
"The period during which the employee may take a leave of absence (a) begins on the day on which the death or disappearance, as the case may be, occurs; and (b) ends 156 weeks after the day on which the death or disappearance, as the case may be, occurs."

This indicates that the leave can last for a maximum of 156 weeks, commencing on the day of the death or disappearance and concluding 156 weeks thereafter.

The section also addresses the scenario where a child who disappeared is subsequently found:
"Despite paragraph (5)(b), in the case of a child who disappears and who is subsequently found, the period referred to in subsection (5) ends (a) on the 14th day after the day on which the child is found, if the child is found during the 156-week period, but no later than the end of the 156-week period; or (b) 156 weeks after the day on which the disappearance occurs if subsection (2) applies to the child."

This clarifies that if a child who disappeared is found within the 156-week period, the leave ends 14 days after the child is found, but no later than the end of the 156-week period. If the child is found after the 156-week period, the leave ends 156 weeks after the disappearance.

Finally, the section sets an aggregate limit on the leave taken by employees under this section for the same death or disappearance of a child:
"The aggregate amount of leave that may be taken by employees under this section in respect of the same death or disappearance of a child — or the same children who die or disappear as a result of the same event — must not exceed 156 weeks."

This means that all employees collectively can take a maximum of 156 weeks of leave for the same child's death or disappearance.

## Circumstances for Leave of Absence in Canada

### Membership in the Reserve Force
"An employee who is a member of the reserve force and has completed at least three consecutive months of continuous employment with an employer — or a shorter period that is prescribed for a class of employees to which the employee belongs — is entitled to and shall be granted a leave of absence from employment to take part in the following operations or activities: (a) an operation in Canada or abroad — including preparation, training, rest or travel from or to the employee’s residence — that is designated by the Minister of National Defence; (b) an activity set out in the regulations; (c) Canadian Armed Forces military skills training; (d) training that they are ordered to take under paragraph 33(2)(a) of the National Defence Act ; (e) duties that they are called out on service to perform under paragraph 33(2)(b) of the National Defence Act ; (f) service in aid of a civil power for which they are called out under section 275 of the National Defence Act ; or (g) treatment, recovery or rehabilitation in respect of a physical or mental health problem that results from service in an operation or activity referred to in this subsection."

This section of the Canada Labour Code outlines a specific circumstance under which an employee is entitled to a leave of absence: membership in the Canadian Reserve Force. It details a minimum continuous employment period of three consecutive months, or a shorter period prescribed for a specific employee class. The leave can be used for a wide range of Reserve Force activities, including operations in Canada or abroad, military skills training, duties called upon during service, and treatment for health problems resulting from service.

### Other Entitlements to Leave
"Every employee is entitled to and shall be granted a leave of absence from employment to attend court to (a) act as a witness in a proceeding; (b) act as a juror in a proceeding; or (c) participate in a jury selection process."

This section of the Canada Labour Code specifies another circumstance for leave of absence: attendance at court. It states that every employee is entitled to leave to act as a witness, serve as a juror, or participate in a jury selection process.

### Leave for Work-Related Illness and Injury
"If you are an employee who suffers from a work-related illness or injury, you are entitled to leave.  Employers must subscribe to a plan that will replace the wages for this kind of leave. The rate will be a rate equivalent to the one provided by the provincial or territorial workers’ compensation in your province of permanent residence.  Where reasonably practicable, your employer shall return you to work after a work-related illness or injury. Your employer may reassign you to a different position, with different terms and conditions of employment, if you are unable to perform your work due to a work-related illness or injury."

This section of the Canada Labour Code addresses leave for work-related illness and injury. It states that employees are entitled to leave for such reasons, and employers are required to maintain a plan to replace wages during this leave. The employer is also expected to reasonably attempt to return the employee to work, potentially through reassignment.

### Leave for Medical Reasons
"...interrupt other leaves in order to take:  medical leave (paid or unpaid), or work-related illness and injury leave  The other leaves are:  parental leave compassionate care leave leave related to critical illness leave related to death or disappearance, and  annual vacation  In such a case, the other leave resumes immediately after the medical leave ends."

This section of the Canada Labour Code explains the possibility of interrupting other types of leave to take medical leave. It specifies that medical leave can be paid or unpaid and can be taken in place of other leaves such as parental leave or annual vacation. The other interrupted leave resumes immediately after the medical leave concludes.

### Leave for Court or Jury Duty
"Section 206.9 Every employee is entitled to and shall be granted a leave of absence from employment to attend court to (a) act as a witness in a proceeding; (b) act as a juror in a proceeding; or (c) participate in a jury selection process."

This section reiterates the entitlement to leave for court or jury duty, stating that every employee is entitled to such leave to act as a witness, serve as a juror, or participate in a jury selection process.

### Leave for Maternity-Related Reassignment and Leave
"You are entitled to leave with pay at your regular rate of wages while your employer is examining your request for:  reassignment, or  job modification   This leave will end once the employer either:   modifies your job function reassigns you to another job, or informs you that it is not reasonably practicable to modify your functions or reassign you  For the purposes of calculating and determining your regular hourly rate of wages if you are paid on any basis of time other than hourly, your employer shall divide the wages paid for work performed by the number of hours required to perform the work. Your regular hourly rate of wages may be the rate agreed on under a collective agreement. The wages paid for work performed do not include:  vacation pay general holiday pay other holiday pay  bereavement leave pay, and  wages paid for any hours of overtime  The number of hours required to perform the work does not include hours for which an overtime rate of wages has been paid."

This section of the Canada Labour Code outlines leave for maternity-related reassignment and leave. ## Leave for Traditional Aboriginal Practices

### Entitlement to Leave

According to the Canada Labour Code, Aboriginal employees who have completed three consecutive months of continuous employment with an employer are entitled to and shall be granted a leave of absence from employment of up to five days in every calendar year. This leave is specifically to enable the employee to engage in traditional Aboriginal practices.

### Activities Included in Traditional Practices

The Canada Labour Code explicitly lists the activities included in this traditional Aboriginal leave:
"...including (a) hunting; (b) fishing; (c) harvesting; and (d) any practice prescribed by regulation."

This indicates that the five days of leave are intended to allow Aboriginal employees to participate in a range of traditional activities, encompassing hunting, fishing, harvesting, and any other practices that may be specifically regulated.

### Employer Requirements

The Canada Labour Code outlines certain requirements for employers regarding this leave. Employers may require that each period of leave be not less than one day’s duration. Additionally, employers may request documentation demonstrating that the employee is Aboriginal. This request can be made in writing and no later than 15 days after an employee’s return to work. The employee is only required to provide such documentation if it is reasonably practicable for them to obtain and provide it.

### Definition of Aboriginal

For the purposes of this section, the Canada Labour Code defines "Aboriginal" as "Indian, Inuit or Métis." This ensures clarity on who is eligible for this leave.

## Circumstances Entitling an Employee to a Leave of Absence Under the Canada Labour Code

"Every employee is entitled to and shall be granted a medical leave of absence from employment of up to 27 weeks as a result of (a) personal illness or injury; (b) organ or tissue donation; (c) medical appointments during working hours; or (d) quarantine." This section of the Canada Labour Code clearly outlines the broad circumstances under which an employee is entitled to a medical leave of absence. It covers a range of health-related situations, including personal illness or injury, organ or tissue donation, necessary medical appointments, and quarantine requirements. The maximum duration of such leave is capped at 27 weeks within a 60-month period.

#### Leave with Pay
"If the employee has completed three consecutive months of continuous employment with the employer, the employee is entitled to the first three days of the leave with pay at their regular rate of wages for their normal hours of work, and such pay shall for all purposes be considered to be wages." This subsection specifies the conditions under which an employee is entitled to medical leave with pay. It requires at least three consecutive months of continuous employment before the first three days of the leave are paid at the employee's regular rate of wages.

#### Documentation
"The employer may, in writing and no later than 15 days after an employee’s return to work, request that the employee provide documentation to support the reasons for the leave. The employee shall provide that documentation only if it is reasonably practicable for them to obtain and provide it." This section addresses the employer's right to request medical documentation upon the employee's return to work. This important provision clarifies that an employee's benefits and seniority continue to accrue during a medical leave of absence. This ensures that the employee's entitlements are not negatively impacted by their absence.

individual_results.question: What are the general obligations of an employee who intends to take a leave of absence under section 206 or 206.1 of the Canada Labour Code?
individual_results.answer:
## General Obligations of an Employee Intending to Take a Leave of Absence

### Notification to Employer

Section 207(1) of the Canada Labour Code outlines the general obligations of an employee who intends to take a leave of absence under section 206 or 206.1. It states:
"Every employee who intends to take a leave of absence from employment under section 206 or 206.1 shall (a) unless there is a valid reason for not doing so, give at least four weeks notice in writing to the employer before the day on which the leave is to begin; and (b) inform the employer in writing of the length of leave intended to be taken."

This indicates that an employee planning to take a leave of absence must provide their employer with written notice. The minimum notice period is four weeks, unless there is a valid reason why this cannot be done. The notice must also specify the intended length of the leave.

### Exception to Notice Requirement

Section 207(1.1) provides an exception to the four-week notice requirement. It states:
"If there is a valid reason for not providing notice in accordance with paragraph (1)(a), the employee shall notify the employer in writing as soon as possible that the employee intends to take a leave of absence."

This exception allows an employee to provide notice as soon as reasonably possible if there is a legitimate reason why they cannot provide the full four weeks' notice.

### Notice of Change in Length of Leave

Section 207(2) further details the obligation to provide notice of any change in the intended length of leave. It states:
"Every employee who is on a leave of absence from employment under any of sections 206.3 to 206.9 shall, as soon as possible, provide the employer with a notice in writing of any change in the length of the leave that they intend to take."

This means that if an employee wishes to shorten or extend their leave after initially providing notice, they must inform their employer in writing as soon as possible.

### Notice for Leaves Longer Than Four Weeks

Section 207(3) specifies the notice period required for leaves exceeding four weeks. It states:
"If the length of the leave taken under any of sections 206.3 to 206.5 and 206.9 is more than four weeks, the notice in writing of any change in the length of the leave shall be provided on at least four weeks’ notice, unless there is a valid reason why that cannot be done."

This clarifies that for leaves lasting more than four weeks, the notice period for any subsequent changes must be at least four weeks, unless a valid reason prevents this.

### Documentation

Section 207(4) outlines the employer's right to request documentation. It states:
"The employer may require the employee to provide documentation in support of the reasons for the leave taken under section 206.4, 206.5 or 206.9 and of any change in the length of leave that the employee intends to take."

This indicates that the employer can ask the employee for supporting documentation to justify the reason for the leave and any changes to its duration.

### Postponement of Return to Work

Section 207(5) addresses the situation where an employee wishes to shorten their leave but does not provide the required four weeks' notice. It states:
"If an employee who takes a leave of more than four weeks under any of sections 206.3 to 206.5 wishes to shorten the length of the leave but does not provide the employer with four weeks’ notice, the employer may postpone the employee’s return to work for a period of up to four weeks after the day on which the employee informs the employer of the new end date of the leave. If the employer informs the employee that their return to work is postponed, the employee is not entitled to return to work until the day that is indicated by the employer."

This provision allows the employer to delay the employee's return to work if the employee does not provide the necessary four weeks' notice for a shortened leave.

### Deemed Part of Leave

Section 207(6) clarifies that the period of the postponement is considered part of the leave. It states:
"The period of the postponement is deemed to be part of the leave."

This means that the employer's postponement of the employee's return to work is counted towards the total length of the leave.

## Interrupting a Leave of Absence

### General Requirements for Interrupting Leave

The documents outline the general requirements for an employee who needs to interrupt their leave of absence for various reasons. A key requirement is providing the employer with written notice.
"It is possible for you to interrupt your compassionate care leave in order to take:  medical leave, or work-related illness and injury leave..." This quote directly addresses the possibility of interrupting a compassionate care leave. It specifies the types of leaves that can interrupt it: medical leave and work-related illness and injury leave.
"...you must give your employer a written notice of the interruption before or as soon as possible after it begins." This passage details the mandatory written notice requirement. It states that the employee must inform their employer of the interruption
"...before or as soon as possible after it begins."
"You must also give your employer a written notice of the day on which leave related to death or disappearance will resume, before or as soon as possible after that day." This quote further elaborates on the notice requirement, specifically for leaves related to death or disappearance. It requires the employee to provide written notice of the resumption date.

### Interrupting Leave for Specific Reasons

The documents provide specific details for interrupting leave for certain reasons.

#### Interrupting Compassionate Care Leave
"Compassionate care leave is to resume immediately after the other leave ends. However, it cannot extend beyond 52 weeks after the day on which the leave started." This passage explains the resumption of compassionate care leave after an interruption. It clarifies that it resumes immediately but cannot exceed 52 weeks from the original start date.
"You can take separate, non-consecutive shorter periods of leaves (not to exceed the 28-week maximum) within the 52-week period if your family member has several episodes of a serious medical condition. To do this, you must provide your employer with a medical certificate issued from a health care practitioner for each period of leave." This quote addresses the possibility of taking shorter, non-consecutive periods of compassionate care leave within the 52-week limit. It specifies the requirement for a medical certificate for each period.

#### Interrupting Leave for Medical Leave or Work-Related Illness and Injury Leave
"It is possible for you to interrupt your compassionate care leave in order to take:  medical leave, or work-related illness and injury leave..." This quote reiterates the general possibility of interrupting compassionate care leave for medical leave or work-related illness and injury leave.
"Leave related to critical illness is to resume immediately after the other leave ends, but cannot extend beyond 52 weeks after the leave commenced. If you intend to interrupt the leave related to critical illness, you must give your employer a written notice of the interruption before or as soon as possible after it begins. You must also give your employer a written notice of the day on which leave related to critical illness will resume, before or as soon as possible after that day." This passage provides specific requirements for interrupting leave related to critical illness. It mandates written notice of both the interruption and the resumption date.

#### Interrupting Leave for Death of a Child
"In order for you to qualify for this 156-week leave, it will be necessary to establish that the child has died, and that death was the result of a probable crime. Although this normally requires finding the child’s body, there may be cases where the child’s death and the criminal nature of that death are clear, despite the inability to find or identify the child’s remains." This quote outlines the requirements for interrupting leave related to the death of a child. It states that establishing the child's death and the probable criminal nature of that death is necessary for qualifying for the 156-week leave.

individual_results.question: What are the steps an employee must take if they need to interrupt their maternity or parental leave to care for a hospitalized child, and what are the potential outcomes in terms of leave duration?
individual_results.answer:
## Interrupting Maternity or Parental Leave for a Hospitalized Child

### Steps an Employee Must Take

An employee wishing to interrupt their maternity or parental leave to care for a hospitalized child must follow these steps:
"**You can interrupt maternity or parental leave if your child is hospitalized**  If your child is hospitalized shortly after birth or adoption, you can interrupt maternity or parental leave and temporarily return to work with consent from your employer.  When interrupting maternity or parental leave to return to work, as a result of the hospitalization of your child, you must give your employer written notice, as soon as possible."

This indicates that the initial action is to provide the employer with written notice of the interruption. The employer then has a limited time to respond.
"Your employer must advise you in writing, within a week of receiving the notice, of their decision to accept or refuse your request to return to work."

This passage clarifies the employer's timeframe for responding to the interruption request. The employer must provide a written decision within one week.

If the employer approves the interruption, they may request medical documentation.
"If your employer accepts the request to interrupt the leave, they may ask you to provide a medical certificate within 15 days of your return to work. This certificate must confirm that your child is hospitalized."

This step involves the employer potentially requesting a medical certificate to verify the child's hospitalization.

Finally, the employee must provide the employer with a written notice of the date on which the leave will resume.
"If you have temporarily returned to work, you must also provide your employer with a written notice, as soon as possible, of the date on which the leave will resume."

### Potential Outcomes in Terms of Leave Duration

The potential outcomes regarding leave duration depend on the employer's decision to approve the interruption.

If the employer approves the interruption, the employee can resume their work. However, if the employer refuses the interruption or fails to respond within a week, the employee may extend their leave.
"If your employer refuses your request to return to work or does not advise you within a week, you may extend your leave by the number of weeks during which your child is hospitalized."

This passage explicitly states that if the employer denies the interruption or doesn't respond, the employee can extend their leave by the duration of the child's hospitalization.

The document also outlines the overall time limits for maternity and parental leave, regardless of interruptions.
"...maternity leave must end no more than 52 weeks after the date of birth, and parental leave must end no later than 104 weeks after the day on which your child is born or comes into your actual care..."

This provides the maximum allowable durations for both types of leave. The interruption for a hospitalized child does not change these overall time limits.

### Initial Notice

Section 207(1) states:
"Every employee who intends to take a leave of absence from employment under section 206 or 206.1 shall (a) unless there is a valid reason for not doing so, give at least four weeks notice in writing to the employer before the day on which the leave is to begin; and (b) inform the employer in writing of the length of leave intended to be taken." This establishes the fundamental notice requirement: employees must provide at least four weeks' written notice to their employer before the leave commences, and they must also inform the employer of the intended duration of the leave.

### Notice of Change in Length of Leave

Section 207(2) elaborates on the notice requirement when there is a change in the intended length of the leave:
"Every employee who intends to take or who is on a leave of absence from employment under section 206 or 206.1 shall provide the employer with notice in writing of at least four weeks of any change in the length of leave intended to be taken, unless there is a valid reason why that notice cannot be given, in which case the employee shall provide the employer with notice in writing as soon as possible." This provision mandates that employees must notify their employer of any alteration to the planned leave duration, again with a minimum of four weeks' written notice, unless a valid reason prevents such notice.

### Notice of Reasons for Leave

Section 207.3(1) specifies the information that employees must provide in their written notice of leave:
"Every employee who takes a leave of absence from employment under any of sections 206.3 to 206.9 shall, as soon as possible, provide the employer with a notice in writing of the reasons for the leave and the length of the leave that they intend to take." This clarifies that the notice must include the employee's justification for taking the leave and the planned length of the leave.

## Documentation Requirements for Leaves of Absence (Sections 206.3 to 206.9)

### Documentation in Support of Reasons for Leave

Section 207.3(4) outlines the employer's right to request supporting documentation:
"The employer may require the employee to provide documentation in support of the reasons for the leave taken under section 206.4, 206.5 or 206.9 and of any change in the length of leave that the employee intends to take." This indicates that the employer can ask for evidence to back up the employee's stated reasons for taking the leave and any modifications to the planned duration.

### Documentation in Support of Change in Length of Leave

Section 207(2) also mentions the employer's right to request documentation for changes in the length of leave:
"Every employee who is on a leave of absence from employment under any of sections 206.3 to 206.9 shall, as soon as possible, provide the employer with a notice in writing of any change in the length of the leave that they intend to take. Marginal note: Notice — leave of more than four weeks (3) If the length of the leave taken under any of sections 206.3 to 206.5 and 206.9 is more than four weeks, the notice in writing of any change in the length of the leave shall be provided on at least four weeks’ notice, unless there is a valid reason why that cannot be done." This reinforces the employer's right to request documentation to support any changes to the leave duration.

### Documentation for Leave of More Than Four Weeks

Section 207(3) specifies the minimum notice period for changes in leave length when the initial leave is more than four weeks:
"If the length of the leave taken under any of sections 206.3 to 206.5 and 206.9 is more than four weeks, the notice in writing of any change in the length of the leave shall be provided on at least four weeks’ notice, unless there is a valid reason why that cannot be done." This clarifies that for leaves exceeding four weeks, the employer must receive the change in leave length notice on at least four weeks' notice.

individual_results.question: Under what circumstances can an employer require a pregnant employee to take a leave of absence from work?

## Employer Requirement for Pregnant Employee Leave

### General Prohibition
"Subject to subsection (2), no employer shall require an employee to take a leave of absence from employment because the employee is pregnant." This section establishes a general prohibition against employers mandating a leave of absence for a pregnant employee. It indicates that such a requirement is not permissible unless specific, limited circumstances exist.

### Employer Requirement Due to Inability to Perform Essential Function
"An employer may require a pregnant employee to take a leave of absence from employment if the employee is unable to perform an essential function of her job and no appropriate alternative job is available for that employee." This subsection outlines the sole circumstance under which an employer can require a pregnant employee to take a leave of absence. It hinges on the employee's inability to perform an essential function of her job and the lack of a suitable alternative position. The employer bears the burden of proving this inability.

### Limitation on Leave Duration
"A pregnant employee who is unable to perform an essential function of her job and for whom no appropriate alternative job is available may be required to take a leave of absence from employment only for such time as she is unable to perform that essential function." This further clarifies the duration of such a required leave. It specifies that the leave is limited to the period during which the employee is genuinely unable to perform an essential function of her job and no alternative is available.

### Burden of Proof
"The burden of proving that a pregnant employee is unable to perform an essential function of her job rests with the employer." This subsection explicitly assigns the responsibility of demonstrating the employee's inability to perform an essential function to the employer. This underscores the strict conditions under which an employer can require a pregnant employee to take a leave of absence.

## Pension, Health, Disability Benefits, and Seniority During a Leave of Absence

### General Accumulation of Benefits and Seniority
"The pension, health and disability benefits and the seniority of any employee who takes or is required to take a leave of absence from employment under this Division shall accumulate during the entire period of the leave." This statement from Section 209.2 of the Canada Labour Code directly addresses the accumulation of benefits and seniority during a leave of absence. It clarifies that these benefits and seniority continue to accrue throughout the duration of the leave.

### Contributions During Leave
"Where contributions are required from an employee in order for the employee to be entitled to a benefit referred to in subsection (1), the employee is responsible for and must, within a reasonable time, pay those contributions for the period of any leave of absence under this Division unless, before taking leave or within a reasonable time thereafter, the employee notifies the employer of the employee’s intention to discontinue contributions during that period." This passage from Section 209.2 details the responsibility of the employee for pension, health, and disability benefit contributions during a leave of absence. It states that the employee is responsible for making these contributions within a reasonable time, unless they notify the employer of their intention to discontinue contributions.

### Benefits Upon Return to Work
"Upon your return to work, your employer must reinstate you in your former position or give you a comparable position in the same location and with the same wages and benefits." This section from Section 209.2 outlines the employer's obligation upon an employee's return from leave. It mandates that the employee be reinstated to their previous position or a comparable one with the same wages and benefits.

### Impact of Reorganization
"If, during a leave period, your employer reduces the wages and benefits of a group of employees as part of a reorganization plan and if you are reinstated in that group you will receive no more than the wages and benefits that you would have received if you had been at work during the reorganization. If your employer increases the wages and benefits for your group during the leave, you would be entitled to the increases upon your return to work." This passage from Section 209.2 addresses the impact of reorganization plans on benefits during a leave of absence. It explains that upon reinstatement, an employee will receive no more than the wages and benefits they would have received if they had been at work during the reorganization. Conversely, if the employer increases wages and benefits during the leave, the employee will be entitled to these increases upon their return.

### Application of Section 189

individual_results.question: What protections are afforded to employees who are pregnant or taking a leave of absence under the Code, in terms of their employment status and benefits?
individual_results.answer:
## Protections for Pregnant or Nursing Employees and Those on Leave

### Employment Status During Leave

The Canada Labour Code provides several protections for employees who are pregnant or taking a leave of absence.

#### Right to Leave
"...an employee who is pregnant or nursing may cease to perform her job if she believes that, by reason of the pregnancy or nursing, continuing any of her current job functions may pose a risk to her health or to that of the foetus or child." This section of Section 132 explicitly grants pregnant or nursing employees the right to cease performing their job functions if they reasonably believe it poses a health risk.
"As an employee who is pregnant or nursing, you are entitled to an unpaid maternity-related leave of absence during the period from the beginning of the pregnancy to the end of the 24th week following the birth." This statement in Labour-Standards-5_2 details the entitlement to unpaid maternity leave, which is a significant protection for pregnant employees.

#### Protection Against Dismissal, Suspension, Demotion, or Discipline
"No employer shall dismiss, suspend, lay off, demote or discipline an employee because the employee is pregnant or has applied for leave of absence in accordance with this Division or take into account the pregnancy of an employee or the intention of an employee to take leave of absence from employment under this Division in any decision to promote or train the employee." This provision in Section 209.3 is a strong protection against adverse employment actions taken due to pregnancy or leave requests. It ensures that pregnancy or leave intentions cannot be factors in decisions about promotions or training.

#### Reassignment Options
"For the period during which the employee does not perform her job under subsection (1), the employer may, in consultation with the employee, reassign her to another job that would not pose a risk to her health or to that of the foetus or child." This section of Section 132 outlines the employer's obligation to consider reassignment if the employee cannot continue her current job due to pregnancy or nursing. This aims to maintain the employee's employment status while protecting her health.

#### Status During Leave
"The employee, whether or not she has been reassigned to another job, is deemed to continue to hold the job that she held at the time she ceased to perform her job functions and shall continue to receive the wages and benefits that are attached to that job for the period during which she does not perform the job." This clarifies that an employee on leave retains their employment status and benefits for the duration of the leave, even if reassigned.

### Benefits During Leave

The Canada Labour Code also ensures that employees on leave receive benefits on the same terms as those absent for health-related reasons.

#### Entitlement to Benefits
"Notwithstanding the provisions of any income-replacement scheme or any insurance plan in force at the workplace, an employee who takes a leave of absence under this Division is entitled to benefits under the scheme or plan on the same terms as any employee who is absent from work for health-related reasons and is entitled to benefits under the scheme or plan." This statement in Section 209.21 explicitly states that employees on leave are entitled to benefits under their existing income-replacement or insurance plans, on the same terms as those absent for other health reasons. This ensures continuity of financial support during the leave period.

#### Certificate as Proof
"A certificate issued by a health care practitioner under this Division is conclusive proof of the statements contained in it." This provision in Section 209.22 emphasizes the importance of a medical certificate in establishing the reason for the leave and its duration. The certificate is considered definitive evidence, ensuring that the employee's health needs are respected and that benefits are provided accordingly.

### Employee's Duty to Inform Employer
"An employee whose job functions have been modified, who has been reassigned or who is on a leave of absence shall give at least two weeks’ notice in writing to the employer of any change in the duration of the risk or in the inability as indicated in the certificate issued by a health care practitioner, unless there is a valid reason why that notice cannot be given, and the notice must be accompanied by a new certificate." This section in Section 205.2 outlines the employee's responsibility to inform the employer of any changes to the duration of the risk or inability to work, as indicated in the medical certificate. This ensures that the employer is kept informed and can make necessary adjustments to the employee's work situation.

individual_results.question: What type of regulations can the Governor in Council make in relation to employment leaves and absences under the Canada Labour Code?
individual_results.answer:
## Regulations on Employment Leaves and Absences

### General Regulations

The Governor in Council has broad authority to make regulations concerning employment leaves and absences under the Canada Labour Code. Section 209.4 outlines a comprehensive list of areas where such regulations can be enacted.

#### Specifying Absences Not Interrupting Continuous Employment
"...specifying the absences from employment that are deemed not to have interrupted continuous employment referred to in any of sections 206.6 to 206.8..."
This regulation allows the Governor in Council to define certain types of absences that are not considered to have broken up an employee's continuous employment. This is important for calculating benefits and entitlements related to continuous service.

#### Prescribing Maximum Periods of Leave
"(a.2) prescribing the maximum number of periods of leave of absence that an employee may take under any of sections 206.3 to 206.5..."
This regulation enables the Governor in Council to set limits on the number of separate periods of leave an employee can take under various leave provisions. This helps to balance employee needs with employer operational requirements.

#### Specifying Essential Job Functions
"(b) specifying what does, or does not, constitute an essential function of a job referred to in section 208..."
This regulation allows the Governor in Council to clarify what tasks are fundamental to a job. This is relevant when determining whether an employee is entitled to a leave of absence or if their absence would cause undue hardship to the employer.

#### Specifying Invalid Reasons for Non-Reinstatement
"(c) specifying what does not constitute a valid reason for not reinstating an employee in the position referred to in subsection 209.1(2)..."
This regulation helps to protect employees from unfair dismissal upon their return from a leave of absence. It defines situations where an employer cannot reinstate an employee.

#### Enlarging Meanings and Support in Subsections 206.3(1) and 206.4(1)
"(d) enlarging the meaning of and support in subsections 206.3(1) and 206.4(1), and of critically ill adult and critically ill child in subsection 206.4(1)..."
This regulation allows the Governor in Council to broaden the definitions of certain family members and support persons who are eligible for leave under the Act.

#### Adapting Terminology from Employment Insurance Act
"...adapting the terminology of the definitions of care , critically ill adult , critically ill child , family member and support in the regulations made under the Employment Insurance Act for the purposes of the definitions of those terms in subsections 206.3(1) and 206.4(1) of this Act..."
This regulation enables the Governor in Council to harmonize the definitions of family members and support persons between the Canada Labour Code and the Employment Insurance Act.

#### Prescribing Offences to be Excluded from the Definition of Crime
"(f) prescribing offences to be excluded from the definition of crime in subsection 206.5(1) and prescribing other persons to be included in the definition of parent in that subsection..."
This regulation allows the Governor in Council to clarify who is considered a parent for the purposes of leave provisions and to exclude certain offences from being classified as crimes.

#### Prescribing Shorter Periods of Continuous Employment
"(g) prescribing shorter periods of consecutive months of continuous employment for the purposes of subsections 206.6(2), 206.7(2.1) and 206.8(1)..."
This regulation enables the Governor in Council to adjust the requirements for continuous employment for various leave provisions.

#### Prescribing Cases Where an Employee is Not Entitled to Leave
"(h) prescribing cases, other than the one set out in subsection 206.5(4), in which an employee is not entitled to a leave of absence and cases in which an employee is entitled to a leave of absence even if they are charged with the crime..."
This regulation allows the Governor in Council to specify situations where an employee is not eligible for leave and cases where they are still entitled to leave even if they are facing criminal charges.

#### Defining Family Violence
"(h.1) defining family violence for the purposes of section 206.7..."
This regulation allows the Governor in Council to provide a clear definition of family violence for the purposes of leave provisions related to family violence.

#### Prescribing Cases Where an Employee is Not Entitled to Leave Despite Subsection 206.7(2)
"(h.2) prescribing cases, other than those set out in subsection 206.7(3), in which an employee is not entitled to a leave of absence and cases in which, despite that subsection, an employee is entitled to a leave of absence under subsection 206.7(2)..."
This regulation enables the Governor in Council to clarify situations where an employee is not entitled to leave despite certain exceptions.

#### Prescribing Documentation Requirements
"(h.3) prescribing documentation that the employer may request under any of subsections 206.6(4), 206.7(5) and 206.8(3)..."
This regulation allows the Governor in Council to specify the types of documentation that employers can request from employees seeking leave.

#### Specifying Circumstances Where a Leave May Be Interrupted
"...the circumstances in which a leave under this Division may be interrupted..."
This regulation allows the Governor in Council to define situations where a leave under the Act can be temporarily paused.

#### Extending the Period Within Which a Leave May Be Taken
"...extending the period within which a leave under this Division may be taken."
This regulation enables the Governor in Council to adjust the maximum duration of a leave under the Act.

### Application of Provincial Laws

Section 265 outlines a specific type of regulation the Governor in Council can make in relation to employment leaves and absences, particularly concerning provincial Crown corporations.
"The Governor in Council may by regulation direct that this Part applies in respect of any employment, or any class or classes of employment, on or in connection with a work or undertaking set out in the regulation that is, or is part of, a corporation that is an agent of Her Majesty in right of a province and whose activities are regulated, in whole or in part, pursuant to the Nuclear Safety and Control Act..."
This regulation allows the Governor in Council to extend the application of this Part of the Canada Labour Code to certain employment relationships within provincial Crown corporations that are subject to the Nuclear Safety and Control Act.

### Exclusion from Application

Section 266 details another type of regulation the Governor in Council can make, specifically concerning the exclusion of certain employment relationships from the application of this Part of the Canada Labour Code.
"(1) The Governor in Council may by regulation exclude, in whole or in part, from the application of any of the provisions of this Part any employment, or any class or classes of employment, on or in connection with a work or undertaking set out in the regulation whose activities are regulated, in whole or in part, pursuant to the Nuclear Safety and Control Act..."
This regulation allows the Governor in Council to specifically exclude certain employment relationships within provincial Crown corporations subject to the Nuclear Safety and Control Act from the application of this Part of the Canada Labour Code.

### Section 209.5: General Application of Section 189

#### Summary
Section 209.5 of the Canada Labour Code explicitly states the relationship between itself and Section 189. It declares that
"Section 189 applies for the purposes of this Division." This indicates a direct and encompassing application of Section 189 to the subject matter of Division X, which deals with individual terminations of employment.

#### Analysis
The statement in Section 209.5 is concise and unambiguous. It signifies that the provisions of Section 189 are relevant and operative when considering the individual terminations of employment addressed in Division X. This means that the principles and conditions outlined in Section 189, particularly those concerning the continuity of employment during lease or transfer of work, are applicable in the context of individual terminations.

### Section 189: Annual Vacations: Transfer

#### Summary
Section 189 of the Canada Labour Code focuses on the transfer of work, undertaking, or business between employers and its implications for the continuity of employment. It details how employment is deemed continuous with one employer if the work, undertaking, or business becomes federal due to a lease or transfer. It also addresses situations where a second employer is responsible for carrying out federal work after a retendering process.

#### Analysis
Section 189 provides the foundational context for understanding the application of Section 209.5. It establishes the circumstances under which employment is considered continuous despite a change in employer or the transfer of work. The reference to Section 189 in Section 209.5 directly links the principles of continuity of employment during transfer to the broader context of individual terminations of employment.

In essence, Section 209.5 acts as a specific application of the general principles outlined in Section 189 to the subject of individual terminations of employment. It confirms that the continuity of employment provisions of Section 189 are relevant when considering the termination of an individual's employment following a lease, transfer, or retendering of work.

individual_results.question: What are the conditions and entitlements for an employee to take a leave of absence in the event of the death of a member of their immediate family or a family member?
individual_results.answer:
## Bereavement Leave Entitlements and Conditions

### General Entitlement
"Every employee is entitled to and shall be granted, in the event of the death of a member of their immediate family or a family member in respect of whom the employee is, at the time of the death, on leave under section 206.3 or 206.4, a leave of absence from employment of up to 10 days that may be taken during the period that begins on the day on which the death occurs and ends six weeks after the latest of the days on which any funeral, burial or memorial service of the deceased person occurs." This section of the Canada Labour Code clearly states the general entitlement to bereavement leave. It specifies the maximum duration of the leave, which is up to 10 days, and the timeframe during which the leave can be taken. The leave begins on the day of death and concludes six weeks after the latest of the funeral, burial, or memorial service dates.

### Conditions for Entitlement
"Section 210 (1) Every employee is entitled to and shall be granted, in the event of the death of a member of their immediate family or a family member in respect of whom the employee is, at the time of the death, on leave under section 206.3 or 206.4, a leave of absence from employment of up to 10 days that may be taken during the period that begins on the day on which the death occurs and ends six weeks after the latest of the days on which any funeral, burial or memorial service of the deceased person occurs." This reiterates the general entitlement but also clarifies the conditions. It defines "immediate family" as
"...a member of their immediate family or a family member in respect of whom the employee is, at the time of the death, on leave under section 206.3 or 206.4..." This means that an employee is eligible for bereavement leave if a member of their immediate family dies, or if a family member dies while the employee is already on leave under another provision of the Canada Labour Code.

### Paid Bereavement Leave
"If the employee has completed three consecutive months of continuous employment with the employer, the employee is entitled to the first three days of the leave with pay at their regular rate of wages for their normal hours of work, and such pay shall for all purposes be considered to be wages." This section details the conditions for receiving paid bereavement leave. An employee must have completed three consecutive months of continuous employment with the employer to be eligible for paid leave. If they meet this condition, they are entitled to the first three days of the leave with pay at their regular rate of wages for their normal hours of work.

### Extension of Leave
"At the request of the employee, the employer may extend, in writing, the period during which the leave of absence from employment may be taken." This provision allows for an extension of the bereavement leave. An employee can request an extension in writing, and the employer may grant it.

### Division of Leave
"The leave of absence may be taken in one or two periods. The employer may require that any period of leave be of not less than one day’s duration." This section explains how the bereavement leave can be taken. It can be taken in one or two periods, but each period must be of at least one day's duration.

### Notice to Employer
"Every employee who takes the leave of absence shall, as soon as possible, provide the employer with written notice of the beginning of any period of leave of absence and of the length of that leave." This requires employees to provide written notice to their employer at the earliest opportunity when they begin taking bereavement leave.

individual_results.question: What are the obligations of an employer who plans to terminate the employment of a group of 50 or more employees within a certain timeframe, and what information must be provided to various parties?
individual_results.answer:
## Obligations of an Employer Planning a Group Termination

### Notice Requirements

An employer planning to terminate the employment of a group of 50 or more employees within a certain timeframe has several obligations regarding notice.
"Section 212 (1) Any employer who terminates, either simultaneously or within any period not exceeding four weeks, the employment of a group of 50 or more employees employed by the employer within a particular industrial establishment, or of such lesser number of employees as prescribed by regulations applicable to the employer made under paragraph 227(b), shall, in addition to any notice required to be given under section 230, give notice to the Head, in writing, of his intention to so terminate at least 16 weeks before the date of termination of the employment of the employee in the group whose employment is first to be terminated."

This section of the Canada Labour Code clearly outlines the initial notice requirement. An employer intending to terminate a group of 50 or more employees within a four-week period must provide written notice to the Head of Compliance and Enforcement at least 16 weeks before the first termination date. This notice must state the employer's intention to terminate, the estimated number of employees in each occupational classification whose employment will be terminated, and any other information prescribed by the regulations.

### Information to be Provided to Various Parties

Beyond the initial notice to the Head, employers are obligated to disseminate specific information to several parties.
"...of notice (2) A copy of any notice given to the Head under subsection (1) must be given immediately by the employer to the Minister of Employment and Social Development and the Canada Employment Insurance Commission and any trade union representing a redundant employee, and if any redundant employee is not represented by a trade union, a copy of that notice must be given to the employee or immediately posted by the employer in a conspicuous place within the industrial establishment in which that employee is employed."

This subsection mandates that a copy of the notice provided to the Head must be given to the Minister of Employment and Social Development Canada (ESDC), the Canada Employment Insurance Commission, and any trade union representing redundant employees. If no union represents redundant employees, a copy must be provided to the individual employee or posted prominently within the workplace.
"Contents of notice (3) A notice referred to in subsection (1) shall set out (a) the date or dates on which the employer intends to terminate the employment of any one or more employees; (b) the estimated number of employees in each occupational classification whose employment will be terminated; and (c) such other information as is prescribed by the regulations."

This subsection details the specific information that must be included in the notice provided to the Head and other relevant parties. This information includes the date(s) of termination, the estimated number of employees in each occupational classification to be terminated, and any other information specified in the regulations.
"If you are an employer planning a group termination of employment, you must:  notify the Labour Program’s Head of Compliance and Enforcement in writing at least 16 weeks before the termination of employment is to take effect, and  immediately give a copy of the notice to:             the Minister of Employment and Social Development Canada (ESDC) the Canada Employment Insurance Commission, and any union representing the affected employees, or to the employees if they are not represented by a union, or  immediately post the notice in a visible place within the workplace in which your employees are employed."

This section reiterates the initial notice requirement and specifies the exact parties to whom the notice must be provided. These parties are the Head of Compliance and Enforcement, the Minister of Employment and Social Development Canada (ESDC), the Canada Employment Insurance Commission, any union representing redundant employees, or the individual employees if no union represents them. Additionally, the notice must be posted conspicuously within the workplace.

### Additional Requirements and Waiver Requests

The documents also outline additional requirements and the process for requesting waivers.
"**Additional requirements** As an employer, when a group termination of employment occurs, you are required to:  establish a joint planning committee with an employee representative cooperate with the Canada Employment Insurance Commission, and  provide affected employees with a statement of benefits, which includes information on the employee’s:             wages vacation pay severance pay, if applicable, and any other benefits and pay arising from employment    You must provide the statement of benefits not later than 2 weeks before the date of termination or earlier, if possible."

This section details additional obligations for employers conducting a group termination. These include establishing a joint planning committee with an employee representative and cooperating with the Canada Employment Insurance Commission. Furthermore, employers must provide affected employees with a statement of benefits, which includes information on their wages, vacation pay, severance pay (if applicable), and other benefits. This statement must be provided no later than two weeks before the termination date, or earlier if possible.
"**Requests for waiver** As an employer, you may request that the Minister of Labour waive certain requirements. Three types of waivers may be granted, including the requirement to:  give 16 weeks’ notice provide employees with a written statement of benefits, and/or establish a joint planning committee when you can show that:             it would be unduly prejudicial to your interests or of the affected employees it would be seriously detrimental to the operation of the industrial establishment similar measures are already in place     Note: You may complete the form “Notice to the Head of Compliance and Enforcement of a group termination of employment and Request for waiver under the Canada Labour Code - Part III (ESDC-LAB1197)” to:  provide notice to the Labour Program’s Head of Compliance and Enforcement               and/or make an application to the Minister of Labour for a waiver of the group termination provisions  Any waiver granted will not exceed 6-months duration."

This section explains the process for requesting waivers of certain requirements. Employers can request waivers from the Minister of Labour for the 16-week notice period, the written statement of benefits, and/or the establishment of a joint planning committee. A waiver may be granted if it would be unduly prejudicial to the employer's interests or seriously detrimental to the operation of the industrial establishment, or if similar measures are already in place. Employers can submit a specific form to apply for a waiver. Any waiver granted will not exceed a six-month duration.

### Providing Information to the Minister and Trade Unions

"(2) A copy of any notice given to the Head under subsection (1) must be given immediately by the employer to the Minister of Employment and Social Development and the Canada Employment Insurance Commission and any trade union representing a redundant employee, and if any redundant employee is not represented by a trade union, a copy of that notice must be given to the employee or immediately posted by the employer in a conspicuous place within the industrial establishment in which that employee is employed."

"(3) A notice referred to in subsection (1) shall set out (a) the date or dates on which the employer intends to terminate the employment of any one or more employees; (b) the estimated number of employees in each occupational classification whose employment will be terminated; and (c) such other information as is prescribed by the regulations."

"A joint planning committee established under subsection (1) shall consist of at least four members." This subsection specifies the minimum number of members required for the joint planning committee. It must have a minimum of four individuals.

#### Subsection (3): Appointment of Members
"At least half of the members of a joint planning committee shall be appointed, in accordance with subsections 215(1), (2) and (3), as representatives of the redundant employees and the rest of the members shall be appointed, in accordance with subsection 215(5), as representatives of the employer." This subsection details how the committee members must be appointed. "At least half" of the members must be appointed as representatives of the redundant employees, following the procedures outlined in subsections 215(1), (2), and (3). The remaining "rest" of the members must be appointed as representatives of the employer, following the procedures outlined in subsection 215(5). This ensures a balanced representation of both the employees being terminated and the employer.
