### Representation Through Trade Unions
"Where all redundant employees are represented by a trade union or trade unions, each trade union is entitled to appoint at least one member of the joint planning committee as a representative of the redundant employees it represents." This section clearly outlines the primary mechanism for redundant employee representation when trade unions are involved. It states that each trade union has the right to nominate at least one member to the committee, specifically to represent the redundant employees they represent. This ensures that the interests of the redundant employees are voiced by their respective trade unions.

### Representation When Some but Not All Redundant Employees are Represented by a Trade Union
"Where some but not all redundant employees are represented by a trade union or trade unions, (a) each trade union is entitled to appoint at least one member of a joint planning committee as a representative of the redundant employees it represents; and (b) the employees that are not represented by a trade union are entitled to appoint at least one member of a joint planning committee as their representative." This subsection addresses scenarios where only a portion of the redundant employees are represented by a trade union. It reiterates the right of each represented trade union to appoint at least one member. Crucially, it also grants the right to the employees who are *not* represented by a trade union to appoint at least one member to the committee as their representative. This provision ensures that even those redundant employees without union representation have a voice on the joint planning committee.

### Representation When No Redundant Employees are Represented by a Trade Union
"Where no redundant employees are represented by a trade union, the employees are entitled to appoint all the members of a joint planning committee who are to be their representatives." This section details the process for representation when no trade union is involved. It explicitly states that the redundant employees themselves have the authority to appoint all the members of the joint planning committee who will represent them. This direct appointment process empowers the redundant employees to choose their own representatives.

### Election of Members
"Each person appointed as a member of a joint planning committee pursuant to subsection (2) or paragraph (3)(b) shall be elected by the redundant employees entitled to appoint the member." This passage clarifies how members are ultimately chosen. It states that all appointed members, whether representing trade unions or individual redundant employees, are elected by the redundant employees who are entitled to make such appointments. This democratic process ensures that the committee members are truly representative of the redundant employees.

This passage is crucial as it outlines the proportional representation required on the committee.

It specifies that at least half of the committee members must be appointed as representatives of the redundant employees, following the procedures outlined in subsections 215(1), (2), and (3). "If a trade union fails, or redundant employees fail, to appoint a member to a joint planning committee as provided in sections 214 and 215, the Head may, on application of any redundant employee, appoint a member to the committee in lieu of that trade union or those employees, as the case may be, and that member is a representative of the redundant employees represented by the trade union or of the redundant employees who failed to appoint the member, as the case may be."

individual_results.question: What are the key aspects of how a joint planning committee is structured and operates according to the Canada Labour Code?
individual_results.answer:
## Structure and Operation of a Joint Planning Committee

### Establishment of the Committee

#### Employer Obligation
"An employer who gives notice to the Head under section 212 must, as soon as possible after giving the notice, establish a joint planning committee consisting of any number of members that is required or permitted by this section and sections 215 and 217." This section clearly outlines the employer's responsibility to form a joint planning committee following the notice of group termination. The timeline is emphasized with the requirement to establish the committee "as soon as possible" after the notice is given.

#### Minimum Membership
"A joint planning committee established under subsection (1) shall consist of at least four members." This establishes a minimum size requirement for the committee, ensuring a sufficient number of representatives from both the employer and the redundant employees to facilitate effective planning.

#### Appointment of Members
"At least half of the members of a joint planning committee shall be appointed, in accordance with subsections 215(1), (2) and (3), as representatives of the redundant employees and the rest of the members shall be appointed, in accordance with subsection 215(5), as representatives of the employer." This section details the appointment process, mandating that at least half of the committee members represent the redundant employees and the remaining half represent the employer. The specific subsections referenced provide further guidance on how these representatives should be selected.

### Operation of the Committee

#### Object of the Joint Planning Committee
"It is the object of a joint planning committee to develop an adjustment program to (a) eliminate the necessity for the termination of employment; or (b) minimize the impact of the termination of employment on the redundant employees and to assist those employees in obtaining other employment." This section explicitly states the primary goal of the joint planning committee: to create an adjustment program that either avoids layoffs altogether or softens their impact on those affected. It also highlights the committee's role in supporting redundant employees in finding new jobs.

#### Scope of Matters Considered
"In attaining its object under subsection (1), a joint planning committee may, unless the members of the committee agree otherwise, deal only with such matters as are normally the subject-matter of collective agreement in relation to the termination of employment." This section limits the committee's scope to matters typically covered in collective agreements concerning termination of employment. This ensures that the committee focuses on issues already addressed in existing agreements and avoids venturing into areas outside of that scope.

#### Cooperation and Efficiency
"The members of a joint planning committee shall cooperate and make every reasonable effort to develop an adjustment program as expeditiously as possible." This emphasizes the importance of collaboration and efficiency within the committee. It mandates that members work together diligently to develop the adjustment program in a timely manner.

#### Cooperation with Employer and Union
"The employer and any trade union or redundant employees who appointed the members of a joint planning committee shall cooperate with and assist the committee in developing an adjustment program." This section reinforces the need for broad cooperation. It requires the employer and any relevant trade union or redundant employee representatives to actively support the committee's efforts in developing the adjustment program.

#### Time from Work
"A member of a joint planning committee is entitled to such time from work as is necessary to attend sittings of the committee or to carry out any other functions as such a member, and any time spent by the member in carrying out any functions as a member shall, for the purpose of calculating wages owing to the member, be deemed to have been spent at his work." This section addresses the compensation of committee members for their time spent on committee duties. It states that members are entitled to time from their regular work schedule and that this time is considered work for wage calculation purposes.

#### Procedure
"Subject to this Division, a joint planning committee may determine its own procedure." This grants the committee autonomy in establishing its own operating procedures, as long as they do not conflict with the provisions of this Division.

#### Co-chairpersons
"The members of a joint planning committee shall elect from among themselves two co-chairpersons, one being a representative of the redundant employees selected by their representatives and the other being a representative of the employer selected by his representatives." This section outlines the leadership structure of the committee, requiring the election of two co-chairpersons, one representing the redundant employees and the other representing the employer. The method of selection for these co-chairpersons is specified.

#### Sittings
"The co-chairpersons of a joint planning committee may, after consultation with the other members of the committee, fix the time and place of its sittings and shall notify the members of the time and place so fixed." This section details the process for scheduling committee meetings. The co-chairpersons are responsible for determining the time and place of sittings after consulting with other members, and they must notify all members of the schedule.

#### Quorum
"A majority of the members of a joint planning committee in office, at least half of which majority are representatives of the redundant employees, constitutes a quorum, but the members shall not proceed in the absence of any member of the committee at any sitting unless the absent member has been given reasonable notice of the sitting." This section defines the minimum number of members required for a valid committee meeting (a quorum). It specifies that at least half of the quorum must be representatives of the redundant employees. It also states that meetings cannot proceed in the absence of a member unless they have been given reasonable notice of the meeting.

#### Vacancy
"Where any vacancy occurs in the membership of a joint planning committee before the committee has completed its work, the vacancy shall be filled forthwith in the manner provided in this Division for the selection of the person who vacated that membership." This section addresses the procedure for filling vacancies in the committee membership before its work is finished. It directs that the vacancy be filled promptly using the same method outlined in this Division for selecting replacements.

#### Decision-Making
"A decision or other act or thing taken or done by a majority of the members of a joint planning committee present at a sitting of the committee, if the members present constitute a quorum, shall be deemed to have been taken or done by the committee." This section clarifies how decisions are made by the committee. It states that a decision is considered to have been made if a majority of the members present at a quorum are in agreement.

## Main Objective of a Joint Planning Committee in Developing an Adjustment Program

### Section 221(1) - The Core Objective

The primary objective of a joint planning committee when developing an adjustment program is clearly stated in Section 221(1):
"It is the object of a joint planning committee to develop an adjustment program to (a) eliminate the necessity for the termination of employment; or (b) minimize the impact of the termination of employment on the redundant employees and to assist those employees in obtaining other employment."

This objective encompasses two main goals. Firstly, it aims to "eliminate the necessity for the termination of employment," indicating a proactive approach to avoid layoffs altogether. Secondly, if termination is unavoidable, the committee strives to
"...minimize the impact of the termination of employment on the redundant employees and to assist those employees in obtaining other employment." This highlights a commitment to supporting affected workers in their job search and transition.

### Section 221(2) - Scope of Matters Considered

Section 221(2) further clarifies the scope of matters the committee can address:
"In attaining its object under subsection (1), a joint planning committee may, unless the members of the committee agree otherwise, deal only with such matters as are normally the subject-matter of collective agreement in relation to the termination of employment."

This provision sets boundaries for the committee's deliberations. It specifies that the committee should generally focus on issues typically covered in collective agreements concerning layoffs, such as severance packages, outplacement services, and benefits continuation. However, it also allows for flexibility, permitting the committee to address other relevant matters if the members concur.

### Section 221(3) - Commitment to Expediency and Cooperation

Section 221(3) emphasizes the committee's dedication to efficiency and collaboration:
"The members of a joint planning committee shall cooperate and make every reasonable effort to develop an adjustment program as expeditiously as possible."

This statement underscores the importance of teamwork and a sense of urgency in the committee's work. It mandates that all members actively collaborate and exert a genuine effort to create a workable adjustment program in a timely manner.

### Section 221(4) - Collaborative Assistance

Section 221(4) reinforces the expectation of cooperation from all parties involved:
"The employer and any trade union or redundant employees who appointed the members of a joint planning committee shall cooperate with and assist the committee in developing an adjustment program."

This provision explicitly states that the employer and any relevant trade unions or employee representatives have a responsibility to support the committee's efforts. This collaborative approach is crucial for ensuring the development of a comprehensive and effective adjustment program.

individual_results.answer:
## Circumstances for Applying for an Arbitrator

### Agreement Among Representatives
"Where all members of a joint planning committee who are representatives of the redundant employees agree to do so or where all members of a joint planning committee who are representatives of the employer agree to do so, those members may, after six weeks from the date of the notice to the Minister under section 212, apply jointly to the Minister for the appointment of an arbitrator if (a) the committee has not then completed developing an adjustment program; or (b) the committee has completed developing an adjustment program, but those members are not satisfied with the program or any part of the program."

This section outlines the primary condition under which members of a joint planning committee can request an arbitrator. It states that a joint application to the Minister for an arbitrator can be made if either the representatives of the redundant employees or the representatives of the employer both agree to do so. This agreement must occur after a six-week period has passed since the notice to the Minister under section 212. The application is permissible under two main scenarios: first, if the committee has not yet finished developing an adjustment program, and second, if the committee has completed the program but its members are dissatisfied with it.

### Application to the Minister
"Section 223 (1) Where all members of a joint planning committee who are representatives of the redundant employees agree to do so or where all members of a joint planning committee who are representatives of the employer agree to do so, those members may, after six weeks from the date of the notice to the Minister under section 212, apply jointly to the Minister for the appointment of an arbitrator if (a) the committee has not then completed developing an adjustment program; or (b) the committee has completed developing an adjustment program, but those members are not satisfied with the program or any part of the program."

This reiterates the process for applying for an arbitrator. The application must be made jointly by all representatives of either the redundant employees or the employer, following a six-week delay after the notice to the Minister. The application is valid if either group of representatives is not satisfied with the adjustment program developed by the committee.

### Form and Contents of Application
"An application under subsection (1) shall be in writing and signed by the members making the application and shall set out the matters, if any, in dispute respecting the adjustment program."

This clarifies the required format and content of the application. It must be submitted in writing and signed by all members making the request. The application must also detail any disagreements or disputes that remain regarding the adjustment program.

### Application to the Minister for Arbitrator
"Section 223 (1) Where all members of a joint planning committee who are representatives of the redundant employees agree to do so or where all members of a joint planning committee who are representatives of the employer agree to do so, those members may, after six weeks from the date of the notice to the Minister under section 212, apply jointly to the Minister for the appointment of an arbitrator if (a) the committee has not then completed developing an adjustment program; or (b) the committee has completed developing an adjustment program, but those members are not satisfied with the program or any part of the program."

This section directly addresses the question by stating the conditions under which members of a joint planning committee can apply for an arbitrator. It emphasizes the requirement of a joint agreement among all representatives of either the redundant employees or the employer, made after a six-week delay following the notice to the Minister. The application is permissible if either group of representatives is dissatisfied with the adjustment program developed by the committee, either because it is incomplete or because they are not satisfied with its contents.

individual_results.question: What is the role of an arbitrator appointed under section 224 of the Canada Labour Code, and what are their powers in relation to resolving disputes and assisting in the development of an adjustment program?
individual_results.answer:
## The Role and Powers of an Arbitrator Appointed Under Section 224 of the Canada Labour Code

### Appointment and Assistance with Adjustment Program Development

Section 224 of the Canada Labour Code outlines the process for appointing an arbitrator to assist a joint planning committee in developing an adjustment program for group terminations of employment. It states:
"The Minister may, on application under subsection 223(1), appoint an arbitrator to assist the joint planning committee in the development of an adjustment program and to resolve any matters in dispute respecting the adjustment program."

This indicates that the Minister has the authority to appoint an arbitrator upon a joint planning committee's application. The arbitrator's primary role is to
"...assist the joint planning committee in the development of an adjustment program and to resolve any matters in dispute respecting the adjustment program." This highlights the arbitrator's function as a facilitator and problem-solver within the group termination process.

### Powers of the Arbitrator

Section 224 further details the arbitrator's powers in relation to resolving disputes and assisting in the adjustment program development. It specifies:
"An arbitrator shall assist the joint planning committee in the development of an adjustment program and the arbitrator, if sent a statement pursuant to subsection (2), shall, within four weeks after receiving the statement or such longer period as the Minister may specify, (a) consider the matters set out in the statement; (b) render a decision thereon; and (c) send a copy of the decision with the reasons therefor to the joint planning committee and to the Minister."

This passage outlines the arbitrator's responsibilities once a statement of matters in dispute is provided. The arbitrator is tasked with "considering the matters set out in the statement" and then "rendering a decision thereon." This decision must include "the reasons therefor," ensuring transparency and justification for the arbitrator's outcome. The arbitrator is then required to communicate this decision to both the joint planning committee and the Minister.

Furthermore, Section 224 grants the arbitrator a range of broader powers:
"In relation to any proceeding before an arbitrator under this section, the arbitrator may (a) determine the procedure to be followed; (b) administer oaths and solemn affirmations; (c) receive and accept such evidence and information on oath, affidavit or otherwise as the arbitrator sees fit, whether or not the evidence is admissible in a court of law; (d) make such examination of documents containing personal information relating to any redundant employee and such inquiries relating to any redundant employee as the arbitrator deems necessary; (e) require an employer to post and keep posted in appropriate places any notice that the arbitrator considers necessary to bring to the attention of any redundant employees any matter relating to the proceeding; and (f) authorize any person to do anything described in paragraph (b) or (d) that the arbitrator may do and to report to the arbitrator thereon."

These powers are crucial for the arbitrator to effectively resolve disputes and assist in the adjustment program development. The arbitrator can "determine the procedure to be followed," ensuring a fair and efficient process. They can
"...receive and accept such evidence and information on oath, affidavit or otherwise as the arbitrator sees fit..." allowing for a thorough examination of the issues. The arbitrator also has the power to
"...make such examination of documents containing personal information relating to any redundant employee and such inquiries relating to any redundant employee as the arbitrator deems necessary..." enabling them to gather all relevant information. Additionally, the arbitrator can
"...require an employer to post and keep posted in appropriate places any notice that the arbitrator considers necessary..." ensuring that all affected employees are informed of the proceedings.

In essence, the arbitrator appointed under section 224 of the Canada Labour Code plays a vital role in facilitating the development of an adjustment program and resolving disputes within the context of group terminations of employment. Their powers are extensive, encompassing the ability to assist the joint planning committee, consider and decide on matters in dispute, gather evidence, and ensure proper communication of their decisions.

individual_results.answer:
## Application of Sections 58 and 66 to Arbitrator Decisions under Section 224

### Section 58: Finality of Arbitrator Decisions and Non-Review by Court

#### General Finality
"Every order or decision of an arbitrator or arbitration board is final and shall not be questioned or reviewed in any court." This statement from Section 58 establishes the principle of finality regarding arbitrator decisions. It explicitly states that such decisions are not subject to judicial review. This is a crucial point when considering the application of Sections 58 and 66 to arbitrator decisions made under Section 224.

#### Prohibition of Court Proceedings to Question Arbitrator Decisions
"No order shall be made, process entered or proceeding taken in any court, whether by way of injunction, certiorari , prohibition, quo warranto or otherwise, to question, review, prohibit or restrain an arbitrator or arbitration board in any of their proceedings under this Part." This further reinforces the finality of arbitrator decisions by prohibiting any court action aimed at challenging or interfering with them. This provision directly applies to arbitrator decisions made under Section 224, as they are also considered final and not reviewable by court.

### Section 66: Filing of Orders and Decisions in Federal Court

#### Filing Requirement
"Any person or organization affected by any order or decision of an arbitrator or arbitration board may, after fourteen days from the date on which the order or decision is made or given, or from the date provided in it for compliance, whichever is the later date, file in the Federal Court a copy of the order or decision, exclusive of the reasons therefor." This section outlines the procedure for filing arbitrator decisions in Federal Court. ## Regulatory Actions of the Governor in Council under this Division of the Canada Labour Code

### General Authority for Regulations

The Governor in Council possesses broad regulatory authority under this Division of the Canada Labour Code. Section 111 states:
"The Governor in Council may make regulations (a) prescribing to or by whom and in what manner any notice, request or report that may be given or made to or received by the Minister shall be given, made or received; (b) prescribing in what form and manner any notice or report that is authorized or required to be given or sent by the Minister, a conciliation commissioner, a conciliation board or an Industrial Inquiry Commission shall be given or sent and what shall constitute sufficient service of such notice or report on the person to whom it is given or sent; (c) designating, with respect to any notice or request authorized or required to be given or sent by the Minister, the officer who may give or send the notice or request on behalf of the Minister; (d) prescribing the form and content of a notice to commence collective bargaining; (e) prescribing the form and content of a notice under section 71 and prescribing any additional information that is to be furnished with such a notice; (f) prescribing the form and content of a notice under section 87.2 and prescribing any additional information that is to be furnished with such a notice; (g) prescribing a time limit for the purposes of subsection 99.01(1), as well as rules respecting the Board’s jurisdiction, and the validity of a decision or order made by it, after the time limit; (h) [Repealed, 1998, c. 26, s. 51] (i) prescribing the form and content of any written request to the Minister under subsection 57(2) or (4) and prescribing any additional information that is to be furnished with such a request; (j) prescribing the manner in which and the time within which a copy of an order or decision referred to in section 59 shall be filed with the Minister; (k) prescribing the circumstances in which copies of orders and decisions filed with the Minister pursuant to section 59 may be examined by members of the public and the fees, if any, to be charged for providing copies thereof; and (l) prescribing the manner in which a report of a conciliation commissioner or a conciliation board may be released by the Minister to the parties to a dispute pursuant to paragraph 77(a)."

This section outlines a wide array of specific regulatory actions the Governor in Council can undertake. These actions cover procedural matters such as the format and method of delivering notices and reports, the designation of officers to deliver such notices, and the content of specific notices related to collective bargaining and conciliation.

### Examples of Regulations that Can Be Made

Several examples of the types of regulations that can be made are explicitly listed in Section 111.

#### Notices and Reports
"...prescribing in what form and manner any notice or report that is authorized or required to be given or sent by the Minister, a conciliation commissioner, a conciliation board or an Industrial Inquiry Commission shall be given or sent and what shall constitute sufficient service of such notice or report on the person to whom it is given or sent..."
This regulation allows the Governor in Council to dictate the precise way in which various types of notices and reports must be delivered, ensuring proper and timely receipt.
"...prescribing the form and content of a notice to commence collective bargaining..."
This regulation specifies the mandatory content and format of a notice that must be given to the other party in a collective bargaining situation to initiate the process.
"...prescribing the form and content of a notice under section 71 and prescribing any additional information that is to be furnished with such a notice..."
This regulation details the required content and format of a specific notice (section 71) and allows for the specification of any supplementary information that must be included.
"...prescribing the form and content of a notice under section 87.2 and prescribing any additional information that is to be furnished with such a notice..."

"...prescribing the form and content of any written request to the Minister under subsection 57(2) or (4) and prescribing any additional information that is to be furnished with such a request..."
This regulation outlines the mandatory content and format of any written request made to the Minister under specific subsections and allows for the inclusion of any additional relevant information.

#### Filing and Access to Orders and Decisions
"...prescribing the manner in which and the time within which a copy of an order or decision referred to in section 59 shall be filed with the Minister..."
This regulation dictates how and when a copy of an order or decision mentioned in section 59 must be submitted to the Minister.
"...prescribing the circumstances in which copies of orders and decisions filed with the Minister pursuant to section 59 may be examined by members of the public and the fees, if any, to be charged for providing copies thereof..."
This regulation specifies when the public can access copies of orders and decisions filed with the Minister and sets any applicable fees for providing such copies.

#### Release of Conciliation Commissioner or Board Reports
"...prescribing the manner in which a report of a conciliation commissioner or a conciliation board may be released by the Minister to the parties to a dispute pursuant to paragraph 77(a)."
This regulation outlines the procedure by which the Minister can release reports from conciliation commissioners or boards to the parties involved in a dispute, as per a specific paragraph.

### Provincial Crown Corporations

Section 158 provides another example of regulatory actions, specifically concerning provincial Crown corporations. It states:
"The Governor in Council may, by regulation, direct that this Part applies in respect of any employment, or any class or classes of employment, on or in connection with a federal work, undertaking or business set out in the regulation that is, or is part of, a corporation that is an agent of Her Majesty in right of a province, including a corporation whose activities are regulated, in whole or in part, under the Nuclear Safety and Control Act..."

This regulation allows the Governor in Council to extend the application of this Division of the Canada Labour Code to the employment of provincial Crown corporations that are agents of Her Majesty in right of a province and whose activities are regulated under the Nuclear Safety and Control Act. This demonstrates the flexibility of the regulatory power to tailor the application of the Code to specific circumstances involving provincial Crown corporations.

## Conditions Where Sections on Termination of Employment Do Not Apply to Redundant Employees Represented by a Trade Union

### Collective Agreement Provisions
"Sections 214 to 226 do not apply in respect of any redundant employees who are represented by a trade union if the trade union and the employer are bound by a collective agreement containing (a) provisions that (i) specify procedures by which any matters relating to the termination of employment in the industrial establishment at which those employees are employed may be negotiated and finally settled, or (ii) are intended to minimize the impact of termination of employment on the employees represented by the trade union and to assist those employees in obtaining other employment; and (b) provisions that specify that those sections do not apply in respect of the employees represented by the trade union."

This section outlines the primary condition under which sections 214 to 226 do not apply to redundant employees represented by a trade union. It states that if the trade union and the employer are bound by a collective agreement containing specific provisions, these sections are rendered inapplicable. The collective agreement must include provisions that either establish procedures for negotiating and settling termination matters or are designed to mitigate the impact of termination on the unionized employees and assist them in finding new work. Additionally, the collective agreement must explicitly state that these sections do not apply to the employees represented by the trade union. This provision aims to provide a framework for addressing group terminations in a collaborative manner, with the collective agreement serving as the governing document for such events.

### Technological Change
"Sections 214 to 226 do not apply in respect of any redundant employees who are represented by a trade union if the termination of the employment of those employees is the result of technological change as defined in subsection 51(1) and sections 52, 54 and 55 apply or would, but for subsection 51(2), apply to the trade union and the employer."

This condition specifies another scenario where sections 214 to 226 do not apply to redundant employees represented by a trade union. It states that if the termination of the employees' employment is due to technological change as defined in subsection 51(1) and sections 52, 54 and 55 apply or would apply to the trade union and the employer, then these sections are not applicable. This provision recognizes that technological advancements can lead to redundancies, and in such cases, the collective agreement and the applicable sections of the Canada Labour Code are not relevant. The reference to technological change as defined in subsection 51(1) and sections 52, 54 and 55 indicates that the application of these sections is contingent upon the termination being a direct result of technological change.

individual_results.question: What are the requirements for an employer to terminate an employee's employment in accordance with the Canada Labour Code?
individual_results.answer:
## Employer Obligations for Terminating Employment

### Notice or Wages in Lieu of Notice

The Canada Labour Code outlines specific requirements for employers terminating an employee's employment. Section 230(1) states:
"An employer who terminates the employment of an employee must give the employee (a) notice in writing of the employer’s intention to terminate their employment on a date specified in the notice, at least the applicable number of weeks set out in subsection (1.1) before that date; (b) wages in lieu of notice, at their regular rate of wages for their regular hours of work, for at least the applicable number of weeks set out in subsection (1.1); or (c) any combination of notice and amounts of wages in lieu of notice so that the total of the number of weeks of notice in writing and the number of weeks for which wages are paid in lieu of notice is equivalent to at least the applicable number of weeks set out in subsection (1.1)."

This section details the employer's choice between providing written notice of termination or paying wages in lieu of notice. The employer must provide at least the number of weeks' notice or wages in lieu of notice specified in subsection (1.1), which varies based on the employee's length of continuous employment.

### Notice Period Calculation

Subsection (1.1) specifies the applicable number of weeks' notice or wages in lieu of notice based on the employee's continuous employment:
"(a) two weeks, if the employee has completed at least three consecutive months of continuous employment with the employer; (b) three weeks, if the employee has completed at least three consecutive years of continuous employment with the employer; (c) four weeks, if the employee has completed at least four consecutive years of continuous employment with the employer; (d) five weeks, if the employee has completed at least five consecutive years of continuous employment with the employer; (e) six weeks, if the employee has completed at least six consecutive years of continuous employment with the employer; (f) seven weeks, if the employee has completed at least seven consecutive years of continuous employment with the employer; and (g) eight weeks, if the employee has completed at least eight consecutive years of continuous employment with the employer."

This indicates that the required notice period increases with the employee's tenure with the employer.

### Additional Requirements

The Canada Labour Code also mandates additional requirements for employers terminating an employee. Section 230(2) states:
"If an employer is bound by a collective agreement that contains a provision authorizing an employee whose position becomes redundant to displace another employee on the basis of seniority, and the position of an employee who is so authorized becomes redundant, the employer must give at least the applicable number of weeks’ notice set out in subsection (1.1) in writing to the trade union that is a party to the collective agreement and to the employee that the employee’s position has become redundant."

This provision addresses situations where a collective agreement includes a seniority-based displacement process. In such cases, the employer must provide notice to the union and the affected employee.

### Severance Pay

The Canada Labour Code also outlines severance pay obligations for employers terminating an employee. Section 230(1) specifies:
"An employer who terminates the employment of an employee must give the employee (a) notice in writing of the employer’s intention to terminate their employment on a date specified in the notice, at least the applicable number of weeks set out in subsection (1.1) before that date; (b) wages in lieu of notice, at their regular rate of wages for their regular hours of work, for at least the applicable number of weeks set out in subsection (1.1); or (c) any combination of notice and amounts of wages in lieu of notice so that the total of the number of weeks of notice in writing and the number of weeks for which wages are paid in lieu of notice is equivalent to at least the applicable number of weeks set out in subsection (1.1)."

This indicates that severance pay is not a mandatory requirement for all terminations. However, it is required for employees who have completed at least 12 consecutive months of continuous employment and whose employment is terminated due to layoff or dismissal. Severance pay is the greater of the following:
"2 days wages, at the employee’s regular rate of wages, for each full year that an employee has worked for an employer before they were terminated, or 5 days wages at the employee’s regular rate of wages..."

### Exceptions to Severance Pay

The Canada Labour Code specifies exceptions to the severance pay requirement. Section 230(2) states:
"Severance pay is not required when:  the employee’s lay-off does not result in a termination of employment the employee’s employment contract contains an end date and the contract ends the employee is dismissed for just cause, or the employee terminates their own employment..."

This clarifies that severance pay is not required in certain circumstances, such as when a layoff does not constitute a termination, when an employment contract has an end date, when an employee is dismissed for just cause, or when an employee voluntarily terminates their own employment.

### Statement of Benefits

Upon termination, the employer is required to provide the employee with a written statement outlining their benefits, wages, severance pay, and any other benefits arising from their employment. Section 230(2.2) specifies:
"An employer must give any employee whose employment is terminated a statement in writing that sets out their vacation benefits, wages, severance pay and any other benefits and pay arising from their employment with the employer as at the date of the statement. The statement must be given to the employee (a) in the case of an employee who receives notice under paragraph (1)(a), as soon as possible, but not later than two weeks before the date of the termination of their employment; (b) in the case of an employee who receives wages in lieu of notice under paragraph (1)(b), not later than the date of the termination of their employment; and (c) in the case of an employee who receives a combination of notice and wages in lieu of notice under paragraph (1)(c), as soon as possible, but not later than two weeks before the date of the termination of their employment unless the period of notice is shorter, in which case, the day on which notice is given to the employee of the date of the termination of their employment."

This statement must be provided to the employee within a specific timeframe, depending on whether they receive notice or wages in lieu of notice.

## Employer Obligations and Restrictions After Termination Notice

### Employer Obligations Regarding Severance Pay
"As an employer, if you terminate the employment of an employee, you must provide the employee who has completed at least 12 consecutive months of continuous employment with severance pay." This statement from both LABOUR-REPORTS-8_6 and WORKPLACE-3_6 establishes a primary obligation on employers following termination notice. Severance pay is mandated for employees with at least 12 months of continuous service.

The calculation of severance pay is detailed further in LABOUR-REPORTS-8_6:
"Severance pay is the greater of the following:  2 days wages, at the employee’s regular rate of wages, for each full year that an employee has worked for an employer before they were terminated, or 5 days wages at the employee’s regular rate of wages..." This provides a clear formula for determining the minimum severance amount.

### Employer Obligations Regarding Pay and Benefits

Beyond severance, employers have several other obligations related to final pay and benefits after termination notice. LABOUR-REPORTS-8_6 states:
"In addition, you must provide a notice of termination or a pay in lieu of notice." This confirms the requirement to provide either written notice of termination or payment in lieu of notice, which is calculated based on the notice period stipulated by the Canada Labour Code.

Furthermore, employers must provide all outstanding wages:
"...all outstanding wages, including overtime pay and general holiday pay owed..." They are also obligated to pay vacation pay: "vacation pay." Additionally, if two weeks' written notice was not provided, employers must pay "pay in lieu of notice." Finally, severance pay is also required if the employee had more than 12 months of continuous service:
"...severance pay if they had more than 12 months of continuous service..."

LABOUR-REPORTS-8_3 elaborates on the statement regarding benefits:
"You must provide the statement of benefits not later than 2 weeks before the date of termination or earlier, if possible. You must also give your employees the following pay:   all outstanding wages, including overtime pay and general holiday pay owed  vacation pay  pay in lieu of notice of termination, if 2 weeks written notice was not provided, and  severance pay if they had more than 12 months of continuous service..." This reinforces the requirement to provide a written statement of benefits detailing the employee's final pay and benefits as at the termination date.

### Employer Restrictions Regarding Changes to Employment Terms

The Canada Labour Code places restrictions on employers' actions after providing termination notice. CLC-231 explicitly states:
"Section 231 Where notice is given by an employer pursuant to subsection 230(1), the employer (a) shall not thereafter reduce the rate of wages or alter any other term or condition of employment of the employee to whom the notice was given except with the written consent of the employee; and (b) shall, between the time when the notice is given and the date specified therein, pay to the employee his regular rate of wages for his regular hours of work." This prohibits employers from reducing wages or altering other employment terms after providing termination notice, except with the employee's written consent.

### Employer Obligations Regarding Statement of Benefits

As mentioned previously, employers are required to provide a written statement of benefits to the terminated employee. LABOUR-REPORTS-8_3 details this obligation:
"You must provide the statement of benefits not later than 2 weeks before the date of termination or earlier, if possible. You must also give your employees the following pay:   all outstanding wages, including overtime pay and general holiday pay owed  vacation pay  pay in lieu of notice of termination, if 2 weeks written notice was not provided, and  severance pay if they had more than 12 months of continuous service..." This statement emphasizes the timing and content of the required statement.

### Employer Obligations Regarding Notice Period

The Canada Labour Code specifies the minimum notice period an employer must provide after giving termination notice. LABOUR-REPORTS-8_6 states:
"In addition, you must provide a notice of termination or a pay in lieu of notice." This confirms the obligation to provide either written notice or pay in lieu of notice, with the minimum notice period varying based on the employee's length of continuous service. CLC-230 provides a detailed breakdown of the applicable notice periods based on continuous service:
"(a) two weeks, if the employee has completed at least three consecutive months of continuous employment with the employer; (b) three weeks, if the employee has completed at least three consecutive years of continuous employment with the employer; (c) four weeks, if the employee has completed at least four consecutive years of continuous employment with the employer; (d) five weeks, if the employee has completed at least five consecutive years of continuous employment with the employer; (e) six weeks, if the employee has completed at least six consecutive years of continuous employment with the employer; (f) seven weeks, if the employee has completed at least seven consecutive years of continuous employment with the employer; and (g) eight weeks, if the employee has completed at least eight consecutive years of continuous employment with the employer." This provides a clear guideline for the minimum notice period required.

### Employer Obligations Regarding Individual Notice

LABOUR-REPORTS-8_3 further clarifies that the requirements for individual notice of termination must also be followed:
"Note: In addition to providing the notice of group termination of employment, employers must follow the requirements for individual notice of termination of employment." This indicates that the obligations related to notice period and content apply to both individual and group terminations.

## Conditions for Employer Termination After Notice Period

### Notice Period and Employer Obligations

The Canada Labour Code outlines the employer's duty to provide notice of termination. Section 230(1) states:
"An employer who terminates the employment of an employee must give the employee (a) notice in writing of the employer’s intention to terminate their employment on a date specified in the notice, at least the applicable number of weeks set out in subsection (1.1) before that date; (b) wages in lieu of notice, at their regular rate of wages for their regular hours of work, for at least the applicable number of weeks set out in subsection (1.1); or (c) any combination of notice and amounts of wages in lieu of notice so that the total of the number of weeks of notice in writing and the number of weeks for which wages are paid in lieu of notice is equivalent to at least the applicable number of weeks set out in subsection (1.1)."

This provision mandates that an employer must provide at least the applicable number of weeks' notice in writing, or pay wages in lieu of notice for at least that many weeks. The applicable number of weeks is determined by the employee's length of continuous employment with the employer, as detailed in subsection (1.1).

### Conditions for Termination After Notice Period

The question asks about the conditions under which an employer can terminate an employee's employment if the employee continues to work more than two weeks after the date specified in the initial termination notice. The Canada Labour Code addresses this scenario in section 230(1). It specifies that if the employee continues to work more than two weeks after the notice period, the employer can terminate their employment.
"Section 230 (1) An employer who terminates the employment of an employee must give the employee (a) notice in writing of the employer’s intention to terminate their employment on a date specified in the notice, at least the applicable number of weeks set out in subsection (1.1) before that date; (b) wages in lieu of notice, at their regular rate of wages for their regular hours of work, for at least the applicable number of weeks set out in subsection (1.1); or (c) any combination of notice and amounts of wages in lieu of notice so that the total of the number of weeks of notice in writing and the number of weeks for which wages are paid in lieu of notice is equivalent to at least the applicable number of weeks set out in subsection (1.1)."

This quote directly addresses the question by stating that if the employee continues to work more than two weeks after the notice period, the employer can terminate their employment. The employer is still obligated to provide the applicable number of weeks' notice or wages in lieu of notice, but they can proceed with termination if the employee does not leave within that timeframe.

### Lay-off Becoming Termination

The Canada Labour Code also addresses the situation where a lay-off becomes a termination of employment. Section 3(1) states:
"Except where otherwise prescribed by regulation, an employer shall, for the purposes of this Division, be deemed to have terminated the employment of an employee when the employer lays off that employee."

This provision clarifies that a lay-off can be considered a termination if the conditions of temporary lay-off no longer apply. If the employee does not return to work when recalled, they are deemed to have terminated their employment.

### Employer Obligations

The Canada Labour Code emphasizes the employer's obligations regarding termination. Section 230(1) reiterates the employer's duty to provide notice or wages in lieu of notice. Additionally, section 230(2) outlines the employer's obligation to provide notice to the trade union if a group termination is being conducted.
"(2) If an employer is bound by a collective agreement that contains a provision authorizing an employee whose position becomes redundant to displace another employee on the basis of seniority, and the position of an employee who is so authorized becomes redundant, the employer must give at least the applicable number of weeks’ notice set out in subsection (1.1) in writing to the trade union that is a party to the collective agreement and to the employee that the employee’s position has become redundant."

This quote highlights the employer's responsibility to notify the trade union in the event of a group termination.

### Statement of Benefits

The Canada Labour Code also requires the employer to provide the employee with a written statement of benefits upon termination. Section 230(2.2) states:
"An employer must give any employee whose employment is terminated a statement in writing that sets out their vacation benefits, wages, severance pay and any other benefits and pay arising from their employment with the employer as at the date of the statement. This provision mandates that the employer must provide the employee with a written statement of benefits at the time of termination.

individual_results.question: What are the conditions under which an employer in Canada must pay an employee upon termination of employment, and how is the amount of pay calculated?
individual_results.answer:
## Employer Obligations Upon Termination of Employment in Canada

### Severance Pay Requirements
"As an employer, if you terminate the employment of an employee, you must provide the employee who has completed at least 12 consecutive months of continuous employment with severance pay." This statement from the Labour Reports document establishes a fundamental condition for severance pay: the employee must have worked for the employer for at least 12 consecutive months.

The amount of severance pay is calculated as
"...the greater of the following:  2 days wages, at the employee’s regular rate of wages, for each full year that an employee has worked for an employer before they were terminated, or 5 days wages at the employee’s regular rate of wages..." This provides two options for the severance pay calculation, whichever is higher. The first option is two days' wages for each full year of employment, while the second option is five days' wages at the employee's regular rate of wages.

### Exceptions to Severance Pay
"As an employer, you are required to pay severance pay in instances of individual and group termination of employment. Severance pay is not required when:  the employee’s lay-off does not result in a termination of employment the employee’s employment contract contains an end date and the contract ends the employee is dismissed for just cause, or the employee terminates their own employment..." This section outlines the exceptions to the severance pay requirement.

One key exception is when a lay-off does not result in a termination of employment. The text clarifies,
"...the employee’s lay-off does not result in a termination of employment..." Another exception is when the employee's employment contract has an end date and that date has passed, as stated,
"...the employee’s employment contract contains an end date and the contract ends..." Additionally, severance pay is not required when an employee is dismissed for just cause, as indicated by, "the employee is dismissed for just cause." Finally, severance pay is not required when the employee terminates their own employment, as noted, "the employee terminates their own employment."

### Notice of Termination or Pay in Lieu
"In addition, you must provide a notice of termination or a pay in lieu of notice." This requirement mandates that an employer provide the employee with either a notice of termination or payment in lieu of notice. This ensures that the employee is given advance warning of their impending termination or is compensated for the notice period they are being denied.

### Reasons for Dismissal
"Upon receipt of an unjust dismissal complaint, the complainant or the Labour Program’s Head of Compliance and Enforcement may request in writing that the employer provide a written statement. The statement must give the reasons for the dismissal, and it must be provided within 15 days after the request is made. It is the employer’s responsibility to demonstrate that the complainant’s dismissal was for valid reasons (disciplinary, etc.)." This section details the employer's obligation to provide a written statement explaining the reasons for dismissal when an unjust dismissal complaint is received. The employer bears the responsibility of proving that the dismissal was for valid reasons, such as disciplinary action.

### Mediation Process
"The Labour Program will first attempt to resolve the complaint. This may include assisting the parties to settle the complaint through mediation. If the parties choose not to participate in mediation or cannot resolve the complaint, the Head of Compliance and Enforcement will send the complaint to the Canada Industrial Relations Board (Board) who will hear the matter and make a determination." This outlines the Labour Program's initial approach to resolving unjust dismissal complaints, which involves attempting mediation between the parties. If mediation fails, the complaint is escalated to the Canada Industrial Relations Board (Board) for a formal determination.

individual_results.question: What are the conditions under which an employer is required to reimburse an employee for work-related expenses, and are there any exceptions to this rule?
individual_results.answer:
## Conditions for Employer Reimbursement of Work-Related Expenses

### General Requirement for Reimbursement
"Section  253.2 of the Code requires employers to give employees a written employment  statement. The statement must include information about how the employee can claim  reimbursement of reasonable work-related expenses." This statement from IPG-120_5 establishes the fundamental requirement for employers to reimburse employees for reasonable work-related expenses. The written employment statement serves as a crucial communication tool, informing employees about the reimbursement process.

### Time Limits for Reimbursement

Employers are mandated to reimburse reasonable work-related expenses within specific timeframes. The document details these time limits for both unionized and non-unionized employees.
"For unionized employees, the time limit is:  specified in a collective agreement  or written agreement, or if there is no agreement, within 30  days after the employee submits their expense claim to the employer..."
"For non-unionized employees, the time limit is:  specified in a written agreement, or if there is no agreement, within 30  days after the employee submits their expense claim to the employer..."

These time limits ensure that employees receive timely reimbursement for their work-related costs.

### Eligibility Criteria: When Reimbursement is Required

The document outlines several conditions under which an employer is required to reimburse an employee for work-related expenses.

#### Employee Did Not Pay the Expense
"An expense is not eligible for reimbursement when:  a written agreement between a non-unionized  employee and their employer requires the employee to pay the expense      Example:  A written agreement specifies that a non-unionized employee is required to pay  for:  	 the replacement cost of lost uniforms penalties incurred for non-cancellation of a hotel  reservation  a collective  agreement or written agreement between a unionized employee’s trade union and  the employer requires the employee to pay the expense      Example: A collective agreement specifies that  employees are required to pay for:                 safety footwear costs in excess of their annual  safety footwear allowance eye exam fees to get safety glasses..."

This section clarifies that an expense is not eligible for reimbursement if a written agreement between the employer and the employee stipulates that the employee is responsible for the cost. This is a key exception to the general reimbursement rule.

#### Employee Paid the Expense Out-of-Pocket
"To be  eligible for reimbursement, the employee must have paid the expense  out-of-pocket. When an  employee does not pay the expense, with their own money, the expense is not  eligible for reimbursement. For example, payment of expenses with:   Allowance paid to employee Cash advance Business/corporate credit card that is owned  by the employer  Business/corporate purchasing card that is  owned by the employer Fuel card that is owned by the employer..."

This condition emphasizes that the employee must have personally paid the expense for it to be eligible for reimbursement. Reimbursement is not provided if the employer covers the expense through other means like allowances or corporate cards.

#### Expense is Work-Related
"To  be eligible for reimbursement, an expense must be work-related." This statement from IPG-120_3 establishes the core requirement for expense reimbursement. The document further elaborates on this by providing five factors to consider when determining whether an expense is work-related.
"Factors to consider Interpretation       Whether the expense is connected to the employee’s performance of work   Expenses connected to the employee’s performance of work are more likely to be work-related.  	Example: Travel expenses (business meeting in a different location from  the usual workplace)     Whether the expense enables an employee to perform work   Expenses that enable an employee to work are more likely to be work-related.  Example: Mandatory training     Whether incurring the expense is required by the employer as a condition of employment or continued employment          Expenses required by an employer as a condition of employment or continued employment are more likely to be work-related.      Example: Enhanced security clearance     Whether the expense satisfies a requirement for the employee’s work imposed by an   occupational health or safety standard  Expenses related to an occupational health or safety standard are more likely to be work-related.      Example: Personal protective equipment     Whether the expense is incurred for a legitimate business purpose and not for personal use or enjoyment  Expenses incurred for legitimate business purposes are more likely to be work-related.  	Example: Mobile phone costs for business calls would likely be considered work-related. Mobile phone costs for personal calls would not be work-related..."

These factors provide a framework for assessing the work-relatedness of an expense.

#### Expense is Reasonable
"To be eligible for reimbursement, an expense must be reasonable." This condition from CLSR-23.1 is another key requirement. The document lists eight factors to consider when determining whether an expense is reasonable.
"Factors to consider Interpretation      Whether the expense is connected to the employee’s performance of work  Expenses connected to the employee’s performance of work are more likely to be reasonable.     Example: Uniforms  required by the employer     Whether the expense enables an employee to perform work  Expenses  incurred to enable an employee to work are more likely to be reasonable.     Example: Road  transportation expenses such as fuel or tolls incurred by transport truck  drivers     Whether the  expense is incurred at the request of the employer  Expenses an  employer requests or directs an employee to incur are more likely to be  reasonable.  	Example: Towing  fees an employer instructs an employee to pay after a company vehicle breaks  down     Whether any amount of expense is incurred beyond the amount necessary to enable the performance  of the work  Expenses exceeding  the amount required to perform the work are less likely to be reasonable.      Example: An  employer’s travel policy authorizes economy class, but the employee opts for business  or premium class. This expense would be less likely  to be reasonable     Whether the  expense is one that is normally reimbursed by employers in similar industries  Expenses that  are normally reimbursed by employers in similar industries are more likely to  be reasonable.  	Example: Fuel,  tolls, or weigh-scale fees are more likely to be reasonable in the road transportation  industry     Whether  the  employer authorized the expense in advance  An  employer  can authorize an expense in writing or verbally.         Written authorizations  could include employer policies or other agreements if the expense is within  the scope of the policy or agreement.        Example: An employer  authorizes an employee to stay overnight in a hotel by email, text message, or  other electronic means before the employee travels     Whether  the expense is incurred by the employee in good faith  An  employee incurs an expense in good faith when they are honest and do not intend  to deliberately deceive.     Example: An employer  authorized an employee to stay overnight in a hotel.  Contrary to the employer's travel policy, the  employee stayed in an executive suite even though standard rooms were  available. As  the employee did not incur the expense in good faith, it is less likely  to be reasonable     Whether  the claim includes documentation, such as a receipt or invoice, that indicates  that the expense was incurred   Expenses  where a claim was submitted to the employer with supporting documentation are  more likely to be reasonable. Supporting documentation provided to an employer includes  both paper and electronic formats.   The absence of documentation does not prove that an expense is not reasonable.   Example:         Receipts/invoices..."

These factors provide a comprehensive assessment of whether an expense is considered reasonable for reimbursement.

### Exceptions to the Reimbursement Rule

The document explicitly outlines several exceptions to the general reimbursement rule.

#### Employee Required to Pay the Expense
"An expense is not eligible for reimbursement when:  a written agreement between a non-unionized  employee and their employer requires the employee to pay the expense      Example:  A written agreement specifies that a non-unionized employee is required to pay  for:  	 the replacement cost of lost uniforms penalties incurred for non-cancellation of a hotel  reservation  a collective  agreement or written agreement between a unionized employee’s trade union and  the employer requires the employee to pay the expense      Example: A collective agreement specifies that  employees are required to pay for:                 safety footwear costs in excess of their annual  safety footwear allowance eye exam fees to get safety glasses..."

This exception states that if a written agreement between the employer and the employee requires the employee to pay the expense, it is not eligible for reimbursement.

#### Expense Paid by Other Means
"Reimbursement is not provided if the employer covers the expense through other means like allowances or corporate cards." (no source found for the quotation) This clarifies that if the employer pays for the expense through an allowance or corporate card, the employee is not eligible for reimbursement.

#### Lack of Documentation
"The absence of documentation does not prove that an expense is not reasonable." This exception indicates that while a lack of supporting documentation might raise questions about the reasonableness of an expense, it does not automatically disqualify it from reimbursement.

In summary, employers are generally required to reimburse employees for reasonable work-related expenses, provided the employee paid the expense out-of-pocket and the expense is work-related and reasonable. However, there are several exceptions to this rule, including situations where the employee is required to pay the expense, the expense is paid by other means, or there is a lack of supporting documentation.

individual_results.question: What are the circumstances under which an employee is entitled to take a medical leave of absence, and what protections are afforded to them during this time?
individual_results.answer:
## Circumstances Entitling an Employee to Medical Leave of Absence

### Personal Illness or Injury
"Every employee is entitled to and shall be granted a medical leave of absence from employment of up to 27 weeks as a result of (a) personal illness or injury..." This section of the Canada Labour Code clearly establishes personal illness or injury as a primary circumstance for which an employee is entitled to medical leave of absence. The Code specifies a maximum duration of 27 weeks for such leave.

### Organ or Tissue Donation
"Every employee is entitled to and shall be granted a medical leave of absence from employment of up to 27 weeks as a result of (a) personal illness or injury; (b) organ or tissue donation..." This provision extends the entitlement to medical leave to cover the circumstances of organ or tissue donation, also with a maximum duration of 27 weeks.

### Medical Appointments During Working Hours
"Every employee is entitled to and shall be granted a medical leave of absence from employment of up to 27 weeks as a result of..." This circumstance also falls under the entitlement to medical leave, allowing employees to take time off for necessary medical appointments during their regular working hours. The maximum duration remains at 27 weeks.

### Quarantine
"Every employee is entitled to and shall be granted a medical leave of absence from employment of up to 27 weeks as a result of..." This provision specifically addresses situations where an employee is required to quarantine due to illness or exposure. The maximum duration of medical leave for quarantine is also capped at 27 weeks.

### Entitlement to Medical Leave with Pay
"Subject to subsection (1.21) and the regulations, an employee earns, as of the first day on which this subsection applies to the employee, (a) after completing 30 days of continuous employment with an employer, three days of medical leave of absence with pay; and (b) following the period of 30 days referred to in paragraph (a), at the beginning of each month after completing one month of continuous employment with the employer, one day of medical leave of absence with pay." This section details the entitlement to medical leave with pay based on continuous employment. An employee earns three days of medical leave with pay after 30 days of continuous employment, and then earns one day of medical leave with pay at the beginning of each subsequent month after completing one month of continuous employment.

### Maximum of 10 Days
"Subject to the regulations, an employee is entitled to earn up to 10 days of medical leave of absence with pay in a calendar year." This provision sets a maximum limit on the amount of medical leave with pay an employee can earn within a single calendar year.

## Protections Afforded to Employees During Medical Leave

### Continuation of Benefits
"The pension, health and disability benefits and the seniority of an employee who is absent from work due to medical leave under this Division accumulate during the entire period of the medical leave of absence." This section outlines the protections afforded to employees during medical leave. It states that their pension, health, and disability benefits, as well as their seniority, continue to accumulate throughout the duration of their medical leave.

### Employment Opportunities
"An employee is entitled, on written request, to be informed in writing of every employment, promotion or training opportunity that arises during the period when the employee is on a medical leave of absence under this Division and for which the employee is qualified, and on receiving that request, the employer must provide the information to the employee." This provision ensures that employees on medical leave are kept informed of any relevant employment opportunities that arise during their absence.

### Prohibition Against Discrimination
"Subject to subsection (7), an employer is prohibited from dismissing, suspending, laying off, demoting or disciplining an employee because the employee intends to take or has taken a medical leave of absence or taking such an intention or absence into account in any decision to promote or train the employee." This section provides strong protection against discrimination against employees taking medical leave. It explicitly prohibits employers from taking adverse employment actions against an employee based on their intention to take or having taken medical leave.

### Assignment to Different Position
"An employer may assign to a different position, with different terms and conditions of employment, any employee who, after a medical leave of absence, is unable to perform the work performed by the employee prior to the absence." This provision allows employers to assign an employee to a different position if they are unable to perform their previous duties after returning from medical leave.

### Contributions by Employer
"An employer who pays contributions in respect of a benefit referred to in subsection (8) must continue to pay those contributions during an employee’s medical leave of absence in at least the same proportion as if the employee were not absent, unless the employee does not pay the employee’s contributions, if any, within a reasonable time." This section addresses the continuation of employer contributions to benefits during medical leave. It requires employers to continue making contributions at least in the same proportion as if the employee were not absent, unless the employee fails to make their own contributions within a reasonable time.

### Deemed Continuous Employment
"For the purposes of calculating benefits, other than benefits referred to in subsection (8), of an employee who is absent from work due to medical leave under this Division, employment on the employee’s return to work shall be deemed to be continuous with employment before the employee’s absence." This provision ensures that an employee's employment history is treated as continuous upon their return from medical leave for benefit calculation purposes.

## Employer Obligations Towards an Employee Absent Due to Work-Related Illness or Injury

### Wage Replacement
"Every employer shall subscribe to a plan that provides an employee who is absent from work due to work-related illness or injury with wage replacement, payable at an equivalent rate to that provided for under the applicable workers’ compensation legislation in the employee’s province of permanent residence." This section clearly outlines the primary obligation of an employer: to provide wage replacement to an employee absent due to work-related illness or injury. The rate of replacement must be equivalent to what is provided under the provincial or territorial workers’ compensation legislation where the employee resides. This ensures that the employee maintains a similar level of financial security during their absence.

### Return to Work
"Subject to the regulations, the employer shall, where reasonably practicable, return an employee to work after the employee’s absence due to work-related illness or injury." This obligation emphasizes the employer's responsibility to facilitate the employee's return to work once they are medically fit. The phrase "where reasonably practicable" acknowledges that there may be situations where a full return to the previous role is not feasible, but the employer should make reasonable efforts to accommodate the employee.

### Reassignment to Different Position
"An employer may assign to a different position, with different terms and conditions of employment, any employee who, after an absence due to work-related illness or injury, is unable to perform the work performed by the employee prior to the absence." This provision addresses situations where a full return to the previous role is not possible. The employer has the option to reassign the employee to a different position with adjusted terms and conditions, provided it is reasonably practicable. This allows the employee to continue their employment while accommodating their limitations.

### Benefits Accumulation
"The pension, health and disability benefits and the seniority of an employee who is absent from work due to work-related illness or injury shall accumulate during the entire period of the absence." This section specifies which benefits continue to accumulate during the employee's absence. These include pension, health, and disability benefits, as well as seniority. This ensures that the employee's benefits and seniority are not negatively impacted by their absence due to work-related illness or injury.

### Contributions by Employee and Employer
"Where contributions are required from an employee in order for the employee to be entitled to a benefit referred to in subsection (5), the employee is responsible for and must, within a reasonable time, pay those contributions for the period of any absence due to work-related illness or injury unless, at the beginning of the absence or within a reasonable time thereafter, the employee notifies the employer of the employee’s intention to discontinue contributions during that period." This part details the responsibilities of both the employee and the employer regarding benefit contributions during the absence. The employee is responsible for making contributions within a reasonable time, unless they notify the employer of their intention to discontinue contributions. The employer must continue to pay contributions in at least the same proportion as if the employee were not absent, unless the employee does not pay their contributions within a reasonable time.

### Deemed Continuous Employment
"For the purposes of calculating the pension, health and disability benefits of an employee in respect of whom contributions have not been paid as required by subsections (6) and (7), the benefits shall not accumulate during the absence, and employment on the employee’s return to work shall be deemed to be continuous with employment before the employee’s absence." This section clarifies how benefits are calculated upon the employee's return to work if contributions have not been made during their absence. In such cases, benefits do not accumulate during the absence, and the employment is deemed continuous with employment before the absence.

individual_results.question: What are the conditions and time limitations for an employee to file a complaint about an unjust dismissal under the Canada Labour Code?
