## Conditions for Filing an Unjust Dismissal Complaint

### Employment Duration and Collective Agreement Status

According to Section 240(1) of the Canada Labour Code, an employee who has been dismissed and considers the dismissal to be unjust may make a complaint in writing to the Head if they have completed
"12 consecutive months of continuous employment by an employer..." and
"...is not a member of a group of employees subject to a collective agreement." This establishes two key conditions: a minimum employment tenure and non-unionized status.

### Manager Status

Section 240(1) further specifies that an employee is not eligible to file an unjust dismissal complaint if they are a manager. It states, "and not be a manager." This exclusion is likely due to the different rights and protections afforded to managers under the Canada Labour Code.

## Time Limitations for Filing an Unjust Dismissal Complaint

### Initial Complaint Deadline

Section 240(2) sets a strict time limit for filing an unjust dismissal complaint. It states,
"Subject to subsection (3), a complaint under subsection (1) shall be made within ninety days from the date on which the person making the complaint was dismissed." This means that an employee must file their complaint within 90 days of their dismissal.

### Extension of Time

Section 240(3) allows the Head to extend this 90-day period under certain circumstances. It specifies,
"The Head may extend the period set out in subsection (2) (a) if the Head is satisfied that a complaint was made in that period to a government official who had no authority to deal with the complaint but that the person making the complaint believed the official had that authority; or (b) in any circumstances that are prescribed by regulation." This provision provides flexibility in cases where an employee may have been unaware of their right to file a complaint within the initial 90-day window.

### Limitation on Similar Complaints

Section 240(1.1) imposes a limitation on filing multiple complaints based on substantially the same facts. It states,
"A person shall not make a complaint under subsection (1) if they have made a complaint that is based on substantially the same facts under either subsection 246.1(1) or 247.99(1), unless that complaint has been withdrawn." This prevents employees from repeatedly filing complaints about the same issue.

### Suspension of Complaint

Section 240(5) addresses the suspension of a complaint. It states,
"Subject to the regulations, if the person who made the complaint does not, within the period set out in the notice, make a written request that the complaint be referred to the Board, the Head may deem the complaint to be withdrawn." This means that if the employee does not respond to a request from the Head within a specified timeframe, the complaint may be considered withdrawn.

individual_results.question: What are the steps and obligations for an employer and the Head when handling a complaint related to the dismissal of a person described in subsection 240(1) of the Canada Labour Code?
individual_results.answer:
## Steps and Obligations for Employer and Head in Handling Unjust Dismissal Complaints

### Employer Obligations

#### Providing Written Statement of Reasons for Dismissal
"If an employer dismisses a person described in subsection 240(1), the person who was dismissed or the Head may make a request in writing to the employer to provide a written statement giving the reasons for the dismissal, and any employer who receives such a request must provide the person who made the request with such a statement within 15 days after the request is made." This section outlines the employer's obligation to provide a written statement detailing the reasons for the dismissal upon request. The employer has a strict 15-day deadline to fulfill this request.

#### Responding to Complaints
"On receipt of a complaint made under subsection 240(1), the Head must endeavour to assist the parties to the complaint to settle the complaint." While the Head is primarily responsible for facilitating settlement, the employer is implicitly obligated to respond to the complaint and engage in good faith efforts to resolve it. The employer must provide the requested written statement of reasons within the stipulated timeframe.

#### Complying with Board Orders
"If the Board decides that a complainant has been unjustly dismissed, the Board may, by order, require the employer who dismissed the complainant to:   pay the complainant compensation, not higher than the amount of money that is equal to what would have been paid by the employer if they had not dismissed them  reinstate the complainant in their employment, and  order the employer, in a fair way, to resolve or reduce any consequences of the dismissal..." This passage details the employer's obligations if the Board finds the dismissal unjust. The Board can order the employer to provide compensation, reinstate the employee, and address any resulting consequences.

### Head Obligations

#### Facilitating Settlement
"On receipt of a complaint made under subsection 240(1), the Head must endeavour to assist the parties to the complaint to settle the complaint." The Head's primary obligation is to facilitate a settlement between the employer and the complainant. This involves attempting to mediate a resolution and encourage both parties to reach an agreement.

#### Referring Complaints to the Board
"If a complaint is not settled under subsection (2) within the period that the Head considers to be reasonable in the circumstances, the Head must, on the written request of the person who made the complaint that the complaint be referred to the Board, deliver to the Board the complaint made under subsection 240(1), any written statement giving the reasons for the dismissal provided under subsection (1) and any other statements or documents that the Head has that relate to the complaint." If a settlement cannot be reached within a reasonable timeframe, the Head must refer the complaint to the Board upon the complainant's written request. This involves providing the Board with all relevant documentation, including the employer's written statement of reasons.

#### Extending Time Limits
"The Head may extend the period set out in subsection (2) (a) if the Head is satisfied that a complaint was made in that period to a government official who had no authority to deal with the complaint but that the person making the complaint believed the official had that authority; or (b) in any circumstances that are prescribed by regulation." The Head has the discretion to extend the time limit for making a complaint under subsection (1) under certain circumstances.

#### Addressing Incomplete or Erroneous Complaints
"...the making of a complaint under subsection 240(1) of the Act, if a complaint that is based on substantially the same facts was previously made under subsection 246.1(1) or 247.99(1) of the Act in accordance with subsection 246.1(3) or 247.99(2) of the Act, as the case may be, and that complaint was withdrawn; and (b) the making of a complaint under subsection 240(1) of the Act, if a complaint that is based on substantially the same facts of unjust dismissal was previously made under that subsection in accordance with subsection 240(2) of the Act and that complaint was withdrawn because it is incomplete or contains an error." These prescribed circumstances relate to the handling of duplicate or flawed complaints. If a complaint is substantially the same as a previously withdrawn complaint, or if a complaint is incomplete or contains an error, the Head may deem the complaint withdrawn.

#### Providing Notice of Time Limit
"If the person who made the complaint does not reply to a written communication from the Head within a period that the Head considers to be reasonable in the circumstances and a period of at least 30 days, or any longer period that may be prescribed by regulation, have elapsed from the day on which the complaint was made, the Head may give written notice to the person who made the complaint that they have the period of 30 days, or any longer period that may be prescribed by regulation, set out in the notice to make a written request that the complaint be referred to the Board." The Head is required to provide written notice to the complainant if they do not respond to a communication within a reasonable timeframe. This notice sets a new deadline for the complainant to request referral to the Board.

individual_results.question: Under what circumstances can the Board suspend or reject a complaint, and what steps must it take in these situations?
individual_results.answer:
## Suspension of Complaint

### Circumstances for Suspension

The Board can suspend consideration of a complaint under two main circumstances, as outlined in CLC-241.1 and CLC-246.2.

**1. Requirement for Complainant to Take Measures:
"If the Board is satisfied that the complainant must take measures before the Board may continue to deal with the complaint referred to it under subsection 241(3), it may, at any time, suspend consideration of the complaint, in whole or in part." This indicates that the Board may suspend a complaint if it determines that the complainant has a specific obligation to act before the Board can proceed. The Board must first ascertain if these measures are required.

**2. Failure to Take Required Measures within Specified Time:
"If the Board suspends consideration of a complaint, the Board shall notify the complainant in writing and specify in the notice (a) the measures that the complainant must take; and (b) the period within which they must take those measures." This passage details the notification process when a complaint is suspended. The Board must inform the complainant of the required actions and the timeframe within which those actions must be completed. The suspension ends only when the Board is satisfied that the specified measures have been taken.

### Steps Taken During Suspension

When a complaint is suspended, the Board must take specific steps.

**1. Written Notification:
"If the Board suspends consideration of a complaint, the Board shall notify the complainant in writing..." This is the initial step. The Board must communicate the suspension to the complainant in writing.

**2. Specification of Required Measures and Timeframe:
"...and specify in the notice (a) the measures that the complainant must take; and (b) the period within which they must take those measures." The written notification must clearly state the actions the complainant must undertake and the deadline for completing those actions.

**3. Reinstatement of Consideration:
"The suspension ends when, in the Board’s opinion, the measures specified in the notice have been taken." The suspension is lifted only when the Board is convinced that the complainant has fulfilled the required actions within the given timeframe. The Board can then resume consideration of the complaint.

## Rejection of Complaint

### Circumstances for Rejection

The Board can reject a complaint under several circumstances, as detailed in CLC-241.2 and CLC-246.2.

**1. Complaint Not Within Jurisdiction:
"(a) if the Board is satisfied that (i) the complaint is not within its jurisdiction..." This is one primary reason for rejection. The Board can reject a complaint if it falls outside the scope of its authority.

**2. Complaint Frivolous, Vexatious, or Not Made in Good Faith:
"(ii) the complaint is frivolous, vexatious or not made in good faith..." The Board can reject a complaint deemed baseless, intended to harass, or lacking genuine merit.

**3. Complaint Already Settled in Writing:
"(iii) the complaint has been settled in writing between the employer and the complainant..." If the parties have reached a written agreement, the Board can reject the complaint.

**4. Other Means Available to Complainant:
"(iv) there are other means available to the complainant to resolve the subject matter of the complaint that the Board considers should be pursued..." The Board may reject a complaint if there are alternative avenues for resolution that the Board believes the complainant should explore.

**5. Subject Matter Adequately Dealt With:
"(v) the subject matter of the complaint has been adequately dealt with through recourse obtained before a court, tribunal, arbitrator or adjudicator..." If the issue has already been resolved through other legal or quasi-legal processes, the Board can reject the complaint.

**6. Failure to Take Required Measures After Suspension:
"(b) if consideration of the complaint was suspended under subsection 241.1(1) and if, in the Board’s opinion, the measures specified in the notice under subsection 241.1(2) were not taken within the specified period." This circumstance mirrors the suspension process. If a complaint is suspended due to required complainant actions and those actions are not taken within the given timeframe, the Board can reject the complaint.

### Steps Taken During Rejection

When a complaint is rejected, the Board must take specific steps.

**1. Written Notification with Reasons:
"If the Board rejects a complaint, it shall notify the complainant in writing, with reasons." This is the initial step. The Board must inform the complainant of the rejection in writing and provide the reasons for the decision.

**2. End of Suspension (if applicable):
"The suspension ends when, in the Board’s opinion, the measures specified in the notice have been taken." If the complaint was previously suspended due to required complainant actions, the suspension ends upon the Board's satisfaction that those actions have been completed.

## Actions the Board Can Take Upon Finding Unjust Dismissal

### Remedies Ordered by the Board
"If the Board decides that a complainant has been unjustly dismissed, the Board may, by order, require the employer who dismissed the complainant to:   pay the complainant compensation, not higher than the amount of money that is equal to what would have been paid by the employer if they had not dismissed them  reinstate the complainant in their employment, and  order the employer, in a fair way, to resolve or reduce any consequences of the dismissal..."

This passage directly addresses the actions the Board can order when it determines an unjust dismissal has occurred. The Board has the authority to mandate several remedies from the employer. These include financial compensation to the complainant, reinstatement to their former position, and a fair resolution of any resulting damages or consequences. The Board's order is legally binding on the employer, requiring strict compliance.

### Factors Considered by the Adjudicator

### Seriousness of the Problem
"Adjudicators will consider a number of factors when deciding whether or not the dismissal was justified. For example, he or she may consider:   Seriousness of the problem: Did the action/inaction of the employee have serious or only minor consequences for the employer?"

This section outlines several factors an adjudicator will weigh when determining if a dismissal was justified. The "seriousness of the problem" is one such factor. The adjudicator will assess the extent of the negative impact the employee's actions (or inaction) had on the employer. A minor issue would likely not justify an unjust dismissal, while a serious one might.

### Degree of Orientation
"Degree of orientation: Had the workplace rules been clearly explained? Was the employee informed about the employer's job performance expectations?"

The adjudicator will also consider whether the employee was adequately informed about workplace expectations and rules. "Degree of orientation" refers to the extent to which these expectations were communicated. If rules and performance expectations were not clearly explained, it would be less likely to justify an unjust dismissal.

### Past Discipline
"Past discipline: Has the employee been disciplined for improper workplace behaviour in the past?"

The adjudicator will examine the employee's disciplinary history. "Past discipline" is a key factor. If the employee had previously been disciplined for similar improper conduct, it would be more likely to justify an unjust dismissal.

### Employee's Work History
"Employee's work history: Has the employee's work performance been satisfactory in the past?"

The adjudicator will also consider the employee's overall work performance. "Employee's work history" is a relevant factor. If the employee had a satisfactory work record, it would be less likely to justify an unjust dismissal.

### History of Organization's Disciplinary Practice
"History of organization's disciplinary practice: Have other employees who engaged in similar improper conduct been disciplined for it?"

The adjudicator will look at the employer's past disciplinary practices. "History of organization's disciplinary practice" is a factor. If other employees who engaged in similar improper conduct had been disciplined, it would be more likely to justify an unjust dismissal.

### Extenuating Circumstances
"Extenuating circumstances or mitigating factors: Was the employee facing pressures such as personal problems or provocation which may have led to the improper behaviour?"

The adjudicator will also consider any "extenuating circumstances or mitigating factors" that may have contributed to the employee's improper behaviour. These could include personal problems or provocation.

### Past Adjudication Decisions
"Adjudicators might also rely on past unjust dismissal adjudication decisions when deciding your case. They are not obligated to follow those decisions, but they can serve as helpful guides."

The adjudicator may also refer to past unjust dismissal decisions as "helpful guides." While not bound by previous rulings, they can provide insights into how similar cases were handled.

individual_results.question: What is the status of the Board's orders in relation to judicial review?
individual_results.answer:
## Judicial Review of Board Orders

### Finality of Board Orders

The Canada Labour Code explicitly states the finality of the Board's orders and decisions in relation to judicial review.
"Every order of the Board is final and shall not be questioned or reviewed in any court." This statement, found in Section 243(1) of the Canada Labour Code, establishes a strong principle of finality for the Board's orders. It directly addresses the possibility of judicial review, asserting that such review is not permitted.

This finality is further reinforced in Section 22(1), which reiterates that
"...every order or decision made by the Board under this Part is final and is not to be questioned or reviewed in any court..." This repetition underscores the legislative intent to preclude judicial interference with the Board's decisions.

### Prohibition of Court Proceedings to Question Board Actions

The Code also prohibits court proceedings aimed at challenging the Board's actions.
"No order shall be made, process entered or proceeding taken in any court, whether by way of injunction, certiorari , prohibition, quo warranto or otherwise, to question, review, prohibit or restrain the Board in any proceedings under section 242." This provision, found in Section 243(2), is a direct response to potential attempts to use the courts to overturn or modify the Board's orders. It explicitly forbids such actions, regardless of the legal mechanism employed.

This prohibition extends to all proceedings related to the Board's work. Section 22(2) states that
"...no order, decision or proceeding of the Board made or carried on under or purporting to be made or carried on under this Part shall (a) be questioned, reviewed, prohibited or restrained, or (b) be made the subject of any proceedings in or any process of any court, whether by way of injunction, certiorari , prohibition, quo warranto or otherwise, on any ground..." This broad prohibition ensures that the courts cannot intervene in the Board's processes or outcomes.

### Exceptions to Judicial Review

While judicial review is generally prohibited, the Code does provide limited exceptions.

Section 251.12(1) states that
"The Board may, in an appeal under this Part, make any order that is necessary to give effect to its decision, including an order to (a) confirm, rescind or vary, in whole or in part, the decision being appealed..." This indicates that the Board itself has the authority to make orders to implement its decisions, and these orders are also final and not subject to judicial review.

Furthermore, Section 22(1) mentions an exception related to the Federal Courts Act:
"Subject to this Part and to any regulations made under paragraph 111.01(1)(g), every order or decision made by the Board under this Part is final and is not to be questioned or reviewed in any court, except in accordance with the Federal Courts Act on the grounds referred to in paragraph 18.1(4)(a), (b) or (e) of that Act." This allows for judicial review only on very specific grounds outlined in the Federal Courts Act, such as jurisdictional issues.

In summary, the Canada Labour Code establishes a robust framework for the finality of the Board's orders, effectively barring judicial review in most circumstances. However, it does permit judicial review only on narrow grounds as specified in the Federal Courts Act.

individual_results.question: How can an order of the Board be enforced in the Federal Court?
individual_results.answer:
## Enforcement of Board Orders in the Federal Court

### Filing in Federal Court

Section 22(1) of the Canada Labour Code establishes the finality of Board orders and decisions, stating,
"Subject to this Part and to any regulations made under paragraph 111.01(1)(g), every order or decision made by the Board under this Part is final and is not to be questioned or reviewed in any court..." However, it also outlines a specific process for enforcement through the Federal Court.

Section 23(1) details this process:
"The Board shall, on the request in writing of any person or organization affected by any order or decision of the Board made under this Part, file a copy of the order or decision, exclusive of reasons, in the Federal Court, unless, in the opinion of the Board, (a) there is no indication of failure or likelihood of failure to comply with the order or decision; or (b) there is other good reason why the filing of the order or decision in the Federal Court would serve no useful purpose." This indicates that any party impacted by a Board order can request the Board to file a copy of the order with the Federal Court.

Section 23(2) further clarifies the acceptance of the filed order:
"Where the Board files a copy of any order or decision in the Federal Court pursuant to subsection (1), it shall specify in writing to the Court that the copy of the order or decision is filed pursuant to that subsection and, where the Board so specifies, the copy of the order or decision shall be accepted for filing by, and registered in, the Court without further application or other proceeding." This means that once the Board files the order, the Federal Court will accept it for registration without needing any further action from the requesting party.

### Registration and Legal Force

Section 23(3) explains the legal effect of the Federal Court registration:
"When a copy of any order or decision of the Board is registered pursuant to subsection (2), the order or decision has the same force and effect as a judgment obtained in the Federal Court and, subject to this section and the Federal Courts Act , all proceedings may be taken thereon by any person or organization affected thereby as if the order or decision were a judgment of that Court." This is a crucial aspect of the enforcement mechanism. By registering the order in the Federal Court, it gains the same legal standing as a judgment issued by that Court. Consequently, all legal actions related to the order can be pursued in the Federal Court as if it were a judgment.

### No Review by Certiorari, etc.

Section 156(1) explicitly states the finality of Board orders and decisions, emphasizing that they
"...shall not be questioned or reviewed in any court." This reinforces the limited scope of judicial review available for Board orders. It further clarifies this point in a marginal note: "No review by certiorari , etc." This directly addresses the question by stating that an order of the Board cannot be challenged or reviewed in any court, including the Federal Court, except under very specific circumstances outlined in the Federal Courts Act.

In summary, an order of the Board can be enforced in the Federal Court by requesting the Board to file a copy of the order with the Court. Upon filing, the Court will register the order, granting it the same legal force and effect as a judgment obtained in that Court. However, it is important to note that Board orders are final and cannot be questioned or reviewed in any court, except under limited circumstances as specified in the Federal Courts Act.

## Effect of Sections 240 to 245 on Civil Remedies

### Section 246

#### Application of Section 189
"Section 189 applies for the purposes of this Division." This statement directly addresses the effect of sections 240 to 245 on an employee's civil remedies. It indicates that the provisions within sections 240 to 245 do not suspend or affect the employee's existing civil remedies against their employer. Instead, Section 189 is the governing provision for this entire Division, meaning that the civil remedies remain available.

### Section 246.1

#### Limitation on Subsequent Complaints
"An employee shall not make a complaint under subsection (1) if they have made a complaint that is based on substantially the same facts under either subsection 240(1) or 247.99(1), unless that complaint has been withdrawn." This section clarifies that the complaint process outlined in sections 240 to 245 is not limited by prior complaints based on substantially the same facts. An employee cannot file a new complaint under sections 240 to 245 if they have already filed a complaint based on the same facts, unless the previous complaint has been withdrawn. This means that the civil remedies remain open even after a prior complaint has been withdrawn.

### Section 246.1

#### Burden of Proof
"A complaint made under subsection (1) is itself evidence that the reprisal was actually taken and, if a party to the complaint proceedings alleges that the reprisal was not taken, the burden of proof is on that party." This section highlights the significance of a complaint made under sections 240 to 245. It states that the complaint itself serves as evidence that the reprisal occurred. If a party to the complaint proceedings disputes the occurrence of the reprisal, the onus is on that party to prove that it did not happen. This reinforces the availability of civil remedies even after a prior complaint has been withdrawn, as the new complaint provides evidence of the reprisal.

### Section 246

#### No Suspension or Effect
"No civil remedy of an employee against his employer is suspended or affected by sections 240 to 245." This is the most direct answer to the question. It explicitly states that sections 240 to 245 do not suspend or affect an employee's existing civil remedies against their employer. Therefore, the civil remedies remain available even after a prior complaint has been withdrawn.

individual_results.question: What recourse do employees have under the Canada Labour Code if they believe their employer has taken disciplinary action against them in response to certain protected activities, such as filing a complaint or providing information to authorities?
individual_results.answer:
## Recourse for Employees Facing Disciplinary Action for Protected Activities

### Section 147: General Prohibition on Disciplinary Action

Section 147 of the Canada Labour Code establishes a general prohibition against employers taking disciplinary action against employees because they have exercised their rights under the Part of the Code that deals with concerted activities and other protected actions.
"No employer shall dismiss, suspend, lay off or demote an employee, impose a financial or other penalty on an employee, or refuse to pay an employee remuneration in respect of any period that the employee would, but for the exercise of the employee’s rights under this Part, have worked, or take any disciplinary action against or threaten to take any such action against an employee because the employee (a) has testified or is about to testify in a proceeding taken or an inquiry held under this Part; (b) has provided information to a person engaged in the performance of duties under this Part regarding the conditions of work affecting the health or safety of the employee or of any other employee of the employer; or (c) has acted in accordance with this Part or has sought the enforcement of any of the provisions of this Part."

This section directly addresses the question by stating that employers are prohibited from taking disciplinary action against employees for engaging in protected activities. It specifically lists several such activities, including testifying in legal proceedings, providing information to authorities regarding health and safety conditions, and acting in accordance with the provisions of the Code.

### Section 147.1: Abuse of Rights

Section 147.1 provides a limited exception to the general prohibition on disciplinary action. It states that an employer may take disciplinary action against an employee who has "wilfully abused those rights."
"An employer may, after all the investigations and appeals have been exhausted by the employee who has exercised rights under sections 128 and 129, take disciplinary action against the employee who the employer can demonstrate has wilfully abused those rights."

This section clarifies that the protection against disciplinary action does not extend to employees who have acted in bad faith or have sought to undermine their rights under the Code. However, it also includes a requirement for the employer to provide the employee with written reasons for any disciplinary action taken.

### Section 246.1: Complaint to Board Regarding Reprisals

Section 246.1 outlines the process for employees to file a complaint with the Board if they believe their employer has taken disciplinary action against them in response to certain protected activities.
"(1) Any employee may make a complaint in writing to the Board if they believe that their employer has taken any of the following reprisals against them: (a) the employer has taken action against the employee in contravention of subsection 173.01(5), 174.1(4) or 177.1(7) or of section 208, 209.3, 238, 239, 239.1 or 247.96; (a.1) [Repealed, 2021, c. 26, s. 25] (b) dismissing, suspending, laying off, or demoting the employee, imposing a financial or other penalty on the employee, or otherwise taking any disciplinary action against the employee, because the employee (i) has made a complaint under this Part, other than a complaint under section 240, (ii) has provided information regarding the wages, hours of work, annual vacation or conditions of work of any employee to the Head or provided any other assistance to the Minister or the Head in the exercise or performance of the Minister’s or the Head’s powers, duties and functions under this Part (ii.1) has provided information regarding the wages, hours of work, annual vacation or conditions of work of any employee or provided any other assistance to an external adjudicator or a member of the Board in the exercise or performance, in accordance with subsections 12.001(2) or 14(5), of the powers, duties or functions conferred on the Board by this Part, (iii) has testified or is about to testify in a proceeding taken or an inquiry held under this Part, or (iv) has exercised, or sought to exercise, any right conferred on the employee by this Part; (c) taking into account the fact that the employee has taken any of the actions referred to in subparagraphs (b)(i) to (iv) in any decision with respect to the promotion or training of the employee; or (d) threatening to take any of the reprisals referred to in paragraph (b) or (c)."

This section explicitly states that an employee can file a complaint with the Board if they believe their employer has taken disciplinary action in retaliation for engaging in protected activities, such as filing a complaint or providing information to authorities. The complaint must be made in writing to the Board within 90 days of becoming aware of the action.

### Section 133: Complaint to Board Regarding Reprisals

Section 133 provides a similar mechanism for employees to file a complaint with the Board regarding reprisals for protected activities.
"(1) An employee, or a person designated by the employee for the purpose, who alleges that an employer has taken action against the employee in contravention of section 147 may, subject to subsection (3), make a complaint in writing to the Board of the alleged contravention."

This section reiterates the right of employees to file a complaint with the Board if they believe their employer has taken disciplinary action in response to protected activities. It also specifies the timeframe for filing the complaint: no later than 90 days after becoming aware of the action.

### Section 134: Board Orders Regarding Reprisals

Section 134 outlines the powers of the Board to order employers to cease reprisals and to provide remedies to affected employees.
"(1) If, under subsection 133(5), the Board determines that an employer has contravened section 147, the Board may, by order, require the employer to cease contravening that section and may, if applicable, by order, require the employer to (a) permit any employee who has been affected by the contravention to return to the duties of their employment; (b) reinstate any former employee affected by the contravention; (c) pay to any employee or former employee affected by the contravention compensation not exceeding the sum that, in the Board’s opinion, is equivalent to the remuneration that would, but for the contravention, have been paid by the employer to the employee or former employee; and (d) rescind any disciplinary action taken in respect of, and pay compensation to any employee affected by, the contravention, not exceeding the sum that, in the Board’s opinion, is equivalent to any financial or other penalty imposed on the employee by the employer."

This section details the remedies available to employees who have faced disciplinary action in response to protected activities. The Board has the power to order the employer to cease reprisals, reinstate employees, pay compensation, and rescind disciplinary actions.

## Board Actions Regarding Required Employee Measures

### Suspension of Complaint

The Board has the authority to suspend a complaint if it determines that the complainant must take specific actions within a defined timeframe before the complaint can be addressed. This action is taken pursuant to subsection 251.02(1) of the Code.
"A complaint may be suspended at any time, in whole or in part, pursuant to subsection 251.02(1) if the Head is satisfied that the complainant must take certain measures within a specific time period before the complaint can be dealt with."

### Rejection of Complaint Due to Unmet Measures

If the Board is satisfied that the employee did not take the required measures within the specified timeframe, the complaint can be rejected. This is outlined in section 251.05(1)(b) of the Code.
"If the Head is satisfied that the employee did not take the required measures within the specified time period, the complaint can be rejected."

### Information to the Employee Regarding Required Measures

When considering suspending or rejecting a complaint due to unmet measures, the Board must provide the employee with specific information. This includes a written communication outlining the required actions and the timeframe within which they must be completed.
"The letter will advise that they have 30 days to indicate, in writing, that they wish to pursue their complaint."

### Abandonment of Complaint Due to No Response

If the complainant does not respond to a written communication within a reasonable period of time, and at least 30 days have passed since the complaint was received, the complaint may be rejected.
"If no response is received, the complaint may be rejected."

### Other Means Available to the Employee

The Board may also reject a complaint if it determines that other means are available to the complainant to resolve the complaint. This could include pursuing the complaint with another government body, such as the Canadian Human Rights Commission, or utilizing a collective agreement.
"A complaint may be rejected if it is determined that other means are available to the complainant."

In such cases, the Board should consider suspending the complaint under section 251.02 of the Code as the primary option until the other available means have been pursued and concluded. The Board must demonstrate that these other means are appropriate for resolving the complaint.

individual_results.question: Under what circumstances can the Board reject a complaint made under subsection 246.1(1) of the Canada Labour Code?
individual_results.answer:
## Circumstances for Rejection of a Complaint

### Section 246.3: Rejection of Complaint

Section 246.3 outlines several circumstances under which the Board may reject a complaint made under subsection 246.1(1) of the Canada Labour Code. These reasons are categorized under two main points: general reasons for rejection and reasons for rejection following a suspension of the complaint.

#### General Reasons for Rejection

The Board may reject a complaint
"...if the Board is satisfied that (i) the complaint is not within its jurisdiction, (ii) the complaint is frivolous, vexatious or not made in good faith, (iii) the complaint has been settled in writing between the employer and the employee, (iv) there are other means available to the employee to resolve the subject matter of the complaint that the Board considers should be pursued, (v) the subject matter of the complaint has been adequately dealt with through recourse obtained before a court, tribunal, arbitrator or adjudicator, or (vi) in respect of a complaint made by an employee who is subject to a collective agreement, the collective agreement covers the subject matter of the complaint and provides a third party dispute resolution process..."

This section provides a comprehensive list of grounds for rejection. For instance, it states that the Board may reject a complaint
"...if the Board is satisfied that (i) the complaint is not within its jurisdiction..." This means that if the employee's complaint falls outside the scope of the Canada Labour Code, the Board has no authority to address it.

Furthermore, the Board may reject a complaint if it is deemed "frivolous, vexatious or not made in good faith." This indicates that the Board will not entertain complaints that are baseless, intended to harass the employer, or not made with a genuine belief that a reprisal has occurred.

The section also mentions that a complaint may be rejected
"...the complaint has been settled in writing between the employer and the employee..." This implies that if the parties have reached an agreement to resolve the issue, the Board will not proceed with the complaint.

Finally, the Board may reject a complaint
"...there are other means available to the employee to resolve the subject matter of the complaint that the Board considers should be pursued..." This suggests that the Board may advise the employee to explore alternative avenues for resolution, such as seeking legal counsel or engaging in mediation.

#### Reasons for Rejection Following a Suspension

Section 246.3 also addresses situations where the Board suspends consideration of a complaint and subsequently rejects it. It states that the Board may reject a complaint
"...if consideration of the complaint was suspended under subsection 246.2(1) and if, in the Board’s opinion, the measures specified in the notice under subsection 246.2(2) were not taken within the specified time period."

This means that if the Board suspends a complaint and provides the employee with specific steps to take within a certain timeframe, and the employee fails to comply with those steps, the Board may reject the complaint. This provision ensures that the Board does not indefinitely postpone consideration of a complaint without requiring the employee to take reasonable steps to resolve the issue.

### Section 246.1: Complaint to Board

Section 246.1 details the process for an employee to make a complaint to the Board. It states that
"Any employee may make a complaint in writing to the Board if they believe that their employer has taken any of the following reprisals against them..." This indicates that the Board is the designated body to receive and address complaints related to reprisals.

### Section 246.2: Suspension of Complaint

Section 246.2 outlines the circumstances under which the Board may suspend consideration of a complaint. It states that
"If the Board is satisfied that the employee must take measures before the Board may continue to deal with the complaint made under subsection 246.1(1), it may, at any time, suspend consideration of the complaint, in whole or in part." This provision allows the Board to pause consideration of a complaint if it requires the employee to take certain actions before proceeding.

### Section 246.4: Board Orders

Section 246.4 describes the actions the Board may take if it determines that a complaint is justified. It states that
"If the Board determines that a complaint under subsection 246.1(1) is justified, the Board may, by order, require the employer to cease engaging in or to rescind the reprisal and, if applicable, to (a) permit the employee who has made the complaint to return to the duties of their employment; (b) reinstate the employee; (c) pay to the employee compensation not exceeding the sum that, in the Board’s opinion, is equivalent to the remuneration that would, but for the reprisal, have been paid by the employer to the employee; (d) pay to the employee compensation not exceeding the sum that, in the Board’s opinion, is equivalent to any financial or other penalty imposed on the employee by the employer; and (e) do any other thing that the Board considers equitable for the employer to do to remedy or counteract any consequence of the reprisal." This section details the remedies the Board may order if a complaint is found to be justified.

individual_results.question: How can an order of the Board be enforced in the Federal Court?
individual_results.answer:
## Enforcement of Board Orders in the Federal Court

### Filing in Federal Court

Section 22(1) of the Canada Labour Code establishes the finality of Board orders and decisions, stating,
"Subject to this Part and to any regulations made under paragraph 111.01(1)(g), every order or decision made by the Board under this Part is final and is not to be questioned or reviewed in any court..." However, it also outlines a specific process for enforcement through the Federal Court.

Section 23(1) details this process:
"The Board shall, on the request in writing of any person or organization affected by any order or decision of the Board made under this Part, file a copy of the order or decision, exclusive of reasons, in the Federal Court, unless, in the opinion of the Board, (a) there is no indication of failure or likelihood of failure to comply with the order or decision; or (b) there is other good reason why the filing of the order or decision in the Federal Court would serve no useful purpose." This indicates that any party impacted by a Board order can request the Board to file a copy of the order with the Federal Court.

Section 23(2) further clarifies the acceptance of the filed order:
"Where the Board files a copy of any order or decision in the Federal Court pursuant to subsection (1), it shall specify in writing to the Court that the copy of the order or decision is filed pursuant to that subsection and, where the Board so specifies, the copy of the order or decision shall be accepted for filing by, and registered in, the Court without further application or other proceeding." This means that once the Board files the order, the Federal Court will accept it for registration without needing any further action from the requesting party.

### Registration and Legal Force

Section 23(3) explains the legal effect of the Federal Court registration:
"When a copy of any order or decision of the Board is registered pursuant to subsection (2), the order or decision has the same force and effect as a judgment obtained in the Federal Court and, subject to this section and the Federal Courts Act , all proceedings may be taken thereon by any person or organization affected thereby as if the order or decision were a judgment of that Court." This is a crucial aspect of the enforcement mechanism. By registering the order in the Federal Court, it gains the same legal standing as a judgment issued by that Court. Consequently, all legal actions related to the order can be pursued in the Federal Court as if it were a judgment.

### No Review by Certiorari, etc.

Section 156(1) explicitly states the finality of Board orders and decisions, emphasizing that they
"...shall not be questioned or reviewed in any court." This reinforces the limited scope of judicial review available for Board orders. It further clarifies this point in a marginal note: "No review by certiorari , etc." This directly addresses the question by stating that an order of the Board cannot be challenged or reviewed in any court, including the Federal Court, except under very specific circumstances outlined in the Federal Courts Act.

In summary, an order of the Board can be enforced in the Federal Court by requesting the Board to file a copy of the order with the Court. Upon filing, the Court will register the order, granting it the same legal force and effect as a judgment obtained in that Court. However, it is important to note that Board orders are final and cannot be questioned or reviewed in any court, except under limited circumstances as specified in the Federal Courts Act.

individual_results.question: What are the requirements for an employer to pay wages to an employee according to the Canada Labour Code?
individual_results.answer:
## Wage Payment Requirements Under the Canada Labour Code

### Regular Paydays and Vacation Pay
"Your employer must pay your wages on the regular payday established. Any vacation pay you are owed must be paid at the time you take your vacation. If your employment ends and you are owed vacation pay, your employer must pay it within 30 days after your last day of work." This section clearly outlines the fundamental requirement for employers to pay wages on a regular schedule and to provide vacation pay at the time of vacation or upon termination of employment. The "regular payday established" allows for flexibility in payment frequency, but the deadlines for vacation pay are strictly enforced.

### Pay for Work Reported at Employer's Call
"If you report to work at the call of your employer, you must receive wages for at least 3 hours at your regular rate of wages. This applies whether or not your employer asks you to do any work after reporting to work." This requirement ensures that employees are compensated for their time when they are summoned to work. The minimum pay for work reported at the employer's call is three hours at their regular rate, regardless of whether any work is subsequently assigned.

### Pay for Non-Hourly Basis
"If your employer does not pay you on an hourly basis, you must receive at least the equivalent of the minimum wage. Where the basis of your pay is not time (for example, you may be paid an  annual salary or in accordance with a mileage rate), the Minister of Labour may  fix a rate that is equivalent to at least the minimum wage. This rate is  determined by dividing the amount of salary you received (excluding any  vacation pay, general holiday pay, and overtime pay) by the number of hours  worked you performed." This section addresses situations where employees are paid on a non-hourly basis, such as annual salaries or mileage rates. It mandates that such employees receive at least the equivalent of the minimum wage, with the specific rate determined by dividing the total salary by the number of hours worked.

### Exemptions for Apprentices and Employees Receiving Room and/or Board
"If you are registered under and paid according to a provincial apprenticeship act, your employer is exempt from the application of the minimum wage. If your employer provides you with room and/or board, and you accept that arrangement, your employer may reduce your wages below minimum wage. Your employer cannot reduce your wages more than:  50 cents, for each meal, and 60 cents, per day, for living quarters..." This section outlines specific exemptions from the minimum wage requirement for apprentices and employees receiving room and/or board. Apprentices are exempt from the minimum wage if paid according to a provincial apprenticeship act. Employees receiving room and/or board can have their wages reduced below the minimum wage, but only within specified limits for meals and living quarters.

### Getting Paid for Work
"Your employer must pay your wages on the regular payday established. Any vacation pay you are owed must be paid at the time you take your vacation. If your employment ends and you are owed vacation pay, your employer must pay it within 30 days after your last day of work." This reiterates the fundamental requirement for employers to pay wages on a regular payday and to provide vacation pay at the appropriate times. The 30-day deadline for vacation pay upon termination of employment is also emphasized.

individual_results.question: What are the circumstances under which an employee who is a member of the reserve force is entitled to a leave of absence from their employment?
individual_results.answer:
## Entitlement to Leave of Absence for Members of the Reserve Force

### General Entitlement

Section 247.5(1) of the Canada Labour Code outlines the general entitlement to leave of absence for members of the reserve force. It states:
"An employee who is a member of the reserve force and has completed at least three consecutive months of continuous employment with an employer — or a shorter period that is prescribed for a class of employees to which the employee belongs — is entitled to and shall be granted a leave of absence from employment to take part in the following operations or activities..." This establishes a baseline requirement of at least three consecutive months of continuous employment to qualify for leave.

### Specific Operations and Activities

The section then details the specific operations and activities for which an employee is entitled to leave. These include:
"(a) an operation in Canada or abroad — including preparation, training, rest or travel from or to the employee’s residence — that is designated by the Minister of National Defence..."
"(b) an activity set out in the regulations;"
"(c) Canadian Armed Forces military skills training;"
"(d) training that they are ordered to take under paragraph 33(2)(a) of the National Defence Act..."
"(e) duties that they are called out on service to perform under paragraph 33(2)(b) of the National Defence Act..."
"(f) service in aid of a civil power for which they are called out under section 275 of the National Defence Act ; or..."
"(g) treatment, recovery or rehabilitation in respect of a physical or mental health problem that results from service in an operation or activity referred to in this subsection."

These points provide a comprehensive list of the types of reserve force activities for which leave is granted. The inclusion of
"...treatment, recovery or rehabilitation in respect of a physical or mental health problem that results from service in an operation or activity referred to in this subsection." highlights the consideration for health-related needs arising from reserve force duties.

### Maximum Duration of Leave

Section 247.5(1.1) sets a maximum aggregate duration for leaves taken under certain paragraphs. It states:
"Leaves taken by an employee under paragraphs (1)(a) to (d) can total no more than an aggregate of 24 months in any 60-month period." This limitation prevents an employee from taking extended leaves for the same reserve force activity.

### Exceptions to the Maximum Duration

Section 247.5(1.2) specifies an exception to the maximum duration rule. It says:
"Subsection (1.1) does not apply to a leave of absence taken as a result of a , within the meaning of the Emergencies Act..." This indicates that leaves taken as a direct result of an emergency, as defined by the Emergencies Act, are not subject to the 24-month aggregate limit.

### Conditions for Entitlement

Section 247.5(4) outlines a condition under which an employee is not entitled to leave. It states:
"Despite subsection (1), an employee is not entitled to a leave of absence under this Division if, in the opinion of the Head, it would adversely affect public health or safety or would cause undue hardship to the employer if the employee, as an individual or as a member of a class of employees, were to take leave." This provision allows for the denial of leave in cases where it would pose a risk to public safety or create significant difficulties for the employer.

## Notice and Communication Requirements for Leave of Absence

### General Notice Requirements

Section 207(1) of the Canada Labour Code outlines the general notice requirements for an employee taking a leave of absence. It states:
"Every employee who intends to take a leave of absence from employment under section 206 or 206.1 shall (a) unless there is a valid reason for not doing so, give at least four weeks notice in writing to the employer before the day on which the leave is to begin; and (b) inform the employer in writing of the length of leave intended to be taken."
This indicates that employees must provide their employer with a minimum of four weeks' written notice before the leave begins, and they must also inform the employer of the planned duration of the leave. The exception to this rule is when there is a valid reason for not providing the notice, in which case the employee must notify the employer as soon as possible.

### Notice of Change in Length of Leave

Section 207(2) further details the notice requirements for any change in the length of a leave of absence. It specifies:
"Every employee who intends to take or who is on a leave of absence from employment under section 206 or 206.1 shall provide the employer with notice in writing of at least four weeks of any change in the length of leave intended to be taken, unless there is a valid reason why that notice cannot be given, in which case the employee shall provide the employer with notice in writing as soon as possible."
This means that if an employee wishes to shorten or extend their leave, they must inform their employer in writing of the change at least four weeks in advance, unless there is a valid reason why this cannot be done.

### Documentation Requirements

Section 207(4) addresses the employer's right to request supporting documentation. It states:
"The employer may require the employee to provide documentation in support of the reasons for the leave taken under section 206.4, 206.5 or 206.9 and of any change in the length of leave that the employee intends to take."
This allows the employer to verify the reasons for the leave and any changes to its duration.

### Return to Work Postponement

Section 207(5) outlines the employer's ability to postpone an employee's return to work if the employee does not provide the required four weeks' notice of a change in the leave's end date. It says:
"If an employee who takes a leave of more than four weeks under any of sections 206.3 to 206.5 wishes to shorten the length of the leave but does not provide the employer with four weeks’ notice, the employer may postpone the employee’s return to work for a period of up to four weeks after the day on which the employee informs the employer of the new end date of the leave. If the employer informs the employee that their return to work is postponed, the employee is not entitled to return to work until the day that is indicated by the employer."
This provides the employer with a mechanism to manage disruptions to the workforce when an employee changes the length of their leave without providing adequate notice.

### Deemed Part of Leave

Section 207(6) clarifies that the period of any return to work postponement is considered part of the leave. It states:
"The period of the postponement is deemed to be part of the leave."
This ensures that the leave period is accurately calculated, even if the return to work is delayed.

individual_results.question: What are the responsibilities of an employee who takes a leave of absence for military purposes in terms of providing documentation to their employer and notifying them of their return to work?
individual_results.answer:
## Employee Responsibilities Regarding Military Leave Documentation and Return to Work Notification

### Providing Documentation to Employer

#### Request for Proof of Qualification
"Your employer can request within 3 weeks after the start date of the leave, proof that you qualify for this leave. In this case, you must provide documentation approved by the Chief of the Defence Staff or their Commander, unless there is a valid reason not to do so." This passage outlines the employer's right to request documentation verifying the employee's eligibility for the military leave. The employee is then obligated to provide this documentation, which must be approved by a designated authority unless a valid reason exists for not doing so.

#### Timing of Documentation Submission
"Unless there is a valid reason for not doing so, the employee shall provide the document referred to in subsection (1) or (2) within three weeks after the day on which the leave begins." This section specifies the timeframe within which the employee must submit the required documentation upon the commencement of their military leave.

### Notifying Employer of Return to Work

#### Written Notice for Leave Start and End
"To take this leave, you must provide a 4 weeks’ written notice to your employer indicating:  the length of the leave, unless you gave a valid reason not to do so, and your intention to extend or shorten the leave, unless you have a valid reason not to do so..." This passage details the mandatory written notice requirement for initiating a military leave. The employee must provide this notice at least four weeks prior to the leave's start date, specifying the intended duration and any potential extensions or shortenings.

#### Extension or Shortening of Leave
"You may extend or shorten your leave period once it has started. As a reservist, you may extend your leave if you need to receive treatments or undergo a rehabilitation program to recover from a physical or mental problem resulting from your service while on leave.  If you shorten your leave:   you must give at least 4 weeks’ notice before the new date on which it would end, unless you have a valid reason not to do so  If you extend your leave:   you must give at least 4 weeks’ notice before the date on which the leave was previously scheduled to end, unless you have a valid reason no to do so..." This section addresses the possibility of extending or shortening the military leave once it has begun. The employee is required to provide at least four weeks' notice for any such changes, unless a valid reason exists for not doing so.

#### Employer's Right to Postpone Return
"If the employee does not notify the employer at least four weeks before the day on which the leave that is taken under this Division is to end, the employer may postpone the employee’s return to work for a period of up to four weeks after the day on which the employee informs the employer of the end date of the leave." This passage explains the employer's right to postpone the employee's return to work if the required four-week notice for a leave extension or shortening is not provided. The postponement can last up to four weeks after the employer receives the notice.

#### Deemed Part of Leave
"The period of postponement referred to in subsection (1) is deemed to be part of the leave." This clarifies that any return-to-work postponement is considered an extension of the military leave.

individual_results.question: What happens to an employee's employment status and position when they return to work after taking a leave of absence under this Division?
individual_results.answer:
## Employment Status and Position Upon Return from Leave

### Continuous Employment and Benefits
"For the purposes of calculating the benefits of an employee who takes a leave of absence under this Division, employment on the employee’s return to work is deemed to be continuous with their employment before the leave." This section clarifies that an employee's prior employment is considered uninterrupted upon their return from leave. This continuity is crucial for benefit calculations, as it ensures that the employee accrues benefits as if they had never taken the leave.

Furthermore,
"The seniority of an employee who takes a leave of absence under this Division shall accumulate during the leave." This indicates that an employee's seniority, which often impacts benefits and job opportunities, continues to build up even while they are on leave. This ensures that their seniority is not lost and that they retain their standing within the organization upon their return.

### Resumption of Employment in Same Position
"At the end of a leave of absence that is taken under this Division, the employer shall reinstate the employee in the position that the employee occupied on the day before the day on which the leave begins." This is a fundamental provision regarding the employee's position upon return. It mandates that the employer must return the employee to their original role, with the same wages and benefits, as they held before the leave commenced.
"If for a valid reason an employer is not able to reinstate the employee in that position, they shall reinstate the employee in a comparable position with the same wages and benefits and in the same location." This section addresses situations where the original position is no longer available. It stipulates that the employer must instead reinstate the employee in a comparable position, ensuring that they retain their original compensation and work environment.

### Not Able to Perform Work
"Subject to the regulations, if an employee is not able to perform the functions of the position that they occupy before the leave begins — or those of a comparable position, with the same wages and benefits and in the same location — the employer may assign them to a position with different terms or conditions of employment." This provision outlines an exception to the reinstatement requirement. If an employee is no longer able to perform the duties of their original or a comparable position, the employer may assign them to a different position with similar compensation and location. This ensures that the employee remains employed but may need to adjust their role based on their current capabilities.

individual_results.question: What protections are provided to employees who are members of the reserve force and take a leave of absence under the Canada Labour Code?
individual_results.answer:
## Protections for Reserve Force Members Taking Leave

### Entitlement to Leave

#### Section 247.5: Entitlement to Leave
"An employee who is a member of the reserve force and has completed at least three consecutive months of continuous employment with an employer — or a shorter period that is prescribed for a class of employees to which the employee belongs — is entitled to and shall be granted a leave of absence from employment to take part in the following operations or activities: (a) an operation in Canada or abroad — including preparation, training, rest or travel from or to the employee’s residence — that is designated by the Minister of National Defence; (b) an activity set out in the regulations; (c) Canadian Armed Forces military skills training; (d) training that they are ordered to take under paragraph 33(2)(a) of the National Defence Act ; (e) duties that they are called out on service to perform under paragraph 33(2)(b) of the National Defence Act ; (f) service in aid of a civil power for which they are called out under section 275 of the National Defence Act ; or (g) treatment, recovery or rehabilitation in respect of a physical or mental health problem that results from service in an operation or activity referred to in this subsection." This section clearly establishes the right of reserve force members to take a leave of absence. It specifies the conditions for entitlement – at least three consecutive months of continuous employment – and outlines the various operations and activities for which leave can be granted. This provision ensures that reserve force members can fulfill their military obligations without jeopardizing their civilian employment.

#### Section 247.5(1.1): Maximum Leave Duration
"Leaves taken by an employee under paragraphs (1)(a) to (d) can total no more than an aggregate of 24 months in any 60-month period." This subsection sets a limit on the total duration of leave an employee can take under the specified operations and activities. This provision aims to balance the needs of reserve force members with the operational requirements of their employers.

### Resumption of Employment

#### Section 247.91: Continuous Employment Benefits
"For the purposes of calculating the benefits of an employee who takes a leave of absence under this Division, employment on the employee’s return to work is deemed to be continuous with their employment before the leave." This section ensures that employees returning from reserve force leave retain their seniority and benefits as if they had never taken the leave. It states that their employment on their return is considered continuous with their employment prior to the leave.

#### Section 247.92: Application of Section 189
"Section 189 applies for the purposes of this Division." This section refers to another part of the Canada Labour Code that provides further protections for employees on leave. Section 189 deals with the reinstatement of employees in their former positions or comparable positions upon their return from leave.

#### Section 247.93: Resumption of Employment in Same Position
"(1) At the end of a leave of absence that is taken under this Division, the employer shall reinstate the employee in the position that the employee occupied on the day before the day on which the leave begins." This provision reinforces the right to reinstatement in the same position upon return from leave. It mandates that the employer must return the employee to their previous role.

#### Section 247.93(2): Comparable Position
"(2) If for a valid reason an employer is not able to reinstate the employee in that position, they shall reinstate the employee in a comparable position with the same wages and benefits and in the same location." This section provides an alternative to reinstatement in the same position. If reinstatement is not feasible for a valid reason, the employer must offer a comparable position with equivalent wages and benefits.

#### Section 247.95: Prohibition on Adverse Employment Actions
"(1) If, during a leave of absence that is taken under this Division, the wages or benefits of the group of employees of which an employee is a member are changed as part of a plan to reorganize the industrial establishment in which that group is employed, the employee is entitled, on reinstatement under this section, to receive the wages and benefits in respect of that employment that that employee would have been entitled to receive had that employee been working when the reorganization took place." This section protects employees from negative employment actions resulting from a reorganization during their leave. It ensures that upon reinstatement, the employee receives the wages and benefits they would have received had they remained employed during the reorganization.

#### Section 247.96: Prohibition on Discrimination
"(1) No employer may dismiss, suspend, lay off, demote or discipline an employee because they are a member of the reserve force or intend to take or have taken a leave of absence under this Division or take into account the fact that an employee is a member of the reserve force or intends to take or has taken a leave of absence under this Division in a decision to promote or train them." This section explicitly prohibits employers from taking adverse employment actions against reserve force members or those taking leave. It ensures that military service and leave do not negatively impact an employee's career progression or job security.

#### Section 247.96(2): Prohibition on Refusal of Employment
"(2) No person may refuse to employ a person because they are a member of the reserve force." This provision further reinforces the protection against discrimination. It states that employers cannot refuse to hire individuals who are members of the reserve force.

### Employer Obligations During Leave

#### Section 247.92(2): Notice of Wage or Benefit Changes
"(2) The employer of an employee who is on leave and whose wages or benefits would be changed as a result of the reorganization shall, as soon as practicable, send a notice to the employee at their last known address." This section mandates that employers must inform employees on leave of any changes to their wages or benefits resulting from a reorganization. This ensures transparency and allows employees to make informed decisions about their return to work.

individual_results.question: What is the purpose of the regulations that the Governor in Council may make under section 247.97 of the Canada Labour Code?
individual_results.answer:
## Purpose of Regulations under Section 247.97 of the Canada Labour Code

### Overview

Section 247.97 of the Canada Labour Code grants the Governor in Council the authority to enact regulations for carrying out the purposes of Division XV.2, which pertains to Leave of Absence for Members of the Reserve Force. The purpose of these regulations is to provide detailed guidance and specific rules for the application of the provisions outlined in this Division.

### Specific Purposes of the Regulations

The regulations that the Governor in Council may make under section 247.97 serve a variety of specific purposes, as detailed in the text.

#### Specifying Absences Not Interrupting Continuity of Employment
"...specifying the absences that are deemed not to interrupt continuity of employment for the purpose of subsection 247.5(1)..."
This regulation aims to clarify which absences are not considered to break an employee's continuous employment. It provides a framework for determining the impact of reserve force leave on employment status.

#### Defining Operations and Activities
"...specifying what constitutes or does not constitute an operation for the purposes of paragraph 247.5(1)(a)..."
"...setting out the activities for the purposes of paragraph 247.5(1)(b)..."
These regulations focus on defining the scope of "operation" and "activities" as they relate to reserve force leave. This ensures clarity in determining eligibility for leave.

#### Defining Military Skills Training
"...defining “military skills training” for the purposes of paragraph 247.5(1)(c)..."
This regulation provides a precise definition of "military skills training," which is a specific type of activity that may qualify for leave.

#### Limiting Treatment and Recovery
"...limiting the duration of the treatment, recovery or rehabilitation referred to in paragraph 247.5(1)(g) or setting out the terms or conditions for the application of that paragraph..."
This regulation establishes limitations or conditions for the duration of treatment, recovery, or rehabilitation related to reserve force leave.

#### Specifying Undue Hardship
"...specifying what constitutes or does not constitute undue hardship for the purposes of subsection 247.5(4)..."
This regulation aims to define what level of hardship would prevent an employer from granting a leave of absence.

#### Specifying Valid Reasons for Leave
"...specifying what constitutes or does not constitute a valid reason for the purposes of subsection 247.6(1), (2), (3) or (4), 247.7(3) or 247.93(2)..."
This regulation clarifies the acceptable reasons for an employee to request a leave of absence for reserve force duties.

#### Specifying Circumstances Where Sections Do Not Apply
"...specifying the circumstances in which section 247.7, subsection 247.8(1) or subsection 247.91(2) does not apply..."
This regulation outlines situations where certain provisions of the Division would not be applicable.

#### Specifying Circumstances Where Employers May Not Assign Employees to Different Terms
"...specifying the circumstances in which an employer may not assign an employee to a position with different terms or conditions of employment for the purposes of section 247.94..."
This regulation clarifies when an employer might not be able to assign an employee to a position with different terms of employment upon their return from reserve force leave.

#### Prescribing Classes of Employees Not Entitled to Leave
"...prescribing the classes of employees that are not entitled to a leave of absence under this Division if the Governor in Council is satisfied that the fact of taking leave would cause unreasonable consequences..."
"...prescribing the circumstances in which classes of employees are not entitled to a leave of absence under this Division."
These regulations allow the Governor in Council to specify classes of employees who would not be entitled to leave if it would create unreasonable consequences for the employer.

In essence, the regulations under section 247.97 of the Canada Labour Code are designed to provide a comprehensive and detailed framework for the application of the Leave of Absence for Members of the Reserve Force provisions within Division XV.2. They aim to ensure clarity, consistency, and fairness in the process of granting and managing such leaves.

individual_results.question: What protections does the Canada Labour Code provide to employees regarding genetic testing and the disclosure of genetic test results?
individual_results.answer:
## Protections for Employees Regarding Genetic Testing and Disclosure of Results

### Right Not to Undergo or Disclose Genetic Tests

The Canada Labour Code explicitly protects employees' rights regarding genetic testing. Section 247.98(2) states,
"Every employee is entitled not to undergo or be required to undergo a genetic test." This establishes a fundamental right for employees to refuse genetic testing without fear of reprisal.

Furthermore, Section 247.98(3) reinforces this right by stating,
"Every employee is entitled not to disclose or be required to disclose the results of a genetic test." This protects employees from being compelled to share genetic test results, safeguarding their privacy and autonomy.

### Prohibitions Against Reprisal

The Canada Labour Code prohibits employers from taking disciplinary action against employees based on genetic test results or their refusal to undergo or disclose such tests. Section 247.98(4) clearly articulates this protection:
"No employer shall dismiss, suspend, lay off or demote an employee, impose a financial or other penalty on an employee, or refuse to pay an employee remuneration in respect of any period that the employee would, but for the exercise of the employee’s rights under this Division, have worked, or take any disciplinary action against or threaten to take any such action against an employee (a) because the employee refused a request by the employer to undergo a genetic test; (b) because the employee refused to disclose the results of a genetic test; or (c) on the basis of the results of a genetic test undergone by the employee."

This provision ensures that employees will not face negative employment consequences for exercising their rights related to genetic testing.

### Restrictions on Disclosure by Third Parties

The Canada Labour Code also places restrictions on third parties disclosing genetic test results to employers without the employee's written consent. Section 247.98(5) states,
"No person shall disclose to an employer that an employee has undergone a genetic test, or disclose to an employer the results of a genetic test, without the written consent of the employee." This protects employees' privacy by preventing unauthorized disclosure of sensitive genetic information.

### Requirements for Consent Regarding Collection or Use of Genetic Test Results

The Canada Labour Code mandates that employers obtain the employee's written consent before collecting or using the results of a genetic test. Section 247.98(6) specifies,
"No employer shall collect or use the results of a genetic test without the written consent of the employee who has undergone the test." This ensures that employees have control over how their genetic information is used.

### Extension of Time to File a Complaint

The Canada Labour Code provides an extension of time to file a complaint in certain circumstances. Section 247.991(3) states,
"The Head may extend the period of time referred to in subsection (2) (a) if the Head is satisfied that a complaint was made in that period to a government official who had no authority to deal with the complaint but that the employee making the complaint believed the official had that authority; or (b) in any other circumstance that is prescribed by regulation." This allows employees who may have mistakenly filed a complaint with the wrong government official or whose initial complaint was incomplete or contained an error, an additional 14 days to file a complaint with the Labour Program.
