## Steps an Employee Can Take if They Believe Their Employer Has Taken Action Against Them in Contravention of Subsection 247.98(4)

### Filing a Complaint with the Board

According to Section 247.98(4) of the Canada Labour Code, an employee who believes their employer has taken disciplinary action against them because they refused a genetic test, refused to disclose the results of a genetic test, or on the basis of the results of a genetic test undergone by the employee, can file a complaint in writing to the Board.
"No employer shall dismiss, suspend, lay off or demote an employee, impose a financial or other penalty on an employee, or refuse to pay an employee remuneration in respect of any period that the employee would, but for the exercise of the employee’s rights under this Division, have worked, or take any disciplinary action against or threaten to take any such action against an employee (a) because the employee refused a request by the employer to undergo a genetic test; (b) because the employee refused to disclose the results of a genetic test; or (c) on the basis of the results of a genetic test undergone by the employee."

This section explicitly outlines the types of disciplinary actions that are prohibited under subsection 247.98(4). If an employee believes their employer has taken any of these actions due to their refusal of a genetic test or disclosure of results, they can initiate a complaint process with the Board.

### The Role of the Head

The Head plays a crucial role in handling complaints related to genetic testing. According to Section 247.98(5),
"No person shall disclose to an employer that an employee has undergone a genetic test, or disclose to an employer the results of a genetic test, without the written consent of the employee." This indicates that the Head is responsible for ensuring the confidentiality of genetic test results and preventing unauthorized disclosure.

Furthermore, Section 247.98(6) states,
"No employer shall collect or use the results of a genetic test without the written consent of the employee who has undergone the test." This implies that the Head is involved in overseeing the proper collection and use of genetic test results by employers.

### The Role of the Board

The Board is the primary body for hearing complaints related to genetic testing and other prohibited disciplinary actions. Section 247.98(4) details the process for filing a complaint:
"Any employee may make a complaint in writing to the Board if they believe that their employer has taken any of the following reprisals against them: (a) the employer has taken action against the employee in contravention of subsection 173.01(5), 174.1(4) or 177.1(7) or of section 208, 209.3, 238, 239, 239.1 or 247.96; (a.1) [Repealed, 2021, c. 26, s. 25] (b) dismissing, suspending, laying off, or demoting the employee, imposing a financial or other penalty on the employee, or otherwise taking any disciplinary action against the employee, because the employee (i) has made a complaint under this Part, other than a complaint under section 240, (ii) has provided information regarding the wages, hours of work, annual vacation or conditions of work of any employee to the Head or provided any other assistance to the Minister or the Head in the exercise or performance of the Minister’s or the Head’s powers, duties and functions under this Part (ii.1) has provided information regarding the wages, hours of work, annual vacation or conditions of work of any employee or provided any other assistance to an external adjudicator or a member of the Board in the exercise or performance, in accordance with subsections 12.001(2) or 14(5), of the powers, duties or functions conferred on the Board by this Part, (iii) has testified or is about to testify in a proceeding taken or an inquiry held under this Part, or (iv) has exercised, or sought to exercise, any right conferred on the employee by this Part; (c) taking into account the fact that the employee has taken any of the actions referred to in subparagraphs (b)(i) to (iv) in any decision with respect to the promotion or training of the employee; or (d) threatening to take any of the reprisals referred to in paragraph (b) or (c)."

This section outlines the range of reprisals that can be the subject of a complaint to the Board. If an employee believes their employer has taken action against them due to their refusal of a genetic test or disclosure of results, they can file a complaint with the Board, which will then investigate the matter and determine if a violation of subsection 247.98(4) has occurred. The Board has the authority to issue orders to remedy the situation, such as requiring the employer to reinstate the employee or to cease the discriminatory disciplinary action.

individual_results.question: What is the effect of an order made by the Board under section 247.99 of the Canada Labour Code, and how does it interact with the court system?
individual_results.answer:
## Effect of a Board Order under Section 247.99 and Interaction with the Court System

### Finality of Board Orders

Section 247.991 of the Canada Labour Code establishes the finality of Board orders. It states,
"Every order of the Board is final and shall not be questioned or reviewed in any court." This indicates a strong limitation on judicial review of Board decisions made under this section. The language is unequivocal, prohibiting any attempt to challenge the Board's order in the courts.

### Enforcement of Board Orders through Federal Court

Despite the finality of Board orders, the Canada Labour Code provides a mechanism for their enforcement through the Federal Court. Section 246.6 outlines this process:
"Any person affected by an order of the Board under section 246.4, or the Head on the request of such a person, may, after 14 days from the day on which the order is made, or from the day provided in the order for compliance, whichever is later, file in the Federal Court a copy of the order, exclusive of reasons." This passage directly addresses how a Board order is made legally binding. It specifies the timeframe within which a party affected by the order can seek judicial registration.

Furthermore, Section 246.6 details the legal effect of this filing:
"On filing in the Federal Court under subsection (1), an order of the Board shall be registered in the Court and, when registered, has the same force and effect, and all proceedings may be taken in respect of it, as if the order were a judgment obtained in that Court." This is a crucial point regarding the Board order's interaction with the court system. It clarifies that the Federal Court registration imbues the Board order with the same legal power as a judgment issued by the Court itself. This means that all legal proceedings, including injunctions, certiorari, prohibition, quo warranto, and other actions, can be initiated in the Federal Court to enforce the Board order.

### Prohibition of Court Action to Question Board Orders

Section 243(2) reinforces the finality of Board orders by explicitly prohibiting court action to challenge them. It states,
"No order shall be made, process entered or proceeding taken in any court, whether by way of injunction, certiorari , prohibition, quo warranto or otherwise, to question, review, prohibit or restrain the Board in any proceedings under section 242." This passage is a direct and forceful statement against attempting to overturn or interfere with a Board order through the court system. It emphasizes the exclusive jurisdiction of the Board in matters falling under section 242.

### Civil Remedies Remain

Section 247.992 clarifies that filing a complaint under section 247.99 does not impact an employee's civil remedies against their employer. It states,
"The making of a complaint under subsection 247.99(1) does not suspend or affect an employee’s civil remedies against their employer." This indicates that the Board's order process does not preclude employees from pursuing other legal avenues against their employers.

In summary, an order made by the Board under section 247.99 of the Canada Labour Code is final and not subject to judicial review in any court. However, it can be enforced through the Federal Court by registering the Board order as a judgment. The Canada Labour Code also explicitly prohibits court action to question or restrain the Board in any proceedings under section 242, further solidifying the finality of Board orders. Importantly, the Board's order process does not affect an employee's civil remedies against their employer.

individual_results.question: What actions can the Minister take to investigate employment in industrial establishments, and who can be appointed to carry out this investigation?
individual_results.answer:
## Minister's Actions to Investigate Employment

### Initiating an Inquiry

The Minister has several actions they can take to investigate employment in industrial establishments. One primary action is to
"...cause an inquiry to be made into and concerning employment in any industrial establishment..." This is explicitly stated in Section 248(1) of the Canada Labour Code. The Minister can also
"...appoint one or more persons to hold the inquiry." This indicates the Minister has the authority to select individuals to lead or participate in the investigation.

### Utilizing Special Committees

The Minister can also establish
"...committees of persons to assist or advise the Minister on any matter that the Minister considers advisable concerning occupational health and safety related to employment to which this Part applies." This is outlined in Section 138(1). These committees can be appointed to provide support and expertise to the Minister in addressing occupational health and safety concerns within industrial establishments.

### Requesting an Inquiry through the Governor in Council

The Minister can also request an inquiry be held under Section 12.08. This is done by
"...the Governor in Council to have an inquiry held under section 12.08..." Upon receiving such a request, the Governor in Council may appoint a judge of a superior court to conduct the inquiry, "on the recommendation of the Minister of Justice."

## Who Can Be Appointed to Carry Out the Investigation

Several types of individuals can be appointed to carry out the investigations initiated by the Minister.

### Commissioners under the Inquiries Act

A person appointed pursuant to subsection (2) of Section 248
"...has all of the powers of a person appointed as a commissioner under Part I of the Inquiries Act..." This means that commissioners appointed to conduct inquiries have the same legal authority as those appointed under the Inquiries Act.

### Judges of a Superior Court

The Governor in Council may appoint a judge of a superior court to conduct an inquiry upon the Minister's request, "on the recommendation of the Minister of Justice." This appointment grants the judge all the powers, rights, and privileges vested in a superior court, including the power to issue summonses, administer oaths, and examine witnesses.

### Members of Special Committees

The Minister can appoint "committees of persons" to assist or advise them on occupational health and safety matters. These committee members can play a significant role in conducting investigations, gathering information, and providing expert opinions.

### Inquirers Appointed by the Governor in Council

The Governor in Council may appoint an inquirer to conduct an inquiry upon the Minister's request, "on the recommendation of the Minister of Justice." This appointment allows for the selection of individuals with specific expertise or experience relevant to the inquiry's subject matter.

## Head's Powers to Gather Information and Conduct Inspections

### Conducting Inspections

The Head possesses significant powers to gather information through inspections. Section 141.1 outlines the Head's authority to conduct workplace inspections. It states,
"If the Head conducts an inspection of the work place at the work place, it shall be done in the presence of (a) an employee member and an employer member of the work place committee; or (b) the health and safety representative and a person designated by the employer." This indicates that inspections are conducted with the involvement of workplace representatives, ensuring transparency and potentially facilitating cooperation.

Furthermore, Section 249 details the Head's power to
"...inspect and examine all books, payrolls and other records of an employer that relate to the wages, hours of work or conditions of employment affecting any employee..." This broad power allows the Head to delve into employer records to gather comprehensive information about employee terms and conditions. The Head can also
"...take extracts from or make copies of any entry in the books, payrolls and other records mentioned in paragraph (a)..." This enables the Head to retain and analyze specific data for further investigation.

The Head also has the authority to
"...require any employer to make or furnish full and correct statements, either orally or in writing, in such form as may be required, respecting the wages paid to all or any of his employees, and the hours of work and conditions of their employment..." This power ensures that employers provide accurate and complete information regarding their employees' compensation and working conditions.

### Powers for Inquiry and Delegation

The Head has extensive powers to gather information through inquiries. Section 248 states,
"The Minister may, (a) for any of the purposes of this Part, cause an inquiry to be made into and concerning employment in any industrial establishment; and (b) appoint one or more persons to hold the inquiry." This grants the Minister the authority to initiate formal inquiries into employment matters.

Section 249 elaborates on the Head's power to delegate these powers. It states,
"Subject to any terms and conditions specified by the Minister, the Head may delegate to any qualified person or class of persons any of the powers the Head is authorized to exercise or any of the duties or functions the Head is authorized to perform for the purposes of this Part." This allows the Head to distribute the burden of information gathering and inspection to qualified individuals or groups.

The Head can also make these delegations subject to specific terms and conditions. Section 249(1.1) mandates that the Head furnish a certificate of authority to every person to whom powers, duties, or functions are delegated. This certificate must be produced upon request when entering a federal work, undertaking, or business.

### Assistance and Accompaniment

The Head can be assisted or accompanied by various individuals during inspections and inquiries. Section 249(3) states,
"The person in charge of any federal work, undertaking or business and every person employed in it or in connection with its operation shall give the Head all reasonable assistance to enable the Head to carry out the Head’s duties and functions under this Part or the regulations." This ensures that employers and their representatives cooperate with the Head's information-gathering efforts.

Section 249(4) further clarifies that the Head may
"...be accompanied or assisted by any persons that the Head considers necessary." This allows the Head to bring along experts or other individuals whose assistance may be beneficial during inspections and inquiries.

### Powers Regarding Oaths and Records

The Head also has powers to gather information through oaths and records. Section 250 states,
"The Head may administer all oaths and take and receive all affidavits and statutory declarations required with respect to the Head’s powers set out in subsection 249(2) and certify to the administration, taking or receiving of them." This allows the Head to obtain sworn statements and declarations from individuals relevant to the inquiries and inspections.

Section 249(2) grants the Head the power to
"...inspect and examine all books, payrolls and other records of an employer that relate to the wages, hours of work or conditions of employment affecting any employee..." This broad power allows the Head to access a wide range of employer records to gather comprehensive information.

individual_results.question: What happens if an employer is found to have failed to pay an employee the wages or other amounts they are entitled to under the Canada Labour Code, and how does this impact potential prosecution?
individual_results.answer:
## Employer Failure to Pay Wages and Potential Prosecution

### Consequences of Failure to Pay Wages

According to the Canada Labour Code, if an employer is found to have failed to pay an employee the wages or other amounts they are entitled to, several consequences can occur.

#### Labour Program Findings and Potential Enforcement Actions

The Labour Program will issue written findings to both the employee and the employer. This may include a Notice of Unfounded Complaint, which states the employer is in compliance and explains the reasons, while also providing the employee with an opportunity to request a review. However, if the Labour Program identifies a pattern of non-compliance, it will advise the employer on their responsibilities under the Code. Failure to comply can lead to various enforcement actions.

The Labour Program may initiate compliance orders to stop ongoing non-compliance. As of January 1, 2021, they can issue a compliance order to prevent future violations of the Code and its Regulations. Additionally, the Labour Program may issue an administrative monetary penalty (AMP) notice if the employer does not correct a contravention.

#### Payment Orders and Collection

If the employer does not voluntarily comply, the Labour Program can issue a payment order to the employer or to a director of the corporation to collect unpaid wages. An administrative fee will be added to the payment order, either a flat fee of \$200 or 15% of the total amount owed, whichever is greater.

If the employer or their director does not pay the payment order, the Labour Program can collect the amounts owed from various sources, including the debtor's debtors, their financial institution, or the debtors or financial institution of one or more directors of their corporation.

#### Director's Liability

In situations where wage recovery from the employer is unlikely or impossible, the Labour Program may hold the corporation's directors jointly and individually liable for the amounts employers owe to employees during their time as director. This liability is capped at 6 months' wages. The Labour Program can then collect from a director’s debtors or financial institution.

### Potential Prosecution

The Labour Program has the option to pursue prosecutions if the employer does not correct a contravention of the Code or Regulations, particularly if the employer is fully aware of their legal obligations and still willfully breaks the law. Repeat contraventions are considered intentional or willful actions.

If found guilty, the employer may be subject to significant fines. A corporation can face fines up to \$50,000 for the first offence, \$100,000 for the second, and \$250,000 for the third (and subsequent) offences. An employer who is not incorporated can face fines up to \$10,000 for the first offence, \$20,000 for the second, and \$50,000 for the third (and subsequent) offences.

#### Public Naming of Employers

The Labour Program will also publish information about employers who violate the Code, including all payment orders of \$5000 or greater filed in federal court, administrative monetary penalties (with some exceptions), and prosecutions. This public naming serves as a deterrent to other employers who may be considering non-compliance.

In summary, if an employer is found to have failed to pay an employee the wages or other amounts they are entitled to under the Canada Labour Code, the Labour Program can take a range of enforcement actions, including issuing compliance orders, payment orders, and administrative monetary penalties. Furthermore, the Labour Program has the power to pursue prosecutions against employers who do not correct their non-compliance, potentially leading to substantial fines for the corporation and its directors.

individual_results.question: What are the circumstances under which the Head may order an employer to conduct an internal audit of its practices and records, and what information must be included in the report?
individual_results.answer:
## Circumstances for Ordering an Internal Audit

### General Authority for Ordering an Internal Audit

The Head possesses the authority to order an employer to conduct an internal audit under specific circumstances. This authority is exercised through a written order. The purpose of such an order is to "verify compliance or preventing non-compliance with this Part." This indicates that the Head can initiate an internal audit to ensure adherence to the provisions of the Canada Labour Code and its regulations.

### Specific Circumstances Triggering an Internal Audit Order

The Head may issue an internal audit order based on several specific circumstances. These include:

1.  **Verifying Compliance:** The primary reason for an internal audit order is to
"...compliance with any provision of this Part or the regulations..." This means the Head can order an audit to check if the employer is following the rules outlined in the Canada Labour Code and its associated regulations.
2.  **Preventing Non-Compliance:** The Head can also order an internal audit "for preventing non-compliance." This suggests a proactive approach, where the Head can initiate an audit to identify and address potential violations before they occur.
3.  **Specific Industrial Establishments and Employee Classes:** The Head must specify in the order
"...any industrial establishment and class of employees to which it applies..." This ensures that the internal audit is targeted and relevant to the employer's specific operations and workforce.
4.  **Audit Period:** The order must also state
"...the period of time to be covered by the internal audit..." This defines the timeframe for the audit, allowing the Head to focus on a particular period of the employer's practices and records.
5.  **Specific Provisions Under Review:** The Head must identify
"...the provisions of this Part or the regulations with respect to which the internal audit was ordered..." This clarifies the specific areas of compliance that the internal audit is intended to address.
6.  **Report Deadline and Format:** The order must include
"...the date by which the employer is to provide the report..." and "the form of the report." This sets a timeline for the report submission and specifies the required format for the report.

## Information Required in the Report

The report submitted by the employer following an internal audit must contain specific information.

### General Contents of the Report

The employer must
"...set out in the report the nature of the employer’s non-compliance and the steps that have been or will be taken by the employer to comply with the provision." This means the report must detail any instances of non-compliance identified during the audit and the employer's plans to rectify those issues.

### Specific Information on Wages and Other Amounts

If the employer determines that any wages or other amounts to which an employee is entitled under the Part are owed, the report must include detailed information. This includes
"...the name of the employee, the amount owed for the period of time covered by the internal audit, the method used to determine the amount owed and any payment subsequently made to the employee with respect to that amount owed." This ensures transparency and accountability regarding employee entitlements.

### Additional Information the Head May Specify

The Head may also mandate the inclusion of additional information in the report. The Head can
"...also specify in the order that the report is to contain any information that the Head considers appropriate." This allows the Head to request any other relevant details that may be necessary to assess compliance.

### False Information Prohibition

The employer is strictly prohibited from providing false or misleading information in the report. The text states,
"No employer shall make a false or misleading statement in a report." This underscores the importance of accuracy and honesty in the internal audit report.

individual_results.question: What is the process and timeframe for employees to make complaints about potential contraventions of the Canada Labour Code by their employer?
individual_results.answer:
## Process and Timeframe for Employees to Make Complaints

### Making a Complaint

#### To Whom Complaints Can Be Made
"...any person or organization may make a complaint in writing to the Board that (a) an employer, a person acting on behalf of an employer, a trade union, a person acting on behalf of a trade union or an employee has contravened or failed to comply with subsection 24(4) or 34(6) or section 37, 47.3, 50, 69, 87.5 or 87.6, subsection 87.7(2) or section 94, 95 or 96.1; or (b) any person has failed to comply with section 96." This section outlines the broad scope of who can file a complaint. It specifies that not only employees but also trade unions and individuals acting on their behalf can lodge complaints. The complaint is directed to the Labour Program, which is now referred to as the Board in this section.

#### Format of the Complaint
"...a complaint pursuant to subsection (1) must be made to the Board not later than ninety days after the date on which the complainant knew, or in the opinion of the Board ought to have known, of the action or circumstances giving rise to the complaint." This passage details the required format and timeframe for submitting a complaint. It mandates a written complaint and sets a strict deadline of ninety days from when the complainant became aware of the alleged contravention.

#### Grounds for Complaint
"A complaint in respect of the exercise of a right under section 128 or 129 may not be made unless the employee has complied with subsection 128(6) or the Head has received the reports referred to in subsection 128(16), as the case may be, in relation to the matter that is the subject-matter of the complaint." This section clarifies that complaints regarding the exercise of certain employee rights are subject to specific procedural requirements. It states that the employee must have followed the established grievance or appeal process, or the Head must have received the relevant reports.

#### Restrictions on Complaints Against Trade Unions
"Subject to subsection (5), no complaint shall be made to the Board under subsection (1) on the ground that a trade union or any person acting on behalf of a trade union has failed to comply with paragraph 95(f) or (g) unless (a) the complainant has presented a grievance or appeal in accordance with any procedure that has been established by the trade union and to which the complainant has been given ready access; (b) the trade union (i) has dealt with the grievance or appeal of the complainant in a manner unsatisfactory to the complainant, or (ii) has not, within six months after the date on which the complainant first presented their grievance or appeal pursuant to paragraph (a), dealt with the grievance or appeal; and (c) the complaint is made to the Board not later than ninety days after the first day on which the complainant could, in accordance with paragraphs (a) and (b), make the complaint." This passage outlines specific conditions under which complaints against trade unions can be made. It requires the complainant to have followed the trade union's grievance procedure and to have found the union's response unsatisfactory or to have not received a timely response. The complaint must then be made to the Board within ninety days of the first opportunity to do so.

### Timeframe for Making Complaints

#### General Timeframe
"...a complaint pursuant to subsection (1) must be made to the Board not later than ninety days after the date on which the complainant knew, or in the opinion of the Board ought to have known, of the action or circumstances giving rise to the complaint." This section reiterates the general timeframe for filing a complaint, which is ninety days from when the complainant became aware of the alleged contravention.

#### Extensions of Time
"The Head may, subject to the regulations, extend the period set out in subsection (2) (a) if the Head is satisfied that a complaint was made within that period to a government official who had no authority to deal with the complaint and that the person making the complaint believed the official had that authority; (b) in any circumstances prescribed by regulation; or (c) in the conditions prescribed by regulation." This passage allows for extensions of the ninety-day timeframe under certain circumstances, as determined by the Head and subject to regulations.

#### Timeframe for Monetary Complaints
"You must file your monetary complaint within 6 months from the last day your employer was required to pay you." This section specifies a shorter timeframe of six months for filing monetary complaints, which relate to unpaid wages and other amounts owed.

#### Timeframe for Non-Monetary Complaints
"You must file your non-monetary complaint within 6 months from the day you were aware of the issue." This section states a six-month timeframe for filing non-monetary complaints, which cover issues like not receiving a response to a flexible work arrangement request.

#### Timeframe for Unjust Dismissal Complaints
"...months from the day on which the subject-matter of the complaint arose." This section specifies a six-month timeframe for filing complaints about unjust dismissal, which includes constructive dismissal.

#### Suspension of Complaints Related to Collective Agreements
"For greater certainty, a complaint is not permitted under this section if it relates to a disagreement whose settlement is governed exclusively by a collective agreement under subsection 168(1.1)." This passage clarifies that complaints cannot be filed regarding disagreements that are solely addressed by a collective agreement.

individual_results.answer:
## Circumstances for Head to Suspend Complaint Consideration

### Employee Required to Take Measures
"If the Head is satisfied that the employee must take measures before the Head may continue to deal with the complaint made under section 251.01, the Head may, at any time, suspend consideration of the complaint, in whole or in part." This section clearly outlines the primary circumstance under which the Head can suspend complaint consideration. The Head must determine that the employee is obligated to undertake specific actions before the complaint can proceed further.

### Head's Notification Requirements
"If the Head suspends consideration of a complaint, the Head must notify the employee in writing and specify in the notice (a) the measures that the employee must take; and (b) the period of time within which the employee must take those measures." This passage details the mandatory requirements for the Head's decision to be implemented. Upon suspension, the Head is obligated to provide the employee with a written notice. This notice must explicitly state the measures the employee is required to take and the timeframe within which those measures must be completed.

### Extension of Time
"The Head may, upon request, extend the time period specified in the notice." This provision allows for flexibility in the timeframe provided to the employee to take the necessary measures. If the employee requires additional time, they can formally request an extension, which the Head may grant at their discretion.

### End of Suspension
"The suspension ends when, in the Head’s opinion, the measures specified in the notice have been taken." This section defines the condition under which the suspension of complaint consideration concludes. The Head will lift the suspension only when they are satisfied that the employee has fulfilled all the measures outlined in the written notice and within the specified timeframe.

individual_results.question: What happens when an employer and employee reach a settlement regarding non-payment of wages or other amounts under the Canada Labour Code, and how does this affect potential prosecution?
individual_results.answer:
## Settlement of Amounts Due

### Agreement and Payment
"If an employer and an employee who has made a complaint relating to the non-payment of wages or other amounts to which they are entitled under this Part reach a settlement in writing on the wages or other amounts to be paid, the employer may pay those amounts to the employee or to the Head." This section of the Canada Labour Code outlines the process when an employer and employee agree on a settlement for unpaid wages. It states that the employer can either pay the agreed-upon amount directly to the employee or to the Head of the Labour Program. This written settlement is a crucial step in resolving wage disputes.

### Impact on Prosecution
"No prosecution for failure to pay an employee the wages or other amounts that were the subject of the complaint may be instituted against an employer, without the written consent of the Minister, if the employer has paid the amounts referred to in subsection (1) to the employee or the Head." This paragraph directly addresses the effect of a settlement on potential prosecution. It clarifies that if the employer fulfills the terms of the written settlement by paying the agreed-upon amount to the employee or the Head, then no criminal prosecution can be initiated against the employer without the explicit written consent of the Minister. This provision encourages employers and employees to reach amicable settlements, as it provides protection from prosecution once the settlement is fulfilled.

### Payment to the Head
"If an employer pays the amounts to the Head, the Head must, without delay after receiving them, pay them over to the employee who is entitled to the amounts." This subsection details the procedure when the employer pays the settlement amount to the Head of the Labour Program. It mandates that the Head must promptly forward the payment to the employee who is rightfully entitled to it. This ensures that the employee receives the wages or other amounts owed to them, even if the employer makes the payment to the Labour Program.

## Conditions for Rejecting a Complaint

### General Grounds for Rejection

Section 251.05(1) outlines several conditions under which the Head may reject a complaint, in whole or in part. These grounds are categorized into several subclauses.

#### Complaint Not Within Jurisdiction
"The Head may reject a complaint made under section 251.01, in whole or in part, (a) if the Head is satisfied (i) that the complaint is not within their jurisdiction..." This indicates that the Head can reject a complaint if it falls outside the scope of their authority to address.

#### Complaint Frivolous, Vexatious, or Not Made in Good Faith
"...that the complaint is frivolous, vexatious or not made in good..." The Head has the power to reject complaints deemed frivolous, vexatious, or lacking good faith. These types of complaints are considered improper uses of the complaint process.

#### Complaint Settled in Writing
"...that the complaint has been settled in writing between the employer and the..." If the parties have already reached a written settlement, the Head can reject the complaint. This is because the underlying dispute has been resolved.

#### Other Means Available
"...that there are other means available to the employee to resolve the subject-matter of the complaint that the Head considers should be..." The Head can reject a complaint if there are alternative avenues for the employee to resolve the issue that the Head believes they should explore.

#### Subject-Matter Adequately Dealt With
"...that the subject-matter of the complaint has been adequately dealt with through recourse obtained before a court, tribunal, arbitrator or..." If the subject of the complaint has already been resolved through other legal or quasi-legal processes, the Head can reject the complaint.

#### Insufficient Evidence
"...that in respect of a complaint other than a complaint of non-payment of wages or other amounts to which the employee is entitled under this Part, there is insufficient evidence to substantiate the..." The Head can reject a complaint if there is not enough evidence to support the allegations made.

#### Collective Agreement Coverage
"...that in respect of a complaint made by an employee who is subject to a collective agreement, the collective agreement covers the subject-matter of the complaint and provides a third party dispute resolution..." If a complaint arises under a collective agreement and the agreement has a dispute resolution process, the Head can reject the complaint.

#### Suspension of Consideration
"...if consideration of the complaint was suspended under subsection 251.02(1) and if, in the Head’s opinion, the other measures specified in the notice under subsection 251.02(2) were not taken within the specified time..." The Head can reject a complaint if its consideration was suspended and the required subsequent measures were not taken within the given timeframe.

#### Failure to Respond to Notice
"...subject to the regulations, if an employee to whom notice is given under subsection (1.1) does not respond within the period set out in the notice." The Head can reject a complaint if the employee does not respond to a written notice within a reasonable period.

### Steps Taken After a Complaint is Rejected

Section 251.05(2) details the steps that must be taken after a complaint is rejected.

#### Written Notification with Reasons
"If a complaint has been rejected, the Head shall notify the employee in writing, with reasons." This mandates that the Head must provide the employee with a written explanation for the rejection.

#### Request for Review
"The employee may, within 15 days after the day on which the employee is notified of the rejection, request in writing, with reasons, that the Head review the Head’s decision." The employee has the right to request a review of the rejection decision within 15 days.

#### Head's Decision
"The Head may confirm the decision, or rescind it and re-examine the complaint." The Head has the discretion to either uphold the rejection or reconsider the complaint.

#### Written Notification of Head's Decision
"The Head shall notify the employee in writing of the Head’s decision." (no source found for the quotation) The Head must inform the employee of their final decision on the rejection request.

#### Finality of Head's Decision
"The Head’s confirmation or rescission is final and conclusive and is not subject to appeal to or review by any court." The Head's decision on the rejection request is binding and cannot be challenged in court.

individual_results.question: What action can the Head take if they believe an employer is violating a provision of the Canada Labour Code, its regulations, or a permit condition, and what are the limitations of this action?
individual_results.answer:
## Head's Powers to Address Employer Violations

### Delegation of Powers

The Head possesses the power to delegate many of their own powers to qualified individuals or groups. This delegation is subject to any terms and conditions specified by the Minister. The Head can also impose additional terms and conditions on the delegation. This mechanism allows the Head to distribute the workload of enforcing the Canada Labour Code.
"Subject to any terms and conditions specified by the Minister, the Head may delegate to any qualified person or class of persons any of the powers the Head is authorized to exercise or any of the duties or functions the Head is authorized to perform for the purposes of this Part. The Head may make the delegation subject to any terms and conditions that the Head considers appropriate."

### Compliance and Enforcement Actions

When the Head finds an employer violating a provision of the Canada Labour Code, its regulations, or a permit condition, they can take a range of escalating compliance and enforcement actions. These actions are designed to ensure employers adhere to the labour standards set out in the Code.

#### Assurance of Voluntary Compliance

The Head can request an employer's written commitment to correct one or more contraventions within a specified timeframe. A contravention can be monetary or non-monetary.

#### Letter of Determination

The Head can issue a formal written request to the employer to correct the non-compliance situation. This letter may specify actions the employer must take, such as paying outstanding wages or implementing appropriate workplace policies.

#### Payment Order

If the employer does not voluntarily comply, the Labour Program can issue a payment order to the employer or to a director of the corporation to collect unpaid wages. An administrative fee is added to the amount owed.

#### Collecting Money

The Labour Program can collect the amounts owed from various sources, including the employer's debtors, financial institutions, or the debtors or financial institutions of one or more directors of the corporation.

#### Compliance Order

As of January 1, 2021, the Labour Program can issue a compliance order to stop non-compliance. This order prevents the reoccurrence of any contravention of the Code and its Regulations.

#### Administrative Monetary Penalty (AMP)

As of January 1, 2021, the Labour Program can issue a notice of violation with an administrative monetary penalty (AMP) if the employer does not correct a contravention of the Code.

#### Filing in Federal Court

The Labour Program can file a payment order and a notice of violation in federal court to ensure its enforceability as a judgment of that court. The Labour Program may also publish information on the Government of Canada website concerning an employer to whom a payment order or notice of violation has been issued.

#### Prosecutions

If the employer does not correct a contravention with the Code or Regulations, the Labour Program may choose to prosecute them. This route is also taken if the employer is fully aware of their legal obligations and still willfully breaks the law. Repeat contraventions indicate an intentional or willful action. If found guilty, the employer may be subject to significant fines, varying based on the number of offences and whether the employer is incorporated.

#### Public Naming of Employers

The Labour Program will publish information about employers who violate the Code, including all payment orders of \$5000 or greater filed in federal court, administrative monetary penalties (with some exceptions), and prosecutions.

### Limitations on Head's Actions

The Head's powers to address employer violations are subject to certain limitations.

#### Prohibition on Disciplinary Action

The Head cannot take any disciplinary action against an employee, including dismissal, suspension, lay-off, demotion, financial or other penalties, or refusal to pay remuneration, because the employee has exercised their rights under this Part. This protection ensures that employees are not retaliated against for engaging in protected activities such as testifying in proceedings or providing information to persons engaged in duties under this Part.
"No employer shall dismiss, suspend, lay off or demote an employee, impose a financial or other penalty on an employee, or refuse to pay an employee remuneration in respect of any period that the employee would, but for the exercise of the employee’s rights under this Part, have worked, or take any disciplinary action against or threaten to take any such action against an employee because the employee (a) has testified or is about to testify in a proceeding taken or an inquiry held under this Part; (b) has provided information to a person engaged in the performance of duties under this Part regarding the conditions of work affecting the health or safety of the employee or of any other employee of the employer; or (c) has acted in accordance with this Part or has sought the enforcement of any of the provisions of this Part."

#### Right to Enter Premises

The Head has the right to enter on any place used in connection with a federal work, undertaking or business for the purpose of making an inspection authorized under subsection (2), and may, for that purpose, question any employee apart from his employer.

#### Reasonable Assistance

The person in charge of any federal work, undertaking or business and every person employed in it or in connection with its operation shall give the Head all reasonable assistance to enable the Head to carry out the Head’s duties and functions under this Part or the regulations.

#### Head Accompanied

The Head may, in carrying out the Head’s duties and functions, be accompanied or assisted by any persons that the Head considers necessary.

#### Evidence Precluded

The Head shall not be required to give testimony in any civil suit or civil proceedings, or in any proceeding under section 242, with regard to information obtained in carrying out those duties and functions. Similarly, no person to whom powers, duties or functions have been delegated under subsection (1), and no person who has accompanied or assisted such a person or the Head in carrying out their duties and functions, shall be required to give testimony in any civil suit or civil proceedings, or in any proceeding under section 242, with regard to information obtained in carrying out those duties and functions or in accompanying or assisting the person, except with the written permission of the Head.

#### Head Not Liable

Neither the Head nor a person to whom powers, duties or functions have been delegated under subsection (1) is personally liable for anything done or omitted to be done by them in good faith under the authority or purported authority of this Part.

individual_results.question: What actions can the Head take if an employer has not paid an employee wages or other amounts to which the employee is entitled under the Canada Labour Code, and what are the limitations and procedures involved?
individual_results.answer:
## Actions the Head Can Take for Non-Payment of Wages

### Issuing a Payment Order
"If the Head finds that an employer has not paid an employee wages or other amounts to which the employee is entitled under this Part, the Head may issue a written payment order to the employer, or, subject to section 251.18, to a director of a corporation referred to in that section, ordering the employer or director to pay the amount in question, and the Head shall send a copy of any such payment order to the employee at the employee’s latest known address."

This section outlines the primary action the Head can take when an employer has not paid wages. The Head can issue a written payment order directly to the employer, compelling them to pay the outstanding amounts. Alternatively, the Head can issue the order to a director of the corporation, holding the director jointly and severally liable for the payment. The Head is then obligated to send a copy of the order to the employee.

### Holding Corporate Directors Liable
"Sometimes, wage recovery from an employer is unlikely or impossible. In this case, the Labour Program may hold the corporation’s directors liable for amounts employers owe to employees during their time as director. Corporate directors are jointly and individually liable for employees’ wages and other amounts to which employees are entitled, up to a limit equivalent to 6 months’ wages."

This action is taken when recovering wages directly from the employer is deemed improbable. In such situations, the Labour Program can hold the corporation’s directors personally liable for the unpaid wages. The directors are jointly and severally liable, meaning each director is responsible for the full amount owed, up to a limit of six months’ wages.

### Collecting from Directors’ Debtors or Financial Institutions
"When an employer or director does not pay a Payment Order, the Labour Program can collect from a director’s debtors or financial institution."

This describes the mechanism the Labour Program employs to recover funds from directors when the employer fails to comply with the Payment Order. The Program can pursue the directors’ other financial assets, such as debtors or financial institutions, to satisfy the outstanding wage obligations.

### Administrative Penalties
"If the employer does not comply with the Code, they may be subject to enforcement action up to and including an administrative monetary penalty."

This action is taken when the employer fails to comply with the Canada Labour Code after a Payment Order has been issued. The employer can face administrative monetary penalties, which can be substantial.

### Rejection of Complaint
"...if the Head concludes that the employer has paid to the employee all wages and other amounts to which the employee is entitled under this Part for the period of six months, plus any extension of the period for making the complaint that is granted by the Head under subsection 251.01(3), immediately before the day on which the complaint was made."

This describes a scenario where the Head will reject a complaint of non-payment if the employer has already paid all the wages and other amounts owed within the specified timeframe. The Head will notify the employee in writing that their complaint is unfounded.

### Limitation on Prosecution
"No prosecution for failure to pay an employee the wages or other amounts that were the subject of the complaint may be instituted against an employer, without the written consent of the Minister, if the employer has paid the amounts referred to in subsection (1) to the employee or the Head."

This section outlines a limitation on criminal prosecution for non-payment. The Minister’s written consent is required to initiate criminal charges against an employer for failing to pay wages, provided the employer has already paid the outstanding amounts to the employee or the Head. This provision aims to prevent unnecessary criminal proceedings when the employer has already fulfilled their wage obligations.

## Disputing Compliance Orders, Payment Orders, or Notices of Unfounded Complaint/Voluntary Compliance

### Review and Appeal of a Notice of Unfounded Complaint or a Notice of Voluntary Compliance
"If you do not agree with the Labour Program’s decision, you may request that the Labour Program review the Notice of Unfounded Complaint or Notice of Voluntary Compliance. To do this, you must make your written request to the Labour Program, with reasons and within 15 days after notice is served." This section outlines the initial step in disputing a notice of unfounded complaint or voluntary compliance. The process involves submitting a written request to the Labour Program, accompanied by the reasons for disagreement, within 15 days of receiving the initial notice.
"Upon completion of the review, the Labour Program may, in writing:  confirm the Notice of Unfounded Complaint, confirm the Notice of Voluntary Compliance, or rescind the notices..." Following the review, the Labour Program has three possible outcomes: they can uphold the original notice, confirm the voluntary compliance, or withdraw the notice.
"In the case of a rescinded notice, the Labour Program will re-examine the complaint. If you are not satisfied with the review decision with respect to a question of law or jurisdiction, you may request an appeal at the Canada Industrial Relations Board (CIRB). You must make your request to the CIRB, in writing and with reasons, within 15 days after the Labour Program review decision is served." If the Labour Program rescinds the notice and the affected person remains dissatisfied, they can appeal the decision to the Canada Industrial Relations Board (CIRB). This appeal must be made in writing, with clear reasons, within 15 days of receiving the Labour Program's review decision.

### Review and Appeal of a Payment Order
"As an employee, employer or a director of the corporation, you may request a review of the Payment Order if you do not agree with the decision. To do this, you must make a request to the Labour Program, in writing and with reasons, within 15 days after the Labour Program’s decision is served." This section details the process for disputing a payment order. The affected party must submit a written request to the Labour Program, providing the reasons for their disagreement, within 15 days of receiving the payment order.
"As the employer or the director, you must also include:  a full payment for the amount indicated in the Payment Order or a Letter of Credit in lieu of payment, and the administrative fee, if applicable..." When requesting a review of a payment order, the employer or director must also provide the full payment or a Letter of Credit, along with any applicable administrative fees.
"Upon completion of the review, the Labour Program can confirm, vary or rescind the Payment Order. If you do not agree with the review decision of the Payment Order, you may request an appeal at the Canada Industrial Relations Board (CIRB). You must make the request to the CIRB, in writing and with reasons, and within 15 days after the Labour Program served the order." If the Labour Program reviews the payment order and the affected person still disagrees, they can appeal the decision to the CIRB. This appeal must be made in writing, with clear reasons, within 15 days of receiving the Labour Program's review decision.

### Review and Appeal of a Compliance Order
"If the Head is of the opinion that an employer is contravening or has contravened a provision of this Part, its regulations or any condition of a permit issued under subsection 176(1), the Head may issue a compliance order in writing requiring the employer to terminate the contravention within the time that the Head may specify and take any step, as specified by the Head and within the time that the Head may specify, to ensure that the contravention does not continue or reoccur." This section explains the process for disputing a compliance order. The affected employer can request a review of the compliance order by submitting a written request to the Labour Program, with the reasons for their disagreement, within 15 days of receiving the order.
"Upon completion of the review, the Labour Program may, in writing:  confirm the Notice of Unfounded Complaint, confirm the Notice of Voluntary Compliance, or rescind the notices..." Following the review, the Labour Program has three possible outcomes: they can uphold the original compliance order, confirm the voluntary compliance, or withdraw the notice.
"In the case of a rescinded notice, the Labour Program will re-examine the complaint. If you are not satisfied with the review decision with respect to a question of law or jurisdiction, you may request an appeal at the Canada Industrial Relations Board (CIRB). You must make your request to the CIRB, in writing and with reasons, within 15 days after the Labour Program review decision is served." If the Labour Program rescinds the compliance order and the affected person remains dissatisfied, they can appeal the decision to the CIRB. This appeal must be made in writing, with clear reasons, within 15 days of receiving the Labour Program's review decision.

individual_results.question: Who can appeal a decision made under subsection 251.101(3) of the Canada Labour Code, and what are the conditions for doing so?
individual_results.answer:
## Who Can Appeal a Decision Made Under Subsection 251.101(3) of the Canada Labour Code?

### General Appeal Eligibility

According to Section 251.11(1) of the Canada Labour Code,
"Subject to subsection (1.1), a person who is affected by a decision made under subsection 251.101(3), other than a decision to rescind a notice of unfounded complaint or a notice of voluntary compliance, may appeal the decision to the Board, in writing, within 15 days after the day on which the decision is served." This indicates that any person "affected by a decision made under subsection 251.101(3)" can appeal to the Board within 15 days of service.

### Exception: Compliance Order

Section 251.11(1.1) introduces an exception to this general appeal eligibility. It states,
"Only an employer to whom a compliance order has been issued may appeal a decision with respect to that order." This means that while other affected parties can appeal, only an employer subject to a compliance order has the right to appeal a decision concerning that order.

### Scope of Appeal

Section 251.11(1.2) further clarifies the scope of the appeal. It specifies,
"Except in the case of a compliance order, the person may appeal the decision only on a question of law or jurisdiction." This means that for appeals not related to a compliance order, the appeal can only be based on legal issues or questions of the Board's authority.

### Conditions for Filing an Appeal

Section 251.11(2) outlines the conditions for filing an appeal. It requires,
"The request for appeal shall contain a statement of the grounds of appeal." This means that the appeal must clearly state the legal basis for challenging the Board's decision.

### Payment of Amount and Administrative Fee

Section 251.11(3) details the financial requirements for filing an appeal. It states,
"An employer or director of a corporation is not permitted to appeal a decision confirming or varying a payment order unless the employer or director pays to the Head the amount indicated in the decision — and, in the case of an employer, the administrative fee specified in the decision in accordance with subsection 251.131(1) — less any amount and administrative fee paid under subsection 251.101(2)." This indicates that an employer appealing a decision confirming or varying a payment order must pay the amount specified in the decision, along with any administrative fee, less any previously paid fees.

### Security

Section 251.11(3.1) provides an alternative to the full payment requirement. It allows,
"The Head may allow an employer or a director of a corporation to give security, in a form satisfactory to the Head and on any conditions specified by the Head, for all or part of the amount and fee referred to in subsection (3)." This means that an employer appealing a payment order can provide security to the Head instead of making the full payment, subject to the Head's approval and conditions.

### Limitation for Directors

Section 251.11(4) applies a limitation to directors appealing payment orders. It states,
"In the case of a director, subsection (3) applies subject to the maximum amount of the director’s liability under section 251.18." This means that a director appealing a payment order is subject to the maximum amount of their liability as defined in section 251.18.

individual_results.answer:
## Responsibilities of the Head and the Board in an Appeal

### Document Provision

#### Head's Responsibilities Regarding Appeal Documents

The Head has several responsibilities concerning the provision of documents in an appeal.
"...the Head shall, on request of the Board, provide to the Board a copy of any document that the Head relied on for the purpose of making the decision being appealed." This passage clearly states that upon the Board's request, the Head must furnish a copy of the documentation that informed their original decision. This ensures the Board has a complete understanding of the basis for the appealable decision.
"...the Head shall, on request of the Board, provide to the Board a copy of any document that the Head relied on for the purpose of issuing the order or notice being appealed." This further elaborates on the Head's document provision duty, specifically in appeals related to orders or notices. The Head must provide the Board with the supporting documentation used to create the challenged order or notice.
"The Board shall, on request of the Head, provide to the Head a copy of any document that is filed with the Board in the appeal." This passage indicates that the Board is also obligated to provide the Head with copies of all documents submitted to the Board as part of the appeal process. This ensures the Head remains informed about all materials considered by the Board.

#### Board's Responsibilities Regarding Appeal Documents

The Board also plays a role in document provision during an appeal.
"The Board shall inform the Head in writing when an appeal is brought under subsection 285(1) and provide the Head with a copy of the request for appeal." This passage outlines the Board's initial responsibility to notify the Head of an appeal and to furnish the Head with a copy of the appeal request. This ensures the Head is promptly aware of the appeal and has access to the initial documentation.
"The Board shall inform the Head in writing when an appeal is brought under subsection 251.11(1) and provide the Head with a copy of the request for appeal." This is a similar provision, but specifically for appeals under subsection 251.11(1). The Board is required to notify the Head and provide the Head with a copy of the appeal request.

### Participation in an Appeal

#### Head's Responsibilities Regarding Evidence and Representations

The Head has the right and responsibility to participate in an appeal by presenting evidence and making representations to the Board.
"The Head may, in an appeal, present evidence and make representations to the Board." This passage explicitly grants the Head the ability to offer evidence and make arguments to the Board during the appeal process. This allows the Head to advocate for their original decision and present any new information relevant to the appeal.

#### Board's Responsibilities Regarding Inquiry and Decision

The Board takes a proactive role in the appeal process by conducting an inquiry and issuing a decision.
"If the Board issues a direction under paragraph (1)(b), the employer shall, without delay, affix or cause to be affixed to or near the machine, thing or place in respect of which the direction is issued a notice of the direction, in the form and containing the information that the Board may specify, and no person may remove the notice unless authorized to do so by the Board." This passage details the Board's power to issue directions and the employer's subsequent responsibility to post a notice of the direction. This ensures transparency and compliance with the Board's decisions.
"The Board shall provide a written decision, with reasons, and a copy of any direction to the employer, employee or trade union concerned and to the Head, and the employer shall, without delay, give a copy of the decision, the reasons, and any direction to the work place committee or health and safety representative." This passage outlines the Board's obligation to issue a written decision with supporting reasons and to distribute copies to relevant parties, including the Head. This ensures the Head is fully informed of the Board's ruling and the rationale behind it.
"...the Board shall, in a summary way and without delay, inquire into the circumstances of the decision or direction, as the case may be, and the reasons for it and may (a) vary, rescind or confirm the decision or direction; and (b) issue any direction that the Board considers appropriate under subsection 145(2) or (2.1)." This passage describes the Board's initial inquiry into the appealable decision or direction and its subsequent power to modify, overturn, or uphold the original decision, and to issue new directions as deemed appropriate. This highlights the Board's central role in the appeal process.

individual_results.question: What are the possible outcomes and implications when the Board makes a decision in an appeal under this Part of the Canada Labour Code (PART III - Standard Hours, Wages, Vacations and Holidays)?
individual_results.answer:
## Possible Outcomes and Implications of a Board Decision in an Appeal

### Correction of Penalty

#### Outcome
"If the Board determines that the amount of the penalty for the violation was not determined in accordance with the regulations, the Board shall correct the amount of the penalty." This section outlines a direct consequence of the Board's decision. If the initial penalty calculation was flawed, the Board has the authority to rectify it.

#### Implications
The Board's correction of the penalty has significant financial implications for the appellant. The appellant will be liable for the revised penalty amount, which could be higher or lower than the original. This outcome directly addresses the appellant's grounds for appeal, which may have centered on the accuracy of the penalty calculation.

### Decision on Violation

#### Outcome
"The Board shall make a decision in writing and provide the appellant and the Head with a copy of the decision, with reasons." This establishes the formal nature of the Board's decision-making process. The decision will be documented in writing and communicated to all relevant parties, including the appellant and the Head of the relevant department.

#### Implications
The Board's decision will determine whether the appellant committed the violation in question. If the Board finds that the appellant committed the violation, the appellant is liable for the penalty. Conversely, if the Board finds that the appellant did not commit the violation, the penalty will be adjusted accordingly. The decision will be accompanied by reasons, providing a detailed explanation of the Board's findings and the basis for its determination.

### Obligation to Pay

#### Outcome
"If the Board determines that the appellant committed the violation, the appellant is liable for the penalty that is set out in the decision." This section directly links the Board's finding of a violation to the appellant's financial obligation.

#### Implications
The Board's determination of a violation creates a legal obligation for the appellant to pay the penalty specified in the decision. This outcome has direct financial consequences for the appellant and reinforces the importance of compliance with the Canada Labour Code.

### Finality of Decision

#### Outcome
"Every decision made under this section is final and shall not be questioned or reviewed in any court." This section emphasizes the binding nature of the Board's decision.

#### Implications
The Board's decision is considered final and cannot be challenged in any court of law. This finality provides certainty and closure to the appeal process. It also underscores the authority and independence of the Board in making its determinations.

### No Review by Certiorari, etc.

#### Outcome
"No order shall be made, process entered or proceeding taken in any court, whether by way of injunction, certiorari , prohibition, quo warranto or otherwise, to question, review, prohibit or restrain the Board in any proceedings under this section." This reinforces the finality of the Board's decision by explicitly stating that no court can review or overturn it through various legal mechanisms.

#### Implications
The Board's decision is immune from judicial review. This finality is a cornerstone of the appeal process, ensuring that the Board's determination is respected and enforced.

### Copy Given by Employer

#### Outcome
"If a decision is made with respect to a notice of violation referred to in subsection 276(3), the employer shall, without delay, give a copy of the decision to the or health and safety representative , as those terms are defined in subsection 122(1)." This section outlines a specific obligation placed on the employer when a decision is made regarding a notice of violation.

#### Implications
The employer is legally required to promptly provide a copy of the Board's decision to the or health and safety representative. This ensures that the relevant parties are informed of the Board's determination and can take any necessary actions.

### Wages for Attendance at Proceeding

#### Outcome
"An employee who has been summoned by the Board to attend at an appeal proceeding under this Part and who attends is entitled to be paid by the employer at the employee’s regular rate of wages for the time spent at the proceeding that would otherwise have been time at work." This section addresses the entitlement of employees who attend appeal proceedings.

#### Implications
Employees who attend appeal proceedings are entitled to be paid their regular rate of wages for the time spent at the proceeding. This ensures that employees are not financially disadvantaged for participating in the appeal process.

## Orders to Debtors of Employers or Directors of Corporations

### General Circumstances

The Head can issue a written order to a person who owes money to an employer or a director of a corporation under specific circumstances. This order directs the debtor to pay the amount owing directly to the Head within 15 days, in satisfaction of the payment order.
"The Head may issue a written order to a person who is or is about to become indebted to an employer to whom a payment order has been issued under subsection 251.1(1), to pay any amount owing to the employer, up to the amount and the administrative fee indicated in the payment order, directly to the Head within 15 days, in satisfaction of the payment order."

This section clearly outlines the primary condition for the Head to issue such an order. It states that the order is directed to a person who is "or is about to become indebted" to the employer, provided that a payment order has already been issued. The order specifies the amount to be paid (up to the amount and administrative fee in the payment order) and the timeframe for payment (within 15 days).

### Order to Debtor of Director of Corporation

The Head also has the authority to issue an order to a person who owes money to a director of a corporation.
"The Head may issue a written order to a person who is or is about to become indebted to a director of a corporation to whom a payment order has been issued under subsection 251.1(1) to pay any amount owing to the director of the corporation, up to the amount indicated in the payment order, directly to the Head within 15 days, in satisfaction of the payment order."

This subsection mirrors the general circumstance but specifically applies to debts owed to a director of a corporation. The order directs the debtor to pay the amount owing to the director directly to the Head within 15 days, in satisfaction of the payment order.

### Banks and Financial Institutions

The authority to issue such orders extends to banks and other financial institutions that hold money on deposit for an employer or a director of a corporation.
"For the purposes of this section, a bank or other financial institution that has money on deposit to the credit of an employer or a director of a corporation shall be deemed to be indebted to that employer or that director."

This provision clarifies that a financial institution holding funds for an employer or director is considered indebted to that entity for the purpose of issuing an order to the bank to make the payment to the Head.

individual_results.answer:
## Enforcement of Orders Filed in Federal Court

### Registration and Legal Force

Section 251.15 of the Canada Labour Code details the process and implications of filing a payment order or Board order in the Federal Court. It states,
"...in the Federal Court under subsection (1) or (2), the order shall be registered in the Court and, when registered, has the same force and effect, and all proceedings may be taken thereon, as if the order were a judgment obtained in that Court." This passage is crucial because it establishes the legal standing of an order once it is filed in the Federal Court.

The registration of an order in the Federal Court is a significant step in its enforcement. It means that the order gains the same legal force as a judgment obtained in that Court. As the text clarifies,
"...all proceedings may be taken thereon, as if the order were a judgment obtained in that Court." This implies that the order can be enforced through the same legal mechanisms available for judgments, such as execution proceedings.

### Limitation on Filing

However, Section 251.15 also includes a limitation on when a payment order can be filed. It specifies,
"However, a payment order is not to be filed while it is or may be the subject of a review under subsection 251.101(1) or an appeal under subsection 251.101(7) or section 251.11 or if an order of the Board is made under paragraph 251.12(1)(a) relating to the payment order." This provision prevents the premature filing of a payment order while it is still under review or appeal. It ensures that the order is only filed after the review or appeal process has concluded.

### Debt to Her Majesty

Section 251.15 further explains the financial implications of an order filed in Federal Court. It states,
"The expenses to be paid in accordance with an order issued under paragraph (1)(d) constitute a debt due to Her Majesty in right of Canada and are recoverable as such in the Federal Court or any other court of competent jurisdiction or in any other manner provided under this Act." This passage clarifies that any costs awarded in an appeal or enforcement proceeding are considered a debt owed to the Crown and can be recovered through the Federal Court or other appropriate courts.

### Enforcement of Orders to Debtors

Section 251.15 also addresses the enforcement of orders against debtors. It mentions,
"After the expiration of the 15 day period specified in an order to a debtor of the employer or of the director of a corporation made under section 251.13, the Head may file a copy of the order in the Federal Court." This indicates that if a debtor fails to comply with an order within the specified timeframe, the Head can file a copy of the order in the Federal Court to initiate enforcement proceedings.

### Copies of Orders Sent

Section 251.12 also outlines the process for distributing orders filed in Federal Court. It states,
"(2) The Board shall send a copy of the decision, with reasons, to each party to the appeal and to the Head." This ensures that all parties involved in the appeal and the Head are informed of the Board's decision and the subsequent filing of the order in Federal Court.

individual_results.question: Can directors of a corporation be held personally liable for unpaid wages and other amounts owed to employees?
individual_results.answer:
## Personal Liability of Directors for Unpaid Wages

### Section 251.18 of the Canada Labour Code
"Directors of a corporation are jointly and severally liable for wages and other amounts to which an employee is entitled under this Part, to a maximum amount equivalent to six months’ wages, to the extent that (a) the entitlement arose during the particular director’s incumbency; and (b) recovery of the amount from the corporation is impossible or unlikely."

This section directly addresses the personal liability of directors for unpaid wages. It states that directors are "jointly and severally liable" for wages and other amounts owed to employees. This means that each director can be held personally responsible for the full amount owed, and the employer can pursue any one of the directors for the entire debt. The liability is capped at six months' wages, and it only applies if the employee's entitlement occurred during the director's time on the board and recovery from the corporation is deemed impossible or unlikely.

### Section 251.19 Regarding Cooperatives
"For the purposes of section 251.18 and subsection 257(3), cooperatives shall be deemed to be corporations."

While this section specifically clarifies the status of cooperatives as corporations for the purposes of section 251.18, it reinforces the principle that directors of corporations, including cooperatives, can be held personally liable for unpaid wages under the conditions outlined in section 251.18.

### Section 12.051 of the Canada Labour Code
"The Chairperson, Vice-Chairpersons, other members and external adjudicators are not personally liable, either civilly or criminally, for anything done or omitted to be done by them in good faith in the exercise or purported exercise of any power, or in the performance or purported performance of any duty or function, conferred on them under this Act."

This section provides a specific exception to the general rule of personal liability for directors. It states that the Chairperson, Vice-Chairpersons, other members, and external adjudicators are not personally liable for actions taken in good faith while exercising their powers or performing their duties under the Act. However, this exception does not apply to the liability of directors for unpaid wages, as outlined in section 251.18.
